tarim-basin: The Tarim Basin is an endorheic basin of about 888,000 square kilometres, bounded by the Tian Shan to the north and the Kunlun Mountains to the south. The Taklamakan Desert fills much of it and is too dry for permanent habitation. The Yarkand, Kashgar and Aksu rivers join to form the Tarim River, which runs along the north side and ends at Lop Nur, a marshy saline depression.

Meltwater from the mountains feeds the oases along which the Silk Road routes ran: one route north of the desert, one south, and a shorter middle route across the Lop Nur region, which became uninhabitable in the 4th century and has been deserted since the 6th. The historical Uyghur name for the basin is Altishahr, meaning six cities.

Bronze appeared in the basin from about 2000 BCE, in six cultural zones. Mummies found at Loulan, the Xiaohe tomb complex and Qäwrighul were once suggested to be Tocharian, but recent evidence points to a distinct population. The Han dynasty came to influence the basin in the reign of Emperor Wu, and General Ban Chao (32–102 CE) wrested control from the Xiongnu at the end of the 1st century. The Chinese administered it as the Protectorate of the Western Regions.

The Kushans expanded into it in the 1st and 2nd centuries and established a kingdom at Kashgar. Kingdoms such as Kucha and Khotan passed Buddhism and other influences between India, Central Asia and China; the monk Kumārajīva came from Kucha.

Under Emperor Taizong the Tang dynasty campaigned against the oasis states, then vassals of the Western Turkic Khaganate: Gaochang was annexed in 640, Karasahr taken in 644 and Kucha conquered in 649. From the late 8th to 9th centuries the region changed hands between the Tang and the Tibetan Empire. Satuq Bughra Khan of the Kara-Khanid Khanate converted to Islam in 966, and Khotan fell to the Kara-Khanid Khanate around 1006; the basin became Islamic over the following centuries. In the early 14th century its eastern parts belonged to the Chagatai Khanate, and the Dughlat tribe held the western basin and raised Tughlugh Timur to the throne in 1347.

The basin lies in the Xinjiang region of north-western China, and Uyghurs form the majority in cities such as Kashgar and Hotan. Xinjiang as a single province dates from 1884, after the Qing conquest of 1759, when the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria had been governed separately. Excavations have found wooden tablets in the Kharosthi script of the 3rd and 4th centuries at Niya, and Buddhist murals at Miran that show links with Central Asia and northern India.
tariq-ibn-ziyad: Medieval Arabic historians give contradictory accounts of Tariq's origins and ethnicity, and details of his personality are uncertain. Many modern scholars hold that he was a Berber mawla, a freedman client, of Musa ibn Nusayr, the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya. According to David Nicolle he came from a Berber tribe native to the Tafna in what is now Algeria, and he first appears in the record as governor of Tangier. Ibn Abd al-Hakam (803–871) says Musa appointed him governor of Tangier after its conquest in 710–711.

An unconquered Visigothic outpost remained at Ceuta, held by a nobleman named Julian, Count of Ceuta. In the story told by Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Julian was enraged because King Roderic had raped his daughter, Florinda la Cava, at the Visigothic court, and so he made a treaty with Tariq and used his merchant ships to carry the Muslim army across the straits. Tariq's army, which landed on or about 26 April 711, consisted of about 7,000 soldiers, largely of Berber stock but with Arab troops, and it gathered at the mountain that became known as Jabal Tariq, or Gibraltar.

Roderic assembled an army said to number 100,000, though the real figure may have been much lower. Most of it was commanded by the sons of Wittiza, whom Roderic had deposed, and it was defeated at the Battle of Guadalete on 19 July, where Roderic was killed. Tariq then divided his army into four. One division took Córdoba under Mughith al-Rumi, others took Granada and further places, and Tariq's own took Toledo before he advanced north to Guadalajara and Astorga. He was de facto governor until Musa arrived a year later, and within a few years the two had taken two-thirds of the peninsula.

In 714 the caliph al-Walid I ordered both Tariq and Musa back to Damascus, where they spent the rest of their lives. Arabic sources differ on their relationship: some tell of Musa's anger and envy at a freedman's conquest, while al-Baladhuri says only that Musa wrote him a severe letter and the two were later reconciled. The historians Ibn Khallikan, in 1274, and al-Maqqari, in the 16th century, attribute to him a long speech to his troops before Guadalete. He also appears in a story of the One Thousand and One Nights.
tarnowskie-gory: Tarnowskie Góry, in German Tarnowitz, lies in Silesia in the Silesian Highlands near Katowice. Its name comes from Tarnowice, a local village, and góry, which in Old Polish meant mines. The German name was introduced in the late 18th century, after the Third Silesian War. In the Middle Ages the region was inhabited by Lechitic Polish tribes, and in the 10th century it became part of the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I.

An outbreak of plague in 1676-77 decimated the population. The Prussian army entered the town on 16 December 1740 during the first of the Silesian Wars, and in 1742 Austrian rule ended and Tarnowskie Góry fell under Prussia. Around 1780 Friedrich Wilhelm von Reden opened a government-controlled mine and a silver and lead foundry. Salomon Isaac, a Jewish trade agent and mining entrepreneur, contributed greatly to Silesian mining and metallurgy, although Jews were restricted or banned from the area.

In 1788 a Newcomen atmospheric engine was imported from Wales to drain the mines, and eventually eight steam engines were used. Drainage tunnels were later cut to replace them, and a 600-metre part of the Fryderyk adit is now a tourist route, the Black Trout Adit. A school of mining was begun in 1803, and the Upper-Silesian Brotherhood Cooperative, an insurance society for miners, had its headquarters in the town. The first railway, to Opole, arrived in 1857, and by the end of the century the town was becoming one of the largest marshalling yards in Europe.

Early in the 20th century the silver ore ran out and mining stopped. After the plebiscite that followed three Silesian uprisings of 1919-1921, the Tarnowitz district voted 61.7 percent to join Poland, although the city itself voted 82 percent for Germany, and in 1922 the town was returned to Poland.

The town, with 61,842 inhabitants in 2021, is in the Silesian Voivodeship. The Historic Silver Mine of Tarnowskie Góry is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Black Trout Adit has been a national Historic Monument since 2004, and the town has a museum opened in 1958 and the 16th-century Gwareks' bell-tower, named for the old Polish word for miners. The Gwarki Tarnogórskie festival has marked mining culture each September since 1957.
tarquinius-priscus: According to Livy, Tarquinius came from the Etruscan city of Tarquinii and was first named Lucumo. Modern scholars note that lucumo was a title of political rank among the Etruscans, meaning king, so the tradition may have mistaken a title for a personal name. His father Demaratus was a Greek merchant from Corinth, who according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus belonged to the Bacchiadae and left the city when Cypselus overthrew them.

After inheriting his father's fortune, Lucumo was denied office at Tarquinii because his father was Greek-born. His wife Tanaquil, gifted in prophecy, persuaded him to move to Rome, where foreigners were said to be readily made citizens. Tradition tells that an eagle took his cap on the Janiculum and replaced it, an omen she read as a sign of kingship. In Rome he took the name Lucius Tarquinius and became the trusted adviser of King Ancus Marcius.

When Ancus died his sons were still boys. Tarquinius sent them off on a hunting trip and then won the Comitia Curiata with a speech, becoming the first king in Roman history to canvass for the throne. He is said to have fought the Latins, the Sabines and the Etruscans, held Rome's first triumph in Etruscan style, and added a hundred men from lesser noble families to the Senate, bringing it to two hundred.

The sources also credit him with building. He is said to have laid permanent seating for the Circus Maximus and to have built the Cloaca Maxima to drain the low ground for the Forum. He began the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill and a stone wall around the city, though neither was finished in his reign; the temple was dedicated under Tarquinius Superbus in 509 BCE. Tradition also gives Rome the fasces, the curule chair and the toga praetexta from him.

According to tradition, assassins organised by the sons of Ancus Marcius killed him with a blow of an axe to the head. Tanaquil is said to have managed the transfer of power so that Servius Tullius took the throne. Modern historians treat most of the account as foundation legend shaped in a later age. Livy and Dionysius wrote about five hundred years after the events, relying on annalists who survive only in fragments. The 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica noted that the story of his Corinthian origins is chronologically impossible. Excavations beneath the Forum have found channels thought to belong to an early Cloaca Maxima.
tarquinius-superbus: Ancient accounts of the regal period mingle history and legend. Tarquin was said to be the son or grandson of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome. The oldest sources make him Priscus's son, but modern historians think that impossible under the traditional chronology. His mother was supposedly Tanaquil, who placed Servius Tullius on the throne after the sons of Ancus Marcius had Priscus assassinated.

Servius married his daughters to Tarquin and his brother Arruns. According to the tradition, the ambitious Tullia Minor and Tarquin conspired to bring about the deaths of her sister and of Arruns, and then married. Tarquin courted the patrician senators with presents, seated himself on the throne in the senate house, denounced Servius, and threw the aged king down the steps; Servius was murdered in the street by Tarquin's assassins.

Tarquin began by refusing to bury Servius and putting to death senators he suspected of loyalty to him. By not replacing them and not consulting the senate he reduced its size and authority. He made an ally of Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, one of the most eminent Latin chiefs, by betrothing his daughter to him, and persuaded the Latins to renew their treaty with Rome.

He took the wealthy town of Suessa Pometia and with its spoils began the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill. When he could not take Gabii by arms, his son Sextus fled there, pretending to have been beaten, won command of its troops and, on a sign from his father, killed or banished its leading men. Tarquin is said to have ordered the excavation of the cloaca maxima, and, by one story, to have bought three of nine Sibylline Books from the Cumaean Sibyl after she burned the others.

In 509 BCE the pace and burden of his building had angered the Roman populace, and Tarquin marched against the Rutuli to besiege Ardea. In the story, his son Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, and she stabbed herself after telling her husband and father. Lucius Junius Brutus persuaded the comitia to revoke the king's imperium and send him into exile, and two consuls were elected in his place.

Tarquin sought help from Etruscan cities and from Lars Porsena of Clusium. In 499 or 496 BCE he joined Octavius Mamilius's Latin army, which Rome defeated. He then went to the court of Aristodemus at Cumae, where he died in 495 BCE. The expression tall poppy syndrome takes its name from Livy's tale of Gabii.
tarragona: Tarragona stands on the Costa Daurada on the Mediterranean shore, around the mouth of the river Francolí. The Romans developed it on a coastal hill, some 75 to 90 metres above sea level, near an earlier Iberian settlement. Its position atop a high rock gave it the epithet arce potens Tarraco. The real founding date is unknown. One Catalan legend says it was named for Tarraho, eldest son of Tubal, and another attributes the name to Tearcon the Ethiopian, a pharaoh of the seventh century BCE.

During the Second Punic War the brothers Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus fortified Tarraco and made it a fortress and arsenal against the Carthaginians. It became the capital of Hispania Citerior and then of Hispania Tarraconensis, and also a bishopric seat. Augustus wintered there after his Cantabrian campaign and gave the city honorary titles. Its Jewish community, established in the Roman era, is among the oldest in Spain.

After the end of the Western Roman Empire the Vandals and the Visigoths took the city, and Visigothic rule ended with the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in 714. It was an important border city of the Caliphate of Córdoba between 750 and 1013. The County of Barcelona took it in 1117, and from 1129 to 1173 it was the capital of the short-lived Principality of Tarragona. It later belonged to the Principality of Catalonia within the Crown of Aragon until 1714.

In the Peninsular War the army of Louis-Gabriel Suchet besieged it from 5 May to 29 June 1811 and stormed the defences, killing or capturing almost all the Spanish garrison. In the Spanish Civil War it stayed with the Republic until Nationalist troops captured it on 15 January 1939.

The Archaeological Complex of Tàrraco is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The remains include parts of the Roman walls, the circus, the second-century amphitheatre and Les Ferreres Aqueduct, 217 metres long. Tarragona Cathedral dates from the 12th and 13th centuries and combines Romanesque and Gothic elements. The Santa Tecla Festival, held from 15 to 24 September, has been held since 1321, and the castells, human towers, are a living tradition there.
tartu: Tartu lies about 186 kilometres southeast of Tallinn on the Emajõgi river, which connects Lake Võrtsjärv with Lake Peipus. Archaeological evidence of permanent settlement on the site dates to as early as the 5th century CE. By the 7th century local inhabitants had built a wooden fortification on the east side of Toome Hill, and around the 9th and 10th centuries the settlement became an inland trading centre. The name is thought to derive from the Estonian word for aurochs, tarvas.

From the 13th century until the end of the 19th, the town was known in most of the world by variants of Dorpat. In 1262 the army of Prince Dmitri of Pereslavl captured and destroyed it but could not take the bishop's fortress on Toome Hill. In the 1280s Dorpat joined the Hanseatic League. In 1558 Tsar Ivan the Terrible began the Livonian War by besieging it, and the local bishop was imprisoned in Moscow, which ended local self-government. The city then passed between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Sweden, which held it for good from 1625.

In 1708 Russian forces blew up the remaining fortifications and houses and deported the citizens to Russia, and with the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 the city became part of the Russian Empire. The Great Fire of 1775 destroyed most of the buildings in the centre, and the town hall was built between 1782 and 1789. In the second half of the 19th century Tartu was the cultural centre of the Estonians: it hosted the first song festival in 1869, the founding of the Vanemuine theatre in 1870 and of the Society of Estonian Literati in 1872. Much of the city was destroyed in the Second World War, and under Soviet rule the population almost doubled from 57,000 to over 100,000 between 1944 and 1991.

Tartu is often called the intellectual capital of Estonia. It is the seat of the Supreme Court of Estonia, the Estonian National Museum, whose new main building opened in 2016, and the Vanemuine theatre, the oldest Estonian-language theatre, and it is the birthplace of the Estonian Song Festivals. After independence was regained in 1991 the old town was renovated and St. John's Church, in ruins since the war, was restored.
tartus: Tartus lies on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean, on a coastal plain bordered to the east by the Syrian Coastal Mountain Range, whose limestone hills in places give way to basalt. Arwad, the only inhabited island on the Syrian coast, lies a few kilometres off the shore. The name derives from the Ancient Greek Antaradus, meaning the town facing Aradus, which became Tortosa in Latin and Ṭarṭūs in Arabic. It has a Mediterranean climate with mild, wet winters and hot, humid summers. The city was governed from Latakia until the 1970s, when Tartus Governorate was created.

Tartus was founded as a Phoenician colony of Aradus, the larger settlement on the island, and was called Antaradus. Little remains of it. In the Greco-Roman and Byzantine periods it had its own bishops, and bishops of Antaradus and of Aradus appear at councils from Chalcedon in 451 onward. The first chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary is said to have been built there in the 3rd century, and the city was favoured by Constantine for its devotion to her cult. Caliphate armies under Ubadah ibn al-Samit conquered it in 636, and Mu'awiya I built an amsar complex there.

Frankish forces captured the city in 1099 during the First Crusade. Raymond of Saint-Gilles recaptured it in February 1102 after a two-week siege, and in 1123 the Crusaders built the semi-fortified Cathedral of Our Lady of Tortosa over a Byzantine church popular with pilgrims.

In 1152 Tortosa was handed to the Knights Templar, who made it a military headquarters and about 1165 built a castle with a large chapel, an elaborate keep and thick double concentric walls. Nur ad-Din Zangi held it briefly. Saladin recaptured it in 1188, but some Templars kept the keep for another hundred years until it fell in 1291, the last Templar outpost on the Syrian mainland. They then held the island of Arwad for another decade. Under the Mamluks the city lost its prestige, which it regained under Ottoman rule through trade with Cyprus and Europe.

Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt conquered Tartus in 1832. The Ottomans regained it in 1839, and in 1840 British frigates and marines attacked the citadel without capturing it. Ottoman rule lasted until 1918.

Tartus is a major port and the second largest port city in Syria after Latakia, with a 2023 population estimated at 458,327. The historic centre is built on and inside the walls of the Templar fortress, whose moat still separates the old town from the modern city. The former cathedral, the Romanesque-Gothic Notre-Dame of Tartus of the 12th century, has housed the National Museum of Tartus since 1956.
tashkent: Tashkent is in northeastern Uzbekistan, on a well-watered plain on the road between Samarkand and Shymkent, just across the border in Kazakhstan. It sits at the confluence of the Chirchiq River and several of its tributaries and is built on deep alluvial deposits up to 15 m deep. The city lies in an active tectonic area and suffers numerous tremors and occasional earthquakes. Its climate is Mediterranean with some humid continental influences: winters are cold and often snowy, and summers are long, hot and dry.

Abu Rayhan Biruni wrote that the name comes from the Turkic tash and the Persian kent, Stone City or City of Stones. The older name Chach has been traced by Ilya Gershevitch to an Old Iranian word for an area of water or lake, though Ünal criticizes that derivation as based on too many assumptions and derives Čač from a Proto-Turkic word for stone.

Tashkent's history stretches back centuries as part of the ancient Silk Road. Before the influence of Islam in the mid-8th century, Sogdian and Turkic culture was predominant. Genghis Khan destroyed the city in 1219, after which it was rebuilt and profited from its place on the Silk Road. From the 18th to the 19th centuries it was an independent city-state, before being re-conquered by the Khanate of Kokand. The Russian Empire took Tashkent in 1865, and it became the capital of Russian Turkestan. In 1868 the Samarkand Kufic Quran was taken as a war trophy from Samarkand to Saint Petersburg, and the Bolsheviks returned it to Tashkent in 1923.

In Soviet times the city grew greatly and its population changed because of forced deportations from throughout the Soviet Union. Thousands of Pontic Greeks were displaced in the early 1940s, and about 11,000 refugees of the Greek Civil War were sent to Tashkent after 1949. Its population was 1,902,000 in 1983 and about 2,136,600 in 1991. The 1966 earthquake destroyed much of the city, which was rebuilt as a model Soviet city and was then the fourth-largest in the Soviet Union, after Moscow, Leningrad and Kiev. The Tashkent Metro, the first in Central Asia, opened in 1977.

Tashkent is the most populous city in Central Asia. Ethnic Uzbeks form the majority, and Uzbek is the main language, with Russian used as a lingua franca. Most of the ancient city was destroyed in the 1917 revolution and the 1966 earthquake. Surviving landmarks include the Kukeldash Madrasah, dating from the reign of Abdullah Khan II (1557-1598), Chorsu Bazaar, the Hazrati Imam Complex and the mausoleum of Qaffol Shoshi, built in 1542. The city marked 2,200 years of written history in 2009.
tassili-najjer: Tassili n'Ajjer, meaning plateau of rivers, is a mountain range and plateau in south-eastern Algeria at the borders of Libya and Niger, covering more than 72,000 square kilometres. Its highest point is Adrar Afao, at 2,158 metres, and the nearest towns are Djanet and Illizi. The range is mostly sandstone stained by desert varnish, and erosion has formed rock forests resembling a lunar landscape, nearly 300 natural rock arches in the south-east, deep gorges and permanent pools in the north.

Because of its height and the water-retaining sandstone, vegetation is more lush than in the surrounding desert, with open woodland of endangered Saharan cypress and Saharan myrtle. It is a national park and Biosphere Reserve and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1982.

The highlands show occupation from 5500 to 1500 BCE, mainly by transhumant pastoralists of the Neolithic who camped there in the dry season, while hearths and stone tumuli in the lowlands date between 6000 and 4000 BCE. Hunter-gatherers lived in the region between about 10,000 and 7500 years ago, and after 7500 years ago people organised into pastoral groups in response to an increasingly unpredictable climate.
Cattle were herded across wide areas as early as 3000 to 2000 BCE, followed by horses before 1000 BCE and then camels, whose arrival reflects the growth of trans-Saharan trade.

European study of Algerian rock art began in 1863. Westerners were widely introduced to Tassili through sketches by French legionnaires, particularly Lieutenant Charles Brenans in the 1930s, who brought the archaeologist Henri Lhote. Lhote returned several times between 1956 and 1970. His expeditions have been heavily criticised, his team being accused of faking images and of damaging paintings by brightening them for tracing and photography.

The rock art, first reported in 1910, includes about 15,000 engravings so far identified. The earliest pieces are presumed to be around 12,000 years old, although sources vary considerably, and most date to between 9,000 and 10,000 years ago or later. The subjects are large wild animals such as antelopes and crocodiles, cattle herds, and humans hunting and dancing. The art falls into five traditions: Archaic, Round Head, Bovidian or Pastoral, Horse and Camel. The Round Head paintings include some of the oldest and largest exposed rock paintings in Africa, with figures over five metres tall, and their concentration in particular places suggests ritual centres.

The Horse period shows chariots and riders beside Libyan-Berber inscriptions that remain undeciphered. The Camel period coincides with caravan routes that carried salt, goods and enslaved people across the Sahara.
tatars: The name Tatar possibly referred first to the Tatar confederation, which Genghis Khan incorporated into the Mongol Empire. Western cartographers later applied the term, often spelled Tartar, to anyone from the northern and central Asian landmass then known as Tartary. The name became that of populations of the former Golden Horde in Europe, such as those of the Kazan, Crimean, Astrakhan, Qasim and Siberian Khanates. The Persian word is first recorded in the 13th century in reference to the hordes of Genghis Khan. Studies of ancestry suggest that the three main groups, the Volga, Crimean and Siberian Tatars, formed independently of one another.

The Volga Tatars descend from Kipchaks of the Golden Horde or from Volga Bulgars who survived the Mongol conquest of 1236 to 1237. About 40 thousand Tatars arrived with Khan Uluk-Muhammad in 1438 to 1445 when the Kazan Khanate was formed. Its conquest by Ivan IV in 1552 followed a six-month siege.

The Crimean Tatars formed between the 13th and 17th centuries, mainly from Kipchaks and Ottoman Turks. Crimea passed to the Giray dynasty, founded by Hacı Giray after an embassy invited him from Lithuania in 1441.

In 1502 the Crimean Khanate defeated the Great Horde, and it was among the strongest powers in Eastern Europe until the early 18th century, formally a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. A major source of income was frequent raids into Eastern Europe and the Caucasus for slaves.

Russia annexed it in 1783, and at least 800 thousand Tatars left Crimea by the early 20th century. In May 1944 the Soviet State Defense Committee ordered the deportation of all Crimean Tatars to Central Asia, and 46 per cent of them are said to have died during the deportation and the first years of exile.

Tatars settled in the Polish-Lithuanian lands between the 13th and 17th centuries. The Lipka Tatars first settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania at the beginning of the 14th century, and Grand Duke Vytautas invited a further, Muslim wave towards the end of it. The grand dukes encouraged the migrations because of the Tatars' reputation as skilled warriors, and the settlers were granted szlachta (noble) status. Estimates for the 17th century put their number at about 15,000, in about 60 villages with mosques.

They kept their religion and culture through royal privileges and internal autonomy, and were allowed to marry Christians, which was uncommon in Europe at the time. By the 18th century they had adopted the local language. The May Constitution of 1791 gave them a seat in the Sejm. Henryk Sienkiewicz's historical novels made their role well known in Poland.
tatarstan: Tatarstan lies in the centre of the East European Plain, about 800 kilometres east of Moscow, between the Volga and the Kama rivers. It covers 68,000 square kilometres and borders Kirov, Ulyanovsk, Samara and Orenburg oblasts and the republics of Mari El, Udmurtia, Chuvashia and Bashkortostan. Its capital and largest city is Kazan. Oil, natural gas and gypsum are its main natural resources.

The earliest known organised state within its present boundaries was Volga Bulgaria (c. 700 to 1238), a mercantile state with trade contacts across Inner Eurasia, the Middle East and the Baltic. Islam was introduced by missionaries from Baghdad around the time of Ibn Fadlan's journey in 922. The Golden Horde and the Khanate of Kazan followed, until Russia conquered the khanate in 1552. In the 19th century the region became a centre of Jadidism, an Islamic movement that preached tolerance of other religions.

During the Civil War of 1918 to 1920 Tatar nationalists tried to found an independent Idel-Ural State with the neighbouring Bashkirs. The Bolsheviks, who had at first supported it, arrested members of its parliament in March 1918. The Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was established on 27 May 1920, with boundaries that did not include a majority of the Volga Tatars. On 30 August 1990 Tatarstan declared its sovereignty. A constitution approved by about 62 per cent of voters in 1992 defined it as a sovereign state, but the Russian Constitutional Court declared the referendum and constitution unconstitutional. Since the 2002 text, the constitution defines Tatarstan as part of the Russian Federation.

Tatarstan is a republic of the Russian Federation. Its two state languages are Tatar and Russian, and the official script is Cyrillic. The 2021 census counted 4,004,809 inhabitants, among them about 2 million Tatars and 1.5 million Russians, with Chuvash, Mari and Udmurts in smaller numbers. Most Tatars are Sunni Muslims, and a minority, the Keräşen Tatars, are Orthodox Christians. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the republic: the Kazan Kremlin, the Bulgarian State Museum-Reserve, and the Assumption Cathedral and Monastery of the town-island of Sviyazhsk.
taunggyi: Taunggyi lies at an elevation of 1,436 metres on a high basin among the mountains of eastern Myanmar, and unlike many towns it is built along the mountain ridges rather than on a valley floor. Its name means big mountain in Burmese and refers to a ridge on its east, part of the Shan Hills, whose high point is called Taung-chun, the Spur. The city has a humid subtropical climate with a dry winter from December to March and a wet summer from April to November, and it is known as a cool hill station. It is 635 kilometres from Yangon by road.

Before the town was founded, villages such as Mon Che, Hum Bwa and Oo See stood in the area under the Nyaungshwe sawbwas. After the British annexation of Upper Burma in 1885 the colonial administration first put its headquarters for the Shan States at Maing Thauk (Fort Stedman) on Inle Lake, but malaria and the damp, low ground made it unsuitable. In 1894 the offices moved to the higher plateau where the village of Taunggyi stood, and the town was planned as a hill station on a grid of streets. By 1906 it housed about 1,000 buildings and was the residence of the British Superintendent of the Southern Shan States.

After independence in 1948 Taunggyi remained the capital of Shan State. Its position on the road to Kengtung and the Thai border made it a junction for trade, and migration brought a mixed population of Pa-O, Shan, Intha and Burmese-Chinese communities.

Taunggyi is the capital of Shan State and its administrative, commercial and educational centre, with several universities. National Highway 4 links it with Meiktila to the west and Kengtung and the Thai border to the east, while the nearest airport is at Heho. The city has Buddhist monasteries, the cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Taunggyi, a Baptist church, mosques and Chinese temples, and a Shan State Cultural Museum. The Tazaungdaing festival, which marks the end of the rainy season, is marked by the Taunggyi Hot Air Balloon Festival. Inle Lake and the Kekku Pagodas, with hundreds of stupas dating from the 16th century, lie nearby.
taunus: The Taunus is the southeastern part of the Rhenish Slate Mountains. This low mountain range is about 75 kilometres long from south-west to north-east and about 35 kilometres wide, and covers some 2,700 square kilometres. The Rhine and the valley of the Lahn bound it on the west and north, the Main and the Rheingau on the south, and the plain of the Wetterau on the east. It is divided into the Vordertaunus, the Hohe Taunus, the Hintertaunus and the Idstein Depression. The highest parts, in the Feldberg massif, are wooded, colder and wetter than the lowlands around them.

Its rocks are mostly slates, phyllites and sandstones laid down in the Ordovician to Devonian periods. Taunus quartzite, a very weather-resistant rock, forms many summits, among them the Altkönig and the Kleiner Feldberg. Iron ore, silver ore and roofing slate were mined in the Lahn area from the 17th to the 20th century, and between Idstein and Usingen pits were worked from the late Middle Ages. The last active lead and silver mine, at Heftrich, closed around 1924.

The Roman frontier, the Limes, was built across the Taunus, and the Saalburg, a restored Roman fort, now houses a museum. After the fall of the Limes in 259 or 260 CE the Alamanni settled in the range, and Alemannic cemeteries survive in its southern foothills. Around 500 CE, after the Battle of Tolbiac, the area passed to the Frankish confederation. The Celtic ring walls on the Altkönig are built of Taunus quartzite.

Until the late 18th century the range was known simply as die Höhe, the height, a name kept in Bad Homburg vor der Höhe and Rosbach vor der Höhe. The name Taunus comes from the Annals of Tacitus, which mention a fort in monte Tauno, probably near present-day Friedberg. In past centuries the Taunus became known among aristocrats for its hot springs.

Several spa towns lie in the Taunus. Bad Schwalbach is mentioned in documents from the 16th century, and Bad Ems has been one of the most reputed therapeutic spas in Germany since the 17th century. By the 19th century the best-known spa towns were Wiesbaden, Bad Homburg vor der Höhe, Bad Nauheim and Bad Soden am Taunus. Groundwater from the quartzite, pumped through four tunnels, contributes much to the water supply of Wiesbaden. The Ford Taunus car line is named after the range.
taurus-mountains: The Taurus Mountains are a mountain complex in southern Turkey, extending in a curve from Lake Eğirdir in the west to the upper reaches of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers in the east. They form part of the Alpide belt of Eurasia and were known in antiquity also as Mons Masius. They are divided into three chains. The Western Taurus arcs around the Gulf of Antalya, with peaks above 3,000 metres; the highest is Kizlarsivrisi, at 3,086 metres, in the Bey Mountains. The Central Taurus includes Mount Demirkazık, at 3,756 metres, and the Bolkar and Aladağlar ranges. The Southeastern Taurus forms the northern boundary of the Southeastern Anatolia Region and North Mesopotamia.

The mountains were formed by the collision of the African and Eurasian tectonic plates and rest mainly on limestone. In the Aladağlar and Bolkar ranges the eroded limestone has formed karst landscapes with waterfalls, underground rivers and some of the largest caves in Asia. The climate is Mediterranean, and at lower elevations evergreen oak and Turkish pine grow, with black pine, Lebanon cedar and Taurus fir above 1,200 metres.

The name appears in the Histories of Polybius as Taûros. According to the scholar Heinrich Kiepert, it was borrowed into Greek from an Old Aramaic root meaning mountain. The bull was a common symbol of the storm gods of the ancient Near East, and the mountains held many storm-god temples. The ancient Syrians held that the thunderstorms of these mountains were the work of the storm god Adad, who made the Tigris and Euphrates rise and flood and so fertilise their land. Modern scholars place the Hurrians, probably the originators of the various storm gods, in the Taurus at their probable earliest origins. At Kestel there is a Bronze Age site where early evidence of tin mining has been found.

The Cilician Gates, or Gülek Pass, crossed the range north of Tarsus and has been the principal route through it since ancient times, linking the coastal plain of Cilicia with central Anatolia. In the Amanus range, a natural frontier with Cilicia to the west and Syria to the east, the passes such as the Amanian Gate were of great strategic importance. In 333 BCE Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at the Battle of Issus in the foothills between two of them. In World War I, the German and Turkish railway through the Taurus was a major objective of the Allies.
tavira: Tavira lies in the east of the Algarve on the south coast of Portugal, 28 kilometres east of Faro and 75 kilometres west of Huelva across the Guadiana into Spain. The Gilão River meets the Atlantic here. The municipality had 26,167 inhabitants in 2011 and covers 606.97 square kilometres. Tavira is the Portuguese representative community for the inscription of the Mediterranean Diet as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity of UNESCO.

The settlement's origins go back to the late Bronze Age. In the 8th century BCE it became one of the first Phoenician settlements in the west of Iberia, with massive walls, at least one sanctuary, two harbours and a regular urban plan, which lasted until the end of the 6th century BCE. Excavations on the hill of Santa Maria found part of a casemate fortification wall and ritual deposits. The site was later revived in the so-called Tartessian period and abandoned again by the end of the 4th century BCE. Under Caesar the Romans built a new port about 7 kilometres from modern Tavira, which prospered and declined with the empire.

The Moorish period, from the 8th to the 13th century, shaped the area's agriculture, culture and architecture, with whitewashed buildings and Moorish style doors. The Moors built Tavira Castle, two mosques and palaces, and the seven-arched bridge once thought Roman proves to be a 12th-century Moorish work. The area stayed mostly rural until the 11th century, when the town grew rapidly into one of the important settlements of the Gharb al-Andalus. In 1242 Dom Paio Peres Correia retook Tavira after seven of his principal knights were killed during a truce. His troops killed most of the population, and the few survivors were confined to a small quarter known as the Mouraria.

In the 18th century the river port shipped salt, dried fish and wine, but the earthquake of 1755 destroyed almost all the town's buildings. It was rebuilt with many 18th-century buildings and has 37 churches. The church of Santa Maria do Castelo, built on the ruins of a mosque and dating to the 13th century, holds the tombs of Paio Peres Correia, who died in Tavira in 1275, and his knights. Fishing was once the main industry but declined, partly because of the changing migration of tuna and the silting of the Gilão. The sand-bar island of Ilha de Tavira forms part of the Ria Formosa wetlands.
tawhid: The word tawhid, an assertion or declaration of oneness, comes from the Arabic verb wahhada, which can mean to make one or to consider to be one. In Islam it holds that God is indivisibly one and single. The first part of the declaration of faith, the shahada, is the declaration of belief in the oneness of God, and Muslims believe that the whole of Islamic teaching rests on it. Chapter 112 of the Quran, al-Ikhlas, states that God is One, never had offspring and was not born, and has no equal. The Quran uses 99 terms, the Excellent Names of God, to express the complexity of the divine nature.

Its opposite is shirk, associating partners with God, a term usually translated as polytheism but understood to be more complex. It is classed as greater shirk, open and apparent, and hidden shirk, such as performing rituals for social recognition. The Quran says that God does not forgive associating others with Him but forgives anything else of whoever He wills.

Muslim theologians have argued for the oneness of God by reason. Against the polytheism of pre-Islamic Arabia, the Quran argues that God as creator of everything excludes lesser gods, who would themselves have to be created, and that the order of the universe shows a single administrator. Verse 21:22 says that had there been gods besides God in the heavens and earth, both would have been ruined. Later theologians reasoned that two gods would sooner or later have conflicting wills, and one would be powerless, which is incompatible with being God. Avicenna (965–1037) proposed an ontological argument in the Metaphysics of The Book of Healing, distinguishing essence from existence.

Scholars have understood tawhid in different ways. Some theologians use it for the whole discussion of God and his attributes, and sometimes for the whole of kalam, Islamic theology. Philosophers such as al-Farabi, al-Razi and Avicenna interpreted it by reason, under the influence of Plotinus's emphasis on divine simplicity. In Sufism it is both an affirmation in speech and a practical realisation of God's unity, through purification from worldliness.

Tawhid shaped Muslim culture widely. Early Muslims understood religion to cover the state, law and society, since God's rule extends to all creatures and to all aspects of life. A single raised index finger is used as a symbol of tawhid. The wish to preserve God's transcendence led to the prohibition of visual depictions of God and of any prophet, and the dominant forms of Islamic art became calligraphy and arabesque. The medieval scholar al-Ghazali held that a believer who thinks himself better than another through wealth or colour adopts the hierarchical principle of Iblis and so falls into shirk.
tawi-tawi: Tawi-Tawi is the southernmost province of the Philippines, part of the Sulu Archipelago between the Sulu Sea in the north and the Celebes Sea in the south. It shares sea borders with the Malaysian state of Sabah and the Indonesian province of North Kalimantan, both on Borneo. It consists of Tawitawi Island and 106 surrounding islands and islets with a land area of 1,087.4 square kilometres, and the main island accounts for 580.5 of them. The name is the Sinama form of jawi-jawi, Malay for the banyan tree, which grows abundantly there. The capital is Bongao, and the island supports several endemic species, among them the Tawitawi brown dove and the Sulu hornbill.

Carbon dating of bones, jars and shells from the Bolobok Rock Shelter places human presence there between 6,810 BCE and 3,190 BCE, among the earliest evidence in Southeast Asia. For centuries the area was a centre of Sama culture, and some islands hold old burial grounds with Sama okil carvings of ancestors. The first mosque in the Philippines, the Sheik Karimol Makhdum Mosque, was established in 1380 by the Arab trader and missionary Makhdum Karim. The area was heavily converted to Islam, especially after the founding of the Sultanate of Sulu, although many Sama kept part of their older animist religions.

Later centuries brought foreign claims. The sultan of Sulu made agreements with Alexander Dalrymple of the British East India Company in 1761 and 1762, and in 1878 Baron von Overbeck leased the sultan's land in Borneo for the British North Borneo Company. The Spanish built a naval base at Tata'an and garrisons at Bongao and Siasi. American forces occupied Jolo in 1899, and by the Treaty of Washington in 1900 Spain ceded Sibutu and Cagayan de Sulu to the United States for US$100,000. The Imperial Japanese Navy used the waters as a fleet anchorage during World War II.

The municipalities of Tawi-Tawi were part of Sulu until 11 September 1973, when Presidential Decree No. 302 made it a province, with Romulo Espaldon as its first governor. Its seat was at first Bato-Bato, in the municipality of Balimbing, and moved to Bongao in 1979. The province lies in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and has 11 municipalities.
taxila: Taxila, known in Sanskrit as Takṣaśilā, lies on the Pothohar Plateau in Punjab, Pakistan, about 25 kilometres north-west of the Islamabad and Rawalpindi area, near the Indus. The Sanskrit name is translated as City of Cut Stone or Rock of Taksha. According to the Ramayana the city was founded by Bharata, brother of Rama, and named for his son Taksha. The modern name derives from the Greek rendering recorded in Ptolemy's Geography.

Settlement in the Taxila valley goes back to the late 4th or early 3rd millennium BCE at Sarai Khola, and the first major settlement, on the Hathial mound, was established around 1000 BCE. Taxila was a capital of the Gandhara kingdom, together with Puṣkalāvatī, though at times it formed its own district or city-state. It may have grown considerably by the time of the Achaemenid conquest of the 6th century BCE. In 326 BCE its king Taxiles, called Āmbhi, surrendered to Alexander the Great without a battle; Greek historians described the city as wealthy, prosperous and well governed, and Alexander kept Taxiles as satrap.

Within about a decade of Alexander's departure Chandragupta Maurya captured the city. Buddhist texts say Chanakya came from Taxila, and under Ashoka, the grandson of Chandragupta, it became a great seat of Buddhist learning. It lay on the ancient Grand Trunk Road linking Pataliputra to Central Asia. In the 2nd century BCE the Indo-Greeks built a new capital, Sirkap, across the river, and Maues overthrew the last Greek king of Taxila around 90 BCE. Inscriptions of 76 CE show Kushan rule, and Kanishka later founded Sirsukh, the latest of the ancient settlements, when the city was known for trade in silk, sandalwood, horses, cotton, pearls and spices.

The invading Hunas devastated Taxila in the 5th century, and by the time the monk Xuanzang described it in the 7th century it was in decline. Its ruins were rediscovered in the mid-19th century by Alexander Cunningham and extensively excavated by Sir John Marshall. UNESCO designated Taxila a World Heritage Site in 1980. Some scholars regard the so-called university of ancient Taxila as one of the earliest centres of education in Asia.
taygetus: The Taygetus massif is about 100 kilometres long, running from the centre of the Peloponnese to Cape Matapan, its southernmost point. It overlooks Sparta and Kalamata and lies within the prefectures of Arcadia, Laconia and Messenia. The Eurotas has some of its headwaters in the northern part of the range, and the slopes are heavily forested, mainly with Greek fir and black pine.

The name is one of the oldest recorded in Europe, appearing in the Odyssey, and in myth it came from the nymph Taygete. In Byzantine times and until the 19th century the mountain was also called Pentadaktylos, Greek for five-fingered. Its highest summit, Profitis Ilias, is probably the classical Mount Taleton mentioned by Pausanias. Geologically the range is a limestone horst beside the Eurotas rift valley, and the Sparta fault below its eastern face caused the earthquake of 464 BCE that levelled Sparta.

The slopes have been inhabited since at least Mycenean times, and near the village of Arna the site of Arkina has three beehive tombs. The mountain was one of Sparta's natural defences. The Spartans threw criminals into a chasm called Ceadas, and remains of adults found there by the University of Athens appear to confirm it as a place of punishment for criminals, traitors and captives.

Plutarch wrote that Spartan elders judged newborn babies and left those thought unfit at the foot of Taygetus. No other ancient source says this, and the bones found at the site belonged to adolescents and adults, not infants. In the age of the barbarian invasions the mountain sheltered the native population, and many villages on its slopes date from then. In Medieval times the citadel and monastery of Mystras was built on its steep slopes and became a centre of Byzantine civilization and the capital of the Despotate of the Morea.

Mystras is occupied by a tiny religious community, its buildings are well preserved, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In antiquity the peak of Taleton was dedicated to Helios, to whom horses were sacrificed, and to Zeus. Today the summit is linked to the Prophet Elias, and each 20 July, his feast day in the Greek Orthodox calendar, a festival with a large bonfire is held at the chapel on the peak. Profitis Ilias is a popular hiking destination, and the European walking route E4 runs along the lower slopes.
tbilisi: Tbilisi stands on the banks of the Kura River. Its name comes from the Old Georgian tpili, meaning warm, because of the area's numerous sulfuric hot springs. Until 1936 the name in English and most other languages followed the Persian pronunciation, Tiflis. On 17 August 1936, by order of the Soviet leadership, the official Russian names of various cities were changed to match the local language, and the Georgian form was modernised from Ṭpilisi to Tbilisi on the proposal of Georgian linguists. Some languages, among them Turkish, Persian, Greek, Spanish and German, have kept a form of Tiflis. Its position at the crossroads between Europe and Asia, near the Silk Road, made it a point of contention among powers.

Archaeologists found evidence of continuous habitation of the suburb of Dighomi since the early Bronze Age, and stone artifacts from the Paleolithic. In the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age it was the largest settlement in the Caucasus. According to legend the site was covered by forest as late as 458. One widely accepted variant of the foundation myth says that King Vakhtang I of Iberia (r. c. 447/49 - 502/22) went hunting with a falcon, which caught or injured a pheasant, and both birds fell into a hot spring and died of burns. The king was so impressed by the springs that he had the forest cleared and built a city there.

King Dachi of Iberia (r. 522-534), Vakhtang's successor, moved the capital of Iberia from Mtskheta to Tbilisi and began building the fortress wall that marked the city's new boundaries. From the sixth century Tbilisi grew steadily because of its strategic position on trade and travel routes between Europe and Asia. It served as the capital of various Georgian kingdoms and republics.

Between 1801 and 1917, as part of the Russian Empire, it was the seat of the Caucasus Viceroyalty, which governed both the northern and southern sides of the Caucasus. Its population has always been diverse in culture, ethnicity and religion, though overwhelmingly Eastern Orthodox Christian.

Tbilisi is the capital and largest city of Georgia, with more than 1.3 million inhabitants, almost one third of the country's population. Its architecture mixes medieval, neoclassical, Beaux Arts, Art Nouveau, Stalinist and modern buildings. Among its landmarks are the Sameba and Sioni cathedrals, the medieval Narikala Fortress and the Georgian National Museum.
tbilisi-state-university: Tbilisi State University was established in 1918, when Georgia had declared itself an independent national democratic state, through the leadership of the historian Ivane Javakhishvili and a group of followers. Among the co-founders were the scientists Giorgi Akhvlediani, Shalva Nutsubidze, Dimitri Uznadze, Grigol Tsereteli, Akaki Shanidze and Andrea Razmadze, and Elizabeth Orbeliani became the first woman to teach there. The chemist Petre Melikishvili was the first rector. Excluding academies and theological seminaries, which had worked in Georgia for centuries, it was the first university in Georgia and the Caucasus, and at the time the only institution of its kind in the region.

The university is housed in the former Georgian Nobility Gymnasium, built by the architect Simon Kldiashvili from 1899 to 1906. Niko Tskhvedadze, a founder of the Society for the Spreading of Literacy among Georgians, oversaw its construction. The university opened on the day of remembrance of the Georgian king David the Builder, with a single faculty, that of philosophy, and Javakhishvili gave the first lecture. At the start of 1918 it had 18 professors and lecturers, 369 students and 89 free listeners.

Georgia had a tradition of education, in the School of Philosophy and Rhetoric of Phazisi in Colchis in the fourth century and the Gelati and Iqalto academies of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, but as a colony of Russia it had no national institution of higher education for centuries. Through the Bolshevik and Communist period, despite forced ideology and fierce censorship, the university kept schools in mathematics, psychology, philosophy, linguistics and historiography, and it encouraged the foundation of the Academy of Science of Georgia. In 1989 it was named after Javakhishvili.

The university has no central campus, and its buildings are spread through the city; the oldest, building number 1, houses the administration. Its yard holds the Pantheon of Tbilisi State University, where its founders are buried. A printing press was set up in 1923, a publishing house in 1933 and the university archive in 1933, and its scholarly Proceedings have appeared since 1919. Medical education was restored in 1994. It now has seven faculties, among them humanities, law, economics and business, and medicine, and branches in cities such as Sokhumi, Poti and Zugdidi.
te-deum: The Te Deum is a Latin Christian hymn, named from its incipit Te Deum laudamus, Thee, God, we praise. Its authorship is traditionally ascribed to Saint Ambrose, who died in 397, or to Saint Augustine, who died in 430, and it is sometimes known as the Ambrosian Hymn, though authorship by Ambrose is unlikely. Nineteenth-century scholarship proposed Saint Hilary of Poitiers and Saint Nicetas of Remesiana, whose name appears with the hymn in manuscripts from the 10th century onward. Hymnologists of the 20th century, especially Ernst Kähler in 1958, showed the link with Nicetas to be spurious. The hymn almost certainly dates to the 4th century, and its authorship is considered uncertain.

The Te Deum has structural similarities with a eucharistic prayer, and it has been proposed that it was originally composed as part of one. It was written on a Gregorian chant melody. It follows the outline of the Apostles' Creed, mixing a poetic vision of the heavenly liturgy with a declaration of faith. The petitions at its end, beginning Salvum fac populum tuum, are a selection of verses from the Psalms added later.

The hymn was part of the Old Hymnal when it was introduced to the Benedictine order in the 6th century and was kept in the Frankish Hymnal of the 8th century. It was removed from the New Hymnal that became prevalent in the 10th century and restored in the 12th century in hymnals that sought to recover the praiseful intent of the Rule of Saint Benedict. In the traditional office it is sung at the end of Matins on days when the Gloria is said at Mass. It is also used in Morning Prayer in the Anglican Book of Common Prayer, as an option in Matins for Lutherans, and in many Reformed churches.
A Te Deum service is a short service of thanksgiving, often held at short notice, to celebrate good news such as a military victory, the signing of a peace treaty or the birth of a royal child.

The text has been set to music by many composers, among them Handel, Haydn, Mozart, Berlioz, Verdi, Bruckner, Dvořák and Britten. The prelude to Marc-Antoine Charpentier's setting is well known in Europe as the theme music of Eurovision broadcasts. William Walton wrote a Coronation Te Deum for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953, and Puccini's opera Tosca features the opening of the hymn at the end of Act I. The 18th-century German hymn Großer Gott, wir loben dich is a free translation of it.
teanum-sidicinum: Teano, the ancient Teanum Sidicinum, is a town in the province of Caserta in Campania, about 30 kilometres northwest of Caserta on the main railway line from Naples to Rome. It stands at the southeast foot of an extinct volcano, Rocca Monfina. Strabo calls Teanum the most important town on the Via Latina, joined by a branch road from Suessa.

Teanum Sidicinum was the capital of the Oscan tribe of the Sidicini, who drove the Aurunci from Roccamonfina. They probably submitted to Rome in 334 BCE, and their troops were grouped with those of Campania in the Roman army. Like Cales, Teanum kept the right of coinage, and like Suessa and Cales it remained faithful to Rome in both the Hannibalic and the Social wars. It was apparently made a colony by Claudius, not by Augustus.

In the 4th century Teano became the seat of a diocese, and it was later an important Lombard county, part of the Duchy of Benevento. Monks from Montecassino took refuge there when their abbey was destroyed in 883, and one of the first documents in the vernacular Italian was issued there in 963. On 26 October 1860 Teano was the site of the Handshake of Teano, when Giuseppe Garibaldi, having wrested the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies from the Neapolitan Bourbons, shook hands with Victor Emanuel II, King of Sardinia, and hailed him as King of Italy.

Roman remains include a theatre of the 2nd century BCE, rebuilt in the 2nd century CE, once one of the largest in Italy at 85 metres in diameter, and extensive baths known as Le Caldarelle. The cathedral of St Clement, begun around 1050 and finished in 1116, uses Corinthian columns taken from the ancient town. The castle, built by the dukes of Sessa in the 15th century on a fortress of the 4th century BCE, served as a prison in the Bourbon era. The cathedral is the see of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Teano-Calvi.
teatro-di-san-carlo: The Teatro di San Carlo stands next to the Royal Palace in Naples and the Piazza del Plebiscito. The Bourbon king Charles VII of Naples commissioned it to replace the old, dilapidated and too small Teatro San Bartolomeo of 1621. It was designed by Giovanni Antonio de Medrano, a Sicilian nobleman and royal architect, with Angelo Carasale, the former director of the San Bartolomeo, responsible for the furnishings. The horseshoe-shaped auditorium was built for 75,000 ducats and had 184 boxes in six orders and a royal box for ten people. Blue and gold, the Bourbon colours, dominated the decoration.

The theatre was inaugurated on 4 November 1737, the king's name day, with Domenico Sarro's opera Achille in Sciro, to a libretto by Metastasio. The first seasons showed the royal preference for dance and featured castrati. Gluck was called to Naples to direct his Clemenza di Tito in 1752. Domenico Barbaia became manager of the royal opera houses in 1809. On 13 February 1816 a fire broke out during a dress rehearsal for a ballet and destroyed part of the building. On the orders of King Ferdinand IV, Barbaia rebuilt it within ten months with the architect Antonio Niccolini, and it reopened on 12 January 1817 with Johann Simon Mayr's Il sogno di Partenope.

Gioachino Rossini was house composer and artistic director of the royal opera houses from 1815 to 1822 and wrote ten operas in this period, among them Otello and Mosè in Egitto. Gaetano Donizetti followed from 1822 until 1838 and composed sixteen operas for the theatre, including Lucia di Lammermoor in 1835. Verdi wrote Alzira and Luisa Miller for it. After the unification of Italy in 1861 Naples lost its status as the musical centre of Italy, and by 1874 falling income closed the house for a year. Bombs damaged it in the Second World War, and its first opera performance after the liberation of Naples in 1943 was La bohème on 26 December.

The San Carlo is the oldest continuously active opera venue in the world, opened decades before Milan's La Scala or Venice's La Fenice. Its opera season runs from late November to July, and its ballet season from December to early June. The seating, once 3,285, has been reduced to 1,386. Since the 1844 redecoration under Niccolini the interior has been red and gold. A renovation costing 67 million euros, carried out in 2008 and 2009, was meant to return the house to its condition after the rebuilding of 1816, and it reopened on 27 January 2010.
tebessa: Tébessa is a city in north-eastern Algeria near the border with Tunisia, the capital of Tébessa Province. Its classical name was Theveste, the Latin form of the Greek Thebeste, and the ancient Greeks also knew it as Hekatompyle, meaning Hundred Gates. It is known for the wall around the city and its gates and for traditional Algerian carpets. The surrounding province has many phosphate mines, among them the Djebel Onk mine, and the city is linked by road and rail with Tunisia and the rest of Algeria.

Once the empire was established, the 3rd Augustan Legion was based at Theveste before it moved to Lambaesis. The town later became a colony, probably under Trajan in the early 2nd century, when it was flourishing with about 30,000 inhabitants.

It became a Christian centre: its bishop Lucius attended the council of Carthage in 256 and died a martyr two years later, Maximilianus was martyred on 12 March 295 and Crispina on 5 December 304. Donatists held a council there, and in the 4th and 5th centuries the city was a hotbed of Manichaeism. A Latin Manichaean codex was found in a cave near the city in June 1918 and is now kept in Cologne.

The Byzantine patrician Solomon rebuilt Theveste and incorporated it into Byzantine North Africa early in the reign of Justinian I. The Muslim conquest in the 7th century reduced its importance without destroying it, and in the 11th century the Banu Hilal settled in the region. In the 16th century the Ottoman Empire placed a small garrison of Janissaries there, and the French occupied the town in 1851. After Algerian independence it became the capital of its own province.

The ruins are rich in ancient monuments. They include the Arch of Caracalla, a triumphal arch of 214, a Roman theatre, the Temple of Minerva of the early 3rd century with mosaics, a 4th-century amphitheatre, and the remains of the basilica of St Crispina, one of the largest in Africa, rebuilt in 535 by Solomon. The Byzantine walls of the 6th century, popularly called Solomon's Walls, are flanked by thirteen square towers, and Solomon also built his own tomb in the town. The city has an archaeological museum.
tecumseh: Tecumseh was born in Shawnee territory in what is now Ohio, probably at the town of Chillicothe on the Scioto River, into the Panther clan of the Kispoko division. His father, the war chief Puckeshinwau, was killed in the 1774 Battle of Point Pleasant, after which the Shawnees ceded Kentucky to the colonists. His older brother Cheeseekau, a noted war chief, taught him.

At the age of fifteen Tecumseh attended an intertribal conference at Lower Sandusky, where speakers such as Joseph Brant argued that Indian lands were held in common and that no more should be ceded without the consent of all the tribes. As a young war leader he joined Chief Blue Jacket's armed struggle, which ended in defeat at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794 and the loss of most of Ohio in the 1795 Treaty of Greenville.

In 1805 his younger brother Lalawéthika, later known as Tenskwatawa, began preaching that Native Americans should reject European influences, stop drinking alcohol and return to a traditional way of life. Tecumseh followed his teachings. In 1808 the brothers established Prophetstown in present-day Indiana, which grew into a large multi-tribal community.

After the Treaty of Fort Wayne Tecumseh became prominent and tried to build a confederacy from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico. In August 1810 he met William Henry Harrison at Vincennes and demanded that the treaty be rescinded, saying that otherwise they would have to fight it out. In 1811, while he was in the South seeking allies, Harrison defeated Tenskwatawa at the Battle of Tippecanoe and destroyed Prophetstown.

In June 1812 Tecumseh joined the British at Fort Malden. He took part in the Siege of Detroit under Major-General Isaac Brock, where he led about 530 warriors, and General William Hull surrendered on 16 August 1812. At Fort Meigs in 1813 he is said to have stopped the killing of American prisoners.

After the American naval victory in the Battle of Lake Erie on 10 September 1813, General Henry Procter decided to retreat from Amherstburg. Tecumseh reluctantly agreed and retreated with him up the Thames River. At the Battle of the Thames on 5 October he held the right with about 500 warriors while Procter's left collapsed, and he was killed in the fighting led by Colonel Richard Mentor Johnson. His confederacy collapsed after his death.

He was admired even by Americans who had fought him, and Harrison called him one of those uncommon geniuses who produce revolutions. He became a folk hero in American, Indigenous and Canadian history.
teesta-river: The Teesta rises at the Teesta Khangtse Glacier, above 5,400 metres, in the eastern Himalayas and flows south through gorges and rapids in Sikkim. Streams from Tso Lhamo Lake, Gurudongmar Lake and the Thangu and Yumthang valleys feed it, and the Rangeet River, its largest tributary, joins it before it turns south into West Bengal. It reaches the plains at Sevoke, about 22 kilometres north-east of Siliguri, where the Coronation Bridge and a railway bridge link the north-eastern states to the rest of India.

Of its 414 kilometres, 305 lie in India and 109 in Bangladesh, and it drains 12,540 square kilometres. It passes Jalpaiguri and Mekhliganj, enters Bangladesh at Dahagram in Rangpur Division and joins the Brahmaputra, there called the Jamuna, near Gaibandha. Tropical deciduous trees cover the lower hills along its route and alpine vegetation the upper ones. During the monsoon landslides often dam parts of the river, and it has caused severe flooding in Bangladesh.

The Teesta once flowed south from Jalpaiguri in three channels, the Punarbhaba, the Atrai and the Karatoya. The flood of 1787 changed its course: it turned south-east and became part of the Brahmaputra system.

Its water has long been disputed between India and Bangladesh. Negotiations began in 1983, when a temporary arrangement gave Bangladesh 36 per cent and India 39 per cent, with the remainder unallocated. A water-sharing treaty signed by both countries in 1996, following the Ganges water dispute, dealt with sharing in general terms, and the sharing of the Teesta itself remains unsettled.

Dams and barrages control the river in both countries. In Sikkim they include the Teesta V Dam, rated at 510 megawatts, while the Teesta Barrage stands at Gajoldoba in Jalpaiguri district and the Barakhata Teesta Barrage in Nilphamari District in Bangladesh. The river area lies in the seismically active Zone V. It is the largest river of Sikkim and the second largest of West Bengal after the Ganges.
tegal: The city developed from a small village called Tetegual. Its modernization began in the early 1530s, and it became part of the Pekalongan Regency, which acknowledged the Pajang Empire, successor of the Sultanate of Demak. Ki Gede Sebayu is named as the founder. Together with the local people he sought to expand agriculture on the fertile soil, and his coronation as leader was held together with a harvest festival. By district ordinance, 28 July is the anniversary of the city.

The colonial sugar industry of the Dutch East Indies originated in Tegal and Pekalongan, and Tegal Regency remained a major sugar centre until the mid-twentieth century. In the 1920s Tegal was a centre of activism for the Communist Party of Indonesia, whose local leaders were among the instigators of the 1926 rebellion. On 8 October 1945 the Three Regions Movement was founded in Tegal, Pekalongan and Brebes to replace the aristocratic regents with ordinary people, accusing them of cooperating with the Japanese in World War II. The republic's government in Yogyakarta declared it illegal, and Indonesian forces defeated the rebels on 21 December 1945.

Tegal lies on the north coast road of Central Java, 329 kilometres east of Jakarta, and covers 39.14 square kilometres. It is administratively separate from Tegal Regency, which borders it to the south and east. It had 273,825 inhabitants at the 2020 census, and its built-up area, which stretches well beyond the city boundary, had 1,602,546. Trade and services are the main sectors of the economy. The city is known for its warung, called warteg, and for tea products, and its language, Bahasa Tegal, resembles the speech of Banyumas in its vocabulary.
tegucigalpa: Tegucigalpa lies in the southern-central highlands of Honduras, in a valley ringed by mountains, in the department of Francisco Morazán, of which it is also the departmental capital. The city stands on a chain of mountains, at elevations of 975 metres at its lowest points and 1,463 metres in its highest suburbs, and is hilly with few flat areas. The Choluteca River separates it from its sister city Comayagüela. The surrounding country was open woodland of pine and oak, and the climate is a tropical savanna one, tempered by the altitude, with a rainy and a dry season.

The Spaniards claimed the site on 29 September 1578 and founded it as the Real de Minas de San Miguel de Tegucigalpa, on the site of an existing settlement of the Lenca and the Tolupans. Juan de la Cueva became its first mayor in 1579. Among its first important buildings were the Dolores Church (1735), the San Miguel Cathedral (1765), the Casa de la Moneda (1780) and the Immaculate Conception Church (1788). The origin of the name is uncertain: the most widely accepted version derives it from a Nahuatl phrase meaning 'hills of silver', although the local people are said to have been unaware of the mineral deposits, and other proposals include 'painted rocks'.

On 30 October 1880 President Marco Aurelio Soto moved the seat of government from Comayagua to Tegucigalpa. The constitution of 1936 made Tegucigalpa and Comayagüela a single Central District, formed on 30 January 1937, and the constitution of 1982 keeps that arrangement as the permanent national capital. In late October and early November 1998 Hurricane Mitch stayed over Honduras for five days; on saturated ground and deforested slopes the rain caused catastrophic flooding, especially in Tegucigalpa, and destroyed parts of the city along the banks of the Choluteca.

Tegucigalpa is the largest city of Honduras and its political and administrative centre, seat of the national government and of the National Autonomous University of Honduras, founded in 1847. Legally the capital is the Municipality of the Central District, though nearly all government institutions stand on the Tegucigalpa side of the river, while Comayagüela on the western bank is largely made up of lower-income neighbourhoods. The census of 2013 counted 1,157,509 people in the Central District. Roman Catholicism has been the leading religion since the Mercedarian missions of about 1548, and the Diocese of Comayagua was moved to the city and renamed the Diocese of Tegucigalpa by 1916.
tehran: Tehran is bounded in the north by the southern end of the Alborz range, whose highest point near the city is Tochal Peak at 3,963 metres. The northern districts begin at about 1,800 metres, with houses and streets on steep slopes, while Rey at the southern end lies at about 1,100 metres beside the single mountain of Raga. Fertile meadows and villages, fed by the Karaj and Jajrud rivers, lie to the west and south-west. Mount Damavand, Iran's highest peak, stands near the city and figures in Ferdowsi's Šāhnāme as the homeland of Keyumars and the place where King Fereydun bound the dragon fiend Zahhak.

The origin of the name is disputed. The city's own account derives it from the Persian words for 'bottom' and 'slope', the foot of the mountain, while the linguist Zana Kamrani proposes that it means 'the warm place', in contrast to Shemiran, 'the cool place'.

Archaeological remains from the ancient city of Ray suggest that settlement in the area is more than 6,000 years old. In the Median period part of present-day Tehran was a suburb of the prominent city of Rhages, which appears in the Avesta and in Old Persian inscriptions as a province; from there Darius I sent reinforcements to his father Hystaspes in Parthia. In 641 the last Sasanian king, Yazdgerd III, issued his final appeal to the nation from Rhages before fleeing to Khorasan. Because the city resisted the Muslim invasion, the Arabs ordered it destroyed and rebuilt by the aristocrat Farrukhzad.

In the ninth century Tehran was a well-known village, though less so than the flourishing Rhages nearby. Agha Mohammad Khan of the Qajar dynasty first chose it as the capital of Iran in 1786, because of its closeness to Iran's contested territories in the Caucasus and to avoid the rival factions of earlier dynasties. Under Reza Shah the city gained Iran's first institute of higher learning, bank, railway line and museum. Large-scale construction began in the 1920s, and Tehran became a destination for mass migration from all over Iran, especially in the 20th century.

Tehran is the capital and largest city of Iran, with 8,693,706 inhabitants at the 2016 census. Persians are the majority, with Azeris the second-largest ethnic group at about 10 to 15 per cent. Its historical sites include the Golestan Palace of the Qajar dynasty, a World Heritage Site, and the Sa'dabad and Niavaran palace complexes; the Azadi Tower was built in 1971 to mark 2,500 years of the Persian Empire.
telangana: Telangana lies on the Deccan Plateau, in the central stretch of the eastern seaboard of the Indian Peninsula, and covers 112,077 square kilometres. It borders Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh to the north and Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka to the south. The Godavari and Krishna rivers drain it, along with smaller rivers such as the Bhima, the Manjira and the Musi, but most of the land is arid. The name comes from Telinga, and was used to set the predominantly Telugu region of the old Hyderabad State apart from Marathwada and Kalyana-Karnataka.

One of the earliest known political formations here was the Aśmaka Mahajanapada, which flourished roughly between 700 and 400 BCE and was the only southern kingdom among the sixteen great Mahajanapadas. Its capital, Podana, is identified by most scholars with present-day Bodhan. The region later belonged to many empires, among them the Maurya, Satavahana, Chalukya, Chola, Rashtrakuta, Delhi Sultanate, Bahmani Sultanate and Golconda Sultanate. The region experienced a golden age under the Kakatiya dynasty, which ruled most of present-day Andhra Pradesh and Telangana from 1083 to 1323; Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra II were prominent rulers. It weakened after the attack of Malik Kafur in 1309 and was dissolved when Muhammad bin Tughluq's forces defeated Prataparudra in 1323.

From the seventeenth to the nineteenth century the Mughals and the Nizams of Hyderabad ruled the region. In 1823 the Nizams ceded the Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts to British India, which left Hyderabad a landlocked princely state. When India became independent in 1947 the Nizam wished to stay independent, and the Government of India annexed Hyderabad State on 17 September 1948 in a military operation called Operation Polo. After decades of protest by the Telangana movement, the state of Telangana was created in 2014 from the Telugu regions of the former Hyderabad State.

Telangana has Hyderabad as its capital. Telugu is the primary official language and Urdu the second; about 75 per cent of people speak Telugu and 12 per cent Urdu. Before 1948 Urdu was the official language of Hyderabad State and the language of the educated elite. At the 2011 census Hindus formed 85.1 per cent of the population and Muslims 12.7 per cent. Warangal Fort, the Kakatiya capital, has the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, which appears on the state emblem, and the Ramappa Temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The state is divided into 33 districts.
telavi: Telavi is the main city and administrative centre of the province of Kakheti. It lies on the foothills of the Tsiv-Gombori Range, 500 to 800 m above sea level, facing the range to the south and south-west and bordering the Alazani Valley to the north and east. The Greater Caucasus Mountain Range, which runs to the north of the valley, can be seen from most of the city.

The first archaeological finds from Telavi date from the Bronze Age. In the 2nd century CE the Greek geographer Claudius Ptolemaeus mentions a name, Teleda, that refers to it. From the 8th century it grew into a fairly important political and administrative centre. The Arab geographer Al-Muqaddasi in the 10th century listed it beside Tbilisi, Ganja, Shamkhor, Shemakha and Shirvan, and noted that most of its population was Christian.

From the 10th to the 12th centuries Telavi was the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti and later of Kakheti-Hereti. During the Georgian state's 12th and 13th centuries it became one of its most important political and economic centres. After the united Georgian Kingdom disintegrated in the 15th century its role declined and it became an ordinary town of trade and crafts. It regained importance in the 17th century as the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti, and by 1762 it was the second capital, after Tbilisi, of the united eastern Georgian Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti.

King Erekle II, who was born and died in Telavi, reigned from 1744 to 1798, and the period was a special epoch for the town. He founded a theological seminary and a theatre there, and Georgians remember him affectionately as Patara Kakhi, the Little Kakhetian. In 1801 Kartli-Kakheti was annexed by the Russian Empire and Telavi lost its status as a capital. In the 19th century it was the centre of the Telavi uezd in the Tiflis Governorate, with small industries such as pottery, leather painting and wine-making. About 12,000 people lived there at the end of the century, around 9,000 of them Armenians and 2,000 Georgians.

Telavi has about 16,800 inhabitants. It keeps four fortification monuments from four periods, which leads scholars to call it the most medieval city in Georgia. They include Batonis Tsikhe, a 17th-century fortress that is one of the few well-preserved medieval royal palaces in the country, and Dzveli Galavani, the fortress of the first Kakhetian kings. Nearby are the 11th-century Alaverdi Cathedral, the Ikalto Academy, where Shota Rustaveli studied, the ruins of Gremi and the Tsinandali Gardens. The Armenian churches of the old town were mostly closed in 1923.
telegraph: Signalling over distance is ancient. The signal towers of the Great Wall of China are among the oldest examples, and by 400 BCE signals could be sent by beacon fires or drum beats. These ancient systems, including Chinese ones, could send only predetermined messages and so were not true telegraphs. The first true telegraph in widespread use was the optical telegraph of Claude Chappe, which operated in France from 1793; its stations signalled to each other with shutters or paddles. The word telegraph, from the Greek for writing at a distance, was coined by Chappe himself.

Early electric telegraphs were electrostatic, with a system over a substantial distance by Ronalds in 1816, which the British Admiralty rejected as unnecessary because its optical telegraph to Portsmouth seemed adequate. Electromagnetic systems replaced the electrostatic ones. The first operative electric telegraph, by Gauss and Weber in 1833, linked Göttingen Observatory to the Institute of Physics about a kilometre away.

Cooke and Wheatstone received a patent for an electric telegraph on 12 June 1837, and the world's first permanent railway telegraph, between London Paddington and West Drayton, was completed in July 1839. Railway companies installed lines first in Germany and Britain, and private companies then offered a public service along them. Samuel Morse developed a rival system in the United States, and the Morse system was adopted as the international standard in 1865, using a modified code developed in Germany in 1848.

Ocean cables needed a flexible insulator that resisted seawater. Gutta-percha, a natural rubber sent to London from Singapore by William Montgomerie in 1843, proved suitable, and a cable between Dover and Calais was laid in 1850, though a French fishing vessel severed it almost at once. It was relaid the next year, and connections to Ireland and the Low Countries followed. Telegrams became popular once prices fell, and at their peak in 1929 an estimated 200 million were sent.

The electric telegraph freed communication from the time constraints of the postal service and revolutionised society and the global economy.
