With the help of the Saxons under Duke Hadugato, Thuringia was conquered. Chlothar received Radegund, daughter of King Berthar, who had been Hermanfrid's brother. Hermanfrid was killed in battle at Unstrut and his kingdom was annexed. The four sons of Clovis then fought the Burgundian kings Sigismund and Godomar. Godomar fled and Sigismund was taken prisoner by Chlodomer, while Theuderic married Sigismund's daughter Suavegotha.

Godomar rallied the Burgundian army and won back his kingdom. Chlodomer, aided by Theuderic, defeated Godomar again but died in the fighting at Vézeronce. After making a treaty with his brother Childebert, Theuderic died, and the throne of Metz passed without hindrance, and unexpectedly, to his son Theudebert. His daughter Theodechild, by Suavegotha, founded the Abbey of St-Pierre le Vif at Sens.
theuderic-ii: Theuderic II was the second son of Childebert II. At his father's death in 595 he received the kingdom of Burgundy that had been Guntram's, with its capital at Orléans, along with lordship over the cities of Toulouse, Agen, Nantes, Angers, Saintes, Angoulême, Périgueux, Blois, Chartres and Le Mans. His elder brother Theudebert II received Austrasia, with its capital at Metz. During his minority, and later, he reigned under the guidance of his grandmother Brunhilda, whom Theudebert had evicted from Austrasia in 599. A peasant found her wandering near Arcis in Champagne and brought her to Theuderic, who welcomed her and readily fell under her influence.

Brunhilda's influence inclined Theuderic toward war with Theudebert, and he defeated him at Sens. Their cousin Clotaire II of Neustria then prompted the brothers to ally against him, and in 600 they defeated Clotaire at Dormelles. They divided the land between the Seine and the Oise, Theuderic receiving the territory between the Seine and the Loire, and campaigned together in Gascony, where they installed Genialis as duke. The brothers then fought each other, and Theuderic defeated Theudebert at Étampes.

In 604 Clotaire invaded Theuderic's kingdom. Theuderic won at Étampes on the Louet, though his mayor of the palace, Berthoald, was killed, and the next mayor, Protadius, a partisan of Brunhilda, was assassinated by nobles when he urged war with Austrasia. In 610 Theuderic lost Alsace, the Saintois, the Thurgau and Champagne to his brother, and his men east of the Jura were defeated by the Alemanni. He routed Theudebert at Toul about 611 and at Tolbiac in 612, captured him and gave him over to Brunhilda, who had him put in a monastery and probably had him murdered.

Theuderic married Ermenberga, daughter of the Visigothic king Witteric, at Chalon in 606 but sent her home in disgrace the next year. He had four sons by unnamed mistresses. He died of dysentery at Metz in late 613, while preparing a campaign against Clotaire, who had retaken the duchy of Dentelin under a treaty made during the last war between the brothers. His son Sigebert II succeeded him in both kingdoms under the regency of Brunhilda.
thies: Thiès lies 72 km east of Dakar on the N2 road, at the junction of railway lines to Dakar, Bamako and Saint-Louis. It is the capital of Thiès Region. Before colonisation the Thiès Plateau was a wooded frontier between the kingdoms of Cayor and Baol, inhabited by the Serer-Noon, a sub-group of the Serer people, who speak the Noon language and still live in the Thiès-Nones quarter of the city.

The village of Dianxene, belonging to Cayor, was founded on the plateau in the 17th century and had only 75 inhabitants in 1860. The French founded a military post there in 1864, and the Spiritans later set up a mission. In 1885 the Dakar–Saint-Louis railway, the first line in French West Africa, opened with a stop at Thiès. The Dakar–Niger line, built between 1906 and 1923, made it a junction. The French created the commune of Thiès in 1904.

The railways brought commerce and migrant labourers, including Bambara from eastern Senegal and Mali. The rail workers played a key part in the rise of Senegal's labour movement. A railway strike was violently repressed by France, and the city was a centre of the general strikes of 1945–1946 and 1947–1948, which also marked the growth of the independence movement across French West Africa. Léopold Sédar Senghor, later the first president of independent Senegal, was elected mayor in November 1956.

Thiès is the hub of an agricultural area producing rice, peanuts, manioc, millet and fruit, and a centre of livestock trading and meat packing. Phosphate is worked nearby at Palo Dial and Taïba. A tapestry factory was set up in 1966 to produce work designed by Senegalese artists, and the city has the University of Thiès, a museum and a crafts village. It is twinned with Caen, Sousse and Solingen.
thimphu: Thimphu lies in the western central part of Bhutan, in the narrow, linear valley of the Wang Chhu, also called the Thimphu River, which flows out into India as the Raidāk. The city extends north and south along the west bank and stands between 2,248 and 2,648 metres above sea level, making it the highest capital in Asia. The surrounding hills range from 2,000 to 3,800 metres, and the two altitude zones, warm temperate and cold temperate, decide the vegetation of the valley. At its southern end the Lungten Zampa bridge connects the east and west banks of the river. The city has no airport of its own and relies on Paro, about 52 kilometres away by road.

Before 1960 Thimphu was a group of hamlets scattered across the valley, among them Motithang, Changangkha, Changlimithang, Langchupakha and Taba. In 1885 a battle at what is now the Changlimithang sports ground ended in a decisive victory that opened the way for Ugyen Wangchuck, the first King of Bhutan, to control virtually the whole country. Under the Wangchuck dynasty the country enjoyed peace and progress under reformist monarchs. The third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, abolished serfdom, redistributed land and reformed taxation and the executive, legislative and judicial systems.

The capital was moved from the ancient capital of Punakha to Thimphu, and in 1961 Thimphu was officially declared the capital of the Kingdom of Bhutan by Jigme Dorji Wangchuck. It was then a hamlet of a few houses built around the Tashichho Dzong. It was only after roads were built in the 1960s, and the country opened to the outside world following the coronation of the fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, that the city grew rapidly. India provided financial and other assistance.

Thimphu is the capital and largest city of Bhutan and the seat of most important political institutions, including the National Assembly and the embassies. Dechencholing Palace, the official residence of the King, lies to the north of the city. Vajrayana Buddhism is the state religion, and the chief abbot, the Je Khenpo, spends six months of the year in the Tashichho Dzong in Thimphu and six months in Punakha. The Tshechu festival, held in September or October, features mask dances in the courtyards of the dzong. Other landmarks include the Memorial Chorten, Changangkha Lhakhang, founded in the 13th century, and the National Institute of Zorig Chusum, which teaches the thirteen traditional arts and crafts of Bhutan.
thingvellir: The name Þingvellir comes from the Old Norse Þingvǫllr, from þing, meaning assembly, and vǫllr, meaning field: the assembly fields. A thing was a form of governing assembly found in Germanic societies. The name has the same root as Tynwald on the Isle of Man, Tingwall in Shetland and Tingvoll in Norway.

The site lies in a rift valley that marks the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the boundary between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, about 40 kilometres northeast of Reykjavík. The plates' drift shows in the cracks and faults crossing the area, the largest being the canyon of Almannagjá. To the south lies Þingvallavatn, the largest natural lake in Iceland, and the river Öxará forms a waterfall at Almannagjá.

According to the Book of Settlements, settlement of Iceland began in 874. As the population grew, district assemblies were no longer enough, and chieftains outside the powerful family descended from Ingólfr Arnarson wanted a general assembly to limit its power. Grímur Geitskör was given the task of finding support and a site. The owner of Bláskógar was found guilty of murder and his land was declared public, to be used for the assembly, temporary dwellings, kindling and the grazing of horses. The place was also reachable from the most populous regions. The first proceedings in the summer of 930 are said to mark the founding of the Icelandic nation.

The Alþingi met for two weeks each year from 930 until 1798. Disputes were settled and laws made there. The Lögberg, or Law Rock, was the focal point, and the Lawspeaker, elected for three years, presided and recited the law from memory before it was written down. The Law Council acted as both parliament and supreme court, and only chieftains who held the office of goði, their Þingmen and later bishops had full rights in it. The Alþingi was the legislative and chief judicial authority of the Commonwealth until 1271. Clashes between chieftain families in its last decades brought Iceland under the Norwegian crown, and in 1662 the King of Denmark became its absolute monarch.

Thousands could gather each year. They lived in temporary dwellings with walls of turf and rock, and the only permanent buildings were a farm and later two churches. Merchants, sword-sharpeners and tanners sold goods and services, entertainers performed, and news was told from distant parts.

Legislation of 1928 made Þingvellir the first national park in Iceland, and the park was founded in 1930 to mark the thousandth anniversary of the Althing. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004 on cultural criteria. The parliament has sat in Reykjavík since 1881. The park is part of the Golden Circle of Icelandic sights, with Gullfoss and the geysers of Haukadalur.
third-crusade: After the fall of Edessa in 1144 and the failure of the Second Crusade, Nur al-Din of the Zengid dynasty united Aleppo, Mosul and later Damascus, and reduced the Crusader states. His nephew Saladin became vizier of Egypt in 1169 and, after Nur al-Din's death in 1174, took Syria for himself, defeating the Zengids at the Battle of the Horns of Hama in 1175. Raids by Reynald of Châtillon on caravans gave Saladin a pretext to move against the Franks. News of the loss of Jerusalem reached the West in the autumn of 1187, and within ten days of the death of Pope Urban III, his successor Gregory VIII proclaimed a new crusade.

Emperor Frederick Barbarossa took the cross at Strasbourg and put the Jews of Germany under his protection, since the earlier crusades had brought violence against them in Germany. He set out from Regensburg on 11 May 1189 and led his army through Hungary and the Balkans, where relations with the Byzantine emperor Isaac were strained. In Anatolia the army defeated Turkish forces at Iconium on 18 May 1190, but Frederick drowned while crossing a river on 10 June 1190, and most of his troops returned home.

Henry II of England and Philip II of France ended their war in January 1188 and both took the cross; each imposed a Saladin tithe. Henry died on 6 July 1189 and Richard I took his place. The crusaders besieged Acre, where Saladin's forces in turn besieged them, and disease killed Queen Sibylla of Jerusalem in 1190. Philip left the Holy Land in August 1191. Richard won the Battle of Arsuf on 7 September 1191 and took Jaffa. In the winter he advanced to within 12 miles of Jerusalem but turned back because of bad weather and fear of being trapped. Saladin retook Jaffa in July 1192.

The crusade kept the Crusader states from collapse, and the capture of Cyprus strengthened them, but it failed to retake Jerusalem. Historians have called it a success, a failure or hardly justified by its cost. Neither side was satisfied, though trade flourished along the Mediterranean coast. The failure inspired the Fourth Crusade of 1202 to 1204, and Europeans regained the city only briefly, in the Sixth Crusade in 1229.

On 2 September 1192 Richard and Saladin agreed the Treaty of Jaffa. Muslims kept Jerusalem, but unarmed Christian pilgrims and merchants could visit it. The Christians kept a narrow strip of coast from Tyre to Jaffa, with Ramla and Lydda to be divided, and a three-year truce was agreed. Richard left on 9 October 1192 because of threats to his rule in Europe.
third-dynasty-of-egypt: The Third Dynasty was the first dynasty of the Old Kingdom, whose capital was at Memphis. It followed the turbulent last years of the Second Dynasty, which may have included civil war. Egyptologists now widely believe that Djoser founded it as the direct successor of Khasekhemwy, the last king of the Second Dynasty. Seals naming Djoser were found at the entrance to Khasekhemwy's tomb at Abydos, which shows that Djoser buried him and finished the tomb. Earlier writers such as Wilkinson in 1999 proposed Nebka, also called Sanakht, as founder. Nebka, Sanakht and Sekhemkhet may have been brothers, sons of Khasekhemwy and his favoured consort Nimaathap.

The sources do not agree on the kings. The Turin King List and the Abydos King List each record five, the Saqqara Tablet four, and Manetho nine, many of whom did not exist or are the same king under several names. The Turin King List gives Nebka, Djoser, Djoserti, Hudjefa I and Huni. The archaeological evidence points to the order Djoser, Sekhemkhet, with the Nebty name Djeserty, and Huni, the last king, who may be the same person as Qahedjet or less likely Khaba. The dynasty is credited with about 75 years, but dating is hard. Shaw gives approximately 2686 to 2613 BCE, Baines and Malek 2650 to 2575 BCE, and Dodson and Hilton 2584 to 2520 BCE.

Djoser is the best-known king, for commissioning his vizier Imhotep to build the Step Pyramid, the earliest surviving pyramid. The scribe of the Turin King List wrote his name in red ink, a sign of his importance to the Egyptians. Some authorities believe Imhotep lived into the reign of Huni. Sekhemkhet's reign is thought to have lasted only six or seven years, and his tomb, the Buried Pyramid, was left unfinished. Khaba possibly built the Layer Pyramid at Zawyet el'Aryan, much smaller than intended; whether erosion or an unfinished building explains this is not known.

Reign lengths for Nebka, eighteen years in both Manetho and the Turin Canon, rest on sources written over 1,400 and 2,300 years after his lifetime, so their accuracy is uncertain. Little archaeological evidence survives for Nebka or Sanakht. Some scholars have proposed a southern origin for the dynasty: Flinders Petrie saw it in Sudan from iconographic evidence, while S.O.Y. Keita thought southern Egypt equally likely.
third-dynasty-of-ur: The Akkadian Empire was destroyed in the middle of the 22nd century BCE in circumstances that are not well known, with the Gutians seeming to be the main actors, and Lower Mesopotamia broke into kingdoms centred on cities such as Uruk and Lagash. Utu-hegal of Uruk defeated the Guti king Tirigan but was dethroned after about eight years by court notables led by Ur-Namma, the governor of Ur, who was probably his brother. Ur-Namma (c. 2112 to 2094 BCE) took the title King of Sumer and Akkad, restored cities, sanctuaries and irrigation canals, and issued a law code that presented him as a just king.

His son Shulgi (c. 2094 to 2047 BCE) reigned for about half the dynasty's duration. His campaigns reached the Upper Tigris, the western Zagros and Elam, and he made marriage alliances with kingdoms on the Iranian plateau and with Mari. He was deified, and a literature glorifying him was written. The fall is poorly understood, but Ibbi-Sin held on for about twenty years while controlling only a small part of the empire, after Ishbi-Erra seceded at Isin amid food shortages and revolts. A coalition of Elamite troops from Anshan and Shimashki dealt the fatal blow around 2004 BCE.

The state was a patrimonial system, a hierarchy of households with the royal household at the top, in which all resources belonged to the king and his family. The king, whose power rested on the support of the god Enlil of Nippur, headed the administration and army and appointed high officials. The administration was centralised and bureaucratic, and the vast majority of surviving documents from the period are administrative.

The economy was redistributive. Dependent workers, men and women, were organised in troops and paid in rations of barley, wool and other goods. Textile workshops were the most important, with some 6,000 workers in the province of Girsu under a single office. About 250 trial reports survive, and the Code of Ur-Nammu, known from fragmentary late copies, is the earliest law collection of its kind. Sumerian was the language of administration and literature, and Shulgi sponsored a scribal school, the e2-dubba.

The fall of Ur was a turning point, and a new era, the Old Babylonian period, began. The dynasties of Isin and Larsa that followed claimed its heritage, took up the titles of its kings and wrote lamentations on the fall of Ur, Uruk, Nippur and Eridu, which presented the fall as a divine decision and legitimised the new rulers. Hymns to Ur-Namma and Shulgi continued to be copied in schools. The dynasty never equalled the prestige of the kings of Akkad in tradition, perhaps because its conquests were less impressive.
third-punic-war: The Second Punic War ended in 201 BCE with a treaty that stripped Carthage of its overseas territories and some African ones, and forbade it to wage war outside Africa or, within Africa, without Rome's express permission. Carthage was thereafter politically subordinate to Rome. Masinissa, King of Numidia and an ally of Rome, repeatedly raided and seized Carthaginian land over the following fifty years, and whenever Carthage appealed to Rome for redress or permission to act, Rome backed Masinissa.

Carthage then sent an army under Hasdrubal against the Numidians, treaty or no treaty, and it ended in disaster at the Battle of Oroscopa. A faction in the Roman Senate had long wanted further action against Carthage, among them Cato, whom later tradition credits with ending every speech with Carthago delenda est. The illicit campaign gave them a pretext.

In 149 BCE a large Roman army landed at Utica under the consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus. The Carthaginians tried to appease them and handed over their weapons, including a recorded 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults. Censorinus then demanded that they abandon the city and settle 16 kilometres from the sea. They refused and prepared to defend Carthage. The Roman siege suffered repeated setbacks through 149 and 148 BCE, relieved only by the conduct of Scipio Aemilianus, then a tribune.

In 147 BCE public support for Scipio was so strong that the age limits were set aside and he was elected consul and sent to Africa. He built a large mole to cut off blockade runners. The Carthaginians cut a new channel to the sea and sortied with a rebuilt fleet, but many of their ships were sunk or captured on the withdrawal. Scipio then overran the Carthaginian field army's camp at Nepheris, and most of the towns still holding out surrendered.

In spring 146 BCE the Romans breached the walls. Over six days they worked through the residential quarter, killing everyone they met and burning the buildings behind them. Only on the last day were prisoners taken, 50,000 of whom were sold into slavery. The notion that the site was sown with salt is likely a 19th-century invention. A curse was laid on anyone who resettled the site, which became public land. Carthage's territory became the Roman province of Africa, with Utica as its capital.

Punic culture, language and religion survived in the surviving cities, and the Punic language was still spoken in North Africa until the 7th century CE. Augustus began rebuilding Carthage as a Roman city in 29 BCE. Polybius, the main source, was with Scipio and so presents him favourably.
thirteenth-amendment: From its founding in 1776 the United States was divided into states that allowed slavery and states that prohibited it. The original Constitution recognised slavery implicitly, in the Three-fifths Compromise, which counted three-fifths of each state's enslaved population for representation and taxation, and in the Fugitive Slave Clause. Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation, effective on 1 January 1863, declared free the enslaved in Confederate-controlled areas, about three million people, but their postwar status was uncertain, and it did not affect the border states. To put abolition beyond legal challenge, an amendment to the Constitution was drafted.

The text has two sections. The first says that neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party has been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States or any place subject to their jurisdiction. The second gives Congress power to enforce it by appropriate legislation.

The Senate passed the amendment on 8 April 1864 by 38 votes to 6. On 15 June the House failed to pass it, thirteen votes short of two thirds, but after extensive manoeuvring by Lincoln's administration it passed on 31 January 1865. Opponents argued from federalism and states' rights. It went to the states on 1 February 1865, and under President Andrew Johnson the reconstructed Southern states of Alabama, North Carolina and Georgia agreed, bringing the count to the required 27 of the 36 states on 6 December 1865. It was proclaimed on 18 December.

The amendment made the whole system of chattel slavery illegal. In Kentucky, between 65,000 and 100,000 people were still legally enslaved when it took effect, and in Delaware about nine hundred. Slavery continued under Native American tribes until new treaties in 1866. Some black Americans in the South were subjected to other forms of forced labour under the Black Codes, and many abuses were given cover by the penal labour exception.

It has rarely been cited in court, but it has been used to strike down peonage and some race-based discrimination as badges and incidents of slavery, and it was the first amendment to govern private individuals directly. It was the first of the three Reconstruction Amendments.
thirty-years-war: The Reformation had led to the Schmalkaldic War between Protestants and Catholics within the Holy Roman Empire. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 tried to prevent a recurrence by designating states as Lutheran or Catholic according to the religion of their ruler. It was undermined by the spread of Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, into Catholic areas, and by the fragmented structure of the empire, which had some 300 imperial estates and an Imperial Diet that met rarely. In 1608 Frederick IV, Elector Palatine formed the Protestant Union, and in 1609 Maximilian of Bavaria established the rival Catholic League.

In May 1618 Protestant nobles led by Count Thurn threw two of the Catholic Ferdinand's representatives and their secretary from the windows of Prague Castle, an episode known as the Third Defenestration of Prague. All three survived. Bohemia became the first battleground, and fighting then expanded into the Palatinate, drawing in the Dutch Republic and Spain, and later Christian IV of Denmark. In 1630 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania with nearly 18,000 troops. His line formations and light artillery defeated the army of Tilly at Breitenfeld in September 1631.

The period from 1618 to 1635 was chiefly a civil war within the empire and largely ended with the Peace of Prague. France then entered the war in alliance with Sweden, and the empire became one theatre in a wider struggle against the Habsburgs of Austria and Spain. Related conflicts included revolts in Portugal and Catalonia in 1640, backed by France. Field armies averaged 13,000 to 20,000 men, and the forces deployed by both sides in Germany peaked at 250,000 in 1632.

The Peace of Westphalia consisted of three agreements: the Peace of Münster between Spain and the Dutch Republic, signed on 30 January 1648, the Treaty of Osnabrück between the empire and Sweden, and the Treaty of Münster between the empire and France. Talks had begun in 1642, with 109 delegations attending at one time or another. The settlement confirmed Dutch independence from Spain and reconfirmed the liberties of the German states, ending Habsburg attempts to turn the empire into a centralised state.

Estimates of the dead range from 4.5 to 8 million, most of them civilians and most after Sweden entered the war in 1630; claims of 12 million are no longer considered realistic. Collapse of local government produced landless peasants and rebellions, and witch-hunts began in Franconia in 1626, with over 900 people executed in the Bishopric of Würzburg by 1631. Historians count the war part of the General Crisis of the mid-17th century, and one lesson drawn was the need for permanent state armies.
thiruvananthapuram: The city is built on seven hills by the seashore on the west coast, near the southern tip of mainland India. The Laccadive Sea bounds it on the west and the Western Ghats on the east, and it lies on the shores of the Karamana and Killi rivers. Its name comes from the Malayalam thiru-anantha-puram, the city of Lord Anantha, the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple. It was officially Trivandrum, the anglicised form, until 1991, when the government reinstated the original name; many Malayalees still use the older one.

The earliest known rulers of the region were the Ays, who were more closely related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai than to the rest of Kerala. Vizhinjam, now part of the city, was their capital and an important port from the second century BCE, and the Cholas and Pandyas fought over it. After the death of Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 almost all Ay territory passed to the Chera dynasty. In the tenth century the Cholas sacked Vizhinjam and destroyed its port and the education centre of Kanthalloor Sala. A branch of the Ay family that controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.

Marthanda Varma inherited Venad and expanded it by conquering Kayamkulam, Kottarakkara, Kottayam and other kingdoms, founding the princely state of Travancore in 1729. Travancore defeated the Zamorin of Calicut at Purakkad in 1755, and in 1795 the capital moved to Thiruvananthapuram from Padmanabhapuram. The Sree Moolam Popular Assembly, set up in 1904, was the first elected legislative council in any Indian state. After Travancore joined the Indian union in 1947, Pattom Thanu Pillai headed its first popularly elected ministry from 24 March 1948. The city was capital of Travancore-Cochin from 1949, and of Kerala from 1 November 1956.

The Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple remains the city's best-known landmark, alongside the Sreevaraham and Attukal Bhagavathy temples. The 2011 census counted 957,730 people in the municipal corporation. The University of Kerala and the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre of the Indian Space Research Organisation are based there, and India's space programme began in the city. It is associated with the musician Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma, the painter Raja Ravi Varma and writers such as Kumaran Asan and C. V. Raman Pillai.
thomas-aquinas: Thomas Aquinas was most likely born around 1225 in the family castle of Roccasecca, near Aquino, then controlled by the Kingdom of Sicily. His father, Landulf VI of Aquino, was a knight in the service of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, and his mother was Theodora Galluccio, Countess of Teano. He was the youngest of nine children, and the family intended him to follow his uncle Sinibald into the abbacy of Monte Cassino, where he began his education at five.

In 1239 his parents enrolled him at the studium generale in Naples, where he was presumably introduced to Aristotle, Averroes and Maimonides. At nineteen he resolved to join the Dominican Order, which did not please his family: on his way to Rome his brothers seized him and brought him back to his parents.

Although he wrote actively for only about two decades, Thomas wrote over eight million words. His best-known work is the unfinished Summa Theologiae (1265 to 1274), alongside the Disputed Questions on Truth (1256 to 1259), the Summa contra Gentiles (1259 to 1265) and commentaries on Scripture and on Aristotle.

Thomas treated theology as a science whose data are Scripture and the tradition of the Church, and held that faith and reason, distinct but related, are both necessary for true knowledge of God. He held that rational thinking and the study of nature, like revelation, are valid ways to understand truths about God. His central thought was that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. He never considered himself a philosopher, and he often cites Aristotle simply as the Philosopher.

Thomas died on 7 March 1274. Dante asserts that he died by poisoning, on the order of Charles of Anjou, but the account of one of his friends gives no hint of foul play. In 1277 Étienne Tempier, bishop of Paris, issued a condemnation listing 219 propositions, twenty of them Thomistic, which severely damaged Thomas's reputation for many years. On 18 July 1323 Pope John XXII, seated in Avignon, pronounced him a saint, and his remains were moved to the Church of the Jacobins in Toulouse on 28 January 1369.
thomas-becket: Becket was born at Cheapside in London, on 21 December, the feast day of Thomas the Apostle. His parents were Gilbert and Matilda Beket, both of Norman descent. Gilbert began as a merchant and later lived on the rents of London properties and served as the city's sheriff. At the age of ten Becket was sent to Merton Priory in Surrey, and he later attended a grammar school in London. When his father suffered financial reverses he worked as a clerk, and later he entered the household of Archbishop Theobald of Bec.

Theobald sent him on missions to Rome and to Bologna and Auxerre to study canon law, and in 1154 made him Archdeacon of Canterbury. As chancellor he enforced the king's traditional revenues, including those owed by churches. After Theobald's death Becket was confirmed as archbishop on 23 May 1162, ordained priest on 2 June and consecrated the next day. He resigned the chancellorship and sought to recover and extend the rights of the archbishopric, to the king's displeasure.

At Clarendon Palace on 30 January 1164 Henry presented sixteen constitutions to limit clerical independence and weaken connections with Rome. All the clergy agreed except Becket, who still refused to sign. Summoned to Northampton Castle on 8 October 1164 to answer charges of contempt of royal authority and malfeasance as chancellor, he was convicted and fled to the Continent. Louis VII of France protected him. He spent nearly two years at the Cistercian abbey of Pontigny, until Henry's threats against the order sent him to Sens. Pope Alexander III favoured diplomacy, and in 1170 Henry offered a compromise that allowed Becket to return.

In 1170 the Archbishop of York crowned the heir, Henry the Young King, which breached Canterbury's privilege, and Becket excommunicated those involved. Henry II is said to have spoken words that his men took as a wish to have Becket killed, and the exact wording is in doubt. Four knights, Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy and Richard le Breton, came to Canterbury on 29 December 1170 and killed Becket in the cathedral. The eyewitness Edward Grim, who was wounded, left an account.

Veneration began across Europe at once, and Alexander III canonised him on 21 February 1173. On 12 July 1174 Henry did public penance at his tomb. In 1220 his bones were moved to a gold-plated shrine in the Trinity Chapel, which Henry VIII destroyed in 1538. Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is set among pilgrims travelling to it.
thomas-cranmer: Thomas Cranmer was born at Aslockton in Nottinghamshire on 2 July 1489, a younger son of a family of established gentry of modest wealth. At 14, two years after his father's death, he was sent to the newly created Jesus College, Cambridge. He took his Master of Arts in 1515 after studying the humanists Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples and Erasmus, was ordained by 1520 and received his Doctor of Divinity degree in 1526.

From 1527 he assisted with the annulment of Henry VIII's marriage while remaining a Cambridge don. In 1529, staying at Waltham Holy Cross to avoid the plague, he suggested putting aside the legal case in Rome in favour of canvassing opinions of university theologians across Europe. Henry took an interest, and Cranmer joined the royal team that gathered them.

A royal letter dated 1 October 1532 informed him that he had been appointed Archbishop of Canterbury, a post secured by the family of Anne Boleyn. Cranmer was consecrated as a bishop on 30 March 1533. He was not at once accepted by the bishops of his province, and Thomas Cromwell, as vicegerent, eclipsed him in the king's spiritual jurisdiction. Under Henry he made few radical changes, because conservatives and reformers struggled for power, and the Act of the Six Articles of 1539 affirmed conservative doctrines such as clerical celibacy. He published the first officially authorised English service, the Exhortation and Litany.

When Edward VI came to the throne in 1547, Cranmer promoted faster change. He wrote four of the twelve Homilies and gave refuge to continental reformers such as Martin Bucer, Peter Martyr and Bernardino Ochino. In the House of Lords in December 1548 he revealed that he had abandoned the doctrine of the corporeal real presence. The Act of Uniformity 1549 backed the first Book of Common Prayer, and a second edition followed. He produced the Edwardine Ordinal in 1550 and, in the same year, the Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament.

Cranmer supported Lady Jane Grey's succession in 1553. After the accession of the Catholic Mary I he was put on trial for treason and heresy and imprisoned for over two years. Under pressure he made several recantations and reconciled himself with the Catholic Church, but Mary wanted him executed on the treason charge. He was burned at the stake on 21 March 1556 and publicly withdrew his recantations on the day.

His death was immortalised in John Foxe's Acts and Monuments, first printed in 1563. The Book of Common Prayer and the Thirty-nine Articles, a statement of faith derived from his work, remain part of his legacy in the Church of England, which honours him as a martyr. His children died without issue, and his line became extinct.
thomas-cromwell: Cromwell is thought to have been born around 1485 in Putney, then a village in Surrey. His father, Walter, was an ambitious yeoman landowner who worked as a sheep farmer and fuller, and also ran a tavern and a brewery.

Around the start of the 16th century Cromwell left his family and crossed to continental Europe, allegedly after time in prison, and later admitted to Archbishop Thomas Cranmer that he had been a ruffian in his youth. Accounts of his years in France, Italy and the Low Countries are problematic. By 1520 he was established in London mercantile and legal circles, and in 1523 he obtained a seat in the House of Commons.

Cromwell secured a seat for Taunton in November 1529 and was reported to be in favour with the King. He joined the Privy Council late in 1530. By the autumn of 1531 he had taken control of the supervision of Henry VIII's legal and parliamentary affairs. In April 1534 Henry confirmed him as principal secretary and chief minister, a position he had held for some time in all but name. He enforced the Act of Succession, and when Sir Thomas More and John Fisher refused the oath, both were imprisoned and within a month executed.

In July 1536 he became Lord Privy Seal and Baron Cromwell of Wimbledon. He orchestrated the Dissolution of the Monasteries. He also secured the licence for the Matthew's Bible and obliged every church to own a Bible by 1538, and the Great Bible followed in 1539. Scholars generally agree that he was a Protestant with a Lutheran mindset. His injunctions for the Ten Articles of 1536 provoked the Pilgrimage of Grace.

Cromwell arranged the King's marriage to Anne of Cleves, which took place on 6 January 1540 and was not consummated. Henry made him Earl of Essex on 18 April 1540, but his conservative opponents, notably the Duke of Norfolk, used the King's anger as their opportunity. Cromwell was arraigned under an act of attainder and executed for treason and heresy on Tower Hill on 28 July 1540.

Until the 1950s historians discounted his role. Geoffrey Elton then presented him as the central figure of a Tudor revolution in government, and later historians agree on his importance if not on that term. Diarmaid MacCulloch credits him with guiding the early careers of William Cecil and Nicholas Bacon.
thomas-hobbes: Thomas Hobbes was born in Westport, now part of Malmesbury in Wiltshire. He later reported that his mother, hearing of the coming invasion of the Spanish Armada, gave birth prematurely: "my mother gave birth to twins: myself and fear." His father, also Thomas, was vicar of Charlton and Westport; according to the biographer John Aubrey he was uneducated and disesteemed learning. After a fight with local clergy outside his church he was forced to leave, and the family was left in the care of his older brother Francis, a wealthy glove manufacturer. Hobbes graduated from the University of Cambridge in 1608.

Hobbes became a tutor to the Cavendish family, and in 1636 he visited Galileo Galilei in Florence, then under house arrest. He later joined the philosophical groups in Paris gathered by Marin Mersenne. Back in England in 1637, he had written The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic by the end of the Short Parliament in 1640; it circulated only in manuscript until a pirated edition about ten years later.

When the English Civil War began in August 1642 and the royalist cause declined from mid-1644, many royalists came to Paris, and their company renewed his political interests. From 1647 until 1648 he was mathematical instructor to Charles, Prince of Wales. The exiled royalists led him to write Leviathan, which compares the state to a monster composed of men, created under pressure of human needs and dissolved by civil strife arising from human passions.

In Leviathan Hobbes begins from a mechanistic understanding of human beings and asks what life would be like without government, a state of nature in which each person has a right to everything. This, he argues, would lead to a war of all against all, with life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." In 1658 he published De Homine, completing the system he had planned more than nineteen years before. After the Restoration, his former pupil Charles II granted him a pension of £100. Hobbes died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick Hall, aged 91, and was interred at Ault Hucknall in Derbyshire.
thomas-jefferson: Thomas Jefferson was born on 13 April 1743 (2 April, Old Style) at the family's Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia, the third of ten children. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a planter and surveyor, and his mother was Jane Randolph. He was born into a slave-owning family and remained a slave owner all his life. He was admitted to the Virginia bar in 1767.

Between 1769 and 1775 Jefferson represented Albemarle County in the Virginia House of Burgesses. In 1769 he wrote and sponsored legislation giving masters of slaves discretion to emancipate them; it met strong opposition. Elected to the Second Continental Congress in 1775, he was named to the Committee of Five with John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman. Adams persuaded the committee to choose Jefferson to write the Declaration of Independence, which Congress passed in 1776. Jefferson drafted it largely alone.

In 1784 he joined Franklin and Adams in Paris and then succeeded Franklin as Minister to France, serving five years. President George Washington appointed him the first Secretary of State, and he clashed with Alexander Hamilton over the national debt and the site of the capital, settled by the Compromise of 1790 in favour of the Potomac River. With James Madison he founded the Democratic-Republican Party in 1792. He lost to John Adams in 1796, by 71 votes to 68, and became vice president, then won the presidency in 1800 and was sworn in on 4 March 1801.

As president he defended American shipping against the Barbary pirates and British trade policies, acquired the Louisiana Territory, which doubled the nation's size, and reduced military forces and spending. His second term brought the trial of Aaron Burr and, in 1807, the Embargo Act. In 1819 he founded the University of Virginia, designed its buildings and was its first rector from 1825.

Jefferson followed the ideals of John Locke, Francis Bacon and Isaac Newton. He regarded the independent yeoman as the ideal of republican virtue, distrusted cities and financiers, and favoured decentralised government. He wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and pressed for a wall of separation between church and state. His views became known as Jeffersonian democracy. From 1768 he built Monticello in the Palladian style, with the help of local masons and carpenters and of his slaves. Historians acknowledge his lifelong ownership of large numbers of slaves but differ on his views of slavery.
thomas-more: Thomas More was born in the City of London on 7 February 1478, the second of six children of Sir John More, a successful lawyer and later a judge, and his wife Agnes. He was educated at St. Anthony's School and from 1490 to 1492 served John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor, as a household page. According to his friend Desiderius Erasmus, he once seriously considered becoming a monk, and between 1503 and 1504 he lived near the Carthusian monastery outside the walls of London. He chose to remain a layman, was elected to Parliament in 1504 and married Joanna Colt the following year.

In 1504 More was elected to Parliament for Great Yarmouth, and from 1510 he represented London. Between 1512 and 1519 he worked on a History of King Richard III, which he never finished. Utopia, a frame narrative in Latin, was published by Erasmus at Leuven in 1516; More is a character in it, discussing modern ills in Antwerp with the traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who describes the island of Utopia. After the fall of Wolsey, More became Lord Chancellor in 1529. Heresy was the most time-consuming issue of his chancellorship. He saw the Reformation as a threat to the unity of church and society, and he denied stories of torture of Protestants in his Apologia of 1533. Modern commentators remain divided over his campaign against Protestantism.

In 1533 More refused to attend the coronation of Anne Boleyn, and he was later imprisoned in the Tower of London, where he wrote A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation. At his trial on 1 July 1535 he argued that his silence on the new statutes could be taken as consent. He was executed on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535, declaring that he died the king's good servant, and God's first. He was beatified in 1886 and canonised in 1935, and in 1980 the Church of England added him to its calendar of Reformation martyrs.
thomas-muntzer: Thomas Müntzer was born in late 1489, or possibly early 1490, in the small town of Stolberg in the Harz Mountains of central Germany. The legend that his father was executed by the feudal authorities is untrue. His background appears to have been relatively comfortable, as his lengthy education suggests. In May 1514 he took up a post as priest in Brunswick, where he began to question the practices of the Catholic Church and to criticise, for example, the selling of indulgences.

In May 1520, using a recommendation Martin Luther had made a year earlier, Müntzer stood in for the reformist preacher Johann Sylvanus Egranus at St Mary's Church in Zwickau. He reached Prague in late June 1521, where he wrote a summary of his beliefs known as the Prague Manifesto, which was never published. In April 1523 he became preacher at St John's Church in Allstedt, where he held services in German and drew people from the surrounding country. Luther asked him to come to Wittenberg, and Müntzer refused.

In 1524 Müntzer went to Mühlhausen, where he worked with the lay preacher Heinrich Pfeiffer. A civic coup in late September 1524 was short-lived, and he had to leave the city. He returned in February 1525 and took over the pulpit at St Mary's Church. He then founded the Eternal League of God, an armed militia that met under a white banner painted with a rainbow. After the Battle of Frankenhausen he was captured, tortured and executed.

Müntzer was deeply read in the early Christian fathers, the late medieval mystics Suso and Tauler, humanist ideas and the Bible. He taught that true belief was dictated by spiritual experience, not by written testimony. The Bible was for him evidence of past spiritual experiences, and its words still had to be validated by the working of the Spirit in the believer's heart. He valued dreams and visions, and held that real suffering was essential to Christian belief.

He believed that the whole cosmos stood at a tipping point: God would set right the wrongs of the world, largely by destruction, with the active help of true Christians. In a confession under torture in May 1525 he named omnia sunt communia, all things held in common, as an aim, though this statement stands alone in his writings. Modern researchers agree that his theology, and not any social doctrine, drove his stand against feudal authority.
thomas-paine: Thomas Paine was the son of Joseph Pain, a tenant farmer and stay-maker, and Frances Pain, born Cocke. His father was a Quaker and his mother an Anglican. He attended Thetford Grammar School from 1744 to 1749 and at 13 was apprenticed to his father. At 19 he served as a privateer aboard the King of Prussia, and in 1759 he became a master staymaker in Sandwich, Kent. He married Mary Lambert that year, but his business collapsed, and she and their child died in early labour at Margate. He was using the spelling Paine by 1769, while living in Lewes, Sussex.

Paine barely survived the voyage to Philadelphia, where typhoid fever killed five passengers, and in March 1775 he became editor of the Pennsylvania Magazine. Common Sense appeared on 10 January 1776, signed by an Englishman. He estimated that it sold 100,000 copies in three months, though some historians dispute such figures. Benjamin Rush suggested the title, since Paine had called it Plain Truth.

Rights of Man, a tract of some 90,000 words answering Edmund Burke, appeared on 13 March 1791. Its second part proposed state support for the poor, public education and pensions for workers from the age of 50. Agrarian Justice argued that landed property had robbed most people of a natural inheritance, and proposed a national fund paying fifteen pounds to each person at the age of twenty-one. In The Age of Reason he wrote that he believed in one God and in no church. He was also an abolitionist, and Rush later credited him with a Pennsylvania Magazine article against slavery.

Paine stayed in France until 1802 and returned to the United States at Thomas Jefferson's invitation, to find himself disliked by the devout and by the Federalists. He died on 8 June 1809 at 59 Grove Street in Greenwich Village, aged 72. The Quakers refused to bury him in their graveyard, so he was buried on his farm at New Rochelle. In 1819 William Cobbett dug up the bones to give him a reburial in England that never took place, and they were later lost. His writings gave radical societies in England and Wales in the early 1790s a boost to their confidence. A marble column raised in New Rochelle in 1839 is the oldest memorial to him.
thomas-the-apostle: The name Thomas comes from the Aramaic Tʾōmā, meaning the twin, and the Greek equivalent Didymos is also used in the New Testament. Early Syrian traditions give his full name as Judas Thomas. In the Gospel of John he speaks twice: when Lazarus has died he says, Let us also go, that we may die with him, and later he asks how the disciples can know the way. He is best known as doubting Thomas, because he doubted the resurrection of Jesus until he saw the places where the wounds still appeared fresh, and then confessed his faith with the words My Lord and my God.

The earliest tradition about his mission is that his allotted field was Parthia, a statement of Origen preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea. Churches of the Middle East and southern Asia also name Thomas as their first evangelist. According to the traditional accounts of the Saint Thomas Christians of India, he landed at Muziris on the coast of the Chera kingdom, in present-day Kerala, in 52 CE, and founded seven communities there; historians still dispute the visit. Frykenberg, a historian of religion, notes that whatever the doubtful historicity of such traditions, there can be little doubt as to their great antiquity.

The main source is the apocryphal Acts of Thomas, written about 180–230, which most Christian churches regard as apocryphal or even heretical. The two centuries between the apostle's life and the work cast doubt on its authenticity. It tells that a king was angered when Thomas converted a queen and others of his household.

According to Syrian Christian tradition, Thomas was killed with a spear at St. Thomas Mount in Chennai on 21 December 72 and buried at Mylapore. Ephrem the Syrian, whose hymns are the earliest known record of his death, states that he was killed in India and that his relics were taken to Edessa; tradition says the greater part of them was sent there in 232. In 1258 some relics were brought to Ortona in Italy.

The San Thome Church at Mylapore, said to stand at his tomb, was built in 1523 by Portuguese missionaries. The feast of Saint Thomas was entered in the Roman calendar in the 9th century on 21 December and moved to 3 July in 1969, which is also observed by Indian Christians as Indian Christians' Day. The name Thomas remains popular among the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala.
thor: Thor's name descends from the Proto-Germanic *Þun(a)raz, meaning thunder, and its forms include Old English Thunor, Old Saxon Thunar and Old High German Donar. He closely resembles other Indo-European thunder gods, among them the Celtic Taranis, the Baltic Perkūnas, the Slavic Perun and the Hindu Indra, and scholars compare Indra's slaying of Vritra with Thor's battle with the serpent Jörmungandr. For this reason he is generally accepted as ultimately derived from a Proto-Indo-European deity. Roman writers identified him with Jupiter or Hercules, and the weekday name Thursday is a calque of the Latin Iovis dies.

In Norse mythology Thor is a god associated with thunder, storms, strength, protection, fertility and farmers. He is the son of Odin and Jörð and the husband of the golden-haired Sif. He rides in a cart pulled by two goats, Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr, which he eats and brings back to life, and he wields the hammer Mjölnir, wears the belt Megingjörð and the iron gloves Járngreipr. He is foretold to kill Jörmungandr at Ragnarök and then to take only nine steps before dying of its venom.

The earliest record of the name is on the Nordendorf fibulae from Bavaria, which bear the name Þonar in Elder Futhark. A 9th-century codex from Mainz, the Old Saxon Baptismal Vow, lists Thunaer among three gods to be renounced. According to a near-contemporary account, Saint Boniface felled an oak dedicated to Jove, known as Donar's Oak, in Hesse in the 8th century.

In the 11th century Adam of Bremen wrote that a statue of Thor stood at the centre of a triple throne in the temple at Uppsala, and that sacrifices were offered to him when plague or famine threatened. Around 1000 hammer pendants have been found in the Nordic countries, England, northern Germany, the Baltic countries and Russia, and Personal names containing his name are recorded with great frequency only from the Viking Age.

Thor was still invoked in the 12th century, a century after Norway was officially Christianized, as a runic stick from Bergen shows. His name survives in place names such as Þórslundr in Denmark and in Thundersley in England. Scandinavian folklore kept words such as tordön for thunder, and a belief that lightning frightens away trolls. In the modern period he has been the subject of poems by writers including Adam Gottlob Oehlenschläger and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, and veneration of him has been revived in Heathenry.
thoth: The Egyptian name of Thoth, written ḏḥwty, may derive from ḏḥw, said to be the oldest known name for the ibis, with an ending marking him as having the ibis's attributes, so that it would mean he who is like the ibis. The Greek form Thoth is more common than the Egyptological rendering Djehuti. Thoth was a moon god. The moon allowed time to be measured at night without the sun, and its phases organised much of the rituals and events of Egyptian society, civil and religious. He therefore came to be seen as a god of wisdom, magic and the measurement and regulation of events and time, and as the secretary and counsellor of Ra.

Thoth was most often shown as a man with the head of an ibis, sometimes wearing a lunar disk on a crescent moon, or as a baboon, or as the ibis itself. Scholars suggest the curve of the ibis's beak was seen as the crescent moon. As Aani, an ape in the underworld, he reported when the scales weighing the heart of the dead against the feather of Maat were exactly even. His feminine counterpart is Seshat, and his wife is Ma'at; with Ma'at he stood beside Ra on the solar barque. He was regarded as the scribe of the gods and the inventor of writing and hieroglyphs, and Egyptian scribes worshipped him, keeping a picture of him in their offices.

In myth Plutarch credits him with the 365-day calendar. When the year had only 360 days and the goddess Nut could bear no children, Thoth gambled with the moon for one seventy-second of its light and won five days, on which Osiris, Set, Isis, Horus and Nephthys were born. In the central Osiris myth he gives Isis the words to restore her husband, and after the battle between Horus and Set he offers counsel.

His chief temple was at Hermopolis, called Khemenu in Egyptian, and in the Late Period his cult gained prominence as Khmun also became the capital. Millions of dead ibis were mummified and buried in his honour. The temple was mostly destroyed before the Christian era, and its large pronaos, standing in 1826, was demolished by the mid-19th century and used as fill for the foundation of a sugar factory. The Greeks identified him with Hermes, and his title Thrice Great, trismégistos in Greek, gave the combined figure Hermes Trismegistus.
thrace: Thrace is bounded by the Balkan Mountains to the north, the Aegean Sea to the south and the Black Sea to the east. It comprises present-day south-eastern Bulgaria, north-eastern Greece and the European part of Turkey, known as Northern, Western and Eastern Thrace. Its historical boundaries varied, and the ancient Greeks used the name for all the land north of Thessaly that the Thracians inhabited. The name comes from the Greek Thrake, which at first referred to the Thracians themselves.

The Thracians recorded no collective name for themselves, and the Greeks assigned the name. They were divided into numerous tribes, and the first Greek colonies on the coast were founded in the 8th century BCE. In the late 6th century BCE the Achaemenid Persians took control after Darius the Great's Scythian campaign and made the region the Satrapy of Skudra.

The Thracian tribes formed no lasting political organisation until the Odrysian state, of the 4th century BCE. Most of Thrace was conquered in the 4th century BCE by Philip II of Macedon and his son Alexander the Great, and after Alexander's death it passed to Lysimachus, who was defeated by Seleucus I Nicator at Corupedium in 281 BCE.

After the Third Macedonian War of 171 to 168 BCE, Thrace became a tributary to Rome. Augustus tried indirect rule through a Hellenized client kingdom under the Sapaean family, with Bizye as its first centre, until the Romans turned Thrace into a province in 46 CE. By the mid-5th century Thrace had fallen from Roman authority and for much of the next thousand years it was a battleground.

The Byzantine Empire kept it until the 7th century, when the northern half joined the First Bulgarian Empire. the Bulgarian and Byzantine Empires held it in turns through the 13th and early 14th centuries. The Ottoman Turks first made an incursion in 1352, took Gallipoli in 1354 and made Edirne their capital before taking Constantinople in 1453.

The Congress of Berlin in 1878 made Northern Thrace part of the semi-autonomous Ottoman province of Eastern Rumelia, which united with Bulgaria in 1885. After the First World War and the Greco-Turkish War, Southern Thrace was divided between Turkey in the east and Greece in the west. Thracian is now a geographical term used in Bulgaria, Turkey and Greece. Notable people from the region include the philosophers Protagoras and Democritus, both of Abdera, and Spartacus, who led the slave uprising of 73 to 71 BCE.
thracian-tomb-of-sveshtari: The Getae, a Thracian people, had been federated in the Odrysian kingdom in the fifth century BCE. Philip II of Macedon's Balkan campaigns between 352 and 340 BCE shattered Odrysian authority, and the Getae profited. By the second half of the fourth century they held sites on both banks of the lower Danube. The tomb was built in the first quarter of the third century BCE. It is probably the grave of Dromichaetes, king of the Getae around 300 BCE, and of his wife, a daughter of King Lysimachus, a general and successor of Alexander the Great.

The tomb lies 2.5 kilometres south-west of the village of Sveshtari in Razgrad Province, north-eastern Bulgaria. Its construction follows the basic principles of Thracian cult buildings, but its decoration is considered unique: polychrome caryatids, half human and half plant, and painted murals. The ten female figures carved in high relief on the walls of the central chamber, with the decoration of the lunette in its vault, are the only examples of this type found so far in the Thracian lands.

The tomb was discovered and excavated in 1982, during work on Mound No 7 of the East Mound Necropolis of Sboryanovo, a tumulus of the early Hellenistic period. Near it were found the remains of a large ancient city and dozens of Getic mound tombs, and the tomb is supposed to lie close to the Getic city of Helis. The settlement stood on a plateau among the ravines of the Krapinets River, with a stone wall up to 4 metres thick; amphora stamps and coins show it existed between about 335 and 250 BCE. The tomb is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
thracians: The exact origin of the Thracians is uncertain. It is believed that, like other Indo-European-speaking groups in Europe, they descended from a mixture of Proto-Indo-Europeans and Early European Farmers. During the 5th and 4th millennia BCE the inhabitants of the eastern Balkans formed different groups of indigenous people that the ancient Greeks later named under the single ethnonym Thracians. Their culture emerged during the early Bronze Age, which began about 3500 BCE, and the Getae and Dacians developed from it.

The first record of the name is in the Iliad, where Thracians appear as allies of the Trojans. Only four Thracian inscriptions have been found, among them a gold ring from Ezerovo in Bulgaria, whose text of eight lines in Greek script has not been deciphered.

Greek colonies were founded along the Thracian coasts from the 8th century BCE, and Thracians and Greeks lived side by side. According to Greek and Roman writers the Thracians remained largely disunited until the Odrysian kingdom was established in the early 5th century BCE by King Teres I, after the failure of the Persian invasion of Greece. Teres and his son Sitalces expanded the kingdom, which allied with Athens and joined the Peloponnesian War on its side.

The kingdom showed signs of fatigue by 400 BCE, and Cotys I brought a brief revival that lasted until his murder in 360 BCE. Around 340 BCE it lost independence to Macedon, and around 330 BCE Seuthes III revived a much smaller state with a new capital, Seuthopolis. From the mid-2nd century BCE the Thracians faced gradual conquest by the Romans. The Odrysian heartland became the client Sapaean kingdom, which was finally converted into the Roman province of Thracia.

Greeks and Romans described the Thracians as warlike and barbarian, yet favoured them as mercenaries. They were skilled horsemen and lightly armed skirmishers with javelins, and Thracian peltasts had a notable influence in ancient Greece. In 188 BCE near Cypsela they defeated the troops of the Roman consul Manlius Vulzon. Tattooing was a custom among both men and women.

Their religion was polytheistic. One cult was that of the Thracian horseman, a god of the underworld shown on funeral statues slaying a beast with a spear. Zalmoxis, worshipped by the Getae and Dacians, is the subject of debate over whether his cult was monotheistic.

Later invasions by Romans, Celts, Huns, Goths, Scythians, Sarmatians and Slavs, with hellenization, romanization and later slavicisation, remade the ethnicity, language and culture of Thrace. Writers spoke of a separate Thracian nationality until the early Middle Ages, and the last reported use of a Thracian language was by monks in the 6th century CE. Late in the 4th century Nicetas of Remesiana brought Christianity to the Bessi.
three-kingdoms-of-korea: The Three Kingdoms were founded after the fall of Wiman Joseon and gradually conquered and absorbed many small states and confederacies. After Gojoseon fell, the Han dynasty set up four commanderies in the north-west of the peninsula and in present Liaoning. Three fell quickly to the Samhan, and Goguryeo destroyed the last in 313. The three polities made the transition from walled-town states to full state-level societies between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. The main sources are the Korean histories Samguk sagi and Samguk yusa and the Eastern Barbarians section of the Book of Wei. The Book of Sui records that the customs, laws and clothes of the three kingdoms were generally identical.

Goguryeo arose on the Yalu River and was the largest of the three, holding the north of the peninsula, the Liaodong Peninsula and Manchuria. It was at its height in the 5th century under King Gwanggaeto the Great and his son King Jangsu. Paekche, founded as a member of the Mahan confederacy, controlled most of the western peninsula at its peak in the 4th century and was a maritime power that passed Chinese characters, metallurgy, ceramics, architecture and Buddhism to ancient Japan. Under pressure from Goguryeo it moved its capital south to Ungjin in the late 5th century and later to Sabi.

According to Korean records Silla, in the south-east, began in 57 BCE as a unification of the Jinhan city-states, though other evidence suggests it was the last of the three to build a centralised government. It was the smallest and weakest, but it made pacts with stronger neighbours, took the name Silla in 503 and annexed the Kaya confederacy in the first half of the 6th century. Buddhism became its official religion in 528, after Goguryeo adopted it in 372.
Silla allied with Tang China. Paekche was conquered in 660 and Goguryeo in 668. Silla then drove the Tang forces out of the peninsula and occupied the lands south of Pyongyang.

Silla's unification of the peninsula in the 7th century was the first in Korean history. It was later divided into the Later Three Kingdoms and annexed by Goryeo, a state that revived Goguryeo. The name Samhan, used since the 7th century for the three kingdoms, came to mean Korea as a whole, and the Han in the names Daehan Jeguk and Daehan Minguk refers to it. The Samguk sagi and Samguk yusa, whose titles use the name Three Kingdoms, should not be confused with the Three Kingdoms of China.
three-kingdoms-period: Han power had declined steadily after the death of Emperor He in 105 CE. Boy emperors, imperial relatives and eunuchs struggled for control, and the reigns of Emperor Huan and Emperor Ling were recorded as particularly dark periods. The Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184 began the period of chaotic infighting among warlords. In 189 the eunuchs killed the regent He Jin, Yuan Shao's troops stormed the palace and killed the Ten Attendants, and the warlord Dong Zhuo, invited to Luoyang, took control. After 192 the coalition against him fell apart, and the empire divided among regional warlords.

The majority view dates the period from 220 to 280. On 11 December 220 Emperor Xian abdicated and Cao Pi proclaimed himself emperor of Wei. Liu Bei declared himself Emperor of Han on 15 May 221, in the state known as Shu Han, and Sun Quan, who had recognised Wei, became king of Wu. Strictly, independent states existed only from Sun Quan's proclamation as emperor in 229 until the fall of Shu Han in 263. Zhuge Liang conquered the south of Shu territory up to Lake Dian in Yunnan in 224 to 225.

Wei conquered Shu in 263. In 266 Sima Yan overthrew the Wei emperor and proclaimed the Jin dynasty, and in 280 Jin forces took Jianye and Sun Hao of Wu surrendered. The period was one of the most dangerous in Chinese history, with plagues, famines and civil war. The census of 280 counted 2,459,840 households and 16,163,863 people, against 10,677,960 households and 56,486,856 people in the Han era, though it may not have been accurate. Cao Wei declared silk cloth and grain the main currencies in 221. Technology advanced, and the Wei engineer Ma Jun designed the south-pointing chariot.

The standard history is Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, compiled in the 3rd century, which Pei Songzhi expanded with annotations in 429, nearly doubling its size. All three states claimed the Mandate of Heaven, and later historians disagreed over which, chiefly Wei or Shu, was the legitimate successor to the Han. The period has been romanticised in folklore, opera, novels, film and games, and its best-known fictional treatment is Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a novel by Luo Guanzhong written under the Ming dynasty.
three-principles-of-the-people: Sun Yat-sen founded the anti-Qing Revive China Society in 1894. After a failed uprising in 1895 he went into exile, part of it in England, and later dated the conception of his principles to this period of study. Between 1903 and 1905 he toured overseas Chinese communities to compete for support with the reformists Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. In a speech in Brussels in 1905 he set out the ideas for the first time.

From 1905 to 1907 Sun and collaborators such as Wang Jingwei, Hu Hanmin and Song Jiaoren wrote on the principles in the Tongmenghui's newspaper Minbao. They answered Liang Qichao, who thought China unready for a republic, by arguing that republicanism was the best form of government and had roots in Chinese culture.

The principles are nationalism (Mínzú), democracy (Mínquán) and people's livelihood (Mínshēng). Sun gave a series of weekly lectures on them in 1924, published as The Three Principles of the People, sixteen in all: six on nationalism, six on democracy and four on livelihood. Two more on shelter and transport were planned but never given. Sun died of liver cancer on 12 March 1925.

On democracy Sun proposed a Five Power Constitution, adding to the legislative, executive and judicial branches a control branch derived from the censorate and an examination branch derived from the civil service examinations. He also distinguished the sovereignty of the people (quan) from the ability of the government (neng), which was to be entrusted to experts. Livelihood covered clothing, food, housing and mobility, and called for state enterprises beside private industry and for land equalization, in line with the thought of Henry George.

After the Kuomintang's Northern Expedition the lectures became the canonical statement of Sun's thought. From 1928 the government was organised in the five branches (the Executive, Legislative, Judicial, Control and Examination Yuan), and the principles were treated as dogma with rituals such as bowing to Sun's portrait. His Whampoa address was chosen as the party anthem in 1930 and the national anthem in 1937.

The Chinese Communist Party cooperated with the Kuomintang on this basis in the Second United Front. In On New Democracy (1940) Mao reinterpreted them as New Three Principles. Under Deng Xiaoping, Sun was praised for plans of development linked to the Four Modernizations. The principles also inspired the Vietnamese Quốc Dân Đảng and the Tibetan reformer Pandatsang Rapga, who translated them into Tibetan.
three-principles-of-the-people-song: The text was a collaboration between several Kuomintang members: Hu Hanmin, Tai Chi-tao, Liao Zhongkai and Shao Yuanchong. It was first heard on 16 June 1924, as the opening of a speech by Sun Yat-sen at the opening ceremony of the Whampoa Military Academy. After the success of the Northern Expedition, the Kuomintang chose the text as its party anthem and publicly asked for music to go with it. Cheng Maoyun won a contest of 139 participants.

On 24 March 1930 numerous party members proposed that Sun's speech serve as the words of the national anthem. At the time the anthem of the republic was the Song to the Auspicious Cloud. Because many objected to a political party's symbol representing the whole nation, the National Anthem Editing and Research Committee was set up, and it endorsed the party song. The Central Standing Committee approved the proposal on 3 June 1937, and the song became the official national anthem in the 1940s.

The lyrics are in classical literary Chinese and follow classical poetic conventions. They keep to the ancient Fu style of four-character lines, in which the last character of each line rhymes in -ong or -eng. Several words are archaic: ěr is a literary form of you, here plural, fěi is a classical word for not, and zī is an old interjection no longer used in this sense in the modern language. The words relate to how the vision and hopes of a new nation and its people can be achieved and maintained.

In this respect the anthem differs from the March of the Volunteers, the anthem of the People's Republic of China, which was written a few years later entirely in modern vernacular Chinese. The song is sometimes called San Min Chu-i, after its opening line, which refers to the Three Principles of the People, but the name is never used on formal or official occasions. An official English translation by Theodore B. Tu appears in English-language guides to the Republic of China published by the government.

The anthem became the national anthem in Taiwan on 25 October 1945, after Taiwan returned to Chinese rule following the surrender of Japan. When the government of the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan and the People's Republic was established, the song was discontinued as a national anthem on the mainland and replaced there by the March of the Volunteers. At flag-raising ceremonies it is played first, followed by the National Flag Anthem during the raising itself. For many Taiwanese the anthem carries a number of meanings, often conflicting. Some reject it outright as an anachronistic symbol of the defeated Kuomintang dictatorship.
thrissur: Thrissur is the headquarters of Thrissur district in central Kerala, 284 km north-west of the state capital, Thiruvananthapuram. The city is built around a hillock of 65 acres, Thekkinkadu Maidanam, which holds the Vadakkumnathan temple. From the hillock the land flattens into the Thrissur-Ponnani Kole Wetlands, which act as a natural drainage for the city. The name is a shortened form of the Malayalam Thirusshivaperoor, the city of the sacred Lord Shiva, after the temple's presiding deity. The English form Trichur was the official name until 1990. In ancient times it was also called Vrishabhadripuram.

Numerous prehistoric megaliths and dolmens show that the area was inhabited from at least 1000 BCE to 500 CE. It was once a point of contact for Assyrians, Greeks, Persians, Arabs, Romans, Portuguese, Dutch and English, and Christianity, Islam and Judaism are believed to have entered the subcontinent through Thrissur and its surroundings. In the 16th century the Portuguese had naval influence in much of Kerala, and in the early 17th century the Dutch took their place as the main naval power. With Dutch help the royal family of Cochin recaptured Thrissur from the Zamorin of Calicut in 1710.

Thrissur rose to importance when Maharaja Sakthan Thampuran ascended the throne of Cochin and made it his capital. He invited Syrian Christian families and Brahmins from neighbouring areas, and the city became a financial and commercial hub of South India. Hyder Ali, the Sultan of Mysore, conquered it in 1750–60 and made it a tributary of Mysore.

Sakthan Thampuran's successor, Rama Varma X, signed a treaty with the East India Company that made Cochin a British protectorate. Mahatma Gandhi visited the city in 1927 and 1934 to promote civil disobedience. R. K. Shanmukham Chetty, Diwan of Cochin from 1935 to 1941, built the Thrissur Town Hall and other civic buildings. Thrissur district was formed on 1 July 1949, with its headquarters in the city.

Thrissur is known as the cultural capital of Kerala. Its Thrissur Pooram, held at the Vadakkumnathan temple in April or May, is one of the largest temple festivals in the state, with a large gathering of people and elephants lasting thirty-six hours. The city is a centre of banking, gold jewellery and Ayurvedic drugs, and it holds the Kerala Sangeetha Nadaka Academy, Kerala Lalithakala Akademi and Kerala Sahitya Academy. The Our Lady of Dolours Basilica is the largest church in India.
thubten-gyatso: Thubten Gyatso was born in 1876 in the village of Thakpo Langdun, near Samye Monastery, to a peasant couple, Kunga Rinchen and Lobsang Dolma. In 1878 he was recognised as the reincarnation of the Dalai Lama and escorted to Lhasa, where the Panchen Lama, Tenpai Wangchuk, gave him his novice vows. He was enthroned at the Potala Palace in 1879 but assumed political power only in 1895, from the monasteries that had wielded great influence through the Regent. His tutor and debating partner, the Buryat Mongol Agvan Dorzhiev, later served as his envoy to Russia.

After the British expedition of Sir Francis Younghusband in 1904, Dorzhiev persuaded the Dalai Lama to flee to Urga in Mongolia, a journey of four months. The Treaty of Lhasa was signed by Britain and Tibet on 7 September 1904. The Dalai Lama later stayed at Kumbum Monastery and at Wutai Shan, where he received envoys including Gustaf Mannerheim, and in September 1908 he was received in Beijing by the Guangxu Emperor and Empress Dowager Cixi but refused to kowtow. When a Qing military expedition reached Tibet in 1910 he fled to India, staying in Sikkim and Darjeeling.

After the revolution of 1911 Chinese forces were expelled, and Tibet was proclaimed independent on 4 April 1912. He returned to Lhasa in January 1913 and declared independence on 13 February. He standardised the Tibetan flag, issued Tibet's first stamps and banknotes, built a medical college, set up a taxation system and a police force, and abolished capital punishment. Secular education was added and four students were sent to England. Electricity, the telephone and the first motor cars reached Tibet, and in 1931 a modern army regiment was created. Tibetan forces fought the Sino-Tibetan War of 1930 to 1933, ending in truces in 1933.

The 13th Dalai Lama died on 17 December 1933 and is remembered as the Great Thirteenth. Shortly before his death he predicted that deceptive acts might occur from without and within, and warned that if Tibet did not protect its territory, its spiritual leaders and political system could vanish. He saw at the end of his life that Tibet was about to retreat from outside influences.
thucydides: Little is known of Thucydides's life, and the most reliable information comes from his own History. He identifies himself as an Athenian, gives his father's name as Olorus and names his deme as Halimous. He fought in the war, survived the Plague of Athens, which killed Pericles and many other Athenians, and records that he owned gold mines at Scapte Hyle in Thrace, opposite the island of Thasos. A story that as a boy he heard Herodotus lecture and wept with joy is disputed and most likely comes from a later account.

Because of his influence in the Thracian region, Thucydides was sent as a general to Thasos in 424 BCE. In the winter of 424 to 423 BCE the Spartan general Brasidas attacked Amphipolis, half a day's sail to the west, and the Athenian commander there, Eucles, sent to Thucydides for help. Brasidas, aware of Thucydides's influence with the people of Amphipolis, offered moderate terms, and the city surrendered before Thucydides arrived. Its fall caused consternation in Athens and was blamed on him, although he claimed he had been unable to reach it in time. He was exiled.

Later sources on his life are less reliable. Pausanias says a law passed by Oenobius allowed him to return to Athens after the war ended in 404 BCE and that he was murdered on the way, while Plutarch preserves a tradition that he was murdered at Scapte Hyle and that his remains were brought to Athens. Many doubt the first account, and the evidence suggests he may have lived as late as 397 BCE or slightly later.

Thucydides began to write the History of the Peloponnesian War at the outbreak of the war in 431 BCE, believing it of unmatched importance, and intended it as a possession for all time. It breaks off in the middle of 411 BCE, after the Athenian defeat at Syracuse, so it does not cover the last seven years of the war. The division into eight books was probably made after his death by scholars of Alexandria. He values eyewitness testimony, consulted written documents and interviewed participants, and unlike Herodotus he does not acknowledge divine intervention in human affairs.

He admired Pericles and disliked the demagogues who followed him, such as Cleon and Hyperbolus, but his account is generally even-handed, and he does not minimise the effect of his own failure at Amphipolis. Scholars have seen in him the influence of the Sophists and of Hippocratic medical writing, and the Melian dialogue and his version of Pericles's Funeral Oration are widely studied. Historians such as Jacqueline de Romilly have stressed his concern with Athenian imperialism, and others have read him as a tragedian in the tradition of Homer.
thukela-river: The Thukela, called the Tugela for most of the 20th century, is the largest river in KwaZulu-Natal and one of the most important rivers of South Africa. It rises in the Drakensberg range at Mont-aux-Sources, the source also of the Orange and Caledon rivers, and flows through the KwaZulu-Natal midlands to the Indian Ocean. It drops 1 370 metres in its lower 480 kilometres, and its catchment covers about 29,100 square kilometres, where land use is mainly rural subsistence farming and commercial forestry.

The largest of its tributaries is the Mzinyathi, or Buffalo, River, which joins about 19 kilometres east of Tugela Ferry.
