timgad: Timgad lies in the Aurès Mountains of Algeria, about 35 km east of Batna, at roughly 1,000 metres above sea level. Its full name was Colonia Marciana Ulpia Traiana Thamugadi. Trajan named it for his mother Marcia, his eldest sister Ulpia Marciana and his father Marcus Ulpius Traianus, while Thamugadi is the Berber name of the site, the plural of Tamgut, meaning peak or summit. It has been nicknamed the Pompeii of North Africa.

Trajan founded the city as a colony in about 100 CE, intended chiefly as a Roman bastion against the Berbers of the nearby Aurès Mountains, and it was populated largely by Roman veterans and colonists. After a peaceful early existence it became a centre of Christian activity from the 3rd century and a Donatist centre in the 4th, when its bishop Optatus became spokesman for the Donatist movement.

The Vandals sacked the city in the 5th century, and Berber tribes from the Aurès destroyed it at the end of that century. In 539 the Byzantine general Solomon retook and rebuilt it during the Moorish wars. It was no longer inhabited by the 8th century. The Scottish explorer James Bruce reached the ruins on 12 December 1765, probably the first European to see them in centuries. French colonists took control of the site in 1881 and excavated it systematically until 1960.

The ruins are one of the best surviving examples of the Roman grid plan. The decumanus maximus, running east to west, and the cardo, running north to south, were lined with a Corinthian colonnade. Built to hold about 15,000 people, the city outgrew its plan and spread beyond the grid. The Arch of Trajan, a 12-metre triumphal arch of sandstone, stands at the west end of the decumanus.

A theatre of 3,500 seats is in good condition and is used for contemporary productions. Other buildings include four baths, a basilica and a Capitoline temple dedicated to Jupiter, of about the same dimensions as the Pantheon in Rome. The library, a gift of Julius Quintianus Flavius Rogatianus, probably dates from the late 3rd or the 4th century and could have held about 3,000 scrolls. UNESCO inscribed Timgad as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
timisoara: Timișoara lies on the Bega River, the southernmost tributary of the Tisza, in the south-eastern part of the Pannonian Basin. Archaeological remains show farmers, hunters and artisans living in the fertile lands between the Mureș, the Tisza and the Danube by 4000 BCE. The Bega was canalized, and a navigable canal was built along it between 1728 and 1760. The Hungarian name Temesvár was first recorded as Temeswar in 1315 and refers to a castle on the Timiș River; the Romanian and German forms derive from it.

The city is first officially mentioned in 1212 as a royal fortress, though some historians date its first documentary mention to 1266, when the heir apparent Stephen V of Hungary donated part of a fortress built by his father, Béla IV. After Tatar destruction in the 13th century it was rebuilt under Charles I of Hungary, who ordered stone walls and a royal palace in 1307 and moved the royal seat there from Buda between 1316 and 1323.

After the defeat at Mohács in 1526 the Banat was contested between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. On 22 July 1552 an army led by Kara Ahmed Pasha took the city and made it the capital of the Temeşvar Eyalet; the local commander István Losonczy and other Christians were massacred on 27 July as they tried to escape. In 1716 Prince Eugene of Savoy besieged it for 48 days, and bombardment destroyed much of the city. By the Treaty of Passarowitz (1718) the Banat of Temeswar became a possession of the Habsburg crown under military rule until 1751. From 1848 to 1860 the city was the capital of the Serbian Vojvodina.

Under Austria-Hungary the city grew quickly and its industries included breweries, an iron foundry and a match factory. On 1 November 1918 the Banat Republic was proclaimed briefly. Serbian forces held the city until 1919, and the Treaty of Trianon of 4 June 1920 ceded it to Romania, whose King Ferdinand I made it a university centre that year.

Timișoara is the capital of Timiș County and the main economic and cultural centre of western Romania, with 250,849 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Romanian is the official language; German, Hungarian and Serbian communities remain, and the city has the largest German population in Romania. It was the first city in the Habsburg monarchy with street lighting, in 1760, and the first in Europe lit by electric street lamps, in 1884. It is nicknamed Little Vienna and the City of Roses.
timor: Timor lies in the north of the Timor Sea, at the eastern end of the Lesser Sunda Islands, and its name is a variant of timur, Malay for east. Mainland Australia is less than 500 km away. The island covers 30,777 square kilometres, and its mountains reach nearly 3,000 metres. Mutis is the highest in West Timor and Ramelau the highest in Timor-Leste.

The climate has a long dry season from April to November, with hot winds blowing from Australia. Anthropologists identify eleven ethno-linguistic groups on the island, the largest being the Atoni of the west and the Tetun of the centre and east. Most indigenous languages belong to the Timor-Babar branch of the Austronesian family.

The earliest historical record of Timor is the Chinese Zhu Fan Zhi of the 13th century, which calls it Ti-wu and notes its sandalwood. The Javanese Nagarakretagama of the 14th century names it as an island within the realm of Majapahit. By then Timor was part of Javanese, Chinese and Indian trading networks, exporting sandalwood, slaves, honey and wax.

The Portuguese and the Dutch later settled there, the Dutch from Kupang in the mid-17th century, and they fought for control until a treaty of 1859 divided it, though the boundary was not formally settled until 1912. West Timor was Dutch Timor until 1949, when it joined Indonesia, and East Timor was a Portuguese colony until 1975.

In 1789 William Bligh and the seamen loyal to him reached Timor after the mutiny on the Bounty. In December 1941 Australian and Dutch forces occupied Portuguese Timor, and after the Japanese landed in February 1942 a 400-strong Dutch-Australian force and many Timorese volunteers fought a year-long guerrilla campaign. The Japanese occupation killed between 40,000 and 70,000 Timorese.

After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 the Portuguese withdrew, and in 1975 Indonesia invaded and annexed East Timor, an annexation the United Nations and Portugal never recognised. Falintil resisted in a prolonged guerrilla war until a UN-sponsored referendum in 1999 rejected autonomy within Indonesia. The UN governed the territory until it became independent as Timor-Leste in 2002.

The island is divided between Timor-Leste in the east, with its capital at Dili, and West Timor, part of the Indonesian province of East Nusa Tenggara, whose provincial capital is Kupang. Timor-Leste also holds the exclave of Oecusse within West Timor. The official languages of Timor-Leste are Tetun and Portuguese, and in West Timor Indonesian. Christianity is the dominant religion across the island.
timur: Timur was born in Transoxiana near the city of Kesh, now Shahrisabz in Uzbekistan, about 80 kilometres south of Samarkand, then part of the Chagatai Khanate. He belonged to the Barlas, a Turkicized Mongol confederation. His name, Temur, means iron in Chagatai, his mother tongue. Timurid histories trace his descent in the male line from Tumbinai Khan, an ancestor of Genghis Khan, but no written evidence from his own lifetime links him directly to Genghis Khan. By about 1360 he had become a military leader whose troops were mostly Turkic tribesmen, and he campaigned in Transoxiana with the Khan of the Chagatai Khanate.

Timur reduced the Chagatai khans to figureheads and ruled in their name. Because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, Mongol tradition denied him the title of khan, so he used the title of amir and set up a puppet khan, Suyurghatmish. His first campaigns took Khwarazm and Urgench, and in 1383 he began his conquest of Persia. When Herat did not surrender he reduced it to rubble and massacred most of its citizens.

In 1398 Timur invaded the Indian subcontinent, where the Tughlaq dynasty's Delhi Sultanate had declined and most provincial governors had asserted their independence. He crossed the Indus on 30 September 1398 with a force of 90,000 and sacked Tulamba, massacring its inhabitants. Before the battle for Delhi on 17 December 1398 he slaughtered some 100,000 captives, fearing that they might revolt. In the following years he fought the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I and the Mamluk sultan of Egypt, Nasir-ad-Din Faraj, and had Ming envoys detained. Scholars estimate that his campaigns caused the deaths of millions.

In December 1404 Timur began a winter campaign against Ming China. He fell ill beyond the Syr Daria and died at Farab on 17 or 18 February 1405. He had outlived two chosen heirs, his son Jahangir and his grandson Muhammad Sultan, and on his deathbed named Muhammad Sultan's brother Pir Muhammad. A civil war among his descendants followed, and his youngest son Shah Rukh took the throne only in 1409.

His legacy is mixed. Central Asia flourished under him, while Baghdad, Damascus, Delhi and other cities were sacked and their people massacred. He keeps a positive image in Muslim Central Asia and is vilified in Arabia, Iraq, Persia and India. Two Zafarnamas written under Timurid patronage present him favourably, while the Arabic chronicle of Ahmad ibn Arabshah is far less so.
timurid-empire: Timur belonged to the Barlas tribe, a Mongol group of the Chagatai ulus that had become Turkified in language and culture. He saw himself as the restorer of the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan. Because he could not claim descent from Genghis, he married a Genghisid princess, Saray Mulk Khanum, and took the title Gurkani, meaning son-in-law. He took Samarkand in 1366 and Balkh in 1369, and was recognised as ruler of the region in 1370. He acted officially in the name of the Chagatai khan, but in practice Timur chose the khans, who became puppet rulers.

From 1380 Timur campaigned westwards against the successor states of the Ilkhanate. He removed the Kartids from Herat, captured Isfahan in 1387, drove the Muzaffarids from Shiraz and expelled the Jalayirids from Baghdad. In 1394–1395 he defeated Tokhtamysh, khan of the Golden Horde, after a campaign in Georgia, and enforced his sovereignty in the Caucasus. The costs of his conquests included the deaths of possibly 17 million people.

Timur gave the main governorships to his sons and grandsons. After his death in 1405 the dynasty fell into disputes and civil wars, and many governors became independent. Samarkand and Herat became the centres of the Timurid Renaissance under Shahrukh Mirza (1405–1447) and his son Ulugh Beg (1447–1449), and Herat flowered again under Husayn Bayqara (1469–1506). Meanwhile the Timurid habit of partitioning the realm weakened it. The Aq Qoyunlu took most of Iran, and the Safavid Empire under Shah Ismail I soon took Persia, the Caucasus and Mesopotamia. The Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan overran the central Asian principalities and founded the Khanate of Bukhara.

Babur, a Timurid prince exiled from Fergana, set up a base at Kabul in 1504 and invaded the Delhi Sultanate in 1526. The Mughal dynasty he founded was directly inherited from the Timurids, and the last nominal Mughal rule was abolished by the British after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

The Timurid era combined Turco-Mongol origins with Persian high culture. The military was at first almost wholly Turco-Mongolian, while the administration was Persian, and Persian became the official language, with Chaghatay as the family's home language. The golden age of Persian painting began under the Timurids, with Chinese influence. Their architecture favoured large buildings, double-shelled domes and rich tile decoration, as at the Gur-i Amir Mausoleum and the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in Samarkand. Gawhar Shad was its most important patron in the 15th century. Its style passed to the Safavids, the Mughals and early Ottoman builders.
tin: Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn, from the Latin stannum, and atomic number 50. It is a soft, silvery-white, malleable metal that can be cut with little force, and a bent bar of tin makes a crackling sound known as the tin cry, caused by the twinning of its crystals. It resists corrosion from water. It does not occur as the native element but is extracted from ores, chiefly cassiterite, the only commercially important source, which is almost always associated with granite.

The word tin is shared among the Germanic languages and traces back to a reconstructed Proto-Germanic form; cognates include German Zinn, Swedish tenn and Dutch tin. The Latin name stannum or stagnum originally meant an alloy of silver and lead, and came to mean tin in the fourth century. The earlier Latin word was plumbum candidum, or white lead. The origin of stannum is unknown and may be pre-Indo-European.

Tin extraction and use can be dated to the beginnings of the Bronze Age around 3000 BCE. The earliest bronze objects had a tin or arsenic content of under 2 per cent and are believed to be the result of unintentional alloying. Adding a second metal to copper increases its hardness, lowers its melting temperature and gives a more fluid melt, which allowed the more complex shapes cast in closed moulds of the Bronze Age.

Arsenical bronze appears first in the Near East, where arsenic is commonly found with copper ore, but its health risks were quickly realised, and the quest for sources of the much less hazardous tin began early in the Bronze Age. This created a demand for rare tin and a trade network linking distant sources of tin to the markets of Bronze Age cultures. The first tin alloy used on a large scale was bronze, of one eighth tin and seven eighths copper; after 600 BCE pure metallic tin was produced. Pewter, an alloy of 85 to 90 per cent tin, has been used for flatware since the Bronze Age.
tinian: Tinian is one of the three principal islands of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. It lies about 9.3 kilometres south-west of Saipan, across the Saipan Channel, and with the uninhabited island of Aguijan forms Tinian Municipality. The island has a land area of about 100 square kilometres and is much flatter than Saipan, with limestone cliffs and caves and a highest point of 187 metres on the Kastiyu plateau. Its main village, San Jose, is on the south-west coast, and the Tinian monarch is the island's only endemic bird.

The Mariana Islands were the first islands settled by humans in Remote Oceania, around 1500 to 1400 BCE, by migrants from the Philippines. A people who built stone structures called taga lived on Tinian thousands of years ago. The Spanish formally occupied the island in 1669 with the missionary expedition of Diego Luis de San Vitores, who named it Buenavista Mariana.

The native population, estimated at 40,000 when the Spanish arrived, fell to under 1,400 through introduced diseases and conflicts over land, and the survivors were forcibly moved to Guam in 1720. Spain sold the island to the German Empire in 1899. Japan captured it in 1914 and was given formal control in 1918 under the South Seas Mandate, and settlers from Japan, Korea and Okinawa built large sugar plantations; by June 1944 about 15,700 Japanese civilians lived there.

The Japanese did not garrison Tinian until the late stages of the Second World War, when its value as a base for American B-29 bombers became clear. Allied forces took the island in the Battle of Tinian, from 24 July to 1 August 1944, in which only 313 of the 8,500-man Japanese garrison survived and many hundreds of civilians were killed or took their own lives. The Americans then built the largest airbase of the war, with a naval base for 40,000 personnel. From North Field the B-29s Enola Gay and Bockscar took off carrying the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The loading pits for the atomic bombs and the remains of the bomber base and Japanese fortifications can still be seen at North Field, where a memorial stands over the pits. After the war Tinian became part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands and has been a municipality of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands since 1978. The House of Taga, a site of latte stones quarried from limestone, is one of the most significant structures in the Marianas, although only one of its twelve large structures still stands.
tintagel: Tintagel, also called Trevena, from the Cornish Tre war Venydh, meaning village on a mountain, is a civil parish and village on the Atlantic coast of Cornwall. The origin of the name is uncertain. It may be Norman French, or Cornish, and Oliver Padel proposes din, a fort, with tagell, meaning neck or narrow place. It first appears as Tintagol in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae, written about 1136. The coastline is of old Devonian slate, and the Tintagel slate quarries, worked from the fifteenth until the early twentieth century, are largely responsible for the jagged coast to the south.

The largest Bronze Age barrow in the parish stands at Condolden, and there were probably Iron Age fortifications at Willapark and Barras Head. A Roman milestone found in the churchyard wall in 1889 refers to the Emperor Licinius. Major excavations beginning with C. A. Ralegh Radford in the 1930s showed that the headland was, in the 5th and 6th centuries, either a high-status Celtic monastery, as Radford held, or, according to later excavators, a princely fortress and trading settlement. Finds of Mediterranean oil and wine jars show that Sub-Roman Britain was not as isolated as once thought. The Ravenna Cosmography, of around 700, mentions Purocoronavis, a fort of the Cornovii, which may have stood at Tintagel or at Carn Brea.

A small cliff castle was founded at Bossiney in Norman times, probably before the Domesday Survey of 1086. In 1253 Richard, 1st Earl of Cornwall, established Bossiney and Trevena as a borough, and Tintagel was one of the seventeen ancient manors of the Duchy of Cornwall. From 1552 to 1832 the borough of Bossiney sent two members to the House of Commons.

In Geoffrey's account, Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, placed his wife Igraine in Tintagol while he was at war. Merlin disguised Uther Pendragon as Gorlois so that Uther could enter and father a child, who was Arthur. This became the standard origin story of Arthur in later chronicles and romances, and Alfred, Lord Tennyson's Idylls of the King popularised the link in the modern era. Parts of the Tristan and Iseult legend are also set there. The Artognou stone, found in 1998, is not thought by historians to refer to Arthur.

The parish had 1,725 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Tintagel Old Post Office dates from the 14th century and is a Grade I listed building owned by the National Trust. The Church of St Materiana, also Grade I, stands on the cliffs between Trevena and the castle, and its first church was probably of the 6th century. Tintagel has inspired composers, among them Arnold Bax, who wrote the symphonic poem Tintagel after a visit.
tintoretto: Jacopo Robusti was born in Venice, the son of Battista, a dyer, which gave him the nickname Tintoretto, little dyer. According to his early biographers Carlo Ridolfi and Marco Boschini, his only formal apprenticeship was in the studio of Titian, who dismissed him after a few days. Tintoretto then studied on his own, drawing from models and casts, including models of Michelangelo's figures, and often worked by night. Above his studio he placed the inscription Michelangelo's drawing and Titian's colour.

He often worked for little or nothing to win commissions. The first work to bring him notice on a large scale was the Miracle of the Slave, commissioned in 1548 for the Scuola di S. Marco, which was a success despite some detractors.

After Paolo Veronese arrived in Venice in 1551, Tintoretto offered the church of the Madonna dell'Orto two colossal canvases on a cost-only basis, the Worship of the Golden Calf and the Last Judgment, each 14.5 metres tall and painted about 1559 to 1560. In 1564 he won the commission for the Scuola Grande di San Rocco by installing a full-sized painting on the ceiling and offering it as a gift. Between 1565 and 1567, and again from 1575 to 1588, he painted its walls and ceilings, and the scuola and its church hold fifty-two paintings by him.

His quick technique, called prestezza, and his use of assistants let him produce more paintings for the Venetian state than any competitor. He also worked in the Doge's Palace, where a fire in 1577 destroyed earlier pictures. His Paradise there, 9.1 by 22.6 metres, was reputed to be the largest painting ever done on canvas. The commission passed to him after Veronese died in 1588, and his son Domenico helped to finish it.

Tintoretto's style uses bold brushwork, long strokes, extreme foreshortening and emphatic perspective, and conveys narrative through the gestures of figures rather than their faces. His Saint George, Saint Louis, and the Princess of 1553 shows the princess sitting astride the dragon with a whip. He was Venice's most prolific portrait painter, and painted two self-portraits, one about 1546 to 1547 and one about 1588.

He married Faustina de Vescovi about 1560, and had a daughter, Marietta Robusti, before the marriage. She trained with him as a painter and died in 1590 at thirty. Tintoretto died on 31 May 1594 and was buried in the Madonna dell'Orto beside Marietta. El Greco is thought to have studied his work, which was influential on his painting style.
tipu-sultan: Tipu Sultan was born on 1 December 1751 in Devanahalli, about 33 kilometres north of Bangalore, and was named after the saint Tipu Mastan Aulia of Arcot. His father, Hyder Ali, was illiterate and took care to give his eldest son a religious education and an early exposure to military and political affairs. French officers in his father's employment instructed him in military tactics. At 15 he accompanied his father against the British in the First Anglo-Mysore War in 1766, and at 16 he commanded a corps of cavalry in the invasion of the Carnatic.

In September 1780, during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, Hyder Ali sent him with 10,000 men and 18 guns to intercept Colonel William Baillie. At the Battle of Pollilur Tipu defeated Baillie. Of 360 Europeans about 200 were captured alive, and the sepoys, about 3,800 men, suffered very high casualties.

He became ruler of Mysore on his father's death from cancer in 1782, during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, and on 29 December 1782 he crowned himself Badshah with the title Nawab Tipu Sultan Bahadur. The Treaty of Mangalore of 1784 ended the war with the position as it had stood before. He also fought the Marathas, and he began a navy in 1786. He introduced a new calendar, new coinage and seven new government departments, and he expanded the use of iron-cased rockets.

In December 1789 he attacked the lines of Travancore, an ally of the East India Company, after a dispute over two Dutch-held fortresses in Cochin. Lord Cornwallis then mobilised Company forces and formed alliances with the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad. In the Third Anglo-Mysore War Tipu was forced into the Treaty of Seringapatam and lost a number of territories, including Malabar and Mangalore. A report that he founded a Jacobin Club in 1794 is doubted: the historian Jean Boutier argued in 2005 that the Company fabricated it to justify intervention.

In 1799, in the Fourth Mysore War, three armies marched into Mysore and besieged the capital, Srirangapatna. More than 60,000 Company soldiers faced about 30,000 men of Tipu's forces. He was killed on 4 May 1799 defending Seringapatam, and General Harris is said to have exclaimed 'Now India is ours.'

Tipu endowed about 156 Hindu temples, including the Ranganathaswami Temple at Srirangapatna, and appointed Hindu officers. His coinage and administrative reforms, and the silk industry that grew under his land revenue system, outlasted him. Assessments of him have often been divided. Two of his rockets, captured at Srirangapatna, were displayed in the Royal Artillery Museum in London.
tirana: Tirana lies on the Plain of Tirana in the centre of Albania, between Mount Dajti to the east, hills to the south and a valley to the north that overlooks the Adriatic Sea. Its average altitude is about 110 metres. The Tiranë and Lanë rivers flow through the city. Dajti National Park lies on the mountain above it, with forests of pine, oak and beech, and the city's mountains are a popular retreat in winter, when snow often covers them although the city itself rarely receives it.

The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with the earliest recognised reference at the Cave of Pëllumbas, of the Palaeolithic period. Illyrians were its first population and most likely formed the core of the Illyrian kingdom of the Taulantii. After the Illyrian Wars the Romans integrated the area into their empire. The oldest surviving find from that period is a Roman house of the 3rd century, later turned into a church with a mosaic floor. A castle, possibly known as Tirkan, was built by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I and was restored by Ahmed Pasha Toptani in the 18th century.

Tirana appears in Venetian documents of the 1350s and in 1418. The first Ottoman land registrations of 1431–32 record 60 inhabited areas with nearly 2,028 houses and 7,300 inhabitants. In 1510 Marin Barleti, in his biography of Skanderbeg, called it a small village, distinguishing Little Tirana from Great Tirana. The town was founded in 1614 by the Ottoman Albanian nobleman Sylejman Pasha Bargjini, who built the Old Mosque, a small commercial centre and a hammam. Some sources describe a bazaar with watermills already existing before 1614. In the 16th century craftsmen made silk and cotton fabrics, leather, ceramics and metal artefacts. The Et'hem Bey Mosque was completed in 1821.

The city was fairly unimportant until the 20th century, when the Congress of Lushnjë proclaimed it the capital of Albania following the Albanian Declaration of Independence of 1912. Its present appearance was shaped by two totalitarian regimes: Mussolini's, whose architects Florestano Di Fausto and Armando Brasini designed the ministry buildings, and Enver Hoxha's afterwards. The population tenfolded between 1820 and 1955, and it grew faster after the fall of communism.

Tirana is the capital and largest city of Albania and seat of its government, parliament and highest courts. The centre from the University of Tirana's Mother Teresa Square to Skanderbeg Square was declared a protected cultural area in 2000. The 2023 census counted 598,176 residents in the municipality. The airport is named after Mother Teresa.
tirich-mir: Tirich Mir, also spelled Terich Mir, rises to 7,708 metres in the Chitral District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It overlooks the town of Chitral and can be seen from the main bazaar. The usual approach is up the Tirich valley, which has the Tirich Glacier at its head. The glacier is encircled by three of the 7,000-metre peaks of the Hindu Kush: Tirich Mir, Noshaq and Istor-o-Nal. Their meltwaters flow down the valley to join the Torkhow River and form a major tributary of the Chitral River. The highest permanent settlement is Shagrom, with summer pastures and shepherd huts above it.

The mountain consists mainly of the mid-Cretaceous granitic Tirich Mir pluton, cut by many dykes. The name combines terich, the valley, with mir, which means mountain in the Khowar language. The linguist Georg Morgenstierne derived it from two Sanskrit words, and several scholars have identified Tirich Mir with the sacred Mount Meru of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain literature.

The first recorded ascent was made on 21 July 1950 by an expedition of Arne Næss, Per Kvernberg, Henry Berg and Tony Streather. They approached from the South Barum glacier and climbed the south ridge. A 1952 documentary film, Tirich Mir til topps, depicts the expedition. In 1967 a Czechoslovak expedition established a route by the Upper Tirich Glacier and the northwest ridge, which is now regarded as the normal route.

Local peoples tell different stories about the mountain. According to the polytheist Kalash, who live nearby, it is the domain of the goddess Krumai, who appears as a wild goat and is associated with childbirth. In one legend she disturbed the other gods and was chased by Imra, who threw her into a fast river. She leapt up the river and ran up the cliff, shaping it with her hooves, then revealed her true form and prepared a feast for the gods, who accepted her into their company. The Muslim Chitrali people believe the mountain is the home and fortress of fairies known as Bohtan Doyak, the stone throwers, and hold that anyone who climbs it will die.
tiruchirappalli: Tiruchirappalli lies almost at the geographic centre of Tamil Nadu, 322 kilometres south of Chennai. About 16 kilometres west of the city the Kaveri divides into two streams, the Kaveri and the Kollidam, and the Cauvery Delta begins; the island of Srirangam between them now belongs to the city. The ground is nearly flat, with an average elevation of 81 metres, and a few isolated hillocks rise above it. The highest is the Rockfort, whose rock is estimated to be 3,800 million years old.

Tiruchirappalli is one of the oldest inhabited cities in Tamil Nadu, with settlements dating to the Sangam period. Uraiyur, which is now a neighbourhood, was the capital of the Early Cholas for 600 years from the 3rd century BCE, and Ptolemy called it Orthoura. The Kallanai dam, about 18 kilometres from Uraiyur, was built across the Kaveri by Karikala Chola in the 2nd century CE.

In the 6th century the Pallava king Mahendravarman I had the rock-cut cave temples of the Rockfort made. After the Pallavas fell in the 8th century the Medieval Cholas held the city until the 13th century. The Carnatic kingdom was annexed by the British in July 1801, after the discovery of collusion between Tipu Sultan and the son of the Nawab during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

Trichinopoly joined the Madras Presidency and became the capital of its own district. The 1871 census counted 76,530 people, making it the second largest city of the presidency after Madras. It was known across the British Empire for the Trichinopoly cigar, of which more than 12 million were made and exported each year at the peak, and the South Indian Railway Company had its first headquarters there in 1874. In 1930 the city was the base for the Vedaranyam salt march begun by C. Rajagopalachari.

The city is predominantly Hindu, with a large Muslim minority and a considerable Christian population. Its best-known monuments are the Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam, dedicated to the reclining form of Vishnu, and the Jambukeswarar Temple at Thiruvanaikaval, dedicated to Shiva. Both are built in the Dravidian style and are often counted among its best examples.

The Archaeological Survey of India lists the rock-cut cave temples of the Rockfort, with the gateway and the Erumbeeswarar Temple, as monuments of national importance. Tiruchirappalli has been an educational centre since British rule: St. Joseph's College moved there from Nagapattinam in 1883, and the commissioning of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited in the 1960s began its growth as an engineering centre.
tiryns: Tiryns lies in the Argolis in the Peloponnese, 20 km south of Mycenae, on a hill about 300 metres long and no more than 18 metres high. The area has been inhabited since prehistory, and a small Neolithic settlement thrived there. In the middle of the 3rd millennium BCE it was a flourishing early settlement. From this period survives a circular structure 28 metres across, built of two concentric stone walls, which seems to have been a refuge for the inhabitants in war or a residence of a king. The first Greek inhabitants settled there at the start of the Middle Helladic period, from 2000 to 1600 BCE.

The city grew most in the Late Helladic, the Mycenaean period. The acropolis was built in three phases: at the end of Late Helladic II, then in Late Helladic III, and at the end of Late Helladic III B, in 1300 to 1200 BCE, to which the surviving ruins belong. Around 1300 BCE the citadel and lower town held about 10,000 people. The palace was destroyed around 1200 BCE, yet the population kept growing and reached about 15,000 by 1150 BCE. Around 1180 BCE a hoard of gold and silver objects was placed in a cauldron in the lower town. The palace area stayed inhabited until the middle of the 8th century BCE, and a temple was later built among its ruins.

In the Classical period Tiryns, like Mycenae, became insignificant. According to Herodotus, it sent 400 hoplites to the Battle of Plataea in 480 BCE. In 468 BCE Argos destroyed both Mycenae and Tiryns. Pausanias says the residents were moved to Argos, but Strabo says many Tirynthians went to found Halieis. Greek tradition held that the Cyclopes built the walls for Proetus, who fled to Lycia and returned with Lycian help. Heinrich Schliemann tested the site in 1876 and returned in 1884, and after him Wilhelm Dörpfeld, a director of the German Archaeological Institute, studied the ruins properly.

The walls, usually 6 metres thick and up to 17 metres where the tunnels pass through, survive to a height of up to 7 metres; the original height is estimated at 9 to 10 metres. A transverse wall divides the acropolis, with the palace in the southern part. The palace's megaron has a throne place against the wall and a central hearth ringed by four wooden columns. Tiryns and Mycenae were designated a World Heritage Site in 1999.
tisha-bav: Tisha B'Av, Hebrew for the Ninth of Av, is an annual fast day in Rabbinic Judaism. It falls in July or August in the Gregorian calendar and ends the Three Weeks, a period of communal sorrow that begins on the Seventeenth of Tammuz. It is regarded as the saddest day in the Jewish calendar.

According to the Mishnah, Taanit 4:6, five events on the ninth of Av warrant fasting: the return of the Twelve Spies sent by Moses, whose discouraging report left the Israelites in despair; the destruction of the First Temple built by King Solomon; the destruction of the Second Temple by the Romans in 70 CE; the crushing of the Bar Kokhba revolt and the fall of Betar in 135 CE; and the ploughing of the Temple site by the Roman commander Quintus Tineius Rufus.

The fast lasts just over 25 hours, from sunset on the preceding evening until nightfall. Five prohibitions apply: no eating or drinking, no washing or bathing, no creams or oils, no leather shoes, and no marital relations. They are waived for health reasons on a rabbi's ruling. Torah study is forbidden, as an enjoyable activity, except for distressing texts such as Lamentations, Job and parts of Jeremiah.

The Book of Lamentations is read in synagogue in the evening, and much of the morning is spent reciting kinnot, liturgical dirges composed by poets such as Eleazar beRabbi Qallir and Judah Halevi. Over time the day came to recall later calamities as well: the Rhineland massacres of the First Crusade in 1096, the expulsion of the Jews from England on 18 July 1290, from France in 1306 and from Spanish-ruled territories under the Alhambra Decree in 1492, and the Holocaust.

After the Bar Kokhba revolt the Romans barred Jews from Jerusalem, which was rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina. The Bordeaux Pilgrim, in a travelogue of 333, and Jerome, in the late 4th century, both describe Jews coming to lament on the Temple Mount once a year. The ban ended in 637 with the early Muslim conquest. Mourning customs grew stricter after late antiquity, especially from the 15th to the 18th centuries.

Observance differs among modern movements. Conservative Judaism keeps it as a traditional fast, while Classical Reform discouraged it. In Israel restaurants and places of entertainment are closed by law on the eve of the fast and the following day. Iranian Jews call it Noi.
tisza: The Tisza begins near Rakhiv in Ukraine, at the meeting of the White Tisza, which springs in the Chornohora mountains, and the Black Tisza, from the Gorgany range. It flows west, roughly following Ukraine's borders with Romania and Hungary, briefly forms the border between Slovakia and Hungary, then enters Hungary at Tiszabecs and crosses it from north to south. A few kilometres south of Szeged it enters Serbia and joins the Danube near the village of Stari Slankamen in Vojvodina.

The river has a length of 966 kilometres and drains about 156,087 square kilometres, contributing about 13 percent of the Danube's runoff. It is the Danube's tributary with the largest catchment area, shared by Ukraine, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and Serbia, of which Romania holds 46 percent and Hungary 29 percent. In antiquity it was known as the Tisia, and another ancient name was Pathissus. Attila the Hun is said to have been buried under a diverted section of it.

The length of the Tisza in Hungary used to be 1,419 kilometres. It crossed the Great Hungarian Plain, one of the largest flat areas in central Europe, in many curves and turns, which led to large floods. After several small-scale attempts, István Széchenyi organised the regulation of the Tisza, which began on 27 August 1846 and was substantially finished in 1880. The river's length in Hungary fell to 966 kilometres, with 589 kilometres of dead channels and 136 kilometres of new riverbed.

Until the Treaty of Trianon in 1920 the Tisza was commonly called the most Hungarian river, because unlike the Danube it flowed entirely within the borders of historical Hungary. In early 2000 a series of pollution incidents from mining in Romania released sludge containing cyanide and heavy metals into the river, killing 2,000 tons of fish; examination of the sediments shows that mine pollution had occurred for over a century.

The Tisza is navigable over much of its course. It was opened to international navigation only after Hungary joined the European Union, having previously distinguished national rivers, closed to foreign vessels, from international ones. In the 1970s the Tisza Dam at Kisköre was begun to control floods and store water, and the resulting Lake Tisza became one of the most popular tourist destinations in Hungary. The bird reserve at Tiszafüred shelters over 200 species, and the yearly flowering of the Tisza, when swarms of mayflies appear, is considered a local natural wonder. The river holds a special place in Hungarian folk songs and poems, which describe it as wild and winding.
tithe: Tithing was a widespread practice in the ancient Near East, though none of the surviving extrabiblical laws deal with it and the evidence is scant. Mesopotamian texts record a ten percent tax levied on garments by the local ruler, tithes owed to gods such as Shamash and Ninurta, and officials in charge of the tithe. According to Diodorus Siculus, the Carthaginians, originally Tyrian colonists, customarily sent a tenth of all public revenue to Melqart.

The Torah commands several agricultural tithes, though not all had the proportion of one tenth. The first tithe, a tenth of the crop, went to the Levites, who owned no territorial inheritance and lived by it. Genesis tells that Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of what he had taken in battle, and Jacob promised God a tenth of his possessions.

Many Christian churches practised tithing. It was taught by the Council of Tours in 567, and the Third Council of Mâcon in 585 prescribed excommunication for those who did not pay. In England the right to receive tithes was granted to the churches by King Ethelwulf in 855, and the Saladin tithe of 1188 was a royal tax assessed by ecclesiastical boundaries. The Statute of Westminster of 1285 affirmed the legal validity of the tithe system. William Blackstone divided tithes into predial, from the land, mixed, from stock such as wool and milk, and personal, from trades and fisheries.

The Dissolution of the Monasteries transferred many rights to tithe to secular landowners and the Crown. In the 17th century dissenting groups, among them the Quakers, objected to paying tithes to the Church of England as forced payments for the maintenance of a professional ministry. Adam Smith criticised the system in The Wealth of Nations in 1776.

A tithe is a tenth part of something, paid to a religious organisation or as a compulsory tax; historically it was paid in kind, as farm produce, while modern tithes are normally voluntary and paid in money. Many Christian denominations still teach tithing. In Judaism the agricultural tithes apply only within the Land of Israel, and outside it a customary practice of giving about a tenth of income to charity has developed. Zakat, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, is a share of assets given to the poor, and in Sikhism daswandh is a tenth of income donated in the name of God.
titian: Titian, in Italian Tiziano Vecellio, was born in Pieve di Cadore, near Belluno, in territory ruled by Venice. His birth date is uncertain. In old age he claimed in a letter to Philip II of Spain to have been born in 1474, but most modern scholars think this very unlikely and place his birth between 1488 and 1490.

Giorgione died in 1510 and Giovanni Bellini in 1516, while Sebastiano del Piombo had gone to Rome, which left Titian without a rival in Venice. In 1516 he completed the Assumption of the Virgin for the high altar of the Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari, where it still stands. It is his largest single panel, and its composition joins the apostles on earth, the Madonna rising and God the Father in heaven into one whole. Bacchus and Ariadne, painted in 1520 to 1523, belonged to a series for the Camerino d'Alabastro in the Ducal Palace at Ferrara, commissioned by Alfonso I d'Este from Bellini, Titian and Dosso Dossi.

After meeting Charles V at the imperial court at Augsburg, Titian built a relationship of mutual trust with the emperor. Commissions from Charles and then from his son Philip II dominated his output from the 1550s. The portrait model he developed for the Habsburgs became a standard for princes, nobles and churchmen, and he reorganised his workshop to meet the demand, producing variants and replicas with the help of assistants whose work he retouched. From the mid-1540s most of his work was done for patrons outside Venice, and he lost influence in the city during his long absences.

Titian painted with open, visible brushwork, a technique that was revolutionary and gave his figures an unprecedented sensuous effect. He revised his compositions repeatedly, treated underdrawings as suggestions, and sometimes returned to a background decades after first laying it in. He never engraved, but designed woodcuts in 1515 to 1520, among them a large Drowning of Pharaoh's Army in the Red Sea in twelve blocks, and later supplied drawings to the engraver Cornelis Cort.

Titian died on 27 August 1576 while plague raged in Venice. He was buried beneath the Frari's Altar of the Crucifix, without the Pietà he had designed for his tomb, which the friars had returned to him. His son and heir Orazio died of plague soon afterwards, leaving no will, which complicated the settlement of the estate.
titus: Titus was born in Rome in the year 39, probably on 30 December, the eldest son of Vespasian and Domitilla the Elder. His brother Domitian was born in 51. The Flavian family had risen from obscurity to prominence in four generations under the Julio-Claudian emperors. Suetonius records that Titus was brought up at the imperial court with Britannicus, the son of Emperor Claudius. He served as a military tribune in Germania from about 57 to 59, and also in Britannia, and returned to Rome about 63 to practise law and become a quaestor.

When the Jews of Judaea revolted in 66, Nero sent Vespasian to put down the rebellion, and Titus joined him at Ptolemais with the Fifteenth Legion. By 68 the coast and north of Judaea had been subdued, with victories at Taricheae and Gamala, where Titus distinguished himself. The campaign stopped when news came of Nero's death, and after Vespasian was declared emperor in 69, Titus was left to end the rebellion.

In 70 he besieged and captured Jerusalem, destroying the city and the Second Temple. He returned to Rome in 71 and rode in a triumph with Vespasian and Domitian, in which treasures taken from the Temple were paraded, and the Arch of Titus at the Forum commemorates the victory. The historian Josephus, who wrote the main account of the war, joined his entourage and took the name Flavius, and the neutrality of his work has been questioned.

Titus succeeded Vespasian on his death in the summer of 79, the first Roman emperor to follow his own father. He ended the treason trials that had long troubled the principate. A few months into his reign Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii and Herculaneum. He appointed two ex-consuls to organise relief and gave large sums from the imperial treasury.

A fire in Rome in 80 burned for three days and three nights and destroyed many public buildings, and he again paid for repairs. The Colosseum, begun in 70 under Vespasian, was completed in 80, and its inaugural games lasted a hundred days. Titus died of a fever on 13 September 81 after about two years in office, and Domitian succeeded him and deified him. Suetonius and Cassius Dio say he died naturally, though Philostratus reports a poisoning. Ancient historians judged him a good emperor.
tiye: Tiye's father, Yuya, was a non-royal, wealthy landowner from the Upper Egyptian town of Akhmim, where he served as a priest and as superintendent of oxen or commander of the chariotry. Her mother, Thuya, held many titles in religious cults. Some Egyptologists have suggested that Yuya was of foreign origin, but a growing number of more recent scholars argue that Tiye and her parents were of indigenous Egyptian origin, since Yuya's name shows no phonological features characteristic of a foreign language. Her brother Anen was Second Prophet of Amun.

Tiye was married to Amenhotep III by the second year of his reign. Commemorative scarabs announced her as Great Royal Wife and gave the names of her parents. Because the king was crowned as a child, scholars have proposed that a regency council formed around him, with Tiye's parents among its members. The couple had six confirmed children, among them Thutmose, crown prince and High Priest of Ptah, and Amenhotep IV, who succeeded his father.

Amenhotep III devoted several shrines to her and built a temple for her at Sedeinga in Nubia, where she was worshipped as a form of Hathor-Tefnut. The American Egyptologists David O'Connor and Eric Cline note that no earlier queen figured so prominently in her husband's lifetime: she appears beside him in statuary, tomb and temple reliefs and stelae, and her name is paired with his on small objects and commemorative scarabs. She was even shown as a sphinx, an image formerly reserved for the king.

Tiye became her husband's trusted adviser and was known for her intelligence and strong personality. Foreign kings such as Tushratta of Mitanni were willing to deal with her directly, and she is regarded as the first Egyptian queen to have her name recorded on official acts. In Amarna letter EA 26, Tushratta wrote to her to recall his good relations with her late husband and to ask for friendship with her son. She had a house at Akhetaten, her son's new capital.

In an inscription dated to the twelfth year of Akhenaten's reign, about 1338 BCE, Tiye is mentioned for the last time, and she is thought to have died soon afterwards. She was probably first buried at Amarna and later moved to the Valley of the Kings.

In 1898 Victor Loret found three mummies in a side chamber of the tomb of Amenhotep II, KV35. The older woman was called the Elder Lady, and several researchers argued that she was Tiye. In 2010, DNA analysis confirmed the identification.
tlaloc: Tlaloc was the god of rain in Aztec religion, and also a deity of the fertility of the earth and of water, worshipped as a giver of life and sustenance. He was feared for his power over hail, thunder, lightning and rain, though not as a malicious figure.

Worship of a storm god tied to mountaintop shrines and life-giving rain is at least as old as Teotihuacan, where an underground shrine of Tlaloc has been found, and archaeological evidence shows he was worshipped in Mesoamerica at least 800 years before the Aztecs. Goggle-eyed rain gods of other peoples, such as the Maya Chaac and the Zapotec Cocijo, are often called Tlaloc generally. His name is thought to derive from the Nahuatl word tlalli, earth.

Representations of Tlaloc are marked by fangs and ringed eyes, with lips shaped like a moustache, and he often carries a vessel of water. In Aztec cosmology four Tlalocs mark the corners of the universe, holding up the sky, and he was lord of the third sun, which was destroyed by fire.

In the Codex Borgia the Five Tlaloque water maize fields with different rains, only one of them beneficial. He ruled Tlalocan, a paradise of unending springtime and green plants, where went those who died by lightning, drowning or water-borne diseases; they were buried with seeds planted in their faces. His sister or older relative was sometimes Chalchiuhtlicue, goddess of ground water.

In Tenochtitlan one of the two shrines on top of the Great Temple, the northern one, was dedicated to Tlaloc, beside that of Huitzilopochtli. The most important site of his worship was the peak of Cerro Tlaloc, a mountain of 4,100 metres on the eastern rim of the Valley of Mexico, where the Aztec ruler came each year and pilgrims left offerings of precious stones and figures.

During the festival of Atlcahualo, from 12 February to 3 March, children were taken to mountaintops such as Cerro Tlaloc and sacrificed; their tears were taken as a sign of coming rain. The Book of Gods and Rites reports a child sacrificed in another pilgrimage, though this may be colonial sensationalism.

The colossal statue found at Coatlinchan, weighing 168 tons and long thought to be Tlaloc, was moved to the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City in 1964, although one scholar thinks it may represent a female deity. Stones depicting Tlaloc were set inside the church of Santiago Tlatelolco in the 16th century.
tlemcen: The area around Tlemcen was inhabited in the Neolithic period. It became a military outpost of Rome in the 2nd century CE under the name Pomaria and was the centre of a diocese, whose bishop Victor represented it at the Council of Carthage in 411. A large Christian population remained for many centuries after the Arab conquest in 708. In the later 8th and the 9th century it was a kingdom of Banu Ifran with a Sufri Kharijite orientation, and these Berber Kharijis developed Saharan oases and linked them into trans-Saharan caravan routes ending at Tlemcen. Idris I founded a congregational mosque at the settlement of Agadir around 790.

In 1081 or 1082 the Almoravid leader Yusuf ibn Tashfin founded Tagrart just west of Agadir, with its congregational mosque, the Great Mosque of Tlemcen. The two settlements fused over time into Tlemcen. The Almohad ruler 'Abd al-Mu'min surrounded the city with a wall in 1145, and under the Almohads it rose to prominence as a major trading and administrative centre.

After the end of Almohad rule in the 1230s, Tlemcen became the capital of one of the three successor states, the Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen. Yaghmurasen Ibn Zyan merged Agadir and Tagrart into one city and gave it its name. He moved the seat of power from the Qasr al-Qadim to a new citadel, the Mechouar. Tlemcen was among the most important economic and cultural centres of the region, alongside Fez, Tunis and Granada. It connected the coastal route across the Maghreb with the trans-Saharan caravans, and it housed a funduk, a European trading centre, so that African gold entered European hands.

In the first half of the 14th century it had perhaps 40,000 inhabitants and several well-known madrasas, among them the Tashfiniya Madrasa founded by Abu Tashfin I. The Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan Ali and his son Abu 'Inan twice ruled the city but could not hold the region against local resistance. Zayyanid Tlemcen was intermittently a vassal of Ifriqiya, the Marinid dynasty or Aragon. The Spanish took Oran in 1509 and a campaign against Tlemcen in 1543 ended in the capture of the city. In 1551 it came under Ottoman rule.

Tlemcen is the second-largest city in north-western Algeria after Oran and the capital of Tlemcen Province. Its mix of Arab, Berber, Andalusi, Ottoman and Western influences has earned it the title of capital of Andalusian art in Algeria, and it is also called the Pearl of the Maghreb. The Great Mosque is said to be the finest remaining example of Almoravid architecture. The tomb of Sidi Boumédiène adjoins a mosque. Its textiles and handcrafts and its cool climate in the mountains have made it a centre of tourism.
toamasina: Toamasina is the capital of the Atsinanana region, on the east coast of Madagascar on the Indian Ocean, 215 kilometres northeast of Antananarivo. Its name means like salt or salty. In French it is called Tamatave, and in the past it was also known as Port aux prunes. Its importance comes from a coral reef that forms a spacious harbour, entered by two openings. The city centre is built on a sandy peninsula that projects at right angles from the general coastline, and the mouth of the Ivondro River lies to the south. The climate is a trade-wind tropical rainforest one, with no true dry season. September to November is the driest period and February to April the wettest.

Under French rule Toamasina was the seat of several foreign consuls and of many French officials, and it was the chief port for the capital and the interior. Imports were mainly piece-goods, flour-based foods and iron and steel goods, and the main exports were gold dust, raffia, hides, natural rubber and live animals. Steamers of the Messageries Maritimes and the Havraise companies kept up communication with Europe, and the British Union-Castle Line linked the port with Mauritius and, from there, Sri Lanka.

In the colonial period the soil and a formerly crowded population left the town often plagued by epidemics. Plague broke out in 1898 and again in 1900. The draining of the neighbouring marshes brought some improvement, though malaria and other diseases have continued. The botanist and explorer André Michaux died in Tamatave in 1802.

Toamasina is the chief seaport of Madagascar and the country's main gateway to the Indian Ocean and the world. The railway line to the capital ends here, and National Road 2 runs west to Antananarivo. The town is also the northern end of the Canal des Pangalanes. The University of Toamasina was founded in 1977. Its places of worship are mostly Christian churches, with the Roman Catholic cathedral of St Joseph, and there are also mosques.
tobago: Tobago lies 35 kilometres northeast of Trinidad and about 160 kilometres off the northeastern coast of Venezuela. It has a land area of 300 square kilometres, about 40 kilometres long and 10 wide. The island is hilly and of volcanic origin, with a mountainous spine called the Main Ridge, while the southwest is flat and largely coralline limestone. The Tobago Forest Reserve on the Main Ridge was designated a protected Crown reserve on 17 April 1776 and is the oldest protected rain forest in the Western hemisphere. Christopher Columbus named the island Belaforme, 'because from a distance it seemed beautiful'.

Tobago was settled by people of the Ortoiroid tradition between 3500 and 1000 BCE, followed by Saladoid people in the first century CE, who brought pottery and agriculture. The island linked the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles with their Kalina allies in the Guianas and Venezuela. Columbus sighted it on 14 August 1498 but did not land. A royal order of 1511 authorised the Spanish of Hispaniola to raid it for slaves, and the raids, continuing until at least the 1620s, decimated its population.

The Dutch founded the first European settlement, Nieuw Walcheren, in 1628 at Great Courland Bay. It was abandoned in 1630 after Indigenous attacks, re-established in 1633 and destroyed by the Spanish in Trinidad. English attempts in the 1630s and 1640s also failed. The Curonians, Dutch, English, French, Spanish and Swedish all tried to colonise the island, which changed hands 33 times, the most in Caribbean history, before the Treaty of Paris ceded it to the British in 1814. From about 1672 plantations of sugar, cotton and indigo grew up, worked by enslaved Africans, and France gave up the island to Britain in 1763. The French retook it in 1781.

After 1814 sugar production flourished again, but a hurricane in 1847, the end of slavery in 1834 and European competition ended the sugar trade. Tobago became a ward of Trinidad in 1889, and Hurricane Flora in 1963 devastated the plantations, turning the economy toward tourism.

Trinidad and Tobago became independent in August 1962 and a republic on 31 August 1976. Tobago is a ward of the republic, governed locally by the Tobago House of Assembly, revived in 1980 after local government ended in 1889. Its capital is Scarborough, and the population was 60,874 at the 2011 census, mostly of African descent. The island has coral reefs, including Buccoo Reef, and nesting beaches for the leatherback turtle.
tobolsk: Tobolsk stands in Tyumen Oblast where the Tobol meets the Irtysh, at the point where the Irtysh turns from flowing westward to flowing northward. The town was founded on the site of the Siberian Tatar town of Sibir-Tura, near the ruins of Qashliq, the capital of the Khanate of Sibir. Yermak Timofeyevich's Cossacks took Qashliq on 26 October 1582, and Kuchum, the khan, retreated. Kuchum regrouped and killed Yermak in a surprise attack on 6 August 1584, and Qashliq passed between Tatar and Cossack hands before it was abandoned in 1588.

Cossacks under Daniil Chulkov founded Tobolsk in 1587, the second Russian town in Siberia after Tyumen. It became the centre of the conquest of Siberia: Beryozovo and Mangazeya were built to bring the Nenets under tribute, and Surgut and Tara to protect Tobolsk. The Cossacks finally defeated Kuchum at the Battle of Urmin in 1598, ending the Khanate of Sibir. Tobolsk grew quickly on the Siberian river routes and prospered on trade with China to the east and Bukhara to the south.

In 1708 it became the capital of the new Siberia Governorate, and the first school, theatre and newspaper in Siberia were founded there. After the Battle of Poltava in 1709, many Swedish prisoners of war were sent to the town, where they numbered about a quarter of the population. Its political importance fell as the governorate was divided, and in the 1890s the Trans-Siberian Railway passed to the south. After the Decembrist Revolt of 1825 some exiled Decembrists settled there. In August 1917 the Provisional Government sent the family of Nicholas II to the former Governor-General's house, and in spring 1918 the Bolsheviks moved them to Yekaterinburg. In 1920 Tobolsk Governorate was abolished, ending 218 years as a provincial capital.

Tobolsk is the only town in Siberia with a standing stone kremlin, a city-fortress of the turn of the 17th and 18th centuries. Its monuments include the Cathedral of St. Sophia, built 1683 to 1686, and the Swedish Chamber of 1713 to 1716. Tobolsk is the seat of the first Orthodox diocese in Siberia. The town had 100,352 inhabitants at the 2021 census, and its economy rests on an oil refinery and the petrochemical industry.
tobruk: Tobruk lies on Libya's eastern Mediterranean coast, near the border with Egypt, and has a strong, naturally protected deep harbour, probably the best natural port in northern Africa. Escarpments run south of the town, as across Cyrenaica, and form a substantial barrier between the north and south of Libya in this area. The city is surrounded by desert lightly populated by nomadic herdsmen who travel from oasis to oasis.

An ancient Greek agricultural colony, Antipyrgus, stood on the site, its name roughly meaning across from Pyrgos, a place in Crete. In the Roman era the town became a fortress guarding the Cyrenaican frontier. With the spread of Christianity it became an episcopal see; only one ancient bishop is known by name, Aemilianus, who took part in the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. Later the site became a way station on the caravan route along the coast, and by 1911 it was an Italian military post.

Tobruk's strategic value in the Second World War rested on its harbour, which could never be wholly rendered useless by bombing, its Italian fortifications, its position on a peninsula that a few troops could defend, and the largest airfield in eastern Libya 24 kilometres away. British, Australian and Indian forces captured it on 22 January 1941. After Erwin Rommel's forces drove the Allies back to the Egyptian border, Tobruk was isolated and besieged. Its defenders included the Australian 9th Division and later the British 70th Infantry Division, the Polish Independent Carpathian Rifle Brigade and a Czechoslovak battalion.

Operation Crusader lifted the siege in late 1941. Rommel took the town on 21 June 1942 in an outflanking attack, capturing the largest number of Commonwealth troops since Singapore. A British raid on 13–14 September 1942 failed with almost 800 casualties. The Allies recaptured Tobruk on 11 November 1942, after the Second Battle of El Alamein.

Rebuilt after the war, Tobruk was expanded in the 1960s with a port terminal linked by an oil pipeline to the Sarir oil field. It is the capital of the Butnan District. King Idris of Libya had his palace at Bab Zaytun, and the city was traditionally a stronghold of the Senussi dynasty.
todai-ji: Japan suffered disasters and epidemics in the Tenpyō era, among them a major smallpox outbreak around 735 to 737 and a rebellion led by Fujiwara no Hirotsugu in 740. In 741 Emperor Shōmu issued an edict promoting provincial temples throughout the country, and in 743 he commissioned the Great Buddha. Kinshōsen-ji, the forerunner of Tōdai-ji, was made the provincial temple of Yamato Province and head of all the provincial temples.

According to the temple's records, more than 2,600,000 people contributed rice, wood, metal, cloth or labour, and 350,000 worked directly on the statue. It was cast in eight pours over three years, begun at Shigaraki and resumed in Nara in 745, and finished in 751. The eye-opening ceremony of 752 was attended by 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers.

The Great Buddha Hall houses the Buddha Vairocana, known in Japanese as Daibutsu, said to be the world's largest bronze statue of him. The original complex also had two pagodas of about 100 metres, which an earthquake destroyed.

The hall has been rebuilt twice after fire. The present building, finished in 1709, is 57 metres long, 50 metres wide and 49 metres high, about 30 per cent smaller than its predecessor, which had eleven bays to its seven. It was the world's largest wooden building until 1998.

In the Nara period the state regulated Buddhism closely, and Tōdai-ji served as the central administrative temple for the provincial temples and for the six Buddhist schools of the time, each of which had an office there. All officially licensed monks had to take Vinaya ordination at the temple. In 754 Ganjin, who had reached Japan after twelve years and six attempts to cross the sea from China, ordained Empress Kōken, the former Emperor Shōmu and others.

The temple's authority declined when the centre of Japanese Buddhism moved to Mount Hiei and political power moved to the shōgun's base at Kamakura after the Genpei war. By the 19th century the Great Buddha Hall was in danger of collapse under its heavy roof. A restoration from 1904 to 1913 propped it up, and a second, from 1974 to 1980, fixed the roof with steel frames and gave the hall its present appearance.
todi: Todi stands on a high two-crested hill at an elevation of 447 metres on the left bank of the Tiber, about 40 kilometres from Perugia and 18 kilometres from Spoleto, in the province of Perugia. The town lies between the streams Rivo and Naia, which flow into the Tiber. Its position, commanding distant views in every direction, made it a strong place. Piazza del Popolo occupies the highest point, on the summit of Colle Nidoli, in the area of the Roman forum.

Todi was founded by the Umbri in the 8th or 7th century BCE under the name Tutere, a name that means border, because the city lay on the frontier with the Etruscan lands. Ancient Tuder was one of the most important Umbrian cities and minted its own coinage with the name Tutere. It had strong Etruscan cultural influence before the Roman conquest, which is placed in the 3rd century BCE, and after it Roman customs replaced the earlier Umbrian-Etruscan culture.

The emperor Trajan's family, the gens Ulpia, came from Todi. A legend places the foundation as early as 2707 BCE and says that the first furrow was traced under the guidance of an eagle. Its elevated position made Todi a strong place during the Gothic War and after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, and chronicles say that Saint Fortunatus, bishop of the city, spared it from slaughter and fire.

In the 11th century it set up a free commune with two consuls responsible for administration and justice. Orvieto, helped by Perugia, entered and devastated it by fire and sword after a territorial dispute. In 1311 it fixed its militia at 10,000 cavalry and 3,000 infantry and built fortifications. A plague in the 16th century killed more than two thirds of the population. A period of prosperity is placed between 1566 and 1606 under Bishop Angelo Cesi, and the 17th century brought decline through plagues, wars and famines.

The cathedral, begun in the 12th century and completed in the 14th, stands at the highest point of the city. Around Piazza del Popolo stand the Palazzo del Popolo, built at the beginning of the 13th century and reportedly one of the oldest public palaces in Italy, the Palazzo del Capitano and the Palazzo dei Priori. Roman cisterns beneath the square supported the forum.

Remains of Umbrian-Etruscan walls of large travertine blocks survive at the summit, and an amphitheatre was built outside the walls in the Augustan period. The Mars of Todi, a bronze statue found in the area, is now in the Gregorian Etruscan Museum. The poet Fra Jacopone da Todi, associated with the hymn Stabat Mater, and Pope Martin I were born there.
todor-zhivkov: Todor Hristov Zhivkov was born in the village of Pravets into a peasant family. The exact date of his birth was disputed within the family: his mother insisted on 20 September 1911, but in his memoirs he said that a drunken Orthodox priest had recorded only the day of baptism, and calculated from local custom that the real day was 7 September.

During the Second World War he took part in the resistance and in 1943 helped organise the Chavdar Partisan Brigade around his birthplace. After the uprising of 9 September 1944 he became head of the Sofia police, restyled the People's Militia, and he rose in the Bulgarian Communist Party, joining its Politburo in 1951 and helping counter rural resistance to forced collectivisation.

Zhivkov became First Secretary in 1954, replacing the hardline Valko Chervenkov, who kept most of his powers as prime minister. After Nikita Khrushchev's secret speech against Stalin, the April plenum of 1956 saw Zhivkov criticise Chervenkov, who was demoted, and he became the de facto leader. He served as prime minister from 1962 to 1971 and then as Chairman of the State Council. His government carried out a relative liberalisation and de-Stalinization, removed monuments of personality cults, allowed some market reforms and ended the persecution of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church. In 1965 a plot by officers who wanted a pro-Chinese Stalinist-Maoist leadership was exposed.

He followed the Soviet Union closely, supporting the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, though he also drew advantage from the relationship, notably in Soviet crude oil refined at Burgas and resold. The economy grew from the mid-1960s to the late 1970s, with new industrial plants and the Kozloduy nuclear power station. Dissidents could still be punished, and exit visas were needed to travel abroad.

In December 1984 the government began the Revival Process, a campaign to replace Turkish with Bulgarian names that many Bulgarian Turks resisted and that led to a large-scale expulsion of Turks and Muslims in 1989. A stagnating economy, a worsening international image and corruption in the party weakened him, and under pressure from senior party members he resigned on 10 November 1989. Communist rule effectively ended within a month.

He was tried on five indictments, including the Revival Process and labour camps, was later released, and wrote memoirs. He died on 5 August 1998. Popularly nicknamed bai Tosho, he remains the longest-serving non-royal ruler in Bulgarian history.
toghon-temur: Toghon Temür was born on 25 May 1320 to Kusala, then in exile in Central Asia. His mother, Mailaiti, was a descendant of Arslan Khan, a chief of the Karluks. After the War of the Two Capitals, which followed the death of Yesün Temür in 1328, Kusala died under suspicious circumstances and his younger brother was restored to the throne as Emperor Wenzong. Toghon Temür was removed from court and exiled, first to Goryeo and later to Guangxi. When Wenzong died in 1332, the succession took months to settle, and Toghon Temür was enthroned only in 1333.

The early reign was dominated by powerful ministers, first El Temür and then Bayan, who carried out political purges and suspended the imperial examination system. In 1340 the emperor allied with Bayan's nephew Toqto'a and removed Bayan in a coup. Under Toqto'a the purges were reversed, the examinations restored and many Chinese literati recalled. The official histories of the Liao, Jin and Song dynasties were completed in 1345.

From the mid-1340s droughts, floods and famines struck the countryside, while the government faced currency depreciation and falling tax revenues. In 1348 illicit salt dealers rebelled against the state salt monopoly, setting off further revolts. When the Red Turban Rebellion erupted in 1351, Toqto'a raised a large army against it, but Toghon Temür dismissed him in 1354. The emperor gradually withdrew from active governance, and in 1364 the warlord Bolad Temür occupied Khanbaliq and expelled the crown prince Ayushiridara. The fighting further weakened central authority.

Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty and sent his armies north. In 1368 Toghon Temür abandoned Khanbaliq for his summer capital at Shangdu, which the Ming took in 1369. He retreated to Yingchang, in present-day Inner Mongolia, and died there on 23 May 1370. His son Ayushiridara succeeded him and withdrew the court to Karakorum. The remnant court, called the Northern Yuan, continued to claim the title of Emperor of China.

The Ming held that the Yuan had forfeited the Mandate of Heaven and gave him the posthumous name Emperor Shun, meaning compliant. The Northern Yuan's temple name for him was Huizong. He reigned for 35 years, the longest of any Yuan emperor after Kublai Khan, and patronised the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism. Historians debate how far the dynasty fell from structural problems and how far from his withdrawal from government.
togo: Togo is a small tropical country of 56,785 square kilometres, less than 115 kilometres wide between Ghana and Benin. It extends north from the Gulf of Guinea, where its coast is 56 kilometres long and consists of lagoons with sandy beaches, to the border with Burkina Faso. The south has a savannah and woodland plateau reaching a coastal plain with lagoons and marshes, the centre is hilly, and the north is rolling savannah. The highest mountain is Mont Agou at 986 metres, and the longest river is the Mono, at 400 kilometres.

The name Togo means 'by the water' or 'behind the sea', from the Ewe words to, 'water', and go, 'shore'. It originally referred only to the town of Togo, now Togoville, and the Germans later extended it to the whole country.

Archaeological finds indicate that societies in the area could produce pottery and process iron. Between the 11th and 16th centuries the Ewe entered the area from the west, and the Mina and Gun from the east, and most settled on the coast. The Atlantic slave trade began in the 16th century. For the next two hundred years the coastal region was a trading centre for Europeans in search of slaves, which earned Togo and the surrounding region the name the Slave Coast.

In 1884 a paper was forcibly signed at Togoville with King Mlapa III, whereby Germany claimed a protectorate over a stretch of coast and gradually extended its control inland. In 1905 this became the German colony of Togoland. The local population was forced to work, to cultivate cotton, coffee and cocoa, and to pay taxes, and a railway and the port of Lomé were built for export.

Britain and France invaded in August 1914, and German forces surrendered on 26 August. The territory was partitioned into British and French zones, which on 20 July 1922 became League of Nations mandates. French Togoland became an autonomous republic in 1956, and British Togoland voted to join the Gold Coast, as part of Ghana, in 1957. Togo became independent from France in 1960.

Togo is the Togolese Republic, with its capital, Lomé, on the Gulf of Guinea. French is the official language, and Kabiye and Ewe are national languages. The population is about 8 million, with some 40 ethnic groups, of which the Ewe in the south are the most numerous. Culture draws on Ewe and Mina traditions in the south, including the creator god Mawu and the vodun, and on Kabye and Tem traditions in the north, including the Evala wrestling initiation rite.
tohoku-region: Tōhoku, like most of Japan, is hilly or mountainous, with the Ōu Mountains running north to south. Many of the region's lowlands lie inland, and much of the population is concentrated there. Because the coastlines do not favour seaport development, settlement came to depend far more than usual on land and rail transport. Low points in the central range make communication between the lowlands on either side moderately easy.

The climate is colder than elsewhere on Honshu because of the stronger effect of the Siberian High, and it permits only one crop a year on paddy fields. The Pacific coast is generally much less snowy than the region's popular image. Tōhoku was traditionally considered the granary of Japan, supplying Sendai and the Tokyo-Yokohama market with rice and other farm goods, and it provided 20 percent of the national rice crop.

The area was held by the Emishi, the indigenous peoples of Honshu, and later by the Ainu. Historically it was the Dewa and Mutsu or Michinoku regions, a name first recorded in the Hitachi no kuni Fudoki of 654. Yamato settlement took place between the seventh and ninth centuries, long after Yamato culture was established in central and south-western Japan. As the last stronghold of the Emishi and the site of many battles, the region at times kept a degree of autonomy from Kyoto.

In the 12th century the Northern Fujiwara ruled Tōhoku as their own realm, independent of the imperial court through the strength of their warrior bands. Their first ruler, Fujiwara no Kiyohira, of mixed Yamato and Emishi parentage, ruled from Hiraizumi in what is now Iwate Prefecture from about 1100. Minamoto no Yoritomo, founder of the Kamakura shogunate, defeated them in 1189.

Date Masamune (1567–1636) of the Date clan expanded trade and ruled one of the largest fiefdoms of the later Tokugawa shogunate. He sheltered Christian missionaries and funded an envoy to the Pope, probably in part out of a wish for foreign technology, but reversed course once Tokugawa Ieyasu outlawed Christianity. The haiku poet Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) wrote Oku no Hosomichi, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, on his travels through the region.

The region consists of six prefectures: Akita, Aomori, Fukushima, Iwate, Miyagi and Yamagata. It is often divided into North Tōhoku (Aomori, Akita and Iwate) and South Tōhoku (Yamagata, Miyagi and Fukushima). Sendai is its largest city, with 1,098,000 people, and Miyagi is now the most populated prefecture. Heavy industry began to develop in the 1960s, and tourism became a major industry in the 20th century. Chūson-ji, Hirosaki Castle and the islands of Matsushima Bay are among its historic and scenic sites. A magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami on 11 March 2011 caused 19,759 deaths along the east coast.
tok-pisin: Tok Pisin is the result of contact among Pacific Islanders. Colonial authorities forced people speaking many different languages to work on plantations in Queensland and on various islands during the period of blackbirding, and the labourers developed a pidgin whose vocabulary came mainly from English but also from German, Malay, Portuguese and their own Austronesian languages, perhaps especially Kuanua, the language of the Tolai.

This pidgin evolved into Tok Pisin in German New Guinea, where it became a widely used lingua franca between the colonial authorities and the indigenous population, although the metropolitan language was German. Bislama in Vanuatu and Pijin in the Solomon Islands developed in parallel and have traditionally been treated as varieties of a single Melanesian Pidgin English.

Tok comes from English talk, with a wider sense of word, speech or language, and Pisin from pidgin. Despite the name, Tok Pisin is a creole in linguistic terms, because many people now learn it as a first language. Tense is marked by separate words: bai for the future, from by and by, and bin for the past, from been. The suffix -im marks transitive verbs, as in luk, look, and lukim, see, and adjectives take -pela, from fellow.

A small vocabulary leads speakers to metaphor: gras bilong het, grass of the head, means hair. The current alphabet has 21 letters and four digraphs; the colonial Department of Education created it in 1955 to increase literacy, replacing earlier spellings that followed each word's source language.

Tok Pisin is one of Papua New Guinea's three official languages, with English and Hiri Motu, and is the most widely used language in the country. Between five and six million people use it to some degree, and perhaps one million as a primary language. It is frequently the language of debate in the national parliament, and some schools teach in it for the first three years of elementary education.

Many children learn it as a first language, especially in urban families whose parents speak different local languages. It has increasingly overtaken Hiri Motu among town-dwellers and is slowly crowding out other languages of Papua New Guinea.
tokat: The city was established in the Hittite era. In the time of King Mithradates VI of Pontus it was one of his many strongholds in Asia Minor. It was known as Evdokia or Eudoxia and was later incorporated ecclesiastically into the western part of the Byzantine Greek Empire of Trebizond. Scholars have debated whether Tokat is the ancient and medieval Dazimon, which Guillaume de Jerphanion and William Mitchell Ramsay held, or the town of Dokeia named in a 10th-century text, as Henri Grégoire argued.
