Grégoire thought the name Dokeia had no Greek etymology, and that its derivation from Eudokia was a later folk etymology.

After the Battle of Manzikert the town came under the Seljuk Turks, like most of Asia Minor. After the death of Sultan Suleiman ibn Qutulmish in 1086, the emir Danishmend Gazi took control of the area from his base at Sivas. The Seljuks retook the region only many decades later, in the reign of Kilij Arslan II. After the Battle of Köse Dağ they lost their hold, and local emirs such as the Eretna took power until the Ottomans captured Tokat in 1392 under Sultan Bayazid I.

Tokat is the seat of Tokat Province, in the mid-Black Sea region of Anatolia, at the confluence of the Tokat River with the Yeşilırmak. It was historically a centre of copper working and textiles, with copper manufacturing that relied on the Kempan Maden mine. Its main landmark is Tokat Castle, an Ottoman citadel with 28 towers on a rocky hill, in whose dungeon Vlad the Impaler is said to have been imprisoned. Other monuments include the 12th-century Garipler Mosque, the 16th-century Ali Paşa Mosque and Hatuniye Külliyesi, and the Gök Medrese, built in 1270 as a school of theology and later a museum. Its distinctive foods include Tokat kebabı and Zile pekmezi, a grape-molasses confection.
tokelau: Tokelau consists of three tropical coral atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo, with a combined land area of about 10 square kilometres, between latitudes 8 and 10 degrees south, about midway between Hawaii and New Zealand and some 500 kilometres north of Samoa. The highest point is just 5 metres above sea level, and the islands lie in the Pacific tropical cyclone belt. Swains Island (Olohega), culturally and geographically part of the same archipelago, has been under United States control since about 1900 and is administered as part of American Samoa. The name is a Tokelauan word meaning north wind; European explorers called the group the Union Islands, and it was shortened to Tokelau on 9 December 1976.

Archaeological evidence indicates that the atolls were settled about 1,000 years ago from Samoa. The three atolls functioned separately in politics while keeping social and linguistic cohesion, governed by chiefly clans, with occasional wars between atolls as well as intermarriage; Fakaofo held some dominion over Atafu and Nukunonu. Life was subsistence-based, relying mainly on fish and coconut.

Commodore John Byron sighted Atafu on 24 June 1765, and Captain Edward Edwards visited it in June 1791 in search of the Bounty mutineers. In 1877 an Order in Council placed the islands under United Kingdom protection, and in June 1889 Commander C. F. Oldham of HMS Egeria raised the Union Flag on each atoll. They were annexed on 29 February 1916 and included in the Gilbert Islands. They were placed under the Governor-General of New Zealand in 1925, and New Zealand took over administration on 11 February 1926, though sovereignty remained with the United Kingdom.

Tokelau is a dependent territory of New Zealand, whose King is its head of state, and both governments call it a nation. About 2,500 people live there, and some 94 per cent speak Tokelauan as their first language. Since 1993 the territory has elected its own head of government, the Ulu-o-Tokelau, a post that rotates among the faipule of the three atolls, and the basis of its system is the Tokelau Islands Act 1948. Tokelauans have twice narrowly failed to reach the two-thirds majority needed for further self-determination.
tokhtamysh: Tokhtamysh belonged to the House of Borjigin. Genealogies trace his descent from Tuqa-Timur, the thirteenth son of Jochi, the eldest son of Genghis Khan. His father, Tuy Khwāja, ruled the Mangyshlak peninsula and refused to join his cousin and suzerain Urus Khan in a campaign against Sarai, so Urus had him executed. Tokhtamysh fled, submitted to his father's killer and was forgiven. In 1373 he tried to make himself khan in Sighnaq but was driven out and was forgiven a second time. When Urus took Sarai in 1375 he fled again and in 1376 reached the court of Timur.

Tokhtamysh was defeated once more by a son of Urus, Tīmūr Malik, and again returned to Timur, whose forces took Sawran and Otrar, then won at Qara-Tal and executed Tīmūr Malik in 1379. Installed as khan in Sighnaq, Tokhtamysh advanced on Sarai in 1380 and defeated the commander Mamai on the Kalka river, becoming the first khan in over two decades to rule both wings of the Golden Horde. He restored peace with the Genoese of the Crimea and confirmed the privileges of the emirs and chieftains.

He then turned to the Russian principalities. Dmitry Donskoy, the Grand Prince of Vladimir-Suzdal, acknowledged him as suzerain but withheld tribute. In 1382 Tokhtamysh crossed the Volga, with the princes of Rjazan' and Nižnij Novgorod serving him as guides, and besieged and sacked Moscow, whose prince had left it under a garrison. Dmitry then submitted, gave his eldest son as a hostage and sent tribute in 1383. In the winter of 1384 to 1385 Tokhtamysh stormed Tabriz and took some 200,000 slaves.

His quarrels with Timur then grew. Timur struck into the Golden Horde and forced a battle at the Kondurcha river in June 1391. A second invasion in 1395 ended in a hard-fought battle on the Terek on 15 and 16 April, where dissension among Tokhtamysh's emirs gave Timur the victory.

Tokhtamysh found refuge in Lithuania, and in 1399 he and Grand Duke Vytautas marched against Tīmūr Qutluq and Edigu. He then went to Siberia, where he held parts of the area from 1400. Edigu is said to have fought him sixteen times, and he was killed late in 1406 near Tyumen. He was the last khan of the Golden Horde to mint coins with Mongolian script.

His sack of Moscow undid the setback that Kulikovo had dealt to Mongol domination two years before. But his conflict with Timur set a course for the undoing of his achievements, and his reliance on Moscow and Lithuania strengthened both.
tokugawa-ieyasu: Tokugawa Ieyasu was born Matsudaira Takechiyo at Okazaki Castle on 31 January 1543, the son of Matsudaira Hirotada, daimyo of Mikawa, and Odai no Kata. When he was five, Oda Nobuhide abducted him on his way to Sunpu as a hostage of Imagawa Yoshimoto, and held him at the Honshōji Temple in Nagoya for three years. In 1556 he came of age at a ceremony presided over by Imagawa Yoshimoto. After Yoshimoto was killed at Okehazama, he formed the Kiyosu Alliance with Oda Nobunaga, and in 1567 he took the family name Tokugawa.

Ieyasu served Oda Nobunaga as ally and general, fighting Takeda Shingen's invasion of his lands from 1571. In 1579 Nobunaga accused Ieyasu's wife and heir of plotting with Takeda Katsuyori, and Ieyasu had his wife executed and his son Matsudaira Nobuyasu forced to commit seppuku. Nobunaga died at Honnō-ji in 1582. Ieyasu fought Toyotomi Hideyoshi at the Battle of Komaki and Nagakute, then submitted. After the campaign against the Hōjō in 1590 he was moved to the Kantō plains and built his castle at Edo.

Hideyoshi named Ieyasu the most powerful of five regents for his young son Toyotomi Hideyori before dying on 18 September 1598. Opposition gathered around Ishida Mitsunari, and the Battle of Sekigahara began on 21 October 1600, with Ieyasu's Eastern Army initially numbering 75,000 against 120,000 in the Western Army. Afterwards Ieyasu redistributed the domains of the daimyo. Those who had joined him earlier became known as fudai daimyō, and those who joined after the battle as tozama daimyō.

Emperor Go-Yōzei gave Ieyasu the title of shōgun on 24 March 1603. He resigned in 1605 but remained the effective ruler as retired shōgun, or ōgosho, at Sunpu Castle until his death. He supervised the building of Edo Castle, whose cost the other daimyo bore. He distanced Japan from European influence from 1609, though the Dutch East India Company kept preferential trading rights. In 1614 he besieged Osaka Castle, where samurai had gathered around Hideyori, and he then issued the Buke shohatto code, which allowed each daimyo one castle.
Ieyasu devoted himself to the Jōdo-shū school of Buddhism. He died on 1 June 1616. His successors moved the government to Edo in 1638 and enacted the sakoku policy of isolation in 1639.
tokugawa-yoshinobu: Tokugawa Yoshinobu was born in Edo on 28 October 1837, the seventh son of Tokugawa Nariaki, daimyō of Mito of the Tokugawa branch family of Mito. He was raised in Mito from the age of seven months and educated in the literary and martial arts and in government. At his father's urging he was adopted by the Hitotsubashi-Tokugawa family to improve his chances of the succession, became family head in 1847 and took the name Yoshinobu.

When the thirteenth shōgun, Iesada, died in 1858, Yoshinobu was nominated as a possible successor, but the opposing faction led by Ii Naosuke prevailed, and Tokugawa Yoshitomi became the fourteenth shōgun, Iemochi. Yoshinobu was placed under house arrest in the Ansei Purge, but after Ii's assassination in 1860 he was reinstated and in 1862 became the shōgun's guardian. In 1864, commanding the defence of the imperial palace, he defeated Chōshū forces who tried to seize the Hamaguri Gate in the Kinmon Incident.

Iemochi died without issue in August 1866. Shogunal officials nominated Yoshinobu, who became head of the Tokugawa main family in October but refused the title of shōgun until January 1867. He was the only Tokugawa shōgun to spend his entire tenure outside Edo, and never set foot in Edo Castle as shōgun. He began a government overhaul, with a French military mission.

Samurai of Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa allied against him, fearing a renewed Tokugawa shogunate. On 9 November 1867 Yoshinobu tendered his resignation to the Emperor, stepping down formally ten days later, and withdrew to Osaka. Satsuma and Chōshū, however, secured an imperial edict later shown to be a forgery, and at a court meeting he was stripped of all titles and land.

When Tokugawa troops marched towards Kyoto to deliver a protest they were attacked, which began the Battle of Toba–Fushimi, the first clash of the Boshin War. Yoshinobu left his army when the Satsuma and Chōshū forces raised the imperial banner, and escaped to Edo. On 11 April 1868 Edo Castle was handed over to the imperial army and the city was spared all-out war. He then moved to Shizuoka and lived in quiet retirement.

On 3 June 1902 the Emperor Meiji allowed him to found his own branch house with the rank of prince. He sat in the House of Peers until 1910 and died in November 1913, and he is buried in Yanaka Cemetery, Tokyo.
tokushima-prefecture: Tokushima Prefecture lies on the island of Shikoku and has an area of 4,146 square kilometres. It borders Kagawa Prefecture to the north, Ehime Prefecture to the west and Kōchi Prefecture to the south-west. It faces the Kii Peninsula of Honshu across the Kii Channel, which connects the Pacific Ocean with the Seto Inland Sea. The Sanuki Mountains run along its northern border, and the Yoshino River flows through the prefecture, with rice fields in its lower valley and along the narrow coastal plains.

The capital and largest city is Tokushima, and other major cities include Anan, Naruto and Yoshinogawa. The Ōnaruto Bridge carries a road across the Naruto Strait to Awaji Island, joining the prefecture to Kobe and the San'yō Expressway on Honshu. Until the Meiji Restoration the area was known as Awa Province.

In ancient times Tokushima City belonged to a district known as Myōdō-gun. In the first wave of consolidation after the abolition of the fiefdoms in 1871 it became Myōdō Prefecture, which included the Awa region and Awaji Island. In 1873 it also took in the area of present-day Kagawa Prefecture. In the second wave of consolidation the Sanuki region separated in 1875 to form Kagawa; in 1876 Awaji Island passed to Hyōgo Prefecture and the Awa region became part of Kōchi Prefecture. On 2 March 1880 the prefecture separated from Kōchi and was inaugurated as Tokushima Prefecture.

In August 1945 the Washi no Mon gate of Tokushima Castle was destroyed by fire at the end of the Second World War. The Nankai earthquake of December 1946 caused vast damage throughout the prefecture. Tokushima University was created in 1949, and Naruto, Komatsushima and Anan were inaugurated as cities between 1947 and 1958. Takeo Miki, who was born in Tokushima, was elected Prime Minister of Japan in October 1974. The Ōnaruto Bridge to Hyōgo was completed in 1985, and the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge in 1998 connected Tokushima with the mainland by road.

The prefecture had a population of 682,439 in February 2025. It depends on agriculture, forestry and fisheries, and Japanese indigo is produced only here. Its produce, including Naruto sweet potatoes, sudachi citrus, lotus roots and strawberries, goes mainly to the Kansai region around Kobe, Osaka and Kyoto. Among its cultural sites are Tokushima Castle, the Iya Valley, the Oboke Koboke Gorge, the Naruto whirlpools, the Otsuka Museum of Art and the Awa Marionette Jōruri tradition of puppet theatre. Its sports teams include the football club Tokushima Vortis.
tolfa: Tolfa is a town of medieval origin in the orbit of Viterbo. It was taken into the Papal States and granted first to the Capocci family and then to the Roman nobles Ludovico and Pietro Frangipani, who walled the community. The discovery of large deposits of alunite, the source of alum, in 1461 gave it sudden importance, and after some confrontations with the Frangipani the Camera Apostolica assumed direct control. Alum was an essential mordant in the textile industry. Previously the only supplies had come from the East, from sources controlled by the Ottoman Turks, through Venice.

Pope Pius II placed the distribution of alum solely in the hands of the Medici, with the explicit thought that the income should serve Christendom against the Turks. Later the monopoly in extraction passed as a papal gift to Agostino Chigi. In 1530 Pope Clement VII granted Tolfa the status of comune, as it had outgrown its medieval walls. The workmen's village of Allumiere was built near the mine and became an autonomous comune in 1826. The Frangipani castle, the Rocca di Tolfa, was destroyed by French troops in 1799 after the town had rebelled against the Roman Republic.

Tolfa is the main centre of the Monti della Tolfa, an extinct volcanic group between Civitavecchia and the Lake of Bracciano, in the Metropolitan City of Rome in Lazio. Its town hall houses a collection of Etruscan and Roman antiquities found nearby. Other sights include the Church of Sant'Egidio Abate, the Augustinian convent of the early 16th century, now a library and civic museum, the Capuchin convent of 1621 and Castle Rota.
tomas-garrigue-masaryk: Masaryk was born on 7 March 1850 in Hodonín, Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire, to a poor, working-class family. His father, Jozef Masárik, was a Slovak carter who became steward and coachman at the imperial estate; his mother, Teresie Kropáčková, was a Moravian cook who had received a German education. He grew up in Čejkovice and attended grammar school in Brno and Vienna from 1865 to 1872.

He studied under Franz Brentano at the University of Vienna and took his doctorate there in 1876 with a thesis on Plato. In Leipzig he met Charlotte Garrigue, an American from Brooklyn, whom he married on 15 March 1878; he took her family name as his middle name. He became professor of philosophy at the Czech Charles-Ferdinand University in Prague in 1882, where his students included Edvard Beneš. He challenged the supposedly medieval Czech epic manuscripts and spoke against the blood libel in the 1899 Hilsner trial.

Masaryk sat in the Austrian Reichsrat from 1891 to 1893 with the Young Czech Party and from 1907 to 1914 for the Czech Progressive Party, which he had founded in 1900. At first he favoured restructuring Austria-Hungary as a federal state. When the First World War broke out he concluded that Czechs and Slovaks should seek independence, and in December 1914 he went into exile with his daughter Olga.

He lectured in London and Paris, wrote memoranda, and in January 1917 sent President Woodrow Wilson a first memorandum on an independent Czechoslovak state. He helped organise the Czechoslovak Legion in Russia, which grew to about 40,000 men by 1918 after its performance at the Battle of Zborov in July 1917. In 1918 he travelled to the United States, where he had lectured at the University of Chicago in 1902 and 1907; on 18 October 1918 he submitted the Washington Declaration of Czechoslovak independence to Wilson.

The Allies recognised Masaryk as head of the provisional government, and on 14 November 1918 the National Assembly elected him president while he was in New York. He was re-elected in 1920, 1927 and 1934; the 1920 constitution limited presidents to two terms, but a one-time provision exempted the first holder. The constitution gave the president a limited role, but with ten or more parties in the Assembly and frequent changes of government, his prestige gave the office more influence than its framers intended. He built an informal political network known as the Hrad, the Castle.

He resigned on 14 December 1935 because of old age and poor health and was succeeded by Beneš. He died at Lány on 14 September 1937, at 87, and was buried beside his wife. Masaryk University in Brno bears his name.
tomoyuki-yamashita: Tomoyuki Yamashita was born on 8 November 1885, the second son of a local physician in a village in what is now Kōchi Prefecture on Shikoku. He graduated from the Imperial Japanese Army Academy in 1905 and fought against Germany in Shandong in 1914. He became an expert on Germany and served as assistant military attaché at Bern and Berlin from 1919 to 1922. A leading member of the Imperial Way group, he became a rival of Hideki Tojo. After the February 26 Incident of 1936 he lost the trust of Emperor Hirohito by appealing for leniency for the rebel officers, and he was posted to Korea.

On 6 November 1941 Yamashita took command of the Twenty-Fifth Army. He invaded Malaya on 8 December with a force about one third the size of the British forces, relying on speed, and the campaign ended with the fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942, when 30,000 front-line soldiers took 80,000 British, Indian and Australian prisoners. The occupation of Singapore saw atrocities, among them the Alexandra Hospital and Sook Ching massacres. His responsibility is debated: the order to execute Chinese came, according to postwar testimony, from senior officers on his operations staff.

In July 1942 Yamashita was sent to Manchukuo, probably through Tojo's doing. On 10 October 1944 he took command of the Fourteenth Area Army in the Philippines. US forces landed on Leyte ten days later and on Luzon on 6 January 1945. He did not declare Manila an open city, and Rear Admiral Sanji Iwabuchi, against Yamashita's order, defended it; the fighting and Japanese atrocities killed more than 100,000 Filipino civilians. Yamashita surrendered on 2 September 1945.

An American military tribunal in Manila tried him from 29 October to 7 December 1945 for atrocities against civilians and prisoners of war in the Philippines, charging that he had failed to prevent them. He denied ordering or knowing of the crimes and said he was in effect charged with losing the war.

He was found guilty and sentenced to death. General Douglas MacArthur upheld the sentence, the supreme courts of the Philippines and the United States declined to review it, and Justices Frank Murphy and W. B. Rutledge dissented, criticising the haste of the trial. He was executed on 23 February 1946. The principle that a commander is responsible for crimes of his troops that he did not try to stop is known as the Yamashita standard.
tomsk: Tomsk stands on the Tom River, from which the city takes its name. The river's name may derive from the Ket word toom, meaning river, from the Russian tyomny, meaning dark, or from the Turco-Mongol tom, meaning great. The climate is humid continental, barely escaping a subarctic classification, with severe and lengthy winters; the lowest recorded temperature was −55 °C in January 1931.

The fortress of 1604 followed a request from Toian, the Tatar duke of the Eushta Tatars, for the tsar's protection against the Yenisei Kyrgyz and the Oirats. Boris Godunov sent 200 Cossacks under Vasily Fomich Tyrkov and Gavriil Ivanovich Pisemsky, and Toian ceded the land. In 1804 Tomsk became the seat of the Tomsk Governorate, and gold was found in 1830. In the mid-19th century one fifth of its residents were exiles. When the Trans-Siberian Railway of the 1890s bypassed the city, growth shifted south and Novosibirsk in time surpassed it.

Tomsk then built its name on education. Tomsk Polytechnic University was founded in 1896 and opened in 1900, and by World War II every twelfth resident was a student. After 1917 Tomsk became a notable centre of the White movement, led among others by Anatoly Pepelyayev and Maria Bochkareva. Factories moved there from 1941, which led to the creation of Tomsk Oblast. In the Cold War it was a closed city, and in 1949 the secret settlement of Tomsk-7, home to the Soviet Union's first industrial-scale nuclear power station, was founded nearby; it was renamed Seversk in 1992.

Tomsk is the administrative centre of Tomsk Oblast in Russia, with 556,478 inhabitants at the 2021 census. It has six universities with over 100,000 students, among them Tomsk State University, the oldest university in Siberia. The city is known for the intricate gingerbread decoration of its traditional wooden houses, though their number is falling through redevelopment and fire.
tomyris: Tomyris was the widow of the king of the Massagetae and succeeded him as ruler of the tribe after his death. She is known only from the writings of the Greek historian Herodotus. The few other early sources that cover the period, above all Ctesias, do not mention her. Her name is the Latin form of the Greek Tomuris, itself a Hellenisation of the Saka name *Taumuriyah, which is taken to mean "of family" and is related to Avestan and Old Persian words for seed, germ and kinship.

In the account of Herodotus, Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire, asked for her hand in order to gain her kingdom through marriage. Tomyris understood his aim and refused. On the advice of the Lydian Croesus, Cyrus then decided to invade the Massagetae. While he built a bridge over the Araxes river, Tomyris told him to be content with ruling his own kingdom and to let her rule hers.

Cyrus's first assault was routed by the Massagetae. He then left a banquet with large amounts of wine in the tents of his camp as an ambush and withdrew. The Massagetae, led by Tomyris's son Spargapises, who commanded their army, were used to fermented mare's milk and cannabis rather than wine. They became drunk and were slaughtered, which destroyed a third of their army. Spargapises was captured and, once sober, asked Cyrus to free him. Cyrus agreed, and Spargapises killed himself.

Tomyris sent Cyrus an angry message calling the wine a drug that made men speak evil words, and demanded that he leave her land or she would give him more blood than he could drink. In the battle that followed she defeated the Persians and destroyed most of their army. Cyrus was killed, and she is said to have cut off his head and put it in a bag filled with blood, telling him to drink his fill.

Ctesias recorded another version, in which Cyrus died fighting the Derbices, who were either the Massagetae or one of their sub-tribes. About 520 BCE, and possibly earlier, the tribe was ruled by a king named Skuⁿxa, who rebelled against Persia until Darius I campaigned against the Sakas from 520 to 518 BCE and conquered the Massagetae.

Tomyris became a popular subject in European art and literature from the Renaissance, usually shown receiving the head of Cyrus or placing it in a vessel of blood, within the tradition of the Power of Women. Rubens, Mattia Preti and Gustave Moreau are among the artists who portrayed her. Eustache Deschamps included her among the nine Female Worthies in the late 14th century, and an opera, Thomyris, Queen of Scythia, was staged in London in 1707.
tongatapu: Tongatapu covers about 260 square kilometres and lies in Tonga's southern island group, to which it gives its name. It is built of coral limestone and is rather flat, covered with fertile soil made of volcanic ash from neighbouring volcanoes. On the steep southern coast the land rises to an average of 35 metres and at most 70 metres, then falls gradually towards the north.

To the north lie many small islands and coral reefs, reaching up to 7 kilometres from the shore. The almost closed Fanga'uta and Fangakakau lagoons, fringed with mangroves, are breeding grounds for birds and fish, and were declared a natural reserve in 1974. As the southernmost island group of the country, it has a cooler climate than the north, so fruit production is lower there.

Tongatapu holds one of the densest concentrations of archaeological remains in the Pacific. The earliest Lapita pottery found in Tonga dates from about 900 to 850 BCE, around 300 years after the first settlements. The archaeologist David Burley found it near the Fanga'uta Lagoon, some 2,000 kilometres from the Lapita pottery of Santa Cruz in the Solomon Islands. Nukuleka is possibly the site of the first Lapita settlement.

The island was the seat of the Tuʻi Tonga, whose rule over distances of up to 1,000 kilometres was often only symbolic. Their first capital was at Toloa, about 1,000 years ago, and the second at Heketā, where the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui trilithon stands. The third, at Muʻa, was a capital from 1220 to 1851 and has more than 20 royal grave mounds.

Abel Tasman, commanding the Heemskerck and the Zeehaen for the Dutch East India Company, sighted the island on 20 January 1643 and named it Amsterdam Island for its abundant supplies. James Cook visited later and wrote the name as Tongataboo in 1777. British and American whalers called regularly for provisions, water and wood between 1807 and 1899.

Tongatapu is the most populous island of Tonga, with 74,611 residents in 2016, roughly 70.5% of the national total. It holds the capital, Nukuʻalofa, and has become the country's business, trade and labour centre. Its sites include the royal tombs at Muʻa, the blowholes at Mapu ʻa Vaea, the natural land bridge at Hūfangalupe and Tupou College, the first educational establishment in the kingdom.
tongeren: Tongeren lies in the southeastern corner of the Flemish region of Belgium, in the province of Limburg. It is called the oldest town in Belgium, as the only Roman administrative capital within the country's borders. Before the Roman conquest the area was inhabited by Belgic tribes known as the Germani cisrhenani, of which the Eburones were the largest. Caesar's Aduatuca, the fort of the Eburones, is widely equated with Tongeren, though others argue that Aduatuca was a general word for a fort and that Tongeren shows no sign of pre-Roman occupation.

As Atuatuca Tungrorum the town was the capital of the Civitas Tungrorum. Located on the road linking Cologne to Bavay and surrounded by fertile land, it quickly became one of the largest Gallo-Roman administrative and military towns. It suffered a fire during the Batavian siege in 70 CE and in the second century built a defensive wall, parts of which survive. In 358 the future emperor Julian met a delegation of Salian Franks there. In the 4th century it became the centre of a Christian diocese under Saint Servatius, who died in 384, but the seat later moved to Maastricht and then Liège. The town may have been destroyed by the Huns in 451.

In Carolingian times a church and a chapter of canons were founded where the old bishops' houses stood, and the present basilica was begun at the start of the 13th century. A medieval wall, new churches and the beguinage were built, and the town became one of the good cities of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. Louis XIV's troops burned it almost entirely in 1677. It became part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1815 and of Belgium in 1830.

The Béguinage, founded in 1257, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998, and the bell tower of the Basilica of Our Lady is inscribed with the Belfries of Belgium and France. The Gallo-Roman Museum holds Celtic gold, Roman glassware and a Roman dodecahedron, and more than 1,500 metres of the second-century Roman wall can still be seen. A statue of Ambiorix, leader of the Eburones, was erected in 1866. Every seven years the Kroningsfeesten, a religious procession, commemorates the crowning of the statue of Our Lady in 1890.
tonle-sap: Tonle Sap, whose Khmer name means Fresh River or, commonly, Great Lake, lies in the northwest of the lower Mekong plain in central Cambodia. It is the largest freshwater lake in Southeast Asia. Its basin covers about 86,000 square kilometres. The Tonle Sap River, about 120 kilometres long, joins the lake to the Mekong.

The lake changes enormously with the seasons. In the dry season it covers about 2,500 to 3,000 square kilometres and is about a metre deep. In the rainy season, from May to October, the Mekong's rising water reverses the flow of the Tonle Sap River, so that it runs into the lake for about six months and out again for the other six. The lake then reaches up to 16,000 square kilometres and a depth of 9 to 14 metres, and acts as a natural flood reservoir for the Mekong system.

The lake has long been a vital area for fishing and farming in Cambodia, and it largely sustained Angkor, described as the largest pre-industrial settlement complex in history. Fish came into the flooded forests to spawn, and the Mekong floods brought large numbers of fry. Historical research indicates that the people of Angkor dug large reservoirs to hold water in the wet season and released it in the dry season through an irrigation system, which doubled and sometimes tripled the rice crops each year. That network no longer exists, and farmers now take one crop a year.

Henri Mouhot described the lake in 1864 as covering an immense space for more than five months of the year, swollen by the current of the Mekong. Its most productive fishing grounds were leased by the government for more than a century. Many people of Vietnamese origin live in floating villages on the lake, as do Cham communities.

About 1.2 million people live around the lake and fish its waters, and the catch supplies much of Cambodia's freshwater fish. UNESCO designated the area a Biosphere Reserve in 1997, and a royal decree of 2001 made the lake and nine surrounding provinces the Tonle Sap Biosphere Reserve, with core, buffer and transition zones. The lake supports at least 149 fish species, including the Mekong giant catfish.
topkapi-palace: Mehmed the Conqueror ordered the palace built in 1459, six years after the conquest of Constantinople. It was first called the New Palace, Yeni Saray, to distinguish it from the Old Palace in Beyazıt Square, and received the name Topkapı, Cannon Gate, only later: during the reign of Mahmud I the name of a destroyed seaside palace was transferred to it. The complex expanded over the centuries, with major renovations after the earthquake of 1509 and the fire of 1665. The Conqueror's Pavilion, built about 1460, is among its oldest buildings.

The palace stands on Seraglio Point, a promontory where the Golden Horn, the Bosphorus and the Sea of Marmara meet. It has four main courtyards and many smaller buildings. The First Courtyard, the largest, was an outer precinct known as the Court of the Janissaries, and held the church of Hagia Irene, which the Ottomans used as a storehouse and armoury.

The Second Courtyard, or Divan Square, was probably completed around 1465 and took its final form around 1525 to 1529 under Suleiman I; the Imperial Council building stands there, where the Grand Vizier and other ministers met, with the kitchens, remodelled by the court architect Mimar Sinan after the fire of 1574. Beyond the Gate of Felicity lies the Third Courtyard, the private and residential part, which holds the Audience Chamber and the library of Ahmed III. The Fourth Courtyard has pavilions, gardens and terraces, including the Baghdad Kiosk, built after the Baghdad campaign of Murad IV.

The palace served as the administrative centre of the Ottoman Empire and the main residence of its sultans. The Imperial Harem, with more than 400 rooms, housed the sultan's mother, his consorts and concubines, his children and their servants, under the guard of eunuchs. The Sultan received audiences in the Second Courtyard, seated on the gold-plated Bayram throne.

After the 17th century the palace gradually lost importance, as sultans preferred their new palaces along the Bosphorus, but it kept functions such as the imperial treasury, library and mint. A government decree of 3 April 1924 made it a museum. Its collections include Ottoman clothing, weapons, miniatures, religious relics and illuminated manuscripts, and the palace forms part of the Historic Areas of Istanbul, recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1985.
toronto: Toronto stands on a harbour on the north-western shore of Lake Ontario, on a broad sloping plateau interspersed with rivers, deep ravines and urban forest. The city covers 631 square kilometres and has a 46-kilometre waterfront. The Toronto Islands and Port Lands extend into the lake and shelter the harbour south of downtown. The name was recorded in many spellings. The early form Taronto referred to the Narrows between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching, which the Mohawk called tkaronto, meaning where there are trees standing in the water, a name recorded as early as 1615 by Samuel de Champlain.

Indigenous peoples have inhabited the area for more than 10,000 years. The Wendat, an Iroquoian-speaking agricultural people, farmed it for centuries before European contact, until the Haudenosaunee invaded and massacred them between 1648 and 1650. By the 1660s the Haudenosaunee had two villages in what is now Toronto, Ganatsekwyagon on the Rouge River and Teiaiagon on the Humber River. By 1701 the Mississaugas, an Anishinaabe-speaking people from northern Ontario, had displaced them at the end of the Beaver Wars. A portage route from Lake Ontario to Lake Huron, the Toronto Carrying-Place Trail, led to the wide use of the name.

French traders founded Fort Rouillé in 1750 but abandoned it in 1759 during the Seven Years' War. The British defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, and in 1763 the area became part of the colony of Quebec. After the broadly disputed Toronto Purchase, in which the Mississaugas surrendered the area to the British Crown, the British established the town of York in 1793 and later made it the capital of Upper Canada.

During the War of 1812 York was the site of the Battle of York, which caused heavy damage and a two-week occupation by American troops. It was renamed and incorporated as the City of Toronto in 1834. In 1867, at Canadian Confederation, it became the capital of the province of Ontario. The city grew beyond its original limits by annexation and amalgamation, reaching its present area in 1998. The completion of the St. Lawrence Seaway in 1959 gave ships access to the Great Lakes from the Atlantic.

Toronto is the capital of Ontario and the most populous city in Canada, with 2,794,356 people at the 2021 census. About half of its residents were born outside Canada, over 200 ethnic origins are represented, and more than 160 languages are spoken. It is governed by a mayor and a unicameral city council of 25 councillors. It is Canada's largest financial centre and the home of the Toronto Stock Exchange, and of institutions such as the National Ballet of Canada, the Canadian Opera Company and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra.
torpedo: The word torpedo first named electric rays, from the Latin torpēdō, meaning lethargy or sluggishness. In naval usage the American inventor David Bushnell was reported to have used it for his submarine, and this probably inspired Robert Fulton, who used it for his stationary mines. Historically the term covered primitive naval mines and spar torpedoes, used ad hoc until the late 19th century, and from about 1900 it has been used strictly for self-propelled underwater explosive devices. Around 1280 the engineer Hasan al-Rammah, who worked for the Mamluk Sultanate, described a rocket-propelled surface craft carrying an explosive payload, which historians classify as a surface-skimming rocket rather than an underwater missile.

The first prototype of a self-propelled torpedo came from a commission by Giovanni Luppis, an Austro-Hungarian naval officer from Fiume, and Robert Whitehead, an English engineer who managed a factory there. In 1864 Luppis gave Whitehead the plans of the Salvacoste, a floating weapon steered from the land by ropes, which the naval authorities had dismissed because its steering and propulsion were impractical.

The Whitehead torpedo of 1866, the first successful self-propelled torpedo, used compressed air stored at pressures of up to 2.55 MPa to drive a piston engine turning a single propeller. It travelled about 180 metres at an average speed of 6.5 knots. The Austrian government invested in it, and by 1870 improved devices could run about 900 metres at up to 6 knots. In 1871 the British Admiralty paid Whitehead £15,000 for certain developments. In 1906 his torpedoes covered nearly 1,000 metres at an average of 35 knots. Rivals included the wire-driven Brennan torpedo, the flywheel-driven Howell torpedo and John Ericsson's electric torpedo of 1873.

The Royal Navy frigate HMS Shah first fired a self-propelled torpedo in anger at the Battle of Pacocha on 29 May 1877, against the Peruvian ironclad Huáscar, which outran it. On 16 January 1878 the Turkish steamer Intibah became the first vessel sunk by self-propelled torpedoes, launched from torpedo boats under Stepan Osipovich Makarov during the Russo-Turkish War. Torpedoes allowed small boats to destroy large ships without big guns. In the First World War German submarine torpedoes disrupted supply lines to Britain, and in May 1915 a torpedo from SM U-20 sank the Lusitania off Ireland in eighteen minutes, killing nearly 1,200 civilian passengers.
torquato-tasso: Tasso was born in Sorrento, the son of Bernardo Tasso, a nobleman of Bergamo and a well-known poet, and Porzia de' Rossi, a noblewoman born in Naples. His father served Ferrante Sanseverino, Prince of Salerno, and when the prince was outlawed by the Spanish government of Naples, Bernardo shared his fate and was proclaimed a rebel along with his son. In 1552 Torquato was in Naples, educated by the Jesuits, and at eight he was already known for his precocity.

He later joined his father in exile in Rome. His mother died suddenly in 1556, and his father believed she had been poisoned by her brother. From 1565 Tasso's life centred on the castle at Ferrara, where he wrote love poems for Lucrezia Bendidio and Laura Peverara and was protected by the princesses Lucrezia and Eleonora d'Este.

Gerusalemme liberata, Jerusalem Delivered, takes the First Crusade as its subject and aims to ennoble the Italian epic with a strict unity of plot, with Virgil as model. Its nominal hero is Godfrey of Bouillon, but readers have been drawn more to its romantic episodes: Armida, the witch converted by her love for a crusader, Clorinda, the female warrior baptised as she dies, and Erminia, in love with Tancredi.

His other works include the Rime, nearly two thousand lyrics written between 1567 and 1593 under Petrarch's influence, the tragedy Re Torrismondo, 28 Dialogues, and the Discorsi del poema eroico, published in 1594, his main statement of poetics. In 1592 he published a revised poem, Gerusalemme Conquistata, from which the romantic episodes were removed.

In the 1570s Tasso developed a persecution mania, fearing denunciation to the Inquisition and poison. After quarrels at the Ferrara court he was sent in March 1579 to the madhouse of St. Anna, where he remained until July 1586. His illness is now believed to have been bipolar disorder. He spent his last years moving between Rome, Naples, Florence and Mantua, and died on 25 April 1595, a few days before he was to be crowned on the Capitoline Hill by Pope Clement VIII.

Spenser and Milton were greatly influenced by him, Monteverdi set his verse, and Goethe wrote a play, Torquato Tasso, in 1790. Edward Fairfax's complete English translation, Godfrey of Bouillon, appeared in 1600. Until the early 20th century he remained one of the most widely read poets in Europe.
torshavn: The Viking settlers of the 9th century held their parliaments, called tings, at neutral and uninhabited places so that no location favoured anyone. The main ting met on the flat rocks of Tinganes, the peninsula that divides the harbour in two, which was the most central place in the islands although no settlement stood there. The Færeyinga Saga says the ting of the Faroese was on Streymoy at the harbour called Tórshavn. A market grew beside the ting and gradually became a permanent trading area, and Tórshavn was never a distinct farming community like other Faroese villages.

In 1271 the Norwegian Crown set up a royal trade monopoly at Tórshavn, with two ships sailing regularly from Bergen with salt, timber and cereal. Officials of the Norwegian and then Danish administration made their home there. Around 1580 Magnus Heinason built the small fort of Skansin at the north end of the harbour, and in 1584 the town had 101 inhabitants. From 1655 to 1709 the von Gabel family held the islands and the monopoly, a period known as Gablatíðin, when islanders complained of unjust treatment and fixed prices. A gunpowder explosion burned Tinganes in 1673, and smallpox in 1709 killed about 250 of some 300 inhabitants.

The town began to develop in the later 18th century, while Niels Ryberg ran the trade monopoly. From 1768 he carried on an entrepot trade, mostly smuggling to England, and he was the first to think of profiting from fishing, with salted cod and herring. Tórshavn Cathedral was first built in 1788 and partly rebuilt in 1865.

On 30 March 1808, during the Anglo-Danish Gunboat War, HMS Clio entered the harbour and the fort at Skansin surrendered without firing a shot. The trade monopoly was abolished in 1856, opening the islands to free trade and putting Tórshavn at the centre of a changed economy. Its town council was founded in 1866, and in 1909 it became a market town with the same charter as Danish ones.

Tórshavn is the capital and largest town of the Faroe Islands, on the east coast of Streymoy, with 14,223 inhabitants in 2024 and 22,444 in the greater urban area. Mountains rise to the northwest and southwest, separated by the Sandá River. It is the seat of the Faroese self-rule government, part of which still sits on Tinganes, and of the Løgting. Since 1990 it has been the seat of the Bishop of the Faroe Islands.
tortola: Tortola is a mountainous island of volcanic origin, 19 kilometres long and 5 kilometres wide, with an area of 55.7 square kilometres. Its highest peak is Mount Sage, at 530 metres, and it lies near an earthquake fault, so minor earthquakes are common. Road Town, on its south coast, is the capital of the British Virgin Islands. The name may be an anglicisation of the island's original Dutch name Ter-Tholen, after the Dutch island of Tholen; some sources say that Christopher Columbus named it Tortola, Spanish for turtle dove, while others say he called it Santa Ana.

On his second voyage Columbus sighted the Virgin Islands and named the archipelago after the 11,000 virgins of the martyr Saint Ursula. The Spanish made a few attempts to settle there, but pirates such as Blackbeard and Captain Kidd were the first permanent residents.

The English then established a plantation colony on Tortola and the surrounding islands, and large sugarcane plantations depended on the labour of enslaved Africans. Most early settlers came in the late 18th century, when Loyalists from the Thirteen Colonies received land grants from the Crown after the American Revolutionary War, bringing enslaved people who outnumbered the colonists. Sugar dominated the island's economy for more than a century.

After Britain abolished the international slave trade, the Royal Navy settled Africans freed from illegal slave ships at Kingstown on Tortola, where St Phillip's Church was built as one of the earliest free black churches in the Americas. After slavery was abolished in the British colonies in 1834, planters found it hard to make a profit from free labour, and competition from beet sugar added to the downturn. Many white landowners left, and an earthquake and tsunami struck in 1867.

Tortola is the largest and most populous of the British Virgin Islands, which are under the British flag but use the United States dollar as their official currency because of their trade with the neighbouring American islands. Financial services are a major part of the economy, and the International Business Companies Act of the early 1980s encouraged offshore companies.

In the late 1970s the activist Noel Lloyd led a protest that stopped a plan to lease a large part of the neighbouring island of Anegada for 199 years, and a park on Tortola is named for him. Hurricane Irma caused extensive damage across the islands in September 2017, most severely on Tortola.
tortona: Tortona stands on the right bank of the Scrivia, between the plain of Marengo and the foothills of the Ligurian Apennines, in the Province of Alessandria. It is the capital of the Colli Tortonesi, an area that stretches to the border with Liguria and is known for intensive wine production, including Barbera, Dolcetto, Moscato and Timorasso, the last tracing its origin to the 14th century. It is also the only place in Piedmont with three varieties of truffle.

The Romans knew the city as Dertona, probably their oldest colony in the westernmost section of the valley of the Po. It was founded about 123 to 118 BCE at the junction of the Via Postumia and the Via Aemilia Scauri, which merged to become the Via Julia Augusta, and so became an important military station on the road from Genua to Placentia. It seems to have been recolonised under Augustus, and some inscriptions give it the title Julia Dertona. Brutus encamped there while pursuing Mark Antony after the Battle of Mutina.

A bishopric was founded early. Until the 9th century the city was under the rule of its bishop, and in 1090 it became a free commune. In the Middle Ages it was a faithful ally of the Guelphs and was destroyed several times, notably by Frederick Barbarossa, who took it after a siege in 1155 and razed all its buildings. From 1260 to 1347 a series of Italian noble families and adventurers dominated the city, and in 1347 it was incorporated into the Duchy of Milan.

One of its lords, Facino Cane, left his lordships and wealth to his wife Beatrice, who married Filippo Maria Visconti. After the War of the Polish Succession the King of Sardinia occupied the city and count of Tortona was added to the titles of the House of Savoy.

The cathedral dates from the mid-16th century with a neoclassical façade added in the 19th, and the Bishops' Palace from 1584 has a Renaissance portal. The Romanesque Abbey of Santa Maria di Rivalta, in a hamlet nearby, was founded before 1151. Roman remains in the town are traditionally identified as the Mausoleum of the Emperor Maiorianus. Lorenzo Perosi, composer of church music and Perpetual Director of the Sistine Choir, and the cyclist Fausto Coppi were born in Tortona.
tortosa: Tortosa is the capital of the comarca of Baix Ebre in Catalonia, Spain, standing 12 metres above sea level beside the Ebro river. It is protected on its northern side by the mountains of the Cardó Massif, and across the river rise the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit, a limestone massif that has been inhabited since prehistoric times.

Tortosa, from Latin Dertosa and Arabic Ṭurṭūshah, is probably the ancient Hibera, capital of Ilercavonia, whose settlement may lie on the hill of the Castillo de la Zuda. In Roman times it lay on the Via Augusta. It was occupied about 714 in the Arab conquest of the Visigothic Kingdom and remained under Muslim rule for more than 400 years. King Louis the Pious besieged it in 808–809 and, although the city submitted, did not occupy it.

In 1148 Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona conquered the city as part of the Second Crusade. Following the appeal of Pope Eugene III, crusaders of many origins, among them Anglo-Normans, Occitans, Germans, Flemish and Dutch, aided the siege on their way to the Holy Land, and the chronicler Caffaro narrated it. The city and its territory were then divided among the victors, with lands granted to foreign crusaders and to the military and religious orders.

Tortosa had a sizable Jewish community in the 14th and 15th centuries. In 1413 and 1414, as an attempt to force conversion, Jews were made to defend their religion in the two-week Disputation of Tortosa, held in the cathedral.

The Castle of Sant Joan, or Suda, commands the city from a hill 59 metres high; the Romans first fortified the place, and the present structure dates to the caliph Abd ar-Rahman III. After 1148 it became a residence of the Montcada and the Knights Templar, and from the 13th century a royal mansion. The cathedral was begun in 1347 and consecrated in 1597. The Royal Schools, founded by Charles V for the education of the Moors, are a leading example of Renaissance civil architecture in Catalonia.
torun: Toruń stands on the Vistula in north-central Poland. Archaeologists date the first settlement near it to 1100 BCE, in the Lusatian culture, and there are few traces from the 5th century BCE to the 8th century CE. In the Roman period two settlements and a cemetery have been found, and a river crossing is visible near the village of Stary Toruń. It was first mentioned in 1226 as Thorun, and from the 15th century the form Thorn came into use.

From the 7th to the 13th century an old Slavonic settlement stood at a ford of the Vistula, on the site where the Teutonic Castle was later built. In the 10th century it became part of the emerging Polish state of the Piast dynasty and grew into a fortified stronghold, which was destroyed around the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries, most likely in a Prussian raid. The Teutonic Knights expanded the town in 1233. From 1264 until 1411 it belonged to the Hanseatic League, and by the 17th century it was a leading trading point, which shaped its architecture from Brick Gothic to Mannerist and Baroque.

Nicolaus Copernicus was born there in 1473. John I Albert, king of Poland, died there in 1501 and his heart was buried in St. John's Cathedral. Toruń became a royal city of Poland in 1506, and a royal mint began work in 1528. After the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 it was annexed by Prussia, was part of the Duchy of Warsaw from 1807 to 1815, serving as temporary capital in April and May 1809, and then returned to Prussia.

Under German rule it was a strong centre of Polish resistance to Germanisation, and the Toruń Scientific Society was founded in 1875. It became Polish again after the First World War, and German forces occupied it from 7 September 1939 to 1 February 1945, arresting, deporting and murdering many Poles, especially the Polish elites.

The city was spared bombing in the Second World War, and its Old Town and central marketplace are entirely preserved. The medieval part was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. It has the largest number of preserved Gothic houses in Poland, as well as the 14th-century cathedral, which holds the Tuba Dei, the largest medieval church bell in Poland. Nicolaus Copernicus University, founded in 1945, is the largest institution of higher education in the city.
totila: Totila was the name used by the Byzantine historian Procopius, who accompanied Belisarius during the Gothic War and is the main source for his life. His real name was Baduila, as his coinage shows. Marco Cristini has argued that the consistent use of Totila by Eastern Roman authors may have served a propagandistic purpose, encouraged by Justinian I to delegitimise him as a usurper. He was born in Treviso, a grandnephew of Theudis, king of the Visigoths, and a sword-bearer.

The Ostrogothic nobles elected him king in the autumn of 541, after the killing of Ildibad and then of Eraric, both slain by the Gothic nobility for attempting to surrender to the Romans. The official Byzantine position, adopted by Procopius and by the Romanized Goth Jordanes, was that he was a usurper, but according to Peter Heather he came from a prominent Gothic family.

In 542 Totila defended Verona and defeated a Roman army at the Battle of Faventia, then won at Mucellium, captured Naples in the spring of 543 on generous terms, and by 543 had retaken most of southern Italy. He won support from the lower classes by liberating slaves and distributing land to the peasants, though Cristini holds that Procopius exaggerated the slaves' part in his army. His strategy was to move fast and take the countryside, leaving Byzantine forces in well-defended cities and ports, and he collected rent and taxes instead of plundering. Procopius also records cruelties, including the beheading of Herculanus, bishop of Perugia, and the maiming of the captive general Demetrius.

Totila besieged Rome from December 545 and entered the practically empty city a year later, praying at St. Peter's Basilica. Belisarius dissuaded him from razing it, and retook it by April 546. After Belisarius retreated to Constantinople in 549, Totila recaptured Rome and went on to conquer Sicily, Corsica and Sardinia. A Byzantine fleet defeated his own in 551.

In 552 the eunuch Narses led a force including Lombards, Gepids and Heruls against him at the Battle of Taginae. Ordered to charge with spears alone, the Gothic cavalry rode into the crossfire of Narses's archers and broke. Procopius reports that a Gepid officer, Asbados, speared the fleeing king in the back, and that Totila died at a village called Caprae. A second account says a stray arrow struck him as he fled.

His successor Teia died at the Battle of Mons Lactarius. The Pragmatic Sanction of 554 voided Totila's edicts and called him a most abominable tyrant. Italy was so ravaged by the war that normal life could not return, and in 568 most of the country was conquered by Alboin of the Lombards.
tottori-prefecture: Tottori Prefecture lies in the Chūgoku region of Honshu and has an area of 3,507.13 square kilometres. It borders Shimane Prefecture to the west, Hiroshima to the south-west, Okayama to the south and Hyōgo to the east. Its capital and largest city is Tottori, and other major cities include Yonago, Kurayoshi and Sakaiminato.

The prefecture holds the Tottori Sand Dunes, the largest dune system in Japan, and Mount Daisen, at 1,729 metres the highest peak of the Chūgoku Mountains. The name combines the characters for bird and to get: early residents lived by catching the region's plentiful waterfowl. It first appears in the Nihon shoki, in an account of a swan given to a mute imperial prince.

People settled the area early, as remains from the Jōmon period show. The Mukibanda Yayoi remains, in the foothills of Mount Daisen, are the largest known Yayoi settlement in Japan, and many kofun tumuli date from the Kofun period. Under the Taika reforms of 645 the area became two provinces, Hōki and Inaba.

During the Genpei War of 1180–1185 Tottori was a base for forces opposed to the Taira, notably at the temples of Daisen-ji and Sanbutsu-ji. Successive clans, above all the Yamana, held the region in the Sengoku period. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 the Tokugawa shogunate installed the Ikeda clan at Tottori Castle, and the clan kept control through the Edo period.

The two provinces remained until the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the 20th century Tottori's harbours on the Sea of Japan served as a transit point for goods to Japan's colonial territories. The 1943 Tottori earthquake, of magnitude 7.2, destroyed 80 percent of the city of Tottori. Postwar land reform greatly increased agricultural output.

Tottori is the least populous prefecture of Japan, with about half a million people. It is heavily agricultural, producing nashi pears, nagaimo yams, Japanese scallions, watermelon and rice. Natural parks cover part of its area, including the Daisen-Oki and Sanin Kaigan National Parks. Sanbutsu-ji at Misasa, a Heian period temple, and the Ishitani Residence at Chizu, an Edo period family residence, are each designated a National Treasure of Japan. Sakaiminato Port offers a ferry route to Oki Island, and Sakaiminato's Kitarō Road honours the manga character created by Shigeru Mizuki.
touba: Touba began as a simple hamlet of Baol. Cheikh Amadou Bamba (1853 to 1927), the Sufi founder of the Mouride order, is said to have raised it to prominence when under a large tree there he experienced a cosmic vision of light. He founded Touba in 1887, and the holy site remained a small isolated place in the wilderness until his death and burial, 40 years later, at the site of the Great Mosque. The origin of the name is uncertain. The Encyclopaedia of Islam concludes that it most likely stems from a reference to tuba, blessing, and the name also matches that of a tree in Paradise in Islamic tradition.

Touba is a city in central Senegal, in Diourbel Region, forming an urban agglomeration with Mbacké. It had 1,120,824 inhabitants in 2023. It is the holy city of Mouridism, which Bamba conceived as having a social mission to return society to the Straight Path of Islam. Alcohol and tobacco are forbidden. The Grand Magal pilgrimage attracts around two million people each year, mostly Mourides.

The city is a sacred area with a quasi-extraterritorial status in Senegal, under the control of a general caliph and his helpers. The Great Mosque, completed in 1963 and enlarged since, has five minarets and three large domes; its central minaret, 87 metres high, is called Lamp Fall after Sheikh Ibrahima Fall, one of Bamba's disciples. Bamba is buried there, and nearby are the mausolea of his sons, the caliphs of the order.
toul: Toul was known to the Romans as Tullum Leucorum and was the capital of the Gaulish tribe of the Leuci. The diocese of Toul was founded around 365 and lasted until 1807, so the town was the seat of the bishops of Toul. In 550 King Theudebald convoked a synod here, and in 612 King Theudebert II of Austrasia was defeated near the town by King Theuderic II of Burgundy.

By the Treaty of Meerssen of 870 Toul became part of East Francia, the later Holy Roman Empire. In the High Middle Ages it became a Free Imperial City. King Henry II of France annexed it in 1552, and the Holy Roman Empire recognised this in the Peace of Westphalia of 1648. It then formed part of the French province of the Three Bishoprics.

In the siege of 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War, the last time Toul's defences were used as a classic fortress, 64 guns opened fire at 6:00 a.m. on 23 September. The fortress surrendered at 3:00 p.m. after 2,433 shells had been fired. In the First World War the town was the primary base of the Air Service of the United States Army, and the St. Mihiel Offensive and the Meuse-Argonne Offensive of September 1918 were launched from the Toul Sector.

Toul is a commune in the Meurthe-et-Moselle department and a sub-prefecture of it, between Commercy and Nancy, where the Moselle meets the Canal de la Marne au Rhin. The stone ramparts that encircle the old town are the work of Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban, Louis XIV's military engineer, who designed a new enclosure in 1698, with work beginning in 1699 to 1700. They are not on the UNESCO list of Vauban's fortifications. The old town has a major Gothic cathedral and many houses built as canonical residences in the Late Middle Ages. The surrounding countryside is a wine-growing region, known for the AOC Côtes de Toul and especially the Gris de Toul.
toulon: Toulon lies on the French Riviera at the eastern end of the Gulf of Lion, in the historical region of Provence. Greek colonists from Phocaea founded trading depots along this coast from about the 7th century BCE, and the Ligurians settled the area from the 4th century BCE. After the Romans defeated the Ligurians, a settlement named Telo Martius arose on the site of the city. It became one of the two principal Roman centres for the purple dye used in imperial robes, made from the murex sea snail.

Toulon was Christianized in the 5th century, and its first cathedral was built then. Pirates and Saracens attacked the town often as Roman power crumbled. Provence became part of France in 1486, and in 1494 Charles VIII of France began a military port at the harbour to make France a Mediterranean sea power. In 1524 Francis I completed the Tour Royale at the harbour entrance, but its commander sold it to an imperial commander and Toulon surrendered. In the winter of 1543 the fleet of the Ottoman admiral Barbarossa occupied the town, whose residents were made to leave, under the Franco-Ottoman alliance.

Toulon resisted a siege by the Imperial Army under Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy and Prince Eugene in 1707. In 1720 plague from Marseille killed about 13,000 people, half the population. In 1793 the city joined the Federalist revolts against the First Republic and handed itself and its fleet to the British; Republican forces forced them out, and the town was briefly renamed Port-la-Montagne. From 1803 to 1805 a fleet under Horatio Nelson blockaded the port. In 1849 Georges Eugène Haussmann, then prefect of the Var, laid out the street plan of the city centre. On 27 November 1942 French naval officers scuttled the fleet based there, after German forces occupied southern France, and Allied bombing the following November destroyed much of the port.

Toulon is the prefecture of the Var department and has 179,116 inhabitants in 2023, with a metropolitan area of 591,135. It is the third most populous French city on the Mediterranean, after Marseille and Nice. Its military port is the chief naval centre of France's Mediterranean coast, and the city also has shipbuilding, fishing, winemaking and several manufacturing industries. The University of Toulon opened in 1979.
toulouse: Toulouse lies on the banks of the Garonne, 150 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, 230 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean and 680 kilometres from Paris, on the axis of communication between the two seas. The Garonne valley has been a central point for trade between the Pyrenees, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic since at least the Iron Age. The historical name of the city, Tolosa, and that of its inhabitants, the Tolosates, first recorded in the 2nd century BCE, is of unknown meaning or origin, and has been connected with the Gaulish Volcae Tectosages and, by others, with a root meaning little hill.

Charlemagne created the county of Toulouse in 778 to guard the border of Muslim Spain. The disintegration of the kingdom of Aquitaine and the weakness of royal power in the following centuries led to the de facto independence of the county. The treaty of 1229 made Toulouse subordinate to the kingdom of France, and when Joan of Toulouse and her husband Alphonse of Poitiers died without heirs in 1271 the city had no count and was annexed to the royal domain. Royal officers settled in the city, trade and crafts grew, and in 1298 King Philip the Fair eased the ennobling of the capitouls, whose annually renewed council was increasingly made up of rich merchants.

The University of Toulouse was founded in 1229. In the 16th century the woad trade brought merchants of international stature to the city, and the Parlement of Toulouse made it the judicial capital of much of the south of France.

On 10 April 1814 Wellington's Hispanic-British troops fought the French under Marshal Soult at the Battle of Toulouse, four days after Napoleon's surrender, though neither army yet knew of it; it was the last Franco-British battle on French territory. In the First World War the city, sheltered from attack, gained chemical industries and aviation workshops, which began its aeronautical tradition and gave rise to the airmail company Aéropostale.

Toulouse is the prefecture of the Haute-Garonne department and of the Occitania region, with 514,819 inhabitants within its municipal boundaries in 2023. Its architecture of pinkish terracotta brick has earned it the name La Ville rose. The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, the largest remaining Romanesque building in Europe, and the former hospital Hôtel-Dieu Saint-Jacques are World Heritage Sites for their place on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, as is the Canal du Midi, which begins in the city. Toulouse is the centre of the European aerospace industry, with the headquarters of Airbus, and its rugby club, Stade Toulousain, is among the most successful in Europe.
tournai: Tournai lies on the river Scheldt in the Province of Hainaut, 89 kilometres by road south-west of Brussels. In Roman times it was a place of minor importance, a stopping place where the road from Cologne to Boulogne crossed the Scheldt. It was fortified under Emperor Maximian in the 3rd century CE, when the Roman limes was withdrawn to a string of outposts along the road. The Salian Franks took it in 432, and under King Childeric I it was the capital of the Frankish realm. In 486 Clovis moved the centre of power to Paris.

After the partition of the Frankish Empire, Tournai stayed in the western part, which became France in 987. It joined the 11th-century rise of towns in the Low Countries on a woollen cloth industry, and the rebuilding of its cathedral began in 1030. The commune won independence from the local counts in 1187 and was thereafter directly subject to the French Crown. In 1340 Edward III of England besieged it for a month without success, which bankrupted him and forced the Truce of Espléchin. In the 15th century it was a major supplier of tapestry, and the painters Jacques Daret, Robert Campin and Rogier van der Weyden came from Tournai.

Henry VIII of England captured the city in 1513, making it the only Belgian city ever ruled by England, and it returned to France in 1519 after the Treaty of London. In 1521 Charles V added it to his Low Countries possessions. Tournai became a bulwark of Calvinism in the 16th century, until the Duke of Parma conquered it after a long siege in 1581. The Spanish Netherlands, including Tournai, passed to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1713, and France annexed the region in 1794. From 1815 the city formed part of the United Netherlands and after 1830 of Belgium. It was badly damaged in 1940 and has since been restored.

The mixed Romanesque and Gothic Cathedral of Our Lady and the Belfry, considered the oldest in Belgium, are World Heritage Sites. The cathedral holds the Châsse de Notre-Dame flamande, a 12th-century reliquary. The Bishopric of Tournai was the religious capital of Flanders from 496 to 1559. The Grande Procession, begun by Bishop Radbot II during a plague, has been held every year since 1092 except 1566. French is the dominant language, and the municipality had an estimated 68,518 people in 2022.
tours: In Gallic times Tours was an important crossing of the Loire. It became part of the Roman Empire in the 1st century and was named Caesarodunum, meaning hill of Caesar; by the 4th century the name had changed from Turones to Civitas Turonum and then Tours, and the Tours Amphitheatre was built. Around 380 to 388 it became a metropolis of the Roman province of Lugdunum, dominating Maine, Brittany and the Loire Valley. Its bishop Saint Martin, who shared his coat with a naked beggar at Amiens, made the city a major centre of the medieval West on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela.

In the 6th century Gregory of Tours, author of the Ten Books of History, restored a cathedral destroyed by fire in 561, and Saint Martin's monastery received patronage from the Frankish king Clovis I. In the 9th century Alcuin of York, a book collector and abbot of Marmoutier Abbey, made the city a heart of the Carolingian Renaissance. In 732 Abdul Rahman Al Ghafiqi's army from Al-Andalus, having advanced 500 km into France, was stopped by Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours. Tours repelled a Viking attack by Haesten in 845, but the Vikings sacked it in 852.

Medieval Tours had two competing centres: the City in the east, with the cathedral and the castle of the Counts of Tours, and in the west Châteauneuf around the Abbey of Saint Martin, which became the economic centre after its enclosure around 918. The two were joined in the 14th century. Touraine was disputed between the counts of Blois and Anjou, and Anjou won in the 11th century.

Under Louis XI, who lived at the castle of Montils, Tours was the capital of France, and he introduced the silk industry, which still survives. The kings and court stayed in Touraine until the 16th century, and the Renaissance left the private mansions and châteaux of the Loire. Protestants were imprisoned by the aldermen in the Wars of Religion, which prevented their massacre.

Tours is the largest city of Centre-Val de Loire and the prefecture of Indre-et-Loire, with 138,668 inhabitants in 2022. From 10 to 13 June 1940 it was the temporary seat of the French government, and German incendiary bombs then burned part of the city centre from 20 to 22 June. Its historical centre is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
toussaint-louverture: Louverture was born into slavery in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the eldest son of Hyppolite, a slave from Allada on the slave coast of West Africa, and his second wife Pauline, who was of the Aja ethnic group. He was a devout Catholic and gained some education from his godfather Pierre-Baptiste on the Bréda plantation. Until 1938 historians believed he had been enslaved until the revolution began. A marriage certificate and baptismal record of 1776 to 1777 then showed that he had been freed between 1772 and 1776.

As a free man he worked as a salaried overseer on his former master's plantation and became a slave owner himself, with several coffee plantations. In 1782 he married his second wife, Suzanne Simone-Baptiste. He later told General Caffarelli that he had fathered at least sixteen children.

When the revolution began he was nearly 50, and he started as a lieutenant to Georges Biassou, a leader of the 1791 slave revolt. He allied first with the Spanish of neighbouring Santo Domingo. He then switched to the French when the Republican government moved to abolish slavery in its colonies. Historians debate the timing and his motives: C. L. R. James held that he joined the French on learning of the emancipation decree, while Thomas Ott sees him as both a power-seeker and a sincere abolitionist.

The third commission's Sonthonax promoted him to general. Toussaint negotiated the British withdrawal and trade agreements with the United Kingdom and the United States, and in 1799 he fought a civil war against the southern general André Rigaud. That War of the South lasted more than a year, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who led much of the campaign, became infamous for massacring mulatto captives and civilians. Estimates of the dead range from a few hundred to 10,000.

On 7 July 1801 he promulgated a constitution that made him governor-general for life with near absolute powers, which challenged Napoleon Bonaparte's authority. He restored the plantation system using paid labour.

Napoleon sent troops under his brother-in-law General Charles Emmanuel Leclerc to take the island. In 1802 Louverture was invited to a parley by General Jean-Baptiste Brunet and arrested on arrival. He was deported to France and jailed at the Fort de Joux, where he died. His wife Suzanne was deported to Jamaica and died there in 1816.

Dessalines led the revolution to its end. The final major battle was fought at Vertières on 18 November 1803, and independence was declared on 1 January 1804 under the name Haiti, from the Taíno Ayiti. Louverture is known with Dessalines as one of the Fathers of Haiti, and in the 19th century African Americans cited him as an example of how to reach freedom. John Brown claimed to be influenced by him.
tower-of-belem: In the late 15th century King John II planned a defence system for the mouth of the Tagus, but he died before any plans were drawn for a strong fort. King Manuel I revisited the proposal twenty years later and ordered a military fortification on the northern bank at Belém. The architect Francisco de Arruda was named master of the works, and in 1516 he began to receive blocks of stone, partly from those collected for the Monastery of Santa Maria de Belém.

The tower was built of lioz limestone on a basalt outcrop on a small island near the shore, and was finished in 1519. Gaspar de Paiva was appointed its first Captain-General in 1521, and the fortress was named the Castle of St Vincent, after the patron saint of Lisbon.

The tower served as a point of embarkation and disembarkation for Portuguese explorers and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon. In 1580 its garrison surrendered to Spanish forces under the Duke of Alba after a few hours of battle, and its dungeons served as a prison until 1830. In 1655 an inscription records its function as a customs control point, where ships paid a tax on entering the harbour. French troops were quartered in it from 1808 to 1814, and King Miguel I imprisoned his liberal opponents there. In 1845–46 renovations demolished the Philippine barracks built over the bastion in the late 16th century.

The tower is a principal work of the Manueline style, with elaborate rib vaulting, crosses of the Order of Christ, armillary spheres and twisted rope, while its minarets reflect Moorish influence. It consists of a hexagonal bastion with spaces for 17 cannons and a four-storey tower about 30 metres high. A carved rhinoceros recalls the animal sent to Manuel by an Indian ruler.

It has often been stated that the tower once stood in the middle of the Tagus and was left near the shore when the 1755 earthquake redirected the river, but it was built on a small island near the bank. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 together with the Jerónimos Monastery, and was added to the Seven Wonders of Portugal in 2007.
tower-of-hercules: The tower is known to have existed by the 1st century CE. It was built, or perhaps rebuilt, by Emperor Trajan, possibly on foundations following a design of Phoenician origin and based on the plans of the Lighthouse of Alexandria. A cornerstone at its base is inscribed to Mars and names the architect Gaius Sevius Lupus, from Aeminium (present-day Coimbra, Portugal) in the province of Lusitania, who made it as an offering to the god.

Until the 20th century the tower was known as the Farum Brigantium, and farum derives from the Greek Pharos. The earliest known reference to the lighthouse at Brigantium is by Paulus Orosius, in his Historiae adversum Paganos written around 415 to 417, who calls it a very tall lighthouse set up to look towards Britannia.

The lighthouse stands on a peninsula about 2.4 kilometres from the centre of A Coruña, overlooking the Atlantic coast. It is 55 metres tall: 34 metres of surviving Roman masonry and 21 metres added in the restoration. The original tower was shorter and wider, since its core was surrounded by a spiral ramp, whose outline is still visible in the restored exterior. The final storey was probably topped with a dome.

In the 18th century the naval engineer Eustaquio Giannini restored the surviving core and built a new fourth storey. UNESCO has called the restoration exemplary, praising the protection of the central core of the Roman monument alongside its return to working condition. Within, the much-repaired Roman and medieval masonry remains visible. The Romans who conquered this region believed it to be the end of the Earth, hence the name Finisterra, and the coast is notorious for shipwrecks, earning it the name Costa da Morte.

Many myths of the lighthouse's origin have been told. In one, mixing Celtic and Greco-Roman elements, Hercules slew the giant Geryon after three days and three nights of battle, buried his head with his weapons and ordered a city built on the site. A skull and crossbones beneath the lighthouse appear in the coat of arms of A Coruña. Another legend, from the Irish Lebor Gabála Érenn, has King Breogán build a tower so high that his sons saw a green shore from it and sailed north to Ireland.

In the Middle Ages crusader fleets bound for the Holy Land stopped there, often landing to walk to the shrine of James the Greater at Santiago de Compostela. Some texts spread the belief that Julius Caesar built it, perhaps from a misreading of the ancient inscription. The tower is a National Monument of Spain and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 27 June 2009. A sculpture garden on its grounds has works by Pablo Serrano and Francisco Leiro.
town-musicians-of-bremen: The Brothers Grimm first published the tale in the second edition of Kinder- und Hausmärchen in 1819, where it is number 27, basing it on the account of the German storyteller Dorothea Viehmann, who lived from 1755 to 1815. Contrary to the title, the characters never arrive in Bremen. The tale is classified in the Aarne-Thompson-Uther Index as type ATU 130, The Animals in Night Quarters, and the folklorists Stith Thompson and Barre Toelken see a deep relation between it and type ATU 210, which concerns a cock, hen, duck, pin and needle on a journey.

Four ageing domestic animals, a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster, are neglected, mistreated or marked for death by their masters. They set out together for Bremen, a city known for its freedom, to live without owners and become musicians. On the way they see a cottage with light in the windows, where three robbers are enjoying their ill-gotten gains. Standing on each other's backs, the animals perform their first song, and the robbers run away in fright. The animals eat a meal in the house and settle down for the night, the donkey outside, the dog by the door, the cat on the mantle and the rooster in the loft.

The robbers return, and one goes back to check. He mistakes the cat's shining eyes for coals, and the cat scratches him, the dog bites his leg, the donkey kicks him and the rooster crows in his ear. He tells the others that he was attacked by a witch, a monster with a knife, a giant with a club and a judge calling from the rooftop. The robbers abandon the cottage, and the animals live there happily for the rest of their days.

Several variants exist. In a version said to date from the 12th century the robbers are a brown bear, a lion and a grey wolf, all animals of heraldry, and the townsfolk of Bremen applaud the donkey and his friends for ridding the district of them. In another variant the animals return the stolen wealth to their master so that he can rebuild. The folklorist Antti Aarne proposed an Asian origin for the tale type, and Paul Delarue distinguished a Western form, in which the animals are domestic, from an Eastern one with inferior animals, popular in Japan, China, Korea, Melanesia and Indonesia.
toyotomi-hideyoshi: According to tradition, Hideyoshi was born on 17 March 1537 in Nakamura in Owari Province.
