He had no traceable samurai lineage, and his father Kinoshita Yaemon was an ashigaru, a peasant employed by samurai as a foot soldier, who died in 1543. His childhood name was Hiyoshimaru. Contemporary writings confirm his poor background, and one notes that he had begged in the streets. In 1558 he became an ashigaru of the Oda clan under Oda Nobunaga and soon his sandal-bearer, a position of relatively high status. In 1561 he married Nene, the adopted daughter of Asano Nagakatsu.

Nobunaga and his eldest son were killed in the Honnō-ji incident on 21 June 1582. Hideyoshi made peace with the Mōri clan and defeated the assassin Akechi Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki on 2 July. He then destroyed Shibata Katsuie's forces at the Battle of Shizugatake and fought Tokugawa Ieyasu to a stalemate at Komaki and Nagakute in 1584. He never took the title of shōgun. Instead he was adopted by Konoe Sakihisa of the Fujiwara and became kampaku, imperial regent, in 1585 and daijō-daijin, chancellor, in 1586, when the court gave him the clan name Toyotomi.

He took Shikoku in 1585 and Kyūshū in 1587, where 200,000 soldiers faced about 30,000 Shimazu. He completed the unification at the Siege of Odawara in 1590, during which Ieyasu accepted the eight Hōjō provinces of the Kantō in exchange for his own five. He began Osaka Castle in 1583. He disarmed the peasants, required samurai to live in castle towns, and ordered surveys of land and production. In July 1587 the Bateren Edict ordered Christian missionaries out of Japan.

His only son Tsurumatsu died in September 1591, and in January 1592 Hideyoshi adopted his nephew Hidetsugu and made him kampaku, taking the title of taikō himself. In April 1592 he sent an army to Korea, aiming at the conquest of Ming China. Konishi Yukinaga took Seoul on 19 June, but the war settled into stalemate.

Peace talks collapsed in 1596 when a forged memorial came to light, and a second invasion in 1597 had less success. Hideyoshi died at Fushimi Castle on 18 September 1598, and the Council of Five Elders kept his death secret and ordered the troops home. His young son Hideyori was displaced by Tokugawa Ieyasu at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, which led to the Tokugawa shogunate.
traben-trarbach: Traben-Trarbach lies on the Middle Moselle in the Bernkastel-Wittlich district of Rhineland-Palatinate, some 40 kilometres north-east of Trier and 60 kilometres south-west of Koblenz. Traben stands on the left bank at the foot of the former fort of Mont Royal and stretches in a broad strip along the river. Trarbach lies on the right bank, on the Hunsrück side, and reaches inland between steep mountains up the Kautenbach valley. The municipal area of 31.35 square kilometres, largely wooded, makes it the biggest town by land area on the Middle Moselle. The name Traben comes from a Celtic word, Traven, meaning a small settlement.

The Aachener Hof, an estate at Traben, was mentioned as early as 830, when Emperor Louis the Pious donated Traben with its rights to the minster at Aachen. Trarbach was the main centre of the Hintere, or Rear, County of Sponheim, and after the comital family died out the inheriting landholders made it a Palatine-Badish condominium; Trarbach was also the seat of a Palatine Oberamt. The Grevenburg, built about 1350, was destroyed in 1734 after many sieges. Because the county belonged to the Reformation, the town remained mainly Evangelical.

France seized the area in the War of the Reunions of 1683 to 1684, and at Traben Vauban built the fortress of Mont-Royal. Its main ramparts were 30 metres high and 3 kilometres long, with room for 12,000 troops. It was demolished when the French withdrew after the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, and only its lower foundations remain. The area around Trarbach was annexed to Prussia in 1816, although Zell, not Trarbach, was made the district seat. The two towns were among the first municipalities in Germany to install electric street lighting from the Edison Company, and in 1904 Traben and Trarbach merged into the town of Traben-Trarbach.

The bridge built between the two centres to plans by Bruno Möhring was the first road bridge between Bernkastel and Koblenz and was blown up in 1945, and Möhring also designed the Brückentor and several houses in the town. The Mittelmoselmuseum covers the history of the Moselle valley, the County of Sponheim, Mont Royal and the Grevenburg. Traben-Trarbach is a state-recognized climatic spa, seat of the Verbandsgemeinde of the same name, and home to many wineries.
trabzon: The city stands on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Turkey, on a table-like central hill between the Zağnos (İskeleboz) and Kuzgun streams. The Greek name Trapezous refers to this hill, since the word τράπεζα meant table in Ancient Greek. Before the Greek colony was founded the area was dominated by Colchian and Chaldian tribes, and Greek authors later mentioned the Macrones and the Chalybes as native peoples. The Pontic Mountains rise behind the coast, and the province's total area is 4,685 square kilometres.

The city was founded in 756 BCE as Trapezous by Greeks from Miletus. It was added to the Achaemenid Empire by Cyrus the Great, later belonged to the Kingdom of Pontus, which challenged Rome until 68 BCE, and then passed to the Roman and Byzantine empires. In the time of Justinian I it served as an important base in his Persian Wars, and an inscription above its eastern gate recorded the rebuilding of the walls at his expense after an earthquake. Its university, the Pandidakterion, was re-established before the 7th century and drew students from Armenia as well.

The Empire of Trebizond formed after a Georgian expedition into Chaldia, commanded by Alexios Komnenos a few weeks before the sack of Constantinople in 1204. It was the longest surviving of the Byzantine successor states. Byzantine writers connected with the Lascaris and later the Palaiologos regarded its rulers as not true emperors. The last emperor, David, surrendered the city to Sultan Mehmed II in 1461, and Mehmed sent many Turkish settlers into the area, though the Greek, Laz and Armenian communities remained.

Under the Ottomans the city was a sanjak centre and then part of several provinces. Ottoman tax books of 1523 show that about 85 percent of the population was Christian, mostly Greek, with an Armenian community making up thirteen percent of adult men. In July 1915, during the Armenian genocide, most adult male Armenians of the city were marched south in five convoys and never seen again.

Trabzon is the capital of Trabzon Province and the second largest city and port on the Black Sea coast of Turkey. Its Byzantine Hagia Sophia, now a mosque, is probably its most important sight. From 1683 to 1921 the Phrontisterion of Trapezous, a teachers' college, operated here and helped spread Greek education across the region; its 1902 building survives. Karadeniz Technical University is in the city, and the horon is the dance of the area.
tractor: The word tractor comes from the Latin trahere, to pull, and the earliest recorded use for an engine or vehicle that pulls wagons or ploughs dates from 1896, from the earlier term traction motor of 1859. The first powered farm machines of the early 19th century were portable steam engines on wheels that drove other machinery through a flexible belt. Richard Trevithick designed a semi-portable barn engine in 1812 to drive a corn threshing machine, and William Tuxford of Boston, Lincolnshire, invented a truly portable engine in 1839.

The first gasoline tractors were built in Illinois by John Charter in 1889, combining single-cylinder Otto engines with a Rumely steam engine chassis. John Froelich built another in Clayton County, Iowa, in 1892 and started the Waterloo Gasoline Engine Company, but the venture failed and he was out of business by 1895.

A tractor is designed to deliver high tractive effort at slow speeds, for hauling a trailer or machinery. The earliest, called standard tractors, were meant almost only for ploughing and harrowing, which were difficult tasks for people and draft animals. Implements were first attached by a drawbar, a steel bar to which the implement's hitch was pinned, so the tractor could be used for other tasks daily. Harry Ferguson later developed the three-point hitch, which lets hydraulics raise and lower the equipment. From the 1910s to the 1950s farm mechanics in the United States often converted automobiles, especially Ford Model Ts, into tractors, and dozens of firms sold conversion kits.

Economic historians have called the farm tractor one of the most revolutionary technological innovations in the history of modern agriculture, which vastly increased farm power, raised productivity and reshaped the rural landscape. Adoption met resistance. There were 500 gas tractors in the United States in 1910 and nearly 5,000 in 1920, when 3.6 per cent of American farms had one. The share reached 13.5 per cent by the end of the 1920s and rose to 40 per cent during the Great Depression. By 1935 nearly a million tractors were in use in the United States, against 15,000 in Germany. In the 1910s and 1920s the Nebraska tests, run by the University of Nebraska, helped farmers see through marketing claims.
trail-of-tears: In 1830 the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee and Seminole nations, later grouped as the Five Civilized Tribes, were living autonomously in what would become the American Deep South. Many of their people had become integrated into the regional economy, including the plantation economy and the holding of slaves, who were also forcibly relocated during the removal. American settlers pressed the federal government to remove them, some encroaching on their lands and others wanting more land made available.

President Andrew Jackson, who made removal his top legislative priority, won passage of the Indian Removal Act of 1830, which authorised the government to extinguish Indian title to land claims in the Southeast. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) the Supreme Court held that the Cherokee were not a sovereign and independent nation. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) it ruled that the Cherokee Nation was subject only to federal law, not to the laws of Georgia.

The Choctaw were the first to sign a removal treaty, the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, ratified in early 1831. The Seminole were called to Payne's Landing in 1832; most of their chiefs later renounced the agreement, and in December 1835 Seminoles and Black allies ambushed a US Army company, killing all but three of 110 soldiers. The Muscogee had already lost most of their Georgia lands by the Treaty of Indian Springs of 1825. The Chickasaw were paid for their lands and moved from 1837, merging with the Choctaw nation in Indian Territory.

By 1838 about 2,000 Cherokee had gone voluntarily. Forcible removal began in May 1838, when General Winfield Scott received the order to relocate the remaining Cherokee, enforcing the Treaty of New Echota, which the elected tribal leadership and a majority of the Cherokee never accepted. The people were gathered into camps in groups often over 700, where disease spread quickly. The marchers faced extortion, violence, exposure and starvation, and approximately 4,000 Cherokee died.

In all, about 60,000 people were displaced between 1830 and 1850. Exposure, disease and insufficient rations killed up to one-third of the Choctaw and other nations on the march. Historians and the affected nations debate whether the name should cover the whole history of removals or the Cherokee removal alone, and historians classify the events variously as ethnic cleansing or as genocide.

In the Cherokee language the event is called the place where they cried. In 1987 federal law authorised about 3,500 km of trails, the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, to mark the removal of 17 detachments of the Cherokee. In 1905 the Court of Claims ruled in favour of the Eastern Cherokee Nation's claim, and 1 million dollars was appropriated for eligible individuals and families.
trajan: Trajan was born Marcus Ulpius Traianus at Italica, a Roman colony in Hispania Baetica, near present-day Seville, to a family that came from Tuder in Umbria. His father, of the same name, was a general and distinguished senator who governed Syria in 76 and 77, when Trajan served there as a tribune. In 89 Trajan, commanding a legion in Hispania Tarraconensis, supported Domitian against a revolt on the Rhine led by Antonius Saturninus. He then governed Germania and Pannonia. The elderly and childless Nerva was unpopular with the army, and in the summer of 97 he named Trajan his adoptive son and successor. Some contemporary sources hint that the adoption was imposed on him.

Trajan's entry into Rome in 99 was understated. He gave the people a gift of money but halved the donative to the troops. By showing reluctance to hold power he built a consensus in the Senate, and Pliny the Younger praised him as a ruler who governed by example rather than fear. The Senate gave him the title optimus princeps. He rebuilt the Circus Maximus in stone by 103 and, with the architect Apollodorus of Damascus, built a great bridge over the Danube. He also formalised the alimenta, which supported orphans and poor children in Italy from Dacian war booty, estate taxes and gifts.

In letters to Pliny about the Christians of Pontus he ruled that anonymous denunciations were not to be accepted, though those who admitted the faith and refused to recant were to be executed. He overcame the Dacian king Decebalus, annexed the Nabataean kingdom after Rabbel II's death in 106, and from 113 fought Parthia over Armenia. A Jewish uprising in the eastern provinces in 116 and 117 forced him to withdraw his army.

Trajan fell ill early in 117, sailed for Italy and died at Selinus shortly before 11 August. Tradition places his ashes in the small chamber at the base of Trajan's Column. Dio reports that his wife Pompeia Plotina secured Hadrian's succession by hiding his death until a document of adoption was signed, a story that may rest on rumour. Ancient sources on Trajan are unanimously positive, and in the fourth century emperors were hailed as more fortunate than Augustus and better than Trajan.
trajans-column: Trajan's Column stands in Trajan's Forum, north of the Roman Forum, and commemorates the emperor's victory in the Dacian Wars. It was probably built under the supervision of the architect Apollodorus of Damascus at the order of the Roman Senate, and was completed and dedicated on 12 May 113. It was placed at the northern end of the forum, between two libraries, one for Greek and one for Latin scrolls, and beside the Basilica Ulpia. The Latin library probably held Trajan's own lost account of the Dacian Wars, the Dacica, which many scholars think the sculpted spiral was meant to echo.

The shaft rises from a large pedestal and is hollow: a spiral staircase of 185 steps, lit by 43 window slits, leads to a viewing platform. The frieze winds 23 times round the shaft from base to capital and was an architectural innovation. Its lower half shows the first Dacian war, of 101 to 102, and its upper half the second, of 105 to 106. A personification of Victory writing on a shield separates the two. Repeated scenes show the emperor addressing the army, sacrificing, and the army setting out, while battle scenes are a minority.

Key episodes include the crossing of the Danube, Trajan's voyage up the river, the Dacian surrender at the end of the first war, the assault on the Dacian capital and the death of the Dacian king Decebalus. The relief shows Roman and Dacian arms, forts, ships and costume in detail, and Trajan himself appears 58 times. Some scholars suggest the emphasis on orderly soldiers and construction was meant to reassure the people of Rome, its main audience, about the army.

After Trajan's death in 117 the Senate voted to place his ashes in a chamber in the base, which is decorated with captured Dacian arms; the ashes of his wife Plotina were set there too, in golden urns that later disappeared. His statue on top vanished in the Middle Ages, and on 4 December 1587 Pope Sixtus V crowned the column with a bronze figure of Saint Peter, which remains.

The design inspired later victory columns, among them those of Marcus Aurelius, Arcadius in Constantinople and the Colonne Vendôme in Paris. Its inscription, among the best-known examples of Roman square capitals, is the basis of the typeface Trajan, designed in 1989. Plaster casts of the relief made in the 19th and 20th centuries, now shown in museums in Rome, Bucharest and London, are in some details more legible than the original.
trakai: Trakai lies 28 kilometres west of Vilnius. About 200 lakes lie in the region, the deepest being Galvė with its 21 islands. Trakai Historical National Park was founded on 23 April 1991 to preserve Trakai as a centre of Lithuanian statehood as well as the park's authentic nature. The name was first recorded in 1337, in the chronicles of the Teutonic Knights, and is derived from the Lithuanian word trakai, meaning glades. In Polish the town is called Troki, and the surname Trotsky, adopted by Leon Trotsky as a pseudonym, comes from the name.

According to a legend, Grand Duke Gediminas found a beautiful lake-surrounded place after a hunting party and built a castle at Senieji Trakai, Old Trakai. The year 1337 is considered the official date of the city's foundation. When Gediminas settled in Vilnius, Senieji Trakai passed to his son Kęstutis, who moved the town to its present site. There he built the Peninsula Castle and the Island Castle, and a village grew around them. Both wooden castles were raided several times by the Teutonic Knights.

In 1382 Jogaila tricked Kęstutis and imprisoned him in Kreva, where he died, and the castles went to Jogaila's brother Skirgaila. Vytautas and the Teutonic Knights captured the town in 1383. After the Astrava Agreement of 1392 Vytautas became Grand Duke and regained his father's lands. Although his official capital was Vilnius, Vytautas spent more time in Trakai, and in the early 15th century he replaced the wooden fortress with a stone castle.

In 1409 the town received Magdeburg Rights, and Vytautas made it the capital of Lithuania and moved the State Treasury and the Lithuanian Metrica there. In 1413 it became the seat of the Trakai Voivodeship. After the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was formed in 1569 its importance declined. Sigismund I the Old made the castle a summer residence, but after his death in 1548 it fell into disrepair. Russian forces plundered the town and demolished both castles during the war of 1654 to 1667.

Karaims, a small Turkic-speaking people, were resettled in Trakai by Vytautas in 1397 and 1398 from Crimea, after a campaign against the Golden Horde, and the town remained a centre of Karaim cultural and religious life. Their wooden kenesa, with an interior dome, survives, and the pastry kibinai has become a local speciality.

Historically Lithuanians, Poles, Russians, Jews, Tatars and Karaims lived there together. The Island Castle was reconstructed in stages: the Polish authorities ordered restoration in 1929, work halted in the early 1960s, and it was completed in the early 1990s. A history museum was established in the castle in 1962, and concerts and festivals take place there in summer.
tralee: Tralee, in Irish Trá Lí, formerly Tráigh Lí, meaning strand of the River Lee, is the county town of County Kerry and the largest town in the county. It stands on the northern side of the neck of the Dingle Peninsula, at the confluence of some small rivers and next to marshy ground at the head of Tralee Bay. It lies at the foot of an ancient roadway that heads south over the Slieve Mish Mountains. On this old track stands a large boulder known as Scotia's Grave, reputedly the burial place of an ancient queen.

Anglo-Normans founded the town in the 13th century, and it became a stronghold of the Earls of Desmond, who built Tralee Castle. John Fitz-Thomas FitzGerald founded a Dominican monastery and was buried there in 1260. The medieval town was burnt in 1580 in retribution for the Desmond Rebellions against Elizabeth I. In 1587 she granted Tralee to Edward Denny, and it received a royal charter in 1613 under James I, with the right to elect two members of parliament. The Dennys occupied the Desmond castle only from 1627.

The modern layout dates from the 19th century. Denny Street, a wide Georgian street, was completed in 1826 on the site of the old castle, and the courthouse was built in 1834. The Tralee Ship Canal was built to replace the silting quay at Blennerville, and it opened in 1846 but soon silted itself. Fenit Harbour was built as a deepwater port in the 1880s. The Tralee and Dingle Light Railway opened in 1891 and closed in 1953.

Tralee saw much violence in 1919–1923. In November 1920 the Black and Tans besieged the town in revenge for the killing of two Royal Irish Constabulary men, and near-famine conditions were reported by the end of the week. In August 1922 Free State troops landed at Fenit and took Tralee from the anti-Treaty garrison. In March 1923 nine prisoners were killed by a land mine at nearby Ballyseedy.

Tralee is known for the Rose of Tralee International Festival, held annually in August since 1959 and inspired by a 19th-century ballad about a woman named Mary. The Kerry County Museum, in the Ashe Memorial Hall built in 1928, includes a reconstruction of medieval Geraldine Tralee in 1450. Ratass Church, a tenth-century medieval church with a sixth-century ogham stone, lies in the eastern suburbs. The Dingle Way, a trail of 162 kilometres, begins and ends in Tralee.
trans-siberian-railway: In the late 19th century Siberia's development was hampered by poor transport. Apart from the Great Siberian Route, roads suitable for wheeled traffic were rare, and for about five months of the year rivers were the main means of travel, with horse-drawn sledges over frozen winter roads. Steamboats appeared on the Ob in 1844, but the river systems ran mostly north to south, making west to east transport difficult.

The first Siberian railway projects emerged after the Saint Petersburg–Moscow Railway opened in 1851, among them a proposal by the American entrepreneur Perry Collins. The central government largely ignored them before 1880, and the design of the line then took ten years. On 9 March 1891 the government issued an imperial rescript announcing a railway across Siberia, and Tsarevich Nicholas, later Nicholas II, inaugurated construction at Vladivostok on 19 May that year.

The line was divided into seven sections worked on at once by 62,000 workers, with an estimated cost of £35 million. To save money and avoid disputes with landowners it was laid outside existing cities: the railway crossed the Ob at Novonikolaevsk, later Novosibirsk, 70 kilometres south of Tomsk, which got only a dead-end branch. Lake Baikal was crossed by the ice-breaking train ferry SS Baikal, built in 1897 at Newcastle upon Tyne, until the Circum-Baikal Railway was completed in 1904. The Amur River line, finished in 1916, made the railway continuous from Petrograd to Vladivostok.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905 exposed the limits of a single-track line, where trains waited in sidings to pass one another; this limited capacity and contributed to Russia's defeat. After 1917 the railway was the main line of communication for the Czechoslovak Legion and the Allied forces in the Siberian Intervention. The whole length was double-tracked by 1939.

Siberian grain began moving west on the railway, and from 1896 to 1913 Siberia exported on average about 501,932 metric tons of grain and flour a year. Between 1906 and 1914 about four million peasants migrated to Siberia from western Russia and Ukraine. The historian Christian Wolmar judges the railway a failure, built for narrow political reasons and to a deficient standard, with flimsy rails and rotting ties; others stress the commercial and political importance of its Manchurian section, the Chinese Eastern Railway.

In the Second World War the railway carried Soviet industry eastward from 1941 and, after Germany invaded the Soviet Union, served as a route for Lend-Lease supplies. Electrification began in 1929 and was completed in 2002. The main line runs 9,289 kilometres from Moscow to Vladivostok across eight time zones, with branches known as the Trans-Manchurian and Trans-Mongolian routes.
transhumance: Transhumance is a type of mobile pastoralism in which livestock are driven in herds between several fixed pastures with the seasons. It differs from sedentary pastoralism, where animals stay on one fenced area all year, and from nomadic pastoralism, where animals are moved irregularly in search of pasture. In mountain regions it means moving between high summer pastures and lowland valleys in winter, called vertical transhumance. Movement across the same plains or plateaus is horizontal transhumance.

Usually only the animals and a small number of herders travel, living in camps or huts at the grazing sites, while most of the community lives in permanent settlements. Nomadic pastoralists, by contrast, move whole communities with their herds in portable shelters such as tents and yurts. The milk, butter, yogurt and cheese of the herds may form much of the diet of such societies.

The word comes from French and derives from the Latin trans, across, and humus, ground. Transhumance developed on every inhabited continent and was practised before recorded history; in Europe, isotope studies of livestock bones suggest that certain animals were moved seasonally. Many languages have words for the high summer pastures, often used as place names, such as hafod in Wales, shieling in Scotland, and Alm or Alp in German-speaking regions.

In Wales farm workers spent the summer at a hillside hafod and returned in late autumn to the main house, the hendref. In Ireland the practice was called booleying, after the buaile, the summer pasture; it is mentioned in the Brehon Laws and was widespread in the west until the Second World War. In southern Italy drovers' roads called tratturi, up to 100 metres wide and more than 100 kilometres long, were regulated by law, with a mounted police force as far back as the 17th century. Spanish transhumance is the origin of the cowboys of the United States and the gauchos of South America.

In the Pyrenees herds went to the high mountains from late May or early June to early October, a system that evolved in the Middle Ages and lasted into the 20th century. In the Balkans, Albanians, Sarakatsani, Romanians, Aromanians and Yörük spent summers in the mountains and winters on lowland plains. The Bhotiya of Uttarakhand practised it until the closure of the Sino-Indian border after the war of 1962. Colonists began summer grazing in the Australian Alps in the 1830s.
transoxiana: Transoxiana, the Latin name meaning land beyond the Oxus, lies in lower Central Asia between the Amu Darya to the south and the Syr Darya to the north. It corresponds roughly to eastern Uzbekistan, western Tajikistan, southern Kyrgyzstan and parts of southern Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. The name was coined in the 4th century BCE, when Alexander the Great's troops conquered the region. Khwarazm, Sogdiana, Chaghaniyan and Khuttal lay in its southern part; Chach, Osrushana and Farghana in the north.

Persian writers called it Farā-rūd, 'beyond the river', and ancient Iranians knew the area as Turan, a term used in the Shahnameh. Early Arab writers used Mā Warāʾ an-Nahr, 'what is beyond the river', and Chinese sources called it Hezhong.

Under the Achaemenid Empire the region was a satrapy named Sogdia. Alexander's successors founded the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, whose Greek presence lasted over two hundred years. The region was ruled in turn by the Seleucids, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, the Parthian Empire and the Kushan Empire before Sasanian rule, under which it became a major cultural centre through the wealth of the Northern Silk Road. Hephthalite invaders interrupted Sasanian rule at the end of the 5th century, and it returned only in 565.

Arab conquest came between 705 and 715, under Qutayba ibn Muslim, after rule by the Göktürks; the Abbasid Caliphate replaced the Umayyads in 750. The people spoke Sogdian, and the conquest spread Arabic elite culture and New Persian. Samarkand and Bukhara remained centres of Persian culture and helped revive it through the Samanid Empire. Before Islam the principal religion was Zoroastrianism, with Buddhism, Nestorian Christianity and Manichaeism also present, and this diversity was gradually eroded.

Genghis Khan invaded in 1219 while conquering Khwarezm, and before his death in 1227 assigned the lands of Western Central Asia to his second son, Chagatai Khan, so that the region became the Chagatai Khanate. In 1369 Timur, of the Barlas tribe, became its effective ruler and made Samarkand the capital of his future empire. Transoxiana was flourishing in the mid-14th century and became a great centre of Muslim civilisation.
transvaal-province: The Transvaal took its name from the Latin prefix trans, meaning across, and referred to its position north of the Vaal River. The province lay between the Vaal in the south and the Limpopo River in the north. To its south were the Orange Free State and Natal, to its west the Cape Province and the Bechuanaland Protectorate, to its north Rhodesia, and to its east Portuguese East Africa and Swaziland. Except on the southwest, the borders were mostly defined by natural features. The Waterberg Massif, an ancient geological feature, lies within it. Pretoria was its capital and also the executive capital of the country.

The area has been inhabited since at least the 8th century by the Venda and Sesotho people. From 1817 several Nguni groups, such as the Matabele, who had been expelled from Natal by the Zulus, invaded the region in the Mfecane. At the end of the 1830s the Boers left on the Great Trek into the interior, where the South African Republic was founded. It was an independent country ruled by the Dutch-speaking Boers from 1852 to 1902, and the borders of the later province coincided with it. Pretoria and Johannesburg emerged as major cities in this period. In 1902 the republic was conquered by the United Kingdom and became the Transvaal Colony.

In 1910 four British colonies united to form the Union of South Africa, and the Transvaal Colony became the Transvaal Province. In 1961 the union left the Commonwealth of Nations and became the Republic of South Africa. The conurbation centred on Pretoria and Johannesburg, called the PWV, became the country's economic centre. Several Bantustans lay wholly within the province, among them Venda, KwaNdebele, Gazankulu, KaNgwane and Lebowa, and parts of Bophuthatswana lay there too. The province was a stronghold of the National Party.

In 1994, after the fall of apartheid, a new constitution abolished the former provinces and the Transvaal ceased to exist. Its south-central portion, including the PWV, became Gauteng, its northern portion became Limpopo and its southeastern portion became Mpumalanga. Most of North West came from its southwestern portion, and a small segment joined KwaZulu-Natal. The old regional names Northern, Eastern, Western and Southern Transvaal survive in the names of sporting teams: the Blue Bulls were formerly Northern Transvaal, and the Golden Lions, formed in 1889, were formerly Transvaal.
transylvania: Transylvania is a historical region in Central Europe, bounded on the east and south by the Carpathian Mountains and on the west by the Apuseni Mountains. Its core is the Transylvanian Plateau, 300 to 500 metres high, drained by the Mureș, Someș, Criș and Olt rivers. The name first appears in a Medieval Latin document of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1078 as ultra silvam, meaning beyond the forest. The German name Siebenbürgen refers to the seven cities of the Transylvanian Saxons.

The first known people of the territory were the Agathyrsi, followed by the Celtic La Tène culture from the 4th century BCE and the Dacian tribes, who were united under King Burebista. Trajan's wars created Roman Dacia in 106, and Emperor Aurelian withdrew the legions south of the Lower Danube in 275. The Goths, Huns, Gepids and Avars then held the region in turn, and the First Bulgarian Empire expanded into its south in the 9th century. Hungarian tribes conquered it in the late 9th century, and King Stephen I of Hungary brought it into the Kingdom of Hungary in 1002. Saxon colonists settled in the 12th and 13th centuries.

Historians disagree about the early population. The theory of Daco-Roman continuity holds that Romanians lived there without interruption, while its opponents point to the lack of written, archaeological and linguistic evidence. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the region belonged to the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, from which the Principality of Transylvania emerged in 1570 under the Treaty of Speyer. For most of the 16th and 17th centuries it was a vassal of the Ottoman Empire, with dual Ottoman and Habsburg suzerainty. In 1848 the Hungarian government proclaimed union with Transylvania, but the Compromise of 1867 reincorporated it into the Kingdom of Hungary within the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

The National Assembly of Romanians from Transylvania proclaimed union with Romania on 1 December 1918, and the Treaty of Trianon confirmed new borders in 1920. Over a million Hungarians remained on the Romanian side, mainly in the Székely Land. Northern Transylvania returned to Hungary in 1940 under the Second Vienna Award and to Romania after the Second World War. Its fortified churches, the old town of Sighișoara, the Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains and Roșia Montană are World Heritage Sites. Bram Stoker's 1897 novel Dracula made the region a byword for vampires in popular culture.
treaties-of-tilsit: Two treaties were signed by Napoleon at Tilsit, today Sovetsk in Russia, in the aftermath of his victory at Friedland, at the end of the War of the Fourth Coalition. The first was concluded on 7 July with Alexander I when the two emperors met on a raft in the middle of the Neman river. The second, with Prussia, followed on 9 July. King Frederick William III of Prussia had already agreed to a truce on 25 June after the Grande Armée had captured Berlin and pursued him to the easternmost frontier of his realm.

The raft was meant to express the perfect equality of the two emperors. Tilsit was declared neutral, with one part held by a Russian Guard battalion and the other by a French one. Napoleon gave his Guard the password Alexander, Russia, Greatness, and the Russian Guard was given Napoleon, France, Prowess.

The Franco-Russian treaty ended the war and began an alliance between the two empires. Russia agreed to join the Continental System against the British Empire, and Napoleon persuaded Alexander to enter the Anglo-Russian War and to instigate the Finnish War against Sweden. The tsar was to evacuate Wallachia and Moldavia, and the Ionian Islands and Cattaro, taken by Russian admirals, were to be handed to the French. Napoleon guaranteed the sovereignty of the Duchy of Oldenburg and several small states ruled by the tsar's German relatives.

Prussia lost about half its territory, falling from 5,700 square miles to 2,800 and from 9.75 million inhabitants to no more than 4.5 million. The Kingdom of Westphalia, the Duchy of Warsaw and the Free City of Danzig were formalised, Cottbus went to Saxony and Białystok to Russia. Prussia was to reduce its army to 43,000, and in 1808 France fixed its tribute at 154,500,000 francs, later lowered to 120 million.

Talleyrand had advised milder terms, and the treaties marked an important stage in his estrangement from Napoleon. Many observers in Prussia and Russia viewed them as unequal and a national humiliation. Napoleon's plan to marry the tsar's sister was stymied by Russian royalty, and cooperation broke down in 1810 when the tsar began to admit neutral ships to Russian ports. Napoleon crossed the Neman to invade Russia in June 1812.

The treaties freed French forces for the Peninsular War, which began on 19 November 1807, and Central Europe became a battlefield again in 1809 with the War of the Fifth Coalition. The Congress of Vienna restored many Prussian territories after 1815. By signing, France also left Persia and the Ottomans, which had hoped for its help, in the face of Russian aggression.
treaty-of-adrianople-1829: The treaty was signed in Adrianople on 14 September 1829 by Count Alexey Fyodorovich Orlov for Russia and Abdülkadir Bey for the Ottoman Empire, and its terms favoured Russia. The Ottoman Empire gave Russia access to the mouths of the Danube and the fortresses of Akhaltsikhe and Akhalkalaki in Georgia. The Sultan recognised Russia's possession of Georgia, with Imeretia, Mingrelia and Guria, and of the Khanates of Erivan and Nakhichevan, which Persia had ceded to the tsar in the Treaty of Turkmenchay a year earlier. Russia also took control of the towns of Anape and Poti in the Caucasus, and Russian traders in Turkey were placed under the jurisdiction of the Russian ambassador.

The treaty opened the Dardanelles to all commercial vessels, which freed the trade in grain, livestock and lumber. The Sultan renewed his earlier guarantee of autonomy to Serbia and promised autonomy for Greece. In recognition of the Treaty of London, the independence of Greece, or autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty, was accepted.

Russia was allowed to occupy Moldavia and Wallachia until the Ottoman Empire had paid a large indemnity. The Ottoman Empire kept nominal suzerainty over the Danube states of Moldavia and Wallachia, which for practical purposes were independent. The treaty also fixed the border between the Ottoman Empire and Wallachia on the thalweg of the Danube, transferring to Wallachia the rule of the districts of Turnu, Giurgiu and Brăila. The indemnities were sharply reduced by the later Treaty of Hünkâr İskelesi of 1833, which was also needed finally to settle the Straits Question between the two states.

The annexed territory had a mostly Georgian population, with Azerbaijanis, called Tatars at the time, Turks, Armenians and Kurds. Soon after the fighting ended, the Turks and Kurds left for the Ottoman Empire, and about 30 thousand Ottoman Armenians from the pashaliks of Erzurum and Kars settled in their places. They were settled not only in the regions of Akhaltsikhe and Akhalkalaki but also in Tbilissi, Erevan and Nakhchivan.
treaty-of-aix-la-chapelle-1748: Britain and France opened talks at Breda in 1746. The Duke of Newcastle, who controlled British foreign policy, delayed them in hopes of a better position, but the Dutch army collapsed and British hopes of recovering the Austrian Netherlands failed. France, though victorious in Flanders, was hard pressed by the British naval blockade, and after the Second Battle of Cape Finisterre in October 1747 could no longer protect its merchant convoys. Austria had made peace with Bavaria and Prussia and was kept in the war only by British subsidies. A congress assembled at Aachen on 24 April 1748, and a draft was agreed on 30 April.

The final treaty was signed on 18 October 1748 by Britain, France and the Dutch Republic; Austria, Sardinia, Spain, Modena and Genoa acceded in documents of 4 December 1748 and 21 January 1749. All accepted the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713, and Austria recognised the Prussian acquisition of Silesia. Austria ceded Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla to Philip of Spain and minor territories, including Vigevano, to Sardinia, and withdrew from Modena and Genoa.

France withdrew from the Austrian Netherlands and returned the Dutch Barrier forts, Maastricht and Bergen op Zoom. Britain and France exchanged Louisbourg on Île-Royale for Madras. Spain renewed the Asiento de Negros, the monopoly contract to supply slaves to Spanish America, which Britain had held since 1713; Britain renounced it in the Treaty of Madrid in 1750 for £100,000. France agreed to expel Charles Edward Stuart.

The treaty largely failed to settle the issues that had caused the war. Prussia, which doubled in size and wealth with Silesia, gained most. Maria Theresa resented her exclusion from the talks and the pressure from Britain to cede territory, while many in Britain questioned the value of the subsidies paid to her. These tensions led to the Diplomatic Revolution and the Seven Years' War, which began in 1756. In the Treaty of Aranjuez of 1752 Austria, Spain and Sardinia agreed to respect each other's boundaries in Italy.

In France the return of conquests, forced by the state of its finances, gave rise to the phrase as stupid as the Peace. The treaty ended the First Carnatic War between the British and French in India. Celebrations in London featured George Frideric Handel's Music for the Royal Fireworks.
treaty-of-amiens: The War of the Second Coalition began well for the coalition, but after French victories at Marengo and Hohenlinden Austria eventually signed the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801, leaving Britain the only major power still at war with France. Horatio Nelson's victory at Copenhagen on 2 April 1801 halted the League of Armed Neutrality. Napoleon Bonaparte had made truce proposals as early as 1799, but the foreign secretary Lord Grenville and Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger rejected them. When Pitt resigned in February 1801 over domestic issues, the more accommodating Henry Addington replaced him.

Addington's foreign secretary, Lord Hawkesbury, opened talks with the French commissary Louis Guillaume Otto, and preliminaries were signed in London on 1 October 1801. Lord Cornwallis went to France in November to negotiate the final text against Joseph Bonaparte and Talleyrand, who kept shifting their positions. Pressure on Cornwallis was great, since the British public expected peace and Parliament was discussing the budget. The chief difficulty was Malta.

The treaty called for the restoration of prisoners and hostages. Britain was to return the Cape Colony and most of Dutch Guiana to the Batavian Republic and withdraw its forces from Egypt, while the Batavian Republic ceded Ceylon. Spain accepted British rule of Trinidad, and Menorca went back to Spain. France was to withdraw from the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples, and the Septinsular Republic was recognised. Malta, Gozo and Comino were to be restored to the Knights Hospitaller and declared neutral, and the House of Orange-Nassau was to be compensated for its losses in the Netherlands.

News of the peace was greeted with celebration in Britain and France, and upper-class British visitors flocked to Paris in the second half of 1802. Among them were Charles James Fox, J. M. W. Turner and William Hazlitt, who spent much of three months copying Italian masters in the Louvre. Napoleon used the interlude for reforms, among them the Napoleonic Code and the Concordat with the Vatican, and for a constitution that gave him lifetime control.

The peace did not last. The British objected to Napoleon's exclusion of their trade from France and its client states, and to his reordering of Switzerland, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, while Napoleon objected to Britain's refusal to evacuate Malta. Addington kept a large peacetime army of 180,000 and used the interlude to rebuild British strength. Britain declared war on France on 18 May 1803, and the Napoleonic Wars began.
treaty-of-brest-litovsk: By 1917 the Eastern Front was stalemated and the Russian economy had nearly collapsed. The February Revolution forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate, but the Provisional Government continued the war. After the Red Guards seized the Winter Palace on 7 November in the October Revolution, the new government at once issued a Decree on Peace. An armistice with the Central Powers was concluded on 15 December 1917, and negotiations opened at Brest-Litovsk on 22 December.

The Soviet delegation was led first by Adolph Joffe, with Max Hoffmann, Richard von Kühlmann, Ottokar Czernin and Talaat Pasha among the Central Powers' negotiators. The Soviet side demanded peace with no annexations or indemnities; the Central Powers accepted this only if all belligerents did, and Hoffmann then made clear that Poland, Lithuania and Courland, already occupied, would separate from Russia.

Leon Trotsky replaced Joffe, since the Soviets hoped to prolong the talks until revolutions broke out in Central Europe. The Central Powers signed a treaty with Ukraine on 8–9 February 1918. Trotsky's formula of 'no war, no peace' was announced on 10 February, but on 18 February 53 German divisions advanced against near-empty Soviet trenches. Lenin argued that the Soviets must sign or face an even more ruinous treaty, telling the Central Committee that they must concede space to win time.

After Hoffmann presented harsher terms on 23 February, the Central Committee backed signing, and the All-Russian Central Executive Committee passed it by 116 to 85, with the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries jeering Lenin as a traitor. Grigori Sokolnikov signed on 3 March 1918.

Russia renounced territorial claims in Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, most of Belarus and Ukraine, and the districts of Ardahan, Kars and Batum were to be cleared of Russian troops. It lost 89% of its coalfields and 26% of its railways, and Kotkin writes that no Russian government had ever surrendered so much territory or sovereignty. A supplementary agreement of 27 August 1918 obliged Russia to pay six billion marks.

The occupation proved costly for Germany, with over one million troops staying in the east. The treaty split the Bolsheviks from the Left SRs, who assassinated the German ambassador in July 1918. The Armistice of 11 November 1918 abrogated the treaty. Poland and the Baltic states re-emerged, and at Rapallo in 1922 Germany and Russia renounced all wartime claims.
treaty-of-campo-formio: France had been at war with Austria since 20 April 1792, when the French Legislative Assembly voted to declare war and began the War of the First Coalition. After several years of stalemate along the Franco-Italian border, the French Revolutionary Army under Napoleon Bonaparte went on the offensive on 10 April 1796 against Austria and its Italian ally Sardinia. Sardinia signed a peace treaty with France on 15 May. After several major defeats in Italy and Germany, Austria signed the Peace of Leoben with Bonaparte on 18 April 1797.

The treaty was composed and signed after five months of negotiations, and its terms largely reflected those of Leoben. Campo Formio, now called Campoformido, is a village west of Udine in Friuli, midway between the Austrian headquarters at Udine and Bonaparte's residence at Villa Manin, the mansion of Ludovico Manin, the last Doge of Venice. The treaty was signed in an old house in the main square, owned by a local merchant.

Bonaparte signed for France and Philipp von Cobenzl for Austria on 17 October 1797. The city of Venice with the Terraferma, Venetian Istria, Venetian Dalmatia and the Bay of Kotor were turned over to the Habsburg emperor, while Corfu and other Venetian possessions in the Ionian Sea passed to France. Austria recognised the Cisalpine Republic and the newly created Ligurian Republic as independent powers. The Italian states ceased to owe fealty to the Holy Roman Emperor, ending the formal existence of the Kingdom of Italy.

The public articles concerned only France and Austria and called for a Second Congress of Rastatt to negotiate a final peace between France and the Holy Roman Empire. Secret clauses divided other territories and agreed to extend the borders of France up to the Rhine, the Nette and the Roer, with free French navigation on the Rhine, the Meuse and the Moselle. Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, a prisoner since the Revolution, was released from Austrian captivity.

Austrian troops entered Venice on 18 January 1798. Napoleon's biographer Felix Markham wrote that the partition of Venice was a moral blot on the settlement and left Austria a foothold in Italy that could only lead to further war. The treaty reshaped the map of Europe, yet it proved only a respite: Franco-Austrian tensions led France to declare war on Austria on 12 March 1799, in the War of the Second Coalition.

In the Southern Netherlands the introduction of French conscription helped provoke the Peasants' War of 1798. The passing of the Ionian Islands to French rule also affected later Greek history in ways neither intended nor expected at the time.
treaty-of-frankfurt-1871: Several considerations shaped the new frontier. The German military wanted Alsace up to the Vosges and the route between Thionville and Metz as protection against a future war with France. Politically, without a shift westward the new empire's frontier with France would have lain largely along the states of Baden and Bavaria, whose governments did not welcome a vengeful France on their doorstep and which kept considerable autonomy under the unification treaty.

The new border largely, though not entirely, followed the linguistic border. Most people in the annexed territory spoke Germanic dialects, and the area had once belonged to the Holy Roman Empire, which let Berlin justify the annexation on nationalist grounds. The taking of French-speaking areas such as Metz caused outrage in France.

The treaty was signed in Frankfurt on 10 May 1871 by the German Empire and the French Third Republic. It ceded 1,694 French villages and cities: in Alsace the departments of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin except Belfort and its territory, and in Lorraine most of Moselle, a third of Meurthe including Château-Salins and Sarrebourg, and the cantons of Saales and Schirmeck in Vosges. Residents had the right of option until 1 October 1872 to keep French nationality and emigrate or to stay and become German citizens.

France was to pay five billion francs within five years, with German occupation of parts of France until payment; it paid sooner, and German troops withdrew in September 1873. The treaty also recognised Wilhelm I of Prussia as German Emperor and gave Germany most-favoured-nation terms in trade.

France lost 1,447,000 hectares, 1,597,000 inhabitants and about 20 percent of its mining and steel potential. The treaty shaped French policy towards Germany for some forty years, and recovery of the lost provinces became a revanchist aim, one of the strongest motives for France's part in World War I. In 1918 Woodrow Wilson called for the return of Alsace-Lorraine as the eighth of his Fourteen Points, and it was restored to France by the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.
treaty-of-ghilajharighat: The Treaty of Asurar Ali of 1639 fixed the limit between Ahom and Mughal interests at the Barnadi river on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and the Asurar Ali on the south. During the Mughal war of succession of 1658–1659 Pran Narayan, king of Koch Bihar, attacked the Mughal faujdar at Guwahati. The Ahoms refused a Koch offer to partition Kamrup, drove the Koches out and took the whole valley up to the Sankosh River.

Aurangzeb made Mir Jumla II subahdar of Bengal. He annexed Koch Bihar in December 1661, recovered Guwahati on 5 February 1662 and occupied Garhgaon on 17 March. The rains from April turned the country to marsh and brought food shortage and cholera to the camps, while the Ahoms waged the guerrilla warfare devised by Atan Burhagohain. When the rains ended the Mughals recovered and the king withdrew to Namrup. The Ahom commander-in-chief, Baduli Phukan, defected at the end of November, and Mir Jumla, by then ill, reached Tipam by 18 December with a worn-out army eager to go home.

Atan Burhagohain persuaded the king that further fighting was futile and sent four emissaries offering tribute if the Mughals left Assam. Mir Jumla, who had refused everything short of unconditional surrender, took the opening and left the bargaining to Dilir Khan. The terms are pieced together from Persian and Assamese sources that do not fully agree.

The king accepted Mughal vassalage; his daughter Ramani Gabharu went to the imperial harem with a dowry of 20,000 tolas of gold and 120,000 of silver. The indemnity was 300,000 tolas of silver within a year and 90 elephants in instalments, the annual tribute 20 elephants. Four sons of leading nobles were to be hostages. The ceded land ran from Guwahati to the Bharali River on the north bank and to the Kolong River on the south.

The princess left on 5 January 1663 with the gold, silver and part of the elephants, and Mir Jumla ordered the retreat from Tipam on 10 January. He died on board on 31 March 1663. Jayadhwaj Singha founded a new capital at Bakata and died in November 1663; his cousin succeeded as Chakradhar Singha. Neither king could accept tributary status, and the terms were only partly fulfilled. The treaty was the root of the later conflicts, which ended with the Mughal defeat at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671 and, after the Battle of Itakhuli in 1682, the end of Mughal interests in the Brahmaputra valley.
treaty-of-guadalupe-hidalgo: Mexico had claimed the northern lands since winning its independence from the Spanish Empire in 1821. The Spanish had conquered part of the area from Indigenous peoples over three centuries, but powerful independent Indigenous nations remained there. Most of the land was dry and mountainous, and about 80,000 Mexicans lived in California, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas between 1845 and 1850. The United States annexed the Republic of Texas, which Mexico had never recognised, with effect from 29 December 1845, and Mexico had warned that annexation would be treated as an act of war.

U.S. forces moved quickly beyond Texas to conquer Alta California and New Mexico, and fighting there ended on 13 January 1847. By the middle of September 1847 they had occupied Mexico City. Nicholas Trist, chief clerk of the State Department, accompanied General Winfield Scott as President James K. Polk's representative and negotiated with a commission of José Bernardo Couto, Miguel de Atristain and Luis Gonzaga Cuevas.

Article V set the new border: the Rio Grande to the southern boundary of New Mexico, due west to the 110th meridian, north to the Gila River, and from the mouth of the Gila a straight line to a point one marine league south of the southernmost part of San Diego Bay, so that the United States received San Diego and its harbour. Mexicans in the annexed areas could relocate within Mexico or take U.S. citizenship and full civil rights.

The U.S. Senate ratified the treaty by 38 votes to 16, but removed Article X, which guaranteed land grants, and changed Article IX. A protocol signed at Querétaro on 30 May 1848 explained the amendments. The United States later ignored it, on the grounds that its representatives had over-reached their authority.

The ceded land became all or part of several U.S. states between 1850 and 1912. Disputes over whether to make the new territory slave or free states contributed to the tensions that led to the American Civil War. Surveying the boundary took over seven years, and the border commission contended with difficult terrain, extreme weather and Indigenous Americans who had not been considered in the negotiations. In 1889 the International Boundary and Water Commission was established to maintain the border. Writing many years later, Nicholas Trist called the treaty "a thing for every right-minded American to be ashamed of".
treaty-of-gulistan: Alexander I became tsar in 1801, eager to expand Russia's control over its neighbours. In Iran Fath Ali Shah Qajar had become shah after the assassination of his uncle Agha Mohammad Khan in 1797. Agha Mohammad Khan had re-subordinated the vassals and subjects in what are now eastern Georgia, Armenia, southern Dagestan and Azerbaijan. After his death and that of Heraclius II of Georgia, Russia, seeking territory and trade, took the chance to annex eastern Georgia.

Persia's primary motive in entering the war was to reassert control over Georgia and protect its north-western borders. Its army was as much as five times larger than the Russian force in the Caucasus but lagged behind technologically and was poorly trained. The Persian court declared a jihad against Russia and asked Napoleon for aid, but after the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807 France left Persia unassisted. The turning point was the Battle of Aslanduz on 31 October 1812, a decisive Persian defeat.

The treaty was concluded on 24 October 1813 in the village of Gulistan. The negotiations had been precipitated by General Pyotr Kotlyarevsky's storming of Lankaran on 1 January 1813. The text was prepared by the British diplomat Sir Gore Ouseley, who acted as mediator, and signed by Nikolai Rtischev for Russia and Mirza Abolhassan Khan Ilchi for Persia.

Russia was confirmed in possession of the khanates of Karabakh, Ganja, Shaki, Shirvan, Derbent, Quba and Baku, with part of Talysh and the fortress of Lankaran. Persia abandoned its claims to Dagestan, Georgia, Mingrelia, Imeretia and Abkhazia. Iran lost the right to navigate the Caspian Sea, and Russia received exclusive rights to station a military fleet there. Free trade was agreed, with a 5% duty on imports on both sides, and Russia promised to support Abbas Mirza as heir to the Persian throne.

The treaty did not settle whether the Persian army would be disarmed or allowed to regroup, and both sides saw that Persia might try to reclaim the territories. The costs of the war nevertheless led to relative peace from 1813 to 1826, and permanent diplomatic missions were set up in both countries to keep trade open. The treaty contributed directly to the Russo-Persian War of 1826 to 1828, which ended in the Treaty of Turkmenchay, by which Iran lost its last Caucasian territories.

Iranians regard Gulistan and Turkmenchay as among the most humiliating treaties ever signed, and Fath Ali Shah is judged for it as one of the most incompetent rulers in memory. Imperial Russian historians argued that Russia's absorption of Transcaucasia shielded local populations from Iranian and Ottoman invasions. The ceded territories came under Russian, and later Soviet, control for about 180 years.
treaty-of-hudaybiyyah: Muhammad had migrated to Medina in 622, and armed conflict followed with the Quraysh of Mecca, who kept him and his followers from the Kaaba. In March 628 he set out for the lesser pilgrimage with about 1,500 Muslims, reportedly after a dream in which he circled the Kaaba. The Meccans presumed an attack and sent cavalry to stop them, but Muhammad took an unconventional route and camped at Hudaybiya, on the edge of the sacred territory.

He told the Quraysh he wished to perform the pilgrimage rather than fight, but they refused to let him enter that year. A rumour that Uthman, sent to negotiate, had been killed led the Muslims to swear the Pledge of the Tree to fight, and when it proved false the Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn Amr to settle terms.

The treaty set a truce of ten years. A man of the Quraysh who fled to Muhammad without his guardian's permission would be returned, while a Muslim who went to the Quraysh would not. Any tribe could enter a covenant with either side.

The Muslims would go back to Medina that year but could make the pilgrimage the next, staying three days while the Quraysh left the city, carrying no weapons except sheathed swords. Ali wrote the document. Suhayl objected to the opening Basmala and to the words Messenger of God, and Muhammad accepted the wording Muhammad, son of Abdullah to preserve the agreement; according to tradition, he erased the phrase himself when Ali was reluctant to.

Some followers, Umar among them, reportedly objected to the terms. Abu Jandal, Suhayl's son, converted and was returned to his father under the return clause, but Muhammad did not return believing women who emigrated, citing Quran 60:10. Abu Basir, who was also returned, escaped and with other converts raided Meccan caravans until the Meccans asked Muhammad to take them in.

The treaty held for about two years, until the Banu Bakr, allies of the Quraysh, attacked the Banu Khuza'ah, allies of Muhammad, with help from some Quraysh. The Quraysh would not meet Muhammad's demands, and in 630 he took Mecca. Historians regard the treaty as an important stage in his consolidation of power, since the Quraysh implicitly treated him as an equal.
treaty-of-karlowitz: The treaty was signed on 26 January 1699 at Karlowitz, now Sremski Karlovci in Serbia, in the Military Frontier of the Habsburg monarchy, after a two-month congress. On the principle of uti possidetis, each power kept what it held. The Habsburgs received the Eğri and Varat eyalets, much of the Budin Eyalet, the northern part of the Temeşvar Eyalet and parts of the Bosnia Eyalet, which amounted to much of Hungary, Croatia and Slavonia. The Principality of Transylvania remained nominally independent but was subject to the direct rule of Austrian governors.

The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth recovered Podolia with the fortress of Kamianets-Podilskyi, undoing the loss of the Treaty of Buchach of 1672, and gave back captured fortresses in Moldavia. Venice obtained most of Dalmatia and the Morea, though the Peloponnese was restored to the Ottomans within 20 years by the Treaty of Passarowitz. The Ottomans kept Belgrade and the Banat of Temesvár, as well as suzerainty over Wallachia and Moldavia.

Negotiations with the Tsardom of Russia went on for a further year under a truce agreed at Karlowitz, and ended in the Treaty of Constantinople of 1700, in which the sultan ceded the Azov region to Peter the Great. Russia returned it eleven years later after the Pruth River Campaign. Commissions marked the new borders between the Austrians and the Ottomans, with some parts disputed until 1703, and the work of the Habsburg commissioner Luigi Ferdinando Marsili produced a border marked by physical landmarks for the first time.

The Habsburg gain of about 160,000 square kilometres of Hungarian territory, and of the Banat of Temesvár 18 years later at Passarowitz, made the monarchy the dominant power of Central Europe. For the Ottoman Empire it was a watershed: after three and a half centuries of expansion in Europe it lost substantial territory for the first time. Its borders in the region shifted over the next century, but it never again gained land on the scale of the 15th and 16th centuries.

In the Commonwealth the Sejm judged the Cossack regiments of the Right Bank unneeded, and in 1699 voted to abolish them. This was a primary cause of the Paliy uprising against the nobility in Right-bank Ukraine from about 1700.
treaty-of-kiel: Denmark-Norway and Sweden tried at first to stay neutral in the Napoleonic Wars but joined opposite camps. After a British fleet bombarded Copenhagen in 1807 and seized or destroyed the Dano-Norwegian ships, Denmark-Norway aligned with France. In 1810 the French Marshal Jean Baptiste Bernadotte was elected heir to the Swedish throne. Sweden allied with Russia in 1812 and with the United Kingdom and Prussia in 1813, and Bernadotte made the gain of Norway his condition for joining the anti-Napoleonic alliance, which the United Kingdom and Russia accepted in May 1813.

Denmark, which had kept to its alliance with Napoleon because of the Swedish claim, was isolated and bankrupt after the war. After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig in October 1813, Bernadotte took a combined Swedish and Russian army, defeated the outnumbered Danish army and occupied Holstein and Schleswig in late December. Frederick VI agreed to peace once it was clear that Bernadotte would occupy Jutland and Zealand, if necessary with British naval help, to force the cession of Norway.

The Danish treaty with Britain was negotiated by the Danish diplomat Edmund Bourke and the British envoy Edward Thornton. Britain returned occupied Danish possessions except Heligoland, which George III received in full sovereignty, and the Danish king joined the alliance and undertook to keep 10,000 men with the Allied forces in northern Germany, with British subsidies of 400,000 pounds a year.

In the treaty with Sweden, Frederick VI renounced Norway "irrevocably and forever" and Swedish Pomerania was to pass to Denmark. Greenland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands were excepted from the cession, through an insertion written by Bourke. Sweden took over Norway's debts, and the king promised to maintain the University of Christiania and the University of Greifswald.

The Swedish crown prince intended to invade Norway to enforce the treaty, but the Norwegian elite in Christiania supported resistance. Norway declared its independence, adopted a constitution and elected Crown Prince Christian Frederik as king. After a short war with Sweden, Norway accepted a personal union at the Convention of Moss. The Storting elected Charles XIII as king of Norway on 4 November 1814.

Because Norway refused to submit, Sweden did not hand over Swedish Pomerania. The Congress of Vienna settled the matter in 1815 on a plan of Karl August von Hardenberg: Pomerania passed to Prussia, and Denmark received the Duchy of Lauenburg with a payment of 3.5 million thalers. The Danish claim to all of Greenland was contested by Norway in the Eastern Greenland case of 1931 to 1933, which the Permanent Court of International Justice decided in Denmark's favour on the basis of the Treaty of Kiel and later treaties.
treaty-of-kucuk-kaynarca: The treaty was signed on 21 July 1774 at Küçük Kaynarca, today Kaynardzha in Bulgaria, after the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Kozludzha. Russia was represented by Field-Marshal Count Pyotr Rumyantsev and the Ottoman Empire by Muhsinzade Mehmed Pasha. After the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 the Ottoman Empire had ceased to be an aggressive power, and by the middle of the 18th century the tsars had taken over the Habsburgs' fight against the Turks. The Russians sought the Black Sea, the bulwark of Constantinople.

Russia returned Wallachia and Moldavia to Ottoman control but gained the right to intervene there in case of Ottoman misrule. It kept Kabardia, the port of Azov, the ports of Kerch and Enikale on the Kerch peninsula, and part of the Yedisan region between the Bug and the Dnieper, including the port of Kherson. Russian merchant ships were allowed through the Dardanelles, giving Russia two outlets to the Black Sea.

The Ottomans recognised the Tatars of Crimea as politically independent, although the sultan remained their religious leader as caliph. Article 14 allowed Russia to build a church in Constantinople, under the protection of the Russian minister. The Ottomans also had to pay a large indemnity. Original copies were written in Russian, Italian and Turkish, and the Italian text was to prevail in a divergence.

Russia later read the treaty as giving it the right to protect Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire, and used this claim in the Danubian Principalities. Historians dispute whether the articles gave such a right, since some consider it granted and others think the wording too vague. A French translation made at St Petersburg in 1775 left out the church's Russian character, which helped later Russian claims. The church was most likely never built.

The Crimean Khanate kept nominal independence, while depending on Russia, until Catherine the Great annexed it in 1783. In 1787 Abdul Hamid I declared war on Russia again. The treaty is regarded as a milestone in the decline of the Ottoman Empire, since a foreign power now had a say in the fate of its Orthodox subjects, and it opened the era of the Eastern Question. The Crimean War of 1853 broke out over the Russian claim.
treaty-of-lausanne: The treaty was negotiated at the Lausanne Conference of 1922 to 1923 and signed in the Palais de Rumine in Lausanne on 24 July 1923. It was a second attempt at peace after the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920, which had sought to partition Ottoman territories but was never ratified. The Turkish National Movement rejected its terms.

After the Greek defeat in the Greco-Turkish War, Turkish forces recaptured İzmir, and the Armistice of Mudanya of October 1922 provided for an exchange of Greek and Turkish populations and for civilian passage through the Turkish Straits. The conference opened on 20 November 1922 and took eight months of negotiation, with several Turkish withdrawals. İsmet İnönü was chief negotiator for Turkey, Lord Curzon for the Allies and Eleftherios Venizelos for Greece.

The treaty had 143 articles and was written in English and French. It provided for the independence of the Republic of Turkey, and for the protection of the Greek Orthodox minority in Turkey and the Muslim minority in Greece. Most of both populations had already been moved under the earlier convention on the exchange of populations; only the Greek Orthodox of Constantinople, Imbros and Tenedos, about 270,000 people, and the Muslim population of Western Thrace, about 129,120 in 1923, were excluded.

Islands in the Aegean beyond three miles from the Turkish shore went to Greece, except Imbros, Tenedos and Rabbit Island. Turkey renounced its claims to the Dodecanese, Cyprus, Egypt and Sudan, Syria and Iraq, and left the fate of the province of Mosul to the League of Nations. Greece gave up reparations in exchange for ceding Karaağaç. Annex VIII, the Declaration of Amnesty, granted legal immunity for acts committed between 1914 and 1922 on account of military or political action, which ended efforts to prosecute Ottoman war criminals.

Turkey ratified the treaty on 23 August 1923 and all other signatories had done so by 16 July 1924. It took effect on 6 August 1924. It brought international recognition of the sovereignty of the Republic of Turkey as successor to the Ottoman Empire, and the Ottoman public debt was divided between Turkey and the states that emerged from the empire.

The convention on the Straits lasted thirteen years until the Montreux Convention of 1936. For Greece, the treaty ended the impetus behind the Megali Idea. David Lloyd George called it an abject, cowardly and infamous surrender. Historians such as Norman Naimark describe it as a pivotal precedent for transferring populations against their will in the 20th century.
treaty-of-london-1915: Soon after the outbreak of the First World War the Triple Entente powers, the United Kingdom, France and Russia, sought more allies. The first attempt to bring in Italy came in August and September 1914, on Russian initiative. On 4 August, a day after Italy declared neutrality, its ambassador to Russia said Italy might join the Entente in return for Trentino-Alto Adige, Vlorë and a dominant position in the Adriatic. The British Foreign Secretary, Edward Grey, would consider nothing further until Italy committed itself, and the Italian prime minister, Antonio Salandra, said that was impossible at the time.

Talks were taken up again by Salandra's foreign minister Sidney Sonnino, who on 4 March 1915 presented Grey with sixteen conditions. The Entente was at the same time courting Bulgaria, and the Italian claim to Dalmatia clashed with the Adriatic outlet offered to Serbia as compensation. Grey judged the Italian claims excessive but not against British interests. Russia's foreign minister, Sergey Sazonov, objected to Italian claims in Dalmatia, and negotiations ran on for six weeks.

Article 1 provided for a military agreement guaranteeing the number of troops Russia would commit against Austria-Hungary. Article 2 required Italy to enter the war against all the enemies of the three Entente powers, and Article 3 obliged the French and British navies to support it by destroying the Austro-Hungarian fleet. Article 4 gave Italy Trentino and the southern part of Tyrol, with a new frontier between the Piz Umbrail and Toblach and an eastern frontier from Tarvisio to the Kvarner Gulf that left Rijeka outside Italy.

Article 5 awarded Italy the part of Dalmatia north of a line running northeast from Cape Planka, with Zadar and Šibenik, and all the Austro-Hungarian Adriatic islands except a list of twelve. The remaining coast between Rijeka and the Drin River went to Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro.

Although it was meant to be secret, an outline became known in late April 1915 to the Yugoslav Committee, which with Serbia protested strongly. Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary in May 1915 but waited a year before declaring war on Germany, which France and the United Kingdom resented. At the Paris Peace Conference the United States pressed to void the treaty as contrary to self-determination. Italy received Trentino-Alto Adige and the Julian March, and under the Treaty of Rapallo Istria and Zadar, but the Entente did not provide the promised colonies or part of Asia Minor.

The result turned wartime fervour into nationalist resentment. Gabriele D'Annunzio called the outcome a mutilated victory and led veterans and soldiers to seize Rijeka in the Impresa di Fiume. His short-lived Italian Regency of Carnaro influenced the development of Italian fascism.
treaty-of-nanjing: In the late 18th and early 19th centuries Britain ran a growing trade deficit with China, since it had nothing to offer that matched its imports of tea and porcelain. Opium grown in British India was auctioned to merchants who sold it to Chinese smugglers, although Chinese law forbade its import and sale. When Lin Zexu seized the opium and ordered its destruction at Humen, Britain demanded reparations and then declared what became known as the First Opium War. British military technology brought a major victory.

With British warships poised to attack Nanjing, the officials negotiated on board HMS Cornwallis in the Yangtze. On 29 August 1842 Sir Henry Pottinger for Britain and Keying, Yilibu and Niu Jian for the Qing signed the treaty of thirteen articles.

The treaty's fundamental purpose was to change the Canton system of foreign trade, in force since 1760. Article V abolished the monopoly of the Cohong merchants and their Thirteen Factories, and the ports of Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai opened alongside Canton, where foreign merchants could trade with anyone. Britain could send consuls to the ports, and trade there was to be subject to fixed tariffs agreed between the two governments.

The Qing government was to pay 27 million silver dollars in instalments over three years: 6 million for the opium Lin Zexu had confiscated, 6 million for the Ransom of Canton, 3 million for the debts of Canton merchants to British merchants and 12 million for the cost of the war. Hong Kong Island was ceded to Queen Victoria as a crown colony, in perpetuity, to give British traders a harbour. The treaty did not mention the opium trade, and the British asked the Chinese to legalise it themselves, which they refused.

The Daoguang Emperor ratified the treaty on 27 October and Queen Victoria on 28 December, and the exchange took place in Hong Kong on 26 June 1843. Because the treaty was brief, a supplementary Treaty of the Bogue followed in 1843, giving Britain extraterritorial rights and making its citizens in the treaty ports exempt from Chinese law. Together with the treaties of 1843, 1858 and 1860 it ended the Canton system and set a framework for China's foreign trade that lasted almost a hundred years.

Chinese nationalists later called it an unequal treaty, since its terms were all concessions from China, among them extraterritoriality and fixed tariffs, and counted it the start of a century of humiliation. Joanna Waley-Cohen writes that the Qing did not at the time regard it as very important, since it resembled an earlier treaty with Kokand. Extraterritoriality was not formally abolished until 1943.
treaty-of-neuilly-sur-seine: The Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine was made between the victorious Allies of World War I and Bulgaria, one of the defeated Central Powers. It was signed on 27 November 1919 in the town hall of Neuilly-sur-Seine, just west of Paris. It belonged to the series of treaties after the war, with those of Versailles, Saint-Germain, Trianon and Sevres, that were meant to reduce the military and political strength of the defeated Central Powers. Like the others, it contained the Covenant of the League of Nations, and for that reason the United States did not ratify it.

Bulgaria had to cede Western Thrace to the Entente, which awarded it to Greece at the San Remo conference, cutting Bulgaria off from the Aegean Sea, and to sign a convention on population exchange with Greece. It also had to give up territory on its western border to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and to return Dobruja to Romania, restoring the border set by the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913. It was to return or pay for property taken from occupied territory, to reduce its army to 20,000 men, to pay reparations of 100 million pounds and to recognise the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

The four small regions ceded to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, called the Western Outlands in Bulgarian writing, had been part of Bulgaria since it became a principality in 1878, except the region around Strumitsa, which joined in 1912. The cession was partly compensation for the Bulgarian occupation of southern and eastern Serbia from 1915 to 1918 and partly strategic: the old boundary followed high mountain ridges, while the new one exposed the Bulgarian capital, Sofia.

In Bulgaria the results of the treaty are popularly known as the Second National Catastrophe. Bulgarian sources claim that Bulgarians made up 98 per cent of the population of Bosilegrad and 95 per cent of Tzaribrod at the time. Bulgaria regained Southern Dobruja permanently through the Treaty of Craiova in 1940. During the Second World War, together with Nazi Germany, it temporarily reoccupied most of the other territories that the treaty had taken from it.
treaty-of-nystad: The Treaty of Nystad, also called the Treaty of Uusikaupunki, was the last peace treaty of the Great Northern War of 1700 to 1721. It was concluded between the Tsardom of Russia and the Swedish Empire on 10 September 1721 (30 August in the old calendar) in the then Swedish town of Nystad, in the south-west of present-day Finland. Sweden had already settled with the other parties to the war in Stockholm in 1719 and 1720 and at Frederiksborg in 1720.

During the war Peter I of Russia had occupied all Swedish possessions on the eastern Baltic coast: Swedish Ingria, where in 1703 he began to build the future Russian capital of St Petersburg, Swedish Estonia and Swedish Livonia, which had capitulated in 1710, and Finland.

King Frederick I of Sweden formally recognised the transfer of Estonia, Livonia and Ingria to Russia, while Russia granted toll-free export of grain from Livonia up to a value of 50 000 rubel a year. South-eastern Finland, the county of Kexholm and part of the Karelian Isthmus, passed to Russia in exchange for two million silver riksdaler. Russia returned the bulk of Finland to Swedish rule, which took place within four weeks of ratification.

The treaty also confirmed the rights of the ceded territories to keep their financial system, their customs border, their self-government and their Lutheran religion. For the German Baltic nobility of Estonia and Livonia it protected the German language. This special position within the Russian Empire was reconfirmed by every tsar from Peter the Great to Alexander II.
