Russia gained the right to mediate in conflicts between Sweden and Poland, while promising not to interfere with the Swedish crown and succession, and prisoners of war on both sides, civilians included, were to be released.
Nystad marked a decisive shift in the European balance of power. The Swedish imperial era ended and Sweden entered the Age of Liberty, while Russia emerged as a new empire.

Before 1917, a thoroughfare in the Vyborgsky district of St Petersburg, the district nearest the Russo-Finnish border, was named Nystadt Street after the treaty. The district also holds St Sampsonius' Cathedral, a church commemorating the first Russian victory of the Great Northern War, at the Battle of Poltava.
treaty-of-paris-1763: The treaty was signed on 10 February 1763 by the kingdoms of Great Britain, France and Spain, with Portugal in agreement. Prussia and Austria were not party to it and signed a separate agreement, the Treaty of Hubertusburg, five days later. Most conquered territories went back to their former owners. France and Spain restored all their conquests to Britain and Portugal, and Britain returned Manila and Havana to Spain, and Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Lucia, Gorée and the Indian trading posts to France.

In return France recognised British sovereignty over Canada, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Tobago. France ceded the eastern half of French Louisiana, the area from the Mississippi River to the Appalachian Mountains, and Spain ceded Florida. France kept fishing rights off Newfoundland and regained the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon. In India France regained its factories but recognised British clients as rulers of key native states and pledged not to send troops to Bengal. Britain agreed to demolish its fortifications in British Honduras but kept a logwood-cutting colony there.

Britain had conquered a great deal during the Seven Years' War, from Canada and Guadeloupe to Manila and Havana. The British debated the relative merits of Guadeloupe, which produced £6 million a year in sugar, and Canada, which was expensive to keep. They chose Canada for strategic reasons. The prime minister, Lord Bute, wanted a peace that would not push France toward a second war.

The French Foreign Minister, the Duke of Choiseul, expected war to return but needed peace to rebuild. France preferred its profitable sugar islands to the vast Canadian lands, which had been a financial burden. French diplomats believed that without France to keep them in check the American colonists might attempt to revolt. France also asked for toleration of Roman Catholics in North America.

France lost all its mainland North American territory except Louisiana west of the Mississippi. It had already secretly given that land to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau three months earlier, though Spain did not take possession until 1769 and the transfer was not publicly announced until 1764. Article IV allowed the French inhabitants of Canada eighteen months to emigrate and sold their estates to British subjects, and Britain agreed to grant liberty of the Catholic religion as far as the laws of Great Britain permit.

The treaty ended the conflict between France and Britain over North America and marked the beginning of an era of British dominance outside Europe. The Mississippi corridor in what is now Louisiana was later reunited under the United States after the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 and the Adams–Onís Treaty in 1819.
treaty-of-paris-1783: Peace negotiations began in Paris in April 1782, after the fall of Frederick North's government on 20 March following the British defeat at Yorktown. The United States was represented by Benjamin Franklin, John Jay, Henry Laurens and John Adams, and Britain by David Hartley and Richard Oswald. In September 1782 the French foreign minister Vergennes proposed a settlement that would confine independence to the area east of the Appalachian Mountains, which the American delegation rejected.

John Jay told the British he was willing to negotiate directly with them and bypass France and Spain, and Prime Minister Lord Shelburne agreed. He saw a chance to split the United States from France and to make the new nation a valuable economic partner. The treaty was drafted on 30 November 1782.

The treaty was signed on 3 September 1783 at the Hôtel d'York in Paris by Adams, Franklin, Jay and Hartley. Britain acknowledged the thirteen former colonies, listed by name, as free, sovereign and independent states. The United States gained all the land east of the Mississippi River, north of present-day Florida and south of present-day Canada, and fishing rights on the Grand Banks and in the Gulf of Saint Lawrence. Creditors on either side were to meet no lawful impediment to recovering debts, Congress was to recommend that the states restore confiscated Loyalist property, and prisoners of war were to be released.

Britain signed separate agreements with France, Spain and, provisionally, the Netherlands. East and West Florida went to Spain without a clear northern boundary, and Spain also received Menorca. The Congress of the Confederation ratified the treaty at Annapolis on 14 January 1784, and the ratified copies were exchanged in Paris on 12 May 1784.

Historians have often called the treaty very generous to the United States, and some argue that the British aimed at close economic ties and profitable trade. Much of it did not work as written. The states ignored the recommendation to restore Loyalist property, and Virginia kept laws against paying debts to British creditors. Spain used its control of Florida to block American use of the Mississippi, and a dispute over the Florida boundary lasted until the Treaty of Madrid in 1795.

Britain kept eight forts on what was technically American soil, citing American failure to compensate Loyalists. They were given up peacefully under the Jay Treaty of 1794. Only Article 1, acknowledging the United States as free, sovereign and independent, remains in force.
treaty-of-paris-1814: The treaty was signed on 30 May 1814 and ended the war between France and the Sixth Coalition. It followed an armistice of 23 April between Charles of Bourbon, Count of Artois, acting as Lieutenant General of the Realm, and the allies. Napoleon had abdicated as Emperor on 6 April after negotiations at Fontainebleau. Peace talks began on 9 May, with Talleyrand negotiating on behalf of the exiled Bourbon king Louis XVIII. The allies had defined their common war aim at Chaumont in March.

The signatories were Talleyrand for France, Lords Castlereagh, Aberdeen and Cathcart for Great Britain, Counts Razumovsky and Nesselrode for Russia, Prince Metternich and Count Stadion for Austria, and Baron Hardenberg and Wilhelm von Humboldt for Prussia. Portugal and Sweden also signed, and Spain ratified in July. The allies concluded separate treaties with France rather than a common document.

The allies wished to establish a lasting peace and did not think harsh terms necessary now that France had a monarchy again. France kept the borders of 1792 and was allowed to retain Saarbrücken, Saarlouis, Landau, the County of Montbéliard, part of Savoy with Annecy and Chambéry, and Avignon with the Comtat Venaissin. It also kept the artworks acquired during the war. Britain kept Malta, and the treaty recognised the independence of Switzerland and returned Santo Domingo to Spain.

Article 32 called for a congress of all the belligerents within two months, which became the Congress of Vienna, held from September 1814 to June 1815. The treaty also aimed to end the French slave trade over five years, though not slavery itself, and it left French territories outside this aim. Several powers still feared a revival of French power. The Netherlands, now freed from French rule, accepted William I of the House of Orange as its prince, with the secret support of the great powers.
After Napoleon's brief return to power and his defeat, a second Treaty of Paris was signed on 20 November 1815. For this reason the treaty of 30 May 1814 is sometimes called the First Peace of Paris.
treaty-of-paris-1856: The Crimean War began on 23 October 1853, when the Ottoman Empire formally declared war on Russia after Russian troops occupied the Danubian Principalities. By its end all sides wanted a lasting settlement after the casualties and attrition they had suffered, though competing ideas of resolution complicated the drafting. Russia had lost over 500,000 troops. Alexander II, who took the crown in 1855, sought peace to keep some imperial possessions, to stop the deaths of thousands of army reserves and to prevent an economic crisis.

Britain and France wanted a stable balance of power, preventing Russia and Austria from growing stronger at the Ottoman Empire's expense. Public opinion mattered: the war was one of the first to receive relatively prompt press coverage, and Lord Aberdeen lost a parliamentary vote and resigned in favour of Lord Palmerston.

The treaty was signed on 30 March 1856 by representatives of France, Austria, the United Kingdom, Prussia, Russia, Sardinia and the Ottoman Empire. It admitted the Ottoman Empire to the European concert, and the powers promised to respect its independence and territorial integrity. Russia gave up its claim to a protectorate over Christians in the Ottoman domains, and a European commission was set up to guarantee freedom of commerce and navigation on the Danube. Sevastopol and other towns in southern Crimea went back to Russia.

Moldavia and Wallachia stayed under nominal Ottoman rule but were to have independent constitutions and national assemblies monitored by the powers. Moldavia recovered part of Bessarabia, creating a buffer between the Ottoman Empire and Russia. The treaty also demilitarised the Åland Islands, part of the Russian Grand Duchy of Finland, where British and French forces had destroyed the fortress of Bomarsund in 1854. The Declaration of Paris set new rules of wartime commerce, including that privateering was illegal.

The Black Sea prohibitions were renounced in the Treaty of London in 1871, and Moldavia and Wallachia were united in 1859. The war and its settlement did little to create lasting stability in the Concert of Europe, and the Ottoman Empire faced a number of patriotic uprisings in its provinces in the following decades. By 1877 Russia and the Ottoman Empire were again at war.

Austria, which had mobilised troops against its former ally and sent an ultimatum asking for the withdrawal of Russian armies from the Balkans, saw relations with Russia remain strained. Russia's resentment contributed to its non-intervention in the Franco-Austrian War of 1859, the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 and the Ausgleich with Hungary of 1867.
treaty-of-paris-1898: The Spanish–American War began on 25 April 1898, after escalating disputes between the two nations. Cubans had attempted revolution in 1868 to 1878 and again in the 1890s under José Martí, and in the Philippines a first call to revolt on 26 August 1896, led by Andrés Bonifacio, was followed by the leadership of Emilio Aguinaldo. The war had overwhelming public support in the United States, owing to enthusiasm for Cuban freedom. A protocol signed at Washington on 12 August 1898 provided for each side to appoint up to five commissioners to meet in Paris, and for the United States to occupy Manila until a treaty settled the Philippines.

The American commission was headed by William R. Day, who had resigned as Secretary of State to lead it, and included three senators, which newspapers noted meant they would later vote on their own work. Spain's commission was led by Eugenio Montero Ríos. At the first session, on 1 October, the Spanish demanded the return of Manila, which the Americans refused. Felipe Agoncillo, a Filipino lawyer representing the First Philippine Republic, was denied participation.

For almost a month the talks concerned Cuba. The Teller Amendment made it impractical to annex the island, so it was agreed that Cuba would be independent and that Spain would assume the Cuban debt, and that Spain would cede Guam and Puerto Rico. On the Philippines the Spanish hoped to cede only Mindanao and perhaps Sulu, while some Americans had favoured keeping only Manila or Luzon. President William McKinley cabled that the cession must be of the whole archipelago. The Americans offered 20 million dollars on 21 November, and Queen-Regent Maria Christina accepted. The treaty was signed on 10 December 1898.

The Cortes in Madrid rejected the treaty, but Maria Christina signed it under a clause of the Spanish constitution. In the American Senate, opponents of expansion included George Frisbie Hoar, who said it would make the country an empire controlling subject races. After fighting broke out between Filipino and American forces in Manila on 4 February 1899, the Senate approved the treaty on 6 February by 57 votes to 27, just over the two-thirds required. It came into effect on 11 April 1899. It became a major issue in the election of 1900, in which McKinley was re-elected.

The treaty marked the end of the Spanish Empire apart from small holdings, and its loss produced the cultural movement known as the Generation of '98 in Spain. The Philippine-American War, which began on 4 and 5 February 1899, ended in an American victory in 1902. Philippine revolutionaries had declared independence on 12 June 1898 and continued to resist American sovereignty.
treaty-of-passarowitz: Between 1714 and 1718 the Ottomans had been successful against Venice in Ottoman Greece and Crete, but they were defeated at Petrovaradin in 1716 by the Habsburg troops of Prince Eugene of Savoy. Peace was arranged with the intervention of Great Britain and the Dutch Republic, and the treaty was signed by Sir Robert Sutton and Jacob Colyer on behalf of their governments. The other signatories were Damian Hugo, Count of Virmont, and Michael von Talmann for the Habsburg monarchy, Vendramino Bianchi and Carlo Ruzzini for Venice, and Silindar Ibrahim-aga and Mehmed-efendija for the Ottoman Empire.

The Ottoman Empire lost the Banat of Temeswar, western Wallachia, northern Serbia including the fortress town of Belgrade, and the northern part of Bosnia, the region of Posavina, to the Habsburgs. The Habsburgs also received assurances that their merchants could operate in the Ottoman domain and that Catholic priests would regain revoked privileges. This allowed the Habsburg emperor to interfere in Ottoman affairs through connections with the church community and by championing the Catholic faith.

Venice ceded the Morea, its last outposts in Crete, and the islands of Aegina and Tinos. It retained the Ionian Islands, with Ottoman-occupied Kythira added to them, and the cities of Preveza and Arta on the Epirote mainland. In Dalmatia Venice made small gains by taking the areas of Imotski and Vrgorac.

The treaty gave the Habsburgs control over the northern part of present-day Serbia, which they had temporarily occupied during the Great Turkish War between 1688 and 1690. They established the Kingdom of Serbia as a crown land and formed the Banat into another. In its time the treaty was regarded in Vienna as an extraordinary success and a source of pride, and it marked the end of Ottoman occupation within the Kingdom of Hungary.

Habsburg control lasted 21 years, until the Turks won the Austro-Russian–Turkish War of 1735 to 1739. In the Treaty of Belgrade of 1739 the Ottoman Empire regained northern Bosnia, Habsburg Serbia including Belgrade, and the southern parts of the Banat of Temeswar, and Oltenia was returned to Wallachia.
treaty-of-portsmouth: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905 pitted the Russian Empire, with one of the largest armies in the world, against a Japan only recently industrialised. Russian armies had been driven from southern Manchuria and the Battle of Tsushima was a disaster for the Russian navy. The war was unpopular in Russia, whose government faced growing threat of revolution, while Japan's economy was strained, its foreign debts were mounting and its supply lines in Manchuria were lengthening. As early as July 1904 the Japanese government sought intermediaries.

It approached US President Theodore Roosevelt, who had been pro-Japanese at first but later worried about Japan's growing power. Tsar Nicholas II was at first adamant that Russia would win. After the costly Battle of Mukden the Japanese Foreign Minister, Komura Jutarō, judged that a settlement was critical. Russia replied favourably only after Tsushima, on 8 June 1905. Roosevelt chose Portsmouth, New Hampshire, partly for its cooler summer climate.

The delegations arrived on 8 August. Komura led the Japanese side and the former finance minister Sergei Witte the Russian. They stayed at a hotel in New Castle and were ferried each day to the naval base at Kittery, Maine. Tsar Nicholas had forbidden any territorial concessions or reparations. Twelve sessions were held between 9 and 30 August. In the first eight the delegates agreed on a ceasefire, recognition of Japan's claims to Korea, Russian withdrawal from Manchuria and the transfer to Japan of the leases in southern Manchuria and the South Manchuria Railway. Russia kept the Chinese Eastern Railway.

The last sessions dealt with reparations and territory. Witte offered that Japan keep Sakhalin and drop its claim to reparations, warned that the war would resume, and had his delegation pack its bags. He pressed his case through the American media. Outmanoeuvred, Komura yielded: in exchange for the southern half of Sakhalin, Japan dropped its claim to reparations. The treaty was signed on 5 September, and ratified in Japan on 10 October and in Russia on 14 October 1905.

The treaty brought three decades of peace between the two nations and confirmed Japan as the leading power of East Asia. Its second article acknowledged Japan's paramount interests in Korea, and Korea was annexed in 1910. The Japanese public, unaware how far its country's power was overextended, received the terms badly, and the frustration led to the Hibiya riots and the fall of the First Katsura Cabinet on 7 January 1906. Roosevelt received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906, though he never went to Portsmouth.
treaty-of-rome: In 1951 the Treaty of Paris created the European Coal and Steel Community, an idea conceived by Jean Monnet and announced by Robert Schuman, the French Foreign Minister, on 9 May 1950. Its aim was to pool Franco-West German coal and steel production and to strengthen Franco-German cooperation so as to banish the possibility of war. Two further communities proposed by the French, a European Defence Community and a European Political Community, failed when the French Parliament rejected the first.

Monnet resigned from the High Authority in protest and began work on communities based on economic integration. The Benelux states and West Germany wanted a general common market, which France opposed because of its protectionist policy, so Monnet proposed a common market and a separate nuclear community. The Messina Conference of 1955 appointed Paul-Henri Spaak to chair a preparatory committee, and its report was accepted at the Venice Conference on 29 and 30 May 1956.

The treaty was signed on 25 March 1957 at the Palazzo dei Conservatori on Capitoline Hill in Rome, together with the Euratom Treaty. It proposed the progressive reduction of customs duties and a customs union, and a common market for goods, labour, services and capital across the member states. It also proposed a Common Agriculture Policy, a Common Transport Policy and a European Social Fund, and established the European Commission.

The new communities shared the Common Assembly and the European Court of Justice with the Coal and Steel Community, but not its Council or High Authority. France was reluctant to accept more supranational powers, so the new bodies were called Commissions, with only basic powers, and important decisions had to be approved by the Council of national ministers, which now adopted majority voting.

The treaty came into force on 1 January 1958. In 1965 President Charles de Gaulle recalled French representatives from the Council of Ministers in the Empty Chair Crisis, which was resolved by the Luxembourg Compromise giving members a veto. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 removed the word economic from the title, and in 2009 the Treaty of Lisbon renamed it the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

The historian Tony Judt argued that it did not represent a fundamental turning point, being largely a declaration of future good intentions, with one significant innovation, the European Court of Justice under Article 177, whose importance was unnoticed at the time.
treaty-of-saint-germain-en-laye-1919: On 21 October 1918, 208 German-speaking delegates of the Austrian Imperial Council convened a provisional national assembly of German-Austria, and on 30 October it elected the Social Democrat Karl Renner as state chancellor. The Armistice of Villa Giusti on 3 November sealed the fate of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, and on 11 November Emperor Charles I declared that he would relinquish every participation in the administration. The next day the assembly declared German-Austria a democratic republic. Meanwhile Czechoslovakia, Poland and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes had been proclaimed on the territory of the former Austrian half of the empire, and Italian forces occupied South Tyrol and Trentino.

Renner reached Saint-Germain in May 1919 and found the Austrian delegation excluded from negotiations led by the French prime minister, Georges Clemenceau. After an Allied ultimatum he signed on 10 September 1919, at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye. The treaty declared the Austro-Hungarian Empire dissolved, and in article 177 Austria accepted, with the other Central Powers, responsibility for starting the war. Austria recognised the independence of Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. It also required reparations, though the sum was never fixed or collected.

Cisleithanian Austria lost over 60 percent of its prewar territory. Bohemia and Moravia formed the core of Czechoslovakia, Galicia went to Poland, Bukovina to Romania, and the southern half of Tyrol up to the Brenner Pass, with Trentino, to Italy. Austria received western parts of the Hungarian counties of Moson, Sopron and Vas, though after an uprising and a plebiscite Sopron and eight villages returned to Hungary. The territory finally gained was organised as the state of Burgenland. Article 88 forbade Austria to compromise its independence, which barred union with Germany without the League of Nations council's consent. The army was limited to 30,000 volunteers.

The name German-Austria had to be changed to Austria. The loss of land and population left the new state much reduced relative to the old empire, and the economy suffered most in Vienna, an imperial capital without an empire to support it. For a time the country's very existence was questioned. Many Austrians found the settlement harsh, and the economic weakness that followed was one reason why union with Nazi Germany later proved popular. The Treaty of Trianon in June 1920 completed the disposition of the former Dual Monarchy. The United States did not ratify the treaty and made a separate peace with Austria in 1921.
treaty-of-san-francisco: The treaty, also called the Treaty of Peace with Japan, was signed on 8 September 1951 at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco. China was not invited because the United States and the United Kingdom disagreed on whether the Republic of China on Taiwan or the People's Republic of China represented the Chinese people; the United States recognised the former, while Britain had recognised the latter in 1950. As a compromise neither was invited. Korea was not invited for a similar disagreement, and Italy and Portugal were not invited either. Afghanistan, Burma, India, Nepal, Yemen and Yugoslavia were invited but did not take part. India considered some provisions to limit Japanese sovereignty, and signed a separate treaty on 9 June 1952.

The treaty ended the legal state of war, brought the Allied occupation to an end and returned full sovereignty to Japan. It came into force on 28 April 1952. Japan renounced its rights to Korea, Formosa and the Pescadores, the Kuril Islands, the Spratly Islands, Antarctica and South Sakhalin. Article 3 left the Bonin, Volcano and Ryukyu Islands under a potential United Nations trusteeship, which was never set up. In Article 11 Japan accepted the judgments of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East and other Allied war crimes courts. Article 14 recognised that Japan should pay reparations but that its resources were insufficient to make complete reparation, so it would negotiate with Allied states whose territories it had occupied.

Under Article 16 Japan transferred assets to the International Committee of the Red Cross for former prisoners of war and paid £4,500,000. The Philippines and South Vietnam received compensation in 1956 and 1959, and the last payment went to the Philippines on 22 July 1976. Burma and Indonesia later signed bilateral treaties instead. The Soviet delegation under Andrei Gromyko opposed the draft and refused to sign, as did Czechoslovakia and Poland. Japan and the Soviet Union ended the war by a Joint Declaration on 19 October 1956.

Together with the Security Treaty signed the same day, the treaty began what is called the San Francisco System, which defines Japan's relationship with the United States. It left some questions open. It did not name a recipient for Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China, which was absent, has never recognised the treaty. The absence of clarity over which islands Japan gave up gave rise to the Kuril Islands dispute. A separate treaty between Japan and the Republic of China was signed at Taipei on 28 April 1952, hours before the San Francisco treaty took effect. Because South Korea did not sign, it was not entitled to the benefits of Article 14, and in 1965 Japan agreed to settlements with its government.
treaty-of-san-stefano: The treaty was signed on 3 March [O.S. 19 February] 1878 at San Stefano, then a village west of Constantinople, at the end of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878. Count Nicholas Pavlovich Ignatiev and Aleksandr Nelidov signed for the Russian Empire, and Foreign Minister Saffet Pasha and Ambassador to Germany Sadullah Pasha for the Ottoman Empire. According to the official Russian position, Russia never intended it to be more than a temporary rough draft, so as to allow a final settlement with the other Great Powers.

The treaty created an autonomous Principality of Bulgaria with a Christian government and the right to keep an army, after almost 500 years of Ottoman rule in the Bulgarian lands. Though still tributary to the Ottomans, it would have functioned as an independent nation. It would have included the plain between the Danube and the Balkan mountains, the region of Sofia, Northern Thrace, parts of Eastern Thrace and nearly all of Macedonia, giving it direct access to the Mediterranean. Its prince was to be elected, and Russian troops were to remain for two years.

Montenegro more than doubled its territory, gaining Nikšić, Podgorica and Bar, and the Ottoman Empire recognised its independence. Serbia gained Niš and Leskovac and became independent, and Turkey recognised Romanian independence, while Romania gained Northern Dobruja and ceded Southern Bessarabia to Russia. In exchange for war reparations the Ottomans ceded Ardahan, Artvin, Batum, Kars and other territories in the Caucasus to Russia. Bosnia was to become an autonomous province, and the Straits were declared open to all neutral ships.

The enlarged Bulgaria alarmed France and the United Kingdom, since Russian ships might use Bulgarian Mediterranean ports as naval bases, and Serbia feared for its own interests. British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli was unhappy with the extension of Russian power, and the British Foreign Secretary set out his objections in the Salisbury Circular of 1 April 1878. Three months later the Congress of Berlin replaced the treaty with the Treaty of Berlin, and the enlargement was never implemented. Romania, Austria-Hungary and the Albanians were also disappointed, and the reaction of the Albanians led to the formation of the League of Prizren. Bulgarians celebrate 3 March as Liberation Day.
treaty-of-sevres: France, Britain and Italy had secretly begun planning the partition of the Ottoman Empire as early as 1915. Open negotiations covered more than 15 months, from the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 through the Conference of London in February 1920, and took definite shape only after the San Remo Conference of April 1920. The delay came from disagreement among the powers, which hinged on the outcome of the Turkish National Movement.

The Allies submitted their draft at San Remo and asked for a response within a month. The former Grand Vizier Tevfik Pasha found it incompatible with independence and even statehood. The Ottoman government sent recommendations on 25 June 1920, but the Allies replied that only minor changes were possible. Sultan Mehmed VI convened a council of 57 delegates, none from the Turkish National Movement, and all but one voted to approve the signature.

The treaty was signed on 10 August 1920 at the Manufacture nationale de Sèvres porcelain factory. Its terms were far more severe than those the Treaty of Versailles imposed on Germany. The Ottoman Army was limited to 50,700 men, and an air force was prohibited. The Allies were to control the empire's finances, and the capitulations abolished in 1914 were restored. Article 230 required the surrender of those responsible for the massacres of the war years, including the Armenian genocide, though the Allied attempt to prosecute them was suspended.

Eastern Thrace and the islands of Imbros and Tenedos went to Greece, and Italy received the Dodecanese. Smyrna was left under Turkish sovereignty but administered by Greece, with a plebiscite after five years. A Zone of the Straits would internationalise the Bosporus and Dardanelles. Armenia was recognised as free and independent, a referendum was planned for Kurdistan, and the mandates for Palestine, Syria and Lebanon, and Iraq were settled.

The Ottoman government accepted the treaty, but it was never ratified, and Greece did not ratify it either. Mustafa Kemal Pasha's Grand National Assembly, set up in Ankara in April 1920, declared on 7 June 1920 invalid all treaties signed by the Istanbul government since 16 March 1920. The Turkish War of Independence followed. The Chanak crisis of September 1922 nearly led to war with Britain over the Straits, but the Armistice of Mudanya was concluded on 11 October. The Allies returned to negotiate at Lausanne, and the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 replaced Sèvres, restored a large territory in Anatolia and Thrace to the Turks, did not make Constantinople an international city, and led to the Republic of Turkey.
treaty-of-shimonoseki: The peace conference ran from 20 March to 17 April 1895 at the Shunpanrō hotel in Shimonoseki, Japan. Count Itō Hirobumi and Viscount Mutsu Munemitsu negotiated for Japan, and Li Hongzhang and his son Li Jingfang for the Qing dynasty, with the former American secretary of state John W. Foster advising the Qing side. On 24 March Li Hongzhang was shot and wounded by a right-wing Japanese extremist. The public outcry led the Japanese to temper their demands and agree to a temporary armistice, and the conference resumed on 10 April.

Itō and Mutsu wanted to reduce Qing power not only in Korea but also on Taiwan, whose importance for expansion towards South China and Southeast Asia Mutsu had noticed. Li argued that Taiwan had never been a battlefield in the war and, having been a province since 1885, could not be given away. He finally agreed to the cession of Penghu and part of Liaodong, but under Japan's military advantage he gave up Taiwan too.

The treaty had eleven articles. China recognised the full independence and autonomy of Korea, ending the tribute and ceremonies Korea had performed to China. China ceded the Penghu Islands, Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula, and agreed to pay an indemnity of 200 million Kuping taels, over seven years. It opened Shashi, Chongqing, Suzhou and Hangzhou to Japanese trade and granted Japan most favoured nation status. The Guangxu Emperor ratified the treaty despite vigorous opposition from Chinese scholars and officials.

Russia, France and Germany, which were active in China, intervened and demanded that Japan give up Liaodong, mainly out of concern for Port Arthur. In November 1895 Japan returned the territory in exchange for an additional indemnity of 30 million taels. The cession of Taiwan met strong local resistance, and Japan did not take over the islands until October 1895. Pro-Qing officials and gentry declared a Republic of Formosa that year but gained no international recognition.

In China the treaty was regarded as a national humiliation. It weakened support for the Qing, and the Self-Strengthening Movement was judged a failure, which fed the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 and the uprisings that ended in the fall of the dynasty in 1911. Many Japanese historians regard the Triple Intervention as a turning point towards outright imperialism. The Treaty of Taipei of 28 April 1952 is held to have formally abrogated the Treaty of Shimonoseki, though the cession provision is disputed by some.
treaty-of-tartu-russian-estonian: Estonia had been a province of Imperial Russia since 1721. In 1917, three years into the First World War, the Russian Empire fell into revolution and civil war. As part of this larger conflict the Estonians declared independence from the warring Russian and German empires, and they won their freedom in the Estonian War of Independence of 1918 to 1920.

The treaty established the border between Estonia and Russia, affirmed the right of Estonians to return to Estonia and of Russian people to return to Russia, and required that Estonian movable property evacuated to Russia in the First World War be returned. Russia also agreed to absolve Estonia of Russian Imperial debt and to pay Estonia 15 million gold rubles, a share of the gold reserves of the former Russian Empire.

Russia further agreed to grant concessions to exploit one million hectares of Russian forest land and to build a railway line from the Estonian border to Moscow. Jaan Poska signed for Estonia and Adolf Joffe for Soviet Russia, together with other representatives of both parties. Ratifications were exchanged in Moscow on 30 March 1920, and the treaty was registered in the League of Nations Treaty Series on 12 July 1922.

The treaty has been regarded as the birth certificate of the Republic of Estonia because it was the first de jure recognition of the state. It was also of great importance to diplomatically isolated Soviet Russia, and Lenin expressed satisfaction with it as "an incomparable victory over Western imperialism". Some members of the Entente opposed the treaty, intending to keep Soviet Russia in international isolation.

After the signing, Soviet Russia did not fulfil several points of the treaty. The migration of Estonians was obstructed, and the museum collections of the University of Tartu were not returned from Voronezh. Estonia was occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940 to 1941 and again from 1944 to 1991.
treaty-of-the-pyrenees: France entered the Thirty Years' War after the Spanish Habsburg victories in the Dutch Revolt in the 1620s and at the Battle of Nördlingen in 1634. By 1640 France was aiding the revolt in Catalonia, while Spain responded in 1648 by aiding the Fronde in France. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 France gained the Sundgau and cut Spanish access to the Netherlands from Austria, which increased hostilities. An Anglo-French alliance won the Battle of the Dunes on 14 June 1658, but the war ground to a halt the next year when the French campaign to take Milan was defeated.

The treaty was negotiated and signed on Pheasant Island, in the Bidasoa River on the border between the two countries, by Louis XIV of France and Philip IV of Spain and their chief ministers, Cardinal Mazarin and Don Luis Méndez de Haro. France gained Roussillon, including Perpignan, and the northern half of Cerdanya, along with Montmédy and other parts of Luxembourg, Artois and towns in Flanders such as Arras, Béthune, Gravelines and Thionville. A new border was fixed at the Pyrenees. Because the treaty spoke only of villages, the town of Llívia was unintentionally left to Spain as an exclave, and the border was not properly settled until the Treaty of Bayonne of 1856.

Spain was forced to recognise the French gains of the Peace of Westphalia. In exchange, the French king pledged to stop supporting Portugal and renounced his claim to the Principality of Catalonia. The treaty also arranged the marriage of Louis XIV to Maria Theresa, daughter of Philip IV, who renounced her claim to the Spanish throne in return for a dowry that was never paid, a factor in the War of Devolution of 1667. England received Dunkirk and sold it to France in 1662.

The historian J. H. Elliott sees the treaty as the decisive admission of defeat in Spain's long struggle to maintain the Pax Hispanica. Paul Kennedy identifies it as the climax of the Habsburg bid for mastery, and attributes Spain's fall to imperial overstretch. It was Cardinal Mazarin's last major diplomatic achievement, and together with the Peace of Westphalia it gave Louis XIV stability and diplomatic advantage. By 1660 most of the European continent was at peace, and the Bourbons had ended the dominance of the Habsburgs. In the Pyrenees the treaty established border customs and restricted the free flow of people and goods.
treaty-of-tordesillas: The dispute arose after Christopher Columbus returned in 1493 from his first voyage under the Crown of Castile. He stopped first at Lisbon, and King John II of Portugal then claimed the new lands under the Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1479 and the papal bull Aeterni regis of 1481, which granted Portugal all lands south of the Canary Islands. He wrote a threatening letter to Ferdinand and Isabella and prepared a fleet.

On 4 May 1493 Pope Alexander VI decreed in the bull Inter caetera that lands west of a line 100 leagues west of the Azores or the Cape Verde Islands should belong to Castile. John II felt this gave him too little: by 1493 Portuguese explorers had reached the Cape of Good Hope, and a later bull that named India as Spanish was a major issue for his near-term goal. He therefore negotiated directly with the Catholic Monarchs.

The treaty was signed in Tordesillas on 7 June 1494 and ratified in Setúbal. It placed the line of demarcation 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, with lands to the east for Portugal and to the west for Castile. Portugal had asked for the line to be moved 270 leagues further west than the pope's, to protect its route along the coast of Africa.

The treaty did not define the league or say which Cape Verde island was meant. It provided that these points be settled by a joint voyage, which never took place, and later expert opinions placed the line at roughly 42° to 47° west. It was negotiated without consulting Alexander VI, but Pope Julius II sanctioned it by the bull Ea quae pro bono pacis of 24 January 1506.

Very little of the divided area had been seen by Europeans. In 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral landed on the easternmost part of present-day Brazil on his way to India, and it fell to Portugal. Some historians contend that the Portuguese already knew of the coast. Spain did not resist Portuguese expansion across the meridian in Brazil.

After Portugal reached the Moluccas in 1512, Spain argued that the treaty divided the whole globe in two. The Treaty of Zaragoza of 22 April 1529 set an antimeridian and Spain gave up its claim to the Moluccas for 350,000 ducats of gold. France's Francis I and the Protestant maritime powers, England and the Netherlands, did not recognise a division of the world between two Catholic nations. The Treaty of Madrid of 1750 superseded the Tordesillas line, and UNESCO added the treaty to its Memory of the World register in 2007.
treaty-of-trianon: Hungary had been at war since August 1914 as part of Austria-Hungary. On 31 October 1918, in the Aster Revolution, King Charles IV appointed the liberal Count Mihály Károlyi prime minister, and Hungary declared its independence from Austria. Károlyi had the army, which still numbered more than 1,400,000 soldiers, unilaterally disarmed, and an armistice was signed on 13 November 1918. Serbian, Czechoslovak and Romanian forces crossed the borders in the following days, and Hungary's neighbours blockaded the country.

On 21 March 1919 Béla Kun led a communist coup and proclaimed the Hungarian Soviet Republic. In June the Entente ordered Romania and Czechoslovakia to stop their advance and accept new demarcation lines as future borders. After Kun's fall Admiral Miklós Horthy entered Budapest on 16 November 1919, and Count Albert Apponyi led the Hungarian delegation to the Paris Peace Conference.

The treaty, dictated by the Allies rather than negotiated, was signed in the Grand Trianon at Versailles on 4 June 1920 and came into force on 26 July 1921. It legalised the existing demarcation lines as the new borders. The Allies refused plebiscites, explaining in the Millerand letter that a popular consultation would not produce significantly different results; the letter also suggested that the League of Nations might mediate border corrections, which Hungarian diplomats read as a promise.

Hungary became a landlocked state of 93,073 square kilometres and 7.6 million people, and 3.3 million Hungarians lived in the areas allocated to its neighbours. The army was limited to 35,000 men, heavy artillery, tanks and air force were forbidden, and the Austro-Hungarian Navy ceased to exist. Hungary had to pay reparations and recognise minority rights. The treaty also ended the blockade and ordered the resumption of trade and of coal supplies.

The Hungarian delegation signed under protest, and agitation for revision began at once. Irredentism, the demand for reunification of Hungarian peoples, became a central theme of Hungarian politics and diplomacy. Romanians joined Romania, and Slovaks, Serbs and Croats helped form Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia, but as many as a third of Hungarian speakers found themselves outside the new borders. The economic effects were severe, since the Austro-Hungarian economy had been one unit: mills around Budapest operated at 20% capacity. Hungary's boundaries have remained mostly the same since 1920, apart from the short-lived expansion of 1938–1941. The treaty is known in Hungary as the Peace Dictate of Trianon.
treaty-of-turkmenchay: The treaty was the second of a series of agreements between Qajar Iran and Imperial Russia that forced Iran to cede or recognise Russian influence over territories that had formerly belonged to it. The first was the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813 and the last the Treaty of Akhal of 1881. It was signed on 22 February 1828 in Torkamanchay, a village between Tabriz and Tehran, for Iran by Crown Prince Abbas Mirza and Allah-Yar Khan Asef al-Dowleh, chancellor to Fath-Ali Shah Qajar, and for Russia by General Ivan Paskievich. As with Gulistan, the treaty was imposed after a Russian military victory, and Paskievich threatened to occupy Tehran in five days unless it was signed.

Under Article 4 Iran ceded the Erivan Khanate, the Nakhchivan Khanate and the Talysh Khanate, together with the Ordubad and Mughan regions, and repeated the cessions of Gulistan. The Aras River became the boundary. Iran promised to pay 10 korur in gold or 20 million silver rubles, and Persian ships lost the right to navigate the Caspian Sea, which passed to Russia. Russia promised to support Abbas Mirza as heir to the throne, a clause that became moot when he died before Fath-Ali Shah.

The treaty also recognised capitulation rights for Russian subjects in Iran and allowed Russia to send consular envoys anywhere in the country. Article 15 gave the inhabitants of Iranian Azerbaijan the right to move to Russian districts within one year, and provided for the resettlement of Armenians in the Caucasus.

The historian Alexander Mikaberidze describes the treaty as the definite acknowledgement of the Persian loss of the Caucasus to Russia. The formerly Iranian territories came under Russian, and later Soviet, control for about 180 years. Dagestan remains a constituent republic of the Russian Federation, while Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia, which together held most of the territory ceded at Gulistan and Turkmenchay, became independent after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

Armenians from Iranian Azerbaijan used the freedom to emigrate, and in the years 1828 to 1831 some 45,000 are recorded as moving to Russian Armenia. Anti-Russian feeling was widespread in Persia after the treaty. On 11 February 1829 a mob stormed the Russian embassy in Tehran and killed almost everyone inside, among them the newly appointed ambassador, the playwright Aleksander Griboyedov, who had helped to negotiate the terms. As an apology the shah presented the tsar with the Shah Diamond.
treaty-of-utrecht: The War of the Spanish Succession involved three contenders for the vacant throne of Spain and drew in much of Europe for over a decade. On 2 January 1710 King Louis XIV of France agreed to open peace negotiations at Geertruidenberg in the Netherlands. France and Great Britain came to terms in October 1711, when the preliminaries were signed in London, and these rested on a tacit acceptance of the partition of Spain's European possessions. The Congress of Utrecht opened on 29 January 1712. Little progress came until 10 July 1712, when Philip V signed a renunciation of the French throne.

The peace was a series of treaties signed in Utrecht between April 1713 and February 1715. The main treaties were signed on 11 April 1713, five separate agreements between France and Great Britain, the Dutch Republic, Savoy, Prussia and Portugal. Spain signed treaties with Savoy and Great Britain on 13 July 1713. Philip V, grandson of Louis XIV, remained king of Spain and renounced the French throne for himself and his descendants, with reciprocal renunciations by French Bourbons.

In Article X Spain ceded Gibraltar and Menorca to Britain, which also gained the Asiento de Negros, the monopoly contract to supply slaves to Spain's American colonies, for thirty years. Britain demanded that France level the fortifications of Dunkirk, the main base of French privateers. Savoy received Sicily and parts of the Duchy of Milan, while the former Spanish Netherlands, Naples, Sardinia and most of Milan went to Emperor Charles VI. France ceded Nova Scotia and its claims to Newfoundland and Rupert's Land to Britain, and the French portion of Saint Kitts.

The treaty stipulated that one person should never become king of both France and Spain. Some historians see it as a milestone in the evolution of the balance of power. The Whigs in Britain opposed the peace, but the Tory ministry of Robert Harley and Viscount Bolingbroke persuaded Queen Anne to create twelve new Tory peers to ensure ratification in the House of Lords. Dutch influence was slight, though the talks were held on their territory.

Catalonia received no guarantees of its rights, and the War of the Catalans of 1713 to 1714 followed. The Dutch Republic ended the war effectively bankrupt, and Britain emerged with naval superiority and commercial access to Spain and America. The historian G. M. Trevelyan wrote that the treaty marked the end of danger to Europe from the old French monarchy and the maritime, commercial and financial supremacy of Great Britain.
treaty-of-verdun: After Charlemagne's death Louis I was made ruler of the Frankish Empire, and he divided it so that each of his sons could rule a kingdom under his own greater rule. His eldest son, Lothair I, held the title of emperor, but after several re-divisions and the revolts that followed he became much less powerful. When Louis died in 840, Lothair claimed overlordship over the entire realm. His brother Louis II and his half-brother Charles II refused to accept it and declared war. They defeated Lothair at the Battle of Fontenoy in 841 and sealed their alliance in 842 with the Oaths of Strasbourg, which declared Lothair unfit for the imperial throne. After this he was willing to negotiate.

The treaty was agreed on 10 August 843, after more than a year of negotiations, and ended the civil war. Each brother already held a kingdom: Lothair in Italy, Louis in Bavaria and Charles in Aquitaine. Lothair kept the imperial title, but it now gave only nominal overlordship of his brothers' lands. He received Francia Media, the Middle Frankish kingdom, with the two imperial cities, Aachen and Rome. This domain later covered the Low Countries, Lorraine, Alsace, Burgundy, Provence and the Kingdom of Italy.

Louis received Francia Orientalis, the East Frankish kingdom, all lands east of the Rhine, which became the high medieval Kingdom of Germany. Charles received Francia Occidentalis, all lands west of the Rhône, which eventually became the Kingdom of France.

The division followed the old Frankish custom of partible inheritance among a ruler's sons rather than primogeniture, which both Frankish kingdoms would soon adopt. It was the first of four partition treaties of the Carolingian Empire, followed by those of Prüm in 855, Meerssen in 870 and Ribemont in 880. Only Charles the Fat briefly reassembled Charlemagne's empire.

After Lothair's death in 855 his eldest son Louis II inherited Italy and the imperial claim, and the northern territory was named Lotharingia after Lothair II. With long, vulnerable land borders and poor communications, it was not a viable entity and soon fragmented. Generations of kings of France and Germany failed to establish firm rule there, and Alsace-Lorraine passed between the two powers from the 18th to the 20th century.
treaty-of-versailles: The armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting but left the peace to be settled. It took six months of Allied negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference to conclude a treaty. Talks between the Allies began on 18 January 1919 at the French Foreign Ministry on the Quai d'Orsay, with 70 delegates from 27 nations.

The victors wanted different things. France had lost 1.3 million soldiers and had its industrial north-east devastated, and Clemenceau sought security by weakening Germany. British opinion favoured a just peace in which Germany paid reparations. President Woodrow Wilson, whose Fourteen Points of 8 January 1918 had called for a League of Nations and self-determination, hoped for a peace of reconciliation. The result was a compromise that satisfied none of them.

The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Palace of Versailles, five years to the day after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Germany lost 65,000 km2 of territory and 7 million people. Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, the Saar coalfield passed to France with the territory under League of Nations control for 15 years, and Eupen-Malmedy went to Belgium. Germany's colonies became League of Nations mandates, and its concessions in Shandong were given to Japan.

The army was limited to 100,000 men, conscription was abolished and the General Staff was dissolved. Allied troops were to occupy the Rhineland for up to fifteen years. Article 231, the so-called War Guilt clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of the war, and a Reparation Commission was to fix the sum. The Covenant of the League of Nations formed Part I of the treaty.

Germany protested that it was excluded from the talks. The government of Philipp Scheidemann resigned rather than sign, and Gustav Bauer's government signed after an Allied ultimatum threatening an invasion across the Rhine. The United States Senate never ratified the treaty, and the United States made a separate peace with Germany.

In 1921 the Reparation Commission set Germany's share at 50 billion gold marks, later reduced by the Dawes Plan and the Young Plan. The last Allied troops left the Rhineland on 30 June 1930. Critics such as John Maynard Keynes thought the treaty too harsh, while Marshal Ferdinand Foch thought it too lenient, and historians still disagree about its effects. Resentment of the treaty, together with the stab-in-the-back myth, was exploited by Adolf Hitler, and the treaty has been cited as a cause of the Second World War.
treaty-of-waitangi: In nineteenth-century New Zealand the British wanted to formalise their involvement, protect British interests, regulate land speculation and control violence and disordered settlement. They faced a Māori population that was more numerous, with cultivated land and its own government. The New Zealand Company, acting for settlers and would-be settlers, was establishing a colony, and some Māori leaders had petitioned the British for protection against French ambitions.

With no draft from lawyers or Colonial Office officials, William Hobson wrote the treaty himself with his secretary James Freeman and the British Resident James Busby, neither a lawyer. It was prepared in three days and revised many times, and there were doubts even during drafting that the chiefs would grasp the idea of relinquishing sovereignty. It was translated into Māori overnight on 4 and 5 February 1840.

The treaty has a preamble and three articles, in English and Māori texts that differ. In Article One the Māori text grants kawanatanga, translated by Hugh Kāwharu as complete governance, while the English text cedes all the rights and powers of sovereignty. In Article Two the Māori text promises rangatiratanga, full chieftainship, over lands, villages and treasures, and the English text guarantees full, exclusive and undisturbed ownership, with the Crown holding the exclusive right of pre-emption to buy land.

Article Three gave Māori the Queen's protection and the rights of British subjects. At the signing a further statement was added in writing that the faiths of England, of the Wesleyans, of Rome and also Māori custom would be protected alike.

Hobson read the treaty in English and Henry Williams the Māori text to a hui of northern chiefs on 5 February 1840, and signing began on 6 February. Eight further copies were sent around the country for more signatures; around 530 to 540 Māori signed the Māori version and only 39 the English. On 21 May 1840 Hobson proclaimed sovereignty over the whole country, the North Island by treaty and the South Island and Stewart Island by discovery.

In 1877 Chief Justice Prendergast called the treaty a simple nullity in the case of Wi Parata v Bishop of Wellington, which remained legal orthodoxy until at least the 1970s. A Māori protest movement then called for the government to honour the treaty. The Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 marked a paradigm shift in official discourse on Māori rights, 6 February is now the national day, Waitangi Day, and the treaty entered UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 1997.
trebinje: Trebinje is the southernmost city of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the Trebišnjica river in the region of East Herzegovina, at the foot of Leotar and about 30 kilometres by road from Dubrovnik. The river floods in the winter, and after it passes through Popovo Polje it runs underground towards the Adriatic. It is heavily used for hydroelectric power. The municipality covers 904 square kilometres and lies in the south of Republika Srpska, bordering municipalities of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio mentions the region as Travunija. Prince Vlastimir of Serbia married his daughter to Krajina, son of Beloje, and that family became hereditary rulers there. The town commanded the road from Ragusa to Constantinople, which Raymond IV of Toulouse and his crusaders followed in 1096. At the end of the 12th century Stefan Nemanja conquered Trebinje, and it belonged to the Serbian Kingdom and Empire until the Balšić family took it in 1373. In 1377 it was incorporated into the Bosnian state under Tvrtko I and later belonged to the Kosača family's domains.

Ottoman forces first took Trebinje in 1465, it was returned to Vlatko Hercegović Kosača in 1470, and by 1478 it was finally captured. The Ottomans built the Old Town, called Kastel, on the site of the medieval fortress of Ban Vir. The Arslanagić Bridge, built in the 16th century by Mehmed-Paša Sokolović, stands in a village north of the town. From 1596 the Tvrdoš Monastery was the centre of anti-Ottoman activity in Herzegovina, and the region suffered from raids by uskoks and hajduks. Austria-Hungary administered the town from 1878 to 1918, building fortifications on the hills, a garrison and the present main street.

Under Socialist Yugoslavia, between 1945 and 1980, Trebinje grew rapidly as dams, lakes and hydroelectric plants were built. During the Bosnian War the town was controlled by Bosnian Serb forces and served as a command and artillery base for the Yugoslav People's Army troops besieging Dubrovnik; ten of its mosques were destroyed with explosives. After the Dayton Agreement of 1995 the former Trebinje municipality was divided between Republika Srpska and the Federation. The Old Town and the Arslanagić Bridge remain its best-known monuments.
treblinka-extermination-camp: Treblinka lay in a forest about 80 kilometres northeast of Warsaw. Before the war the site held a gravel mining enterprise owned by the Polish industrialist Marian Łopuszyński, linked by rail to the main cities of central Poland. The Germans found it well connected yet isolated, halfway between some of the largest ghettos in occupied Europe, among them the Warsaw Ghetto and the Białystok Ghetto. It consisted of two camps. Treblinka I, opened on 1 September 1941, was a forced-labour camp through which 20,000 people passed, and about half of them died of exhaustion, hunger and disease. Treblinka II, the extermination camp, was built from 10 April 1942.

Treblinka II was part of Operation Reinhard, the programme for the genocide of the Jews outlined after the Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942. It had one function, to murder those sent there, and it was disguised as a transit camp with a false station, a painted clock and a ticket window. Mass deportation from the Warsaw Ghetto began on 22 July 1942, and the gas chambers began operating the next morning. German records give 265,000 Jews carried from the ghetto between 22 July and 12 September 1942. Almost 20,000 foreign Jews arrived between October 1942 and March 1943. Romani people were also killed there.

Irmfried Eberl, the first commandant, was replaced by Franz Stangl on 1 September 1942, after the early gassing machinery broke down and the mass graves overflowed. From early 1943 the bodies were dug up and burned on open pyres. A small group of prisoners was kept alive to work, and in early 1943 they formed a resistance organisation. On 2 August 1943, about 700 prisoners revolted, set buildings ablaze and attacked the gate; most were shot, but about 200 escaped, half of whom were killed in pursuit. Around 70 are known to have survived the war, among them Samuel Willenberg. Gassing ended in October 1943 and the camp was dismantled, with a farmhouse built on the site and the ground ploughed over.

Soviet forces reached the site in August 1944. Treblinka was long looted by local people digging for valuables, and the site was not at first protected. A memorial designed by Franciszek Duszeńko was begun in 1958, and Treblinka was declared a national monument of martyrdom on 10 May 1964. The first German trials of former SS personnel were held at Düsseldorf in 1964 and 1965. An exhibition centre opened in 2006. Estimates of the number of dead differ between scholars and museums.
trebuchet: A trebuchet is a type of catapult that uses a hinged arm with a sling attached to the tip to launch a projectile. It was a common powerful siege engine until the advent of gunpowder. As a compound machine it makes use of the mechanical advantage of a lever. Typical constructions are large, with a beam as much as 15 metres long. The beam is attached by an axle to a stout frame and base, so that it can rotate vertically through an arc typically over 180 degrees. The projectile section of the beam is usually four to six times longer than the section where force is applied.

The traction trebuchet, which uses manpower to swing the arm, first appeared in China by the 4th century BCE. It spread westward, possibly via the Avars, and was adopted by the Byzantines, Persians, Arabs and other neighbouring peoples by the sixth to seventh centuries CE. The counterweight trebuchet appeared in both Christian and Muslim lands around the Mediterranean in the 12th century and was carried back to China by the Mongols in the 13th century.

There is little consensus on where and when the counterweight trebuchet was first developed. The earliest known description and illustration comes from a commentary on the conquests of Saladin by Mardi ibn Ali al-Tarsusi in 1187, though cases have been made for earlier European and Muslim machines. In China the traction trebuchet was called the pào and the counterweight trebuchet the húihúi pào, the Muslim trebuchet.

With the introduction of gunpowder the trebuchet lost its place as the siege engine of choice to the cannon. Trebuchets were still used at the siege of Burgos in 1475 to 1476 and the siege of Rhodes in 1480. One of the last recorded military uses was by Hernán Cortés at the 1521 siege of Tenochtitlán, where limited gunpowder motivated the attempt. It was reportedly unsuccessful: the first projectile landed on the trebuchet itself and destroyed it.

The methods of construction were lost at the beginning of the 16th century. In 1984 the French engineer Renaud Beffeyte made the first modern reconstruction, based on documents from 1324. Most use in recent centuries has been recreational or educational.
treguier: Tréguier, Landreger in Breton, is a port town and the capital of the province of Trégor. It lies 36 miles north-west of Saint-Brieuc by road. The port is about 5 and a half miles from the English Channel, at the confluence of two streams that form the Tréguier River. Its inhabitants are called trécorrois in French. In the past saw-milling, boat-building and flax-stripping were carried on there, together with trade in cereals, cloth and potatoes, and the port had fishing, coasting and a small foreign trade.

Tréguier, called Trecorum, dates from the sixth century and grew up round a monastery founded by Saint Tudwal, who died about 564. In the 9th century it became the seat of a bishopric, which was suppressed on 12 July 1790 under a decree of 14 November 1789. Count Stephen of Tréguier was the second Earl of Richmond, inheriting the peerage that William the Conqueror had created for his second cousin Alan Rufus.
The United States Navy established a naval air station there on 1 November 1918 to operate seaplanes during the First World War, and it closed shortly after the Armistice of Compiègne.

The cathedral, dating from the 14th and 15th centuries, has three towers over the transept, one of them with a fine spire. It holds the mausoleum of Ivo of Kermartin (Saint Yves), who died in 1303, a canon of the cathedral and patron saint of lawyers, to whom its building was largely due. South of the church is a cloister of 1468. The Pardon of Saint Yves draws lawyers and judges from many countries, and the Tro Breizh pilgrimage links Tréguier with the towns of the other founding saints of Brittany.

A statue of Ernest Renan, born in the town in 1823, stands near the cathedral. Renan was a prominent sceptic, and when the statue was unveiled in 1903 with a figure of the goddess Athena, it provoked widespread protests from the Catholic Church. The town has a museum in his birthplace. Others born there include the critic Ernest Hello and the Dominican Hervaeus Natalis, who was Master General of the order.
trencin: Trenčín lies in the central valley of the Váh River in the Trenčín Basin, near the Czech border and about 95 kilometres from Bratislava, at an altitude of 217 metres. The basin is surrounded by the Strážov Mountains, Považský Inovec and the White Carpathians. It was first mentioned under the Greek name Leukaristos on a world map based on Ptolemy, around 150 CE, and the Roman inscription of 179 CE names the place as Laugaricio. The medieval name probably derives from a personal name, Trnka or Trenka, meaning blackthorn, with a possessive suffix, and the first medieval mentions date from 1111 and 1113.

Trenčín is one of the suggested locations for the capital of Samo's Empire in the 7th century, and Trenčín Castle may have been founded in the Great Moravian era. In 1017 Stephen I of Hungary conquered the region, which stayed part of Hungary until 1918. By the end of the 11th century the castle was the administrative centre of Trencsén county. As one of the few stone castles in the country it resisted the Mongol invasion of 1241. Between 1302 and 1321 it was the seat of the magnate Matthew Csák, who controlled most of present-day Slovakia and challenged King Charles Robert. The Treaty of Trentschin between Bohemia, Hungary and Poland was signed in the city in 1335.

The town gained freedom from tolls in 1324 and free royal town status from King Sigismund in 1412. Imperial troops captured it in 1528 during the conflict between the Habsburgs and the supporters of János Szapolyai. The Ottomans failed to take it in the 17th century. The Battle of Trenčín was fought near the city on 3 August 1708, and a plague killed 1,600 inhabitants two years later. In 1790 the town and castle burned down, and the castle has been a ruin since. The 19th century brought railways and new industries.

Trenčín is the seat of the Trenčín Region and District and has more than 55,000 inhabitants. Trenčín Castle, the third largest in Slovakia, stands on a rock above the city, with its upper castle and central medieval tower. The old town has a large main square, a baroque church and a town tower. The Roman inscription on the rock below the castle, carved in 179 CE during the Marcomannic Wars, is its best-known monument. The historical centre has been largely restored since 1990.
trentino: Trentino, officially the Autonomous Province of Trento, lies in the far north of Italy and covers 6,207 square kilometres. With South Tyrol it forms the autonomous region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol. The province is mountainous and contains much of the Dolomites, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, whose highest peak, the Marmolada, rises to 3,343 metres. The Adige River flows through its centre, and its valley, where the principal towns lie, has long connected Italy with Central Europe. The name derives from the capital, Trento, and originally referred only to the city and its surroundings. Under Austrian rule the common German name was Welschtirol, or Foreign Tyrol.

The valleys were inhabited from the mid-Stone Age. In the early Middle Ages the area belonged to the Kingdom of Italy and the March of Verona. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II established the Bishopric of Trent as a state of the Holy Roman Empire, governed by prince-bishops. The Council of Trent, held in three sessions between 1545 and 1563, set out Roman Catholic doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation.

After the Napoleonic Wars the bishopric was secularised and absorbed into the Austrian County of Tyrol. Trentino lay on the front line between Austria-Hungary and Italy and saw heavy fighting in the First World War. Italy occupied it in November 1918 and it was formally ceded under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1919. After the Second World War the Gruber-De Gasperi Agreement created the autonomous region, and a second Statute of Autonomy in 1972 devolved most powers to the two provinces.

Trentino has more than half a million people and 166 municipalities. Italian predominates, but three indigenous minorities, speakers of Ladin, Mòcheno and Cimbrian, are protected by law. The province has its own elected government and a council of 35 members, one of whom must by law come from the Ladin minority. Since 1996 it has belonged with South Tyrol and the Austrian state of Tyrol to a Euroregion whose boundaries match the old County of Tyrol. Its castles include Castel del Buonconsiglio in Trento and Castel Thun in the Non Valley.
trento: Trento stands on the Adige river, on the river route to Bolzano and the low Alpine passes of the Brenner and the Reschen Pass. It is the capital of the autonomous province of Trento, or Trentino, in the region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, and has 119,359 inhabitants. The city centre lies just under 200 metres above sea level, while the municipality reaches 2,000 metres at Monte Bondone. Before the river was diverted in the mid-nineteenth century the Adige ran through the centre of the town and was a navigable commercial route in the Alps. Its old course is now covered by Via Torre Vanga, Via Torre Verde and Via Alessandro Manzoni.

The origins of Trento are uncertain. Some scholars hold that it was a Rhaetian settlement, though the Adige area was influenced by neighbours including the Veneti, the Etruscans and the Gauls. Other theories say the Gauls founded the city in the fourth century BCE. A late-Roman basilica lies beneath the later cathedral, which can be seen in an underground crypt. The Castello del Buonconsiglio was the seat of the Prince-Bishops of Trento, and the Council of Trent was held in the city in the sixteenth century. It was part of Austria and then of Austria-Hungary before Italy annexed it in 1919.

The railway station opened in 1859 on the Brenner line from Verona to Innsbruck, the main rail link between Italy and Germany. The Teatro Sociale was built in 1819. The University of Trento was founded in 1962 as a Higher University Institute of Social Sciences.

Much of the Late Medieval and Renaissance centre has been restored to its pastel colours and wooden balconies. Part of the medieval walls and a circular tower can be seen in Piazza Fiera. The Romanesque-Gothic Cathedral of Saint Vigilius dates from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and the Piazza Duomo beside it has frescoed Renaissance buildings and the Late Baroque Fountain of Neptune of 1767 to 1768. The Tridentine Diocesan Museum, in the Palazzo Pretorio, shows the artistic treasures of the diocese and the influence of the council on the city. Since 2011 Trento has belonged to the Euroregion Tyrol-South Tyrol-Trentino.
trepanning: The word trepan comes from Old French, from Medieval Latin trepanum and Greek trúpanon, meaning borer or auger. The operation exposes the dura mater and was mainly performed by priests or healers. Its purposes may have included treating intracranial disease, releasing blood that pooled after an injury, removing splinters of bone and relieving pressure. In some societies it was believed to release the evil spirits blamed for abnormal behaviour. Archaeologists identify a trephined skull by the hole, the shape of its edges and signs of healing.

Early tools were hand-held and made of flint, obsidian or harder stone, and later of bronze and copper. In early Peru the tumi, a ceremonial knife, was used, and in the South Pacific sharpened seashells. Five methods are recorded: rectangular intersecting cuts, scraping, circular grooving, cutting with a circular trephine or crown saw, and boring a ring of holes and chiselling between them. The Greeks and Romans were the first to design instruments for the purpose, such as the terebra serrata.

Among the Andean peoples, including the Paracas culture, the Muisca and the Inca, skulls with trepanation are common, between 11 and 40 per cent in parts of Peru, and many holes avoid the midline of the skull, which suggests a wish to reduce risk. Chinese examples include a skull from Shandong dated to about 5,000 years ago. In Europe, Iron Age populations had success rates of 78 per cent, and seven of eight skulls of the 6th to 8th centuries from south-western Germany show healing.

In the 1870s the French anthropologist Paul Broca found several European and South American children's skulls of the Neolithic that had been perforated surgically. He found no fractures to explain the operation and proposed a ritual or religious purpose, perhaps to remove confined demons or to make talismans from the removed bone. He also suggested it might treat childhood conditions such as febrile seizures. The idea that the holes treated headaches spread in the 19th century, but this belief is a myth.

In modern medicine trepanation is the ancestor of the craniotomy, used for epidural and subdural haematomas. Since the 1960s a few people have drilled holes in their own skulls, among them the Dutch librarian Bart Huges in 1965, who claimed it increased brain blood volume. Research has not supported these claims.
tretyakov-gallery: The Muscovite merchant Pavel Mikhailovich Tretyakov began collecting art in the middle of 1850, and the gallery's founding year is taken to be 1856, when he bought two paintings by Russian artists of his day: Temptation by Nikolay Shilder and Skirmish with Finnish Smugglers by Vasily Khudyakov. Earlier, in 1854 and 1855, he had bought 11 drawings and nine pictures by Dutch Old Masters. His aim was a collection that might one day grow into a museum of national art. In 1867 the Moscow City Gallery of Pavel and Sergei Tretyakov was opened, holding 1,276 paintings, 471 sculptures and 10 drawings by Russian artists as well as 84 paintings by foreign masters.

In August 1892 Tretyakov presented his collection to the city of Moscow. It then included 1,287 paintings and 518 graphic works of the Russian school, 75 paintings and eight drawings of European schools, 15 sculptures and a collection of icons. The museum officially opened on 15 August 1893. It was housed in a mansion the Tretyakov family had bought in 1851 and extended several times. The façade, designed by the architect V. Bashkirov from drawings by the painter Viktor Vasnetsov in a Russian fairy-tale style, was built in 1902 to 1904.

On 3 June 1918 the gallery was declared the property of the Russian Federated Soviet Republic and named the State Tretyakov Gallery, with Igor Grabar as its director. In 1932 the former Church of St Nicholas in Tolmachi, closed in 1929, was given to the gallery. In the summer of 1941 the collection was taken to Novosibirsk on a train of 17 wagons, the paintings rolled on wooden shafts and packed in boxes, and the gallery reopened in Moscow on 17 May 1945. The Alexander Ivanov Hall, built for his painting The Appearance of Christ Before the People, was completed in 1956. From 1986 to 1995 the main building in Lavrushinsky Lane was closed for a major renovation.

The State Tretyakov Gallery is considered the foremost depository of Russian fine art in the world. Its collection runs to more than 130,000 exhibits, from the Theotokos of Vladimir to Wassily Kandinsky's Composition VII and Kazimir Malevich's Black Square. In 1977 it kept a significant part of the George Costakis collection. In 1985 it was merged with a gallery of contemporary art in the Central House of the Artists, whose grounds hold Socialist Realism sculpture and statues of the former Soviet Union moved from their original sites. Its organisation also includes branches in Kaliningrad and Vladivostok.
trevoux: The Treaty of Verdun of 843 divided the empire of Charlemagne and made the Saône the frontier between France and the Empire. Trévoux owed its particular political status to this border position. In the 11th century it belonged to the lords of Thoire-Villars, from whom it acquired its freedom. The Bourbons bought it in 1402, and it became the capital of the Dombes and had its own mint. The river toll grew important, and the town built a castle and walls.

On 30 June 1417 the local baron issued a decree allowing the Jewish population to continue to study the Talmud, contrary to a decision taken at Chambéry in January 1417, after which Jewish books had been seized and burned. In 1523 King François I confiscated the Dombes and founded a parliament for the region in Lyon, and in 1560 the Dombes fell to the Bourbons. The town grew rich as capital of the principality and seat of its parliament.

A printing works was established in 1603. In the 18th century the Jesuits printed there the Journal de Trévoux and a universal dictionary, the Dictionnaire de Trévoux, from 1704 to 1771. At the end of the 17th century two sovereign princes, Anne-Marie Louise of Orléans, Duchess of Montpensier, known as la Grande Mademoiselle, and her successor Louis-Auguste of Bourbon, Duke of Maine, raised two monuments that still mark the landscape: the Montpensier hospital and the Palace of the Dombes Parliament. The principality of the Dombes was absorbed definitively into France in 1762.

Trévoux is a commune in the Ain department of eastern France, built on the steeply sloping left bank of the Saône and known for its fort; its inhabitants are called Trévoltiens. It remained a sub-prefecture of Ain until 1926. From the end of the 19th century until the 1950s it was the world capital of the manufacture of synthetic diamonds.
triangular-trade: Triangular trade is trade between three ports or regions. It usually evolves when a region has export commodities that are not required in the region from which its major imports come, and it has been used to offset trade imbalances. The most commonly cited example is the Atlantic slave trade, but others existed. In the seventeenth century manufactured goods went from England to New England and Newfoundland, dried cod went from there to the Mediterranean and the Iberian peninsula, and gold, silver, olive oil, tobacco, dried fruit and sacks of wine came back to England. Maritime carriers called this the sack trade.

In the Atlantic triangle, ships left European ports such as Bristol and Nantes for West Africa loaded with manufactured goods, including copper, cloth, guns and ammunition, which were bartered for enslaved Africans. The second leg, the Middle Passage, carried the enslaved to Brazil, the Caribbean and the American colonies, where they were sold to plantation owners. An estimated 12 to 13 percent died of disease or in rebellions on board, and the average ship carried just over 300 people. The third leg took sugar, rum and molasses, or tobacco and hemp from Virginia, back to Europe.

A classic example is the colonial molasses trade between West Africa, the West Indies and the northern colonies of British North America in the 17th and 18th centuries. Enslaved people grew the sugar used to brew rum, which in turn was traded for more slaves. Great Britain, Portugal and France controlled the transatlantic slave market until the 18th century in terms of the number of enslaved people shipped.

Historians have questioned the neat picture. The triangle route was not generally followed by individual ships: slave ships were built to carry people, not cargo, and often returned with ballast, while cash crops travelled on a separate fleet. No New England trader is known to have completed the full circuit. The idea of a New England triangular trade was first suggested, inconclusively, by George H.
