Moore in 1866, and developed in a lecture by William B. Weeden in 1887. Even so, the Atlantic slave trade was one of the more complex international trades of the modern period, and an estimated 12.5 million people were transported from Africa.
tributary-system: A tribute is wealth, often in kind, that one party gives to another as a sign of submission, allegiance or respect. Various ancient states exacted tribute from the rulers of lands they conquered, and in alliances lesser parties might pay tribute to more powerful ones as a sign of allegiance. Tribute differs from taxes: it is not collected in the same regular, routine manner, and it uniquely requires the payer to recognise political submission to the payee.

Ancient China received tribute from states including Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Cambodia, Borneo, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Myanmar and Central Asia, and the Aztec Empire received tribute from the city-states and provinces it conquered.

The Aztecs used tribute to maintain control over conquered areas. Rather than replacing local rulers or colonising, they collected tribute and ideally did not interfere in local affairs unless it went unpaid. Strategic provinces, regarded as client states, paid consensually in exchange for good relations, while tributary provinces were required to pay regularly whether they wished to or not.

Aztec officials managed the system at several levels. The calpixque collected, transported and received tribute in each province, the huecalpixque managed them, and the petlacalcatl, based in Tenochtitlan, oversaw the whole system. A military official, the cuahtlatoani, was involved only when newly conquered provinces resisted. Tribute took the form of natural resources such as obsidian and salt, of gold, silver and jade, and of goods and rotational labour owed by commoners to their lords, who could also call them for military service and construction.

China received tribute from states under the influence of Confucian civilisation and gave them Chinese products and recognition of their authority in return. The relationship is known as Jimi, Cefeng or Chaogong. According to the Book of Han, the tribes of Japan had entered tributary relationships with China by the first century, though Japan later left the system during the Heian period. Goguryeo sent a diplomatic representative to the Han dynasty in 32 CE, and China's tributary relationship with Korea continued in varying degrees until China's defeat in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894 to 1895.

China ended its suzerainty over Vietnam with the Treaty of Tientsin in 1885, after the Sino-French War. The theoretical justification was the Mandate of Heaven, under which the Chinese emperor ruled with the authority of heaven. The Islamic Caliphate introduced the jizya, a tax on adult men only, unlike Roman tribute, which could be levied on land, landowners and slaveholders. Iberian Christians translated it as tributo, and the Spanish empire later applied it in the New World.
trier: Trier lies in a hollow midway along the Moselle valley, between low vine-covered hills in the west of Rhineland-Palatinate, near the border with Luxembourg, which is some 15 kilometres away. Most of the city is on the east bank of the river. Wooded and vineyard-covered slopes stretch up to the Hunsrück plateau in the south and the Eifel in the north. The city lies within the Moselle wine region.

The Celtic tribe of the Treveri settled the area in the last pre-Christian centuries. The Romans subdued them in the 1st century BCE and founded Augusta Treverorum around 16 BCE. From 293 to 395 the city was one of the residences of the Western Roman emperor, and in the 4th century it was one of the largest cities of the empire, with some 75,000 people and perhaps as many as 100,000. The Porta Nigra dates from this age. Emperor Constantine the Great exiled Athanasius of Alexandria to Trier in 336, and Saint Ambrose was born there. The Franks seized the city in 459.

In 870 Trier became part of Eastern Francia, which developed into the Holy Roman Empire. Relics of Saint Matthias began widespread pilgrimages, and the archbishops grew powerful. The University of Trier was founded in 1473. The Trier witch trials of 1581 to 1593 reached the city itself in 1587 and led to the deaths of about 368 people. France annexed Trier in 1794 and dissolved the electoral archbishopric, and after 1815 it passed to Prussia. Karl Marx was born there in 1818.

Trier is a city of about 110,000 on the Moselle, and several Roman and medieval monuments are a World Heritage Site. They include the Porta Nigra, the best-preserved Roman city gate north of the Alps, the Aula Palatina, the throne hall of Constantine, now a Protestant church, a Roman bridge of the 2nd century still used by traffic, and the largest Roman baths north of the Alps. Trier Cathedral houses the Holy Tunic, one of a number of garments claimed to be the robe Jesus wore when he died.
trieste: Trieste lies at the head of the Gulf of Trieste, on a narrow strip of Italian territory between the sea and Slovenia, which is about 8 km to the east. Most of the city is built on a hillside at the foot of an escarpment that drops from the Karst Plateau towards the sea. The city lies where the Italian region, the Balkan Peninsula and central Europe meet. Its deep-water port is a maritime gateway for northern Italy, Germany, Austria and Central Europe.

The site has been inhabited since the second millennium BCE. The Veneti seem to have given the town its name, Tergeste, from a word for market. It became part of the Roman Republic in 177 BCE during the Second Istrian War. It belonged to the Habsburg monarchy from 1382 until 1918. Venice occupied it in 1508, but the Habsburg Empire recovered it a little over a year later. In 1719 Emperor Charles VI made it a free port, and the reign of Maria Theresa began a very prosperous era.

French troops occupied Trieste in 1797, 1805 and 1809, and from 1809 to 1813 it was part of the Illyrian Provinces, which interrupted its free port status and its autonomy. In the 19th century it was the most important seaport of the Habsburg monarchy and the fourth largest city of Austria-Hungary. James Joyce lived there between 1904 and 1915, working on Dubliners and Ulysses. Italy annexed Trieste at the end of the First World War. In 1947 it was declared the Free Territory of Trieste under United Nations protection, divided into Zones A and B along the Morgan Line; the Free Territory lasted until 1954.

Trieste is the capital and largest city of the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Half the city was built in the Austro-Hungarian period, giving it some of the architecture of Vienna. Its sights include Miramare Castle, built between 1856 and 1860 for Archduke Maximilian, the Roman theatre, and the cathedral of St Justus. Piazza Unità d'Italia is the largest seafront square in Europe.
trigonometry: The word comes from the Ancient Greek trigonon, "triangle", and metron, "measure". Sumerian astronomers studied angle measure, dividing the circle into 360 degrees. They and the later Babylonians studied the ratios of the sides of similar triangles and found some of their properties, but did not make a systematic method for finding the sides and angles of triangles. The ancient Nubians used a similar method. In the 3rd century BCE Hellenistic mathematicians such as Euclid and Archimedes studied chords and inscribed angles in circles and proved theorems equivalent to modern trigonometric formulae, though they presented them geometrically rather than algebraically.

Hipparchus of Nicaea gave the first tables of chords in 140 BCE, and in the 2nd century CE Ptolemy constructed detailed tables in Book 1 of his Almagest. Ptolemy's treatise stayed in use for calculations in astronomy for the next 1,200 years in the Byzantine, Islamic and later Western European worlds.

Trigonometry relates the angles of a right triangle to the ratios of its side lengths. The sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the hypotenuse, the cosine the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and the tangent the ratio of the opposite to the adjacent side. Their reciprocals are the cosecant, secant and cotangent. With the laws of sines and cosines one can find the remaining sides and angles of any triangle once enough of them are known. Spherical trigonometry applies the same ideas to triangles on a sphere, and was long used to locate the sun, moon and stars and to predict eclipses.

The modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Surya Siddhanta, and Aryabhata documented its properties in the 5th century CE. Medieval Islamic mathematicians translated and expanded Greek and Indian works. Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi made the first table of cotangents in 830 CE, and by the 10th century Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani used all six functions, with sine tables in steps of a quarter of a degree.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi was the first to treat trigonometry as a discipline independent of astronomy, and in the 14th century Madhava of Sangamagrama developed infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent. Knowledge reached Western Europe through Latin translations of the Almagest and the works of al-Battani and al-Tusi. Regiomontanus wrote De Triangulis in the 15th century, and Copernicus devoted two chapters of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium to the basics. Bartholomaeus Pitiscus first used the word trigonometry in his Trigonometria of 1595, and Gemma Frisius described the method of triangulation still used in surveying.
trikala: The city straddles the Lithaios river, a tributary of the Pineios, and lies close to Meteora and the southern Pindus mountains. Its name comes from the ancient Trikka or Trikke, itself named after a nymph, a daughter of Peneus or, according to others, of the river god Asopus. The region has been inhabited since prehistoric times: the cave of Theopetra holds the first signs of permanent settlement, from about 49,000 BCE, and Neolithic settlements go back to about 6,000 BCE.

Ancient Trikke was founded around the third millennium BCE on a defensible site between a hill and the Lithaios. In the Mycenean period it was the capital of a kingdom, and later the main centre of the Thessalian region of Estaiotis. Homer's Iliad names it among the cities that sent thirty ships to the Trojan War under Asclepius' sons Machaon and Podalirius. It fell to the Achaemenid Persians in 480 BCE, joined Philip II's Macedonia in 352 BCE, and passed to the Roman Republic after 168 BCE.

The present name appears in the 11th century. After 1204 the town was part of the Despotate of Epirus, and in 1259 it passed to the Empire of Nicaea. In 1348 Stefan Dušan's Serbian Empire took Thessaly, and in 1359 his half-brother Symeon Uroš set up his court at Trikala; about 1366 he founded the Meteora monasteries nearby. The Ottoman conquest of Thessaly came about 1393.

Under the Ottomans the city, called Tırhala, was the centre of the Sanjak of Trikala. Turahan Bey and his son Ömer Bey raised mosques, medreses, a hammam and a khan there. The 17th-century traveller Evliya Çelebi counted 2,300 houses and eight mosques; only the Osman Shah Mosque, built by Mimar Sinan, survives. A great fire in 1749 burned much of the city. It passed to Greece on 23 August 1881 under the Treaty of Constantinople, and in 1906 the first agricultural cooperative of Greece was founded there.

Trikala has 62,064 inhabitants, with 78,605 in the municipality (2021 figures). Its old town below the Byzantine castle keeps churches from the 14th to the 19th centuries, and the Asklepieion of Trikke, which Strabo called the most ancient in Greece, lies beside St. Nicholas Cathedral.
trincomalee: Trincomalee is the main city of the Eastern Province of Sri Lanka and the administrative centre of Trincomalee District, overlooking Trincomalee Harbour. It is built on a peninsula of the same name that divides the inner and outer harbours. The temple on Swami Rock, a cliff that drops 120 metres into the sea, gave the city its Tamil name Thirukonamalai, meaning roughly Lord of the Sacred Hill. Its Sanskrit name Gokarna means Cow's Ear. Tamil-speaking culture has had one of its main centres here for nearly a millennium.

The harbour has drawn seafarers, traders and pilgrims since ancient times, and the town has been a seaport since 400 BCE. The earliest inscriptions found in the city are in Tamil, and Chola inscriptions of 900 to 1000 CE concern the Koneswaram temple. The shrine has a recorded history from the 3rd century BCE and drew pilgrims from all parts of India. The Tevaram hymns of Sambandar, composed around 600, praise its deity.

The Portuguese demolished the temple in 1622 and fortified the heights with its stones. A Danish expedition under Ove Giedde had reached the island in May 1620 and occupied the temple. Fort Frederick was built in 1623 by the Portuguese and captured by the Dutch in 1639. In 1782, during the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, the British took it, after which the French captured it; the French handed it back to the Dutch for a large sum. The British took it again in 1795 and Trincomalee became part of British Ceylon in 1815.

In 1942 the city was attacked by Japan as part of the Indian Ocean raid. After Sri Lanka's independence in 1948, relations between Tamils and Sinhalese worsened, and the city and its district were severely affected by the civil war of thirty years that followed. In 1950 workers digging a well found bronze statues from the 10th century, including Shiva as Somaskanda; they were reinstalled in a restored shrine on 3 March 1963.

The city has a population of 99,135 and holds naval and air force bases at the Trincomalee Garrison. It contains the Hoods Tower Museum and the Dutch fort, and the Koneswaram compound remains a place of pilgrimage sacred to Hindus; some Buddhists also worship at these sites.
trinidad: Trinidad lies 11 kilometres off the north-eastern coast of Venezuela and sits on the continental shelf of South America. It is the southernmost island in the Caribbean, with an area of 4,768 square kilometres, and the fifth largest in the Caribbean. Its landforms include the Northern, Central and Southern Ranges, the Caroni, Nariva and Oropouche swamps and the Caroni and Naparima plains. The highest point is El Cerro del Aripo, at 940 metres. The island's fauna is overwhelmingly of South American origin, and the Pitch Lake and the oil and gas fields of its south belong to its geology.

Kalinago and Arawakan-speaking peoples lived on Trinidad long before Christopher Columbus reached it on 31 July 1498, on his third voyage. The Arawakan name was Iëre, meaning land of the hummingbird. Columbus named the island for the Trinity, fulfilling a vow, after a sailor sighted three peaks. The island remained Spanish until 1797, but it was settled mostly by French colonists from the French Caribbean, especially Martinique.

In 1889 Trinidad and Tobago became a single British crown colony. It was granted self-governance in 1958 and independence from the United Kingdom in August 1962, and became a republic in September 1976. In the 19th century recruiters from India called the island Chinidat, the land of sugar, to lure workers into indentureship, and the Indian ancestry of much of the population is still marked by holidays such as Divali and Indian Arrival Day.

Trinidad is the largest and most populous island of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago. At the 2011 census its population was 37 per cent Indo-Trinidadian, 32 per cent Afro-Trinidadian and 24 per cent mixed race. The steelpan originated on the island and is the national instrument, and Carnival, J'ouvert and the Panorama steelpan competition are among its festivals. Venezuela's influence appears in the parang music style.
trinity-college-dublin: A medieval University of Dublin was founded in 1320 under a papal brief issued by Pope Clement V in 1311. It kept an intermittent existence at St Patrick's Cathedral but did not flourish and ended during the Reformation. In 1592 a small group of Dublin citizens obtained letters patent from Elizabeth I incorporating Trinity College on the site of the disbanded Augustinian Priory of All Hallows, southeast of the city walls, which the Corporation of Dublin provided.

The college was established to consolidate Tudor rule in Ireland. Provost Adam Loftus named it after Trinity College, Cambridge, and it was founded on the model of Oxford and Cambridge. It was the only college ever established within the University of Dublin.

In the 18th century Trinity was the university of the Protestant Ascendancy. The Parliament of Ireland, meeting across College Green, made generous grants for the neoclassical Parliament Square, whose first building was the Old Library, begun in 1712, followed by the Printing House and the Dining Hall. The library has housed the Book of Kells since 1661. Trinity gained the world's oldest chairs in French and German (1776), Irish (1840) and English literature (1867).

Women were admitted as full members for the first time in 1904. From 1904 to 1907 women from Oxford and Cambridge, who were not granted degrees there, came to Trinity to receive them; known as the Steamboat ladies, they paid fees that helped to fund Trinity Hall.

The college is governed by the Provost, Fellows and Scholars under letters patent that later monarchs amended. Charles I in 1637 raised the number of fellows from seven to 16 and established the Board. The university was linked to parliamentary representation from 1613, when James I granted it two seats in the Irish House of Commons; the vote was first limited to the Provost, Fellows and Scholars, extended in 1832 to holders of an MA and in 1918 to all graduates. After the Acts of Union 1800 it elected members to Westminster, among them W. E. H. Lecky and Edward Carson.

Trinity is a sister college of Oriel College, Oxford, and St John's College, Cambridge, and a graduate of any of the three universities may be incorporated into another. Traditions include Commons, a meal in the Dining Hall begun by the slamming of its doors, and Trinity Week in April. The student society The Hist was founded in 1770, and from 1869 to 1893 the college's literary magazine Kottabos was edited by Robert Yelverton Tyrrell.
trinity-lavra-of-st-sergius: Sergius of Radonezh, one of the most venerated Russian saints, founded the monastery in the 14th century by building a wooden church in honour of the Holy Trinity on Makovets Hill. In 1355 he introduced a charter that required auxiliary buildings such as a refectory, kitchen and bakery. It became a model for his many followers, who founded more than 400 monasteries across Russia, including Solovetsky, Kirillov and Simonov.

Sergius supported Dmitri Donskoi against the Tatars and sent two monks, Peresvet and Oslyabya, to the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380. A Tatar raid devastated the monastery by fire in 1408. In 1422 Sergius was declared patron saint of the Russian state, and in the same year a team of Serbian monks who had found refuge there after the Battle of Kosovo built the first stone cathedral. Andrei Rublev and Daniil Chyorny were summoned to decorate it with frescoes.

The monastery grew into one of the wealthiest landowners in Russia. Woods around it were cleared and a village, or posad, grew up near its walls and gradually became the town of Sergiyev Posad. It was also a notable centre of chronicle-writing and icon painting. The six-pillared Assumption Cathedral, commissioned by Ivan the Terrible in 1559, took 26 years to build and holds the burials of Boris Godunov and his family.

In the 1550s a wooden palisade was replaced by stone walls 1.5 km long with twelve towers. They helped the monastery withstand a Polish-Lithuanian siege of 16 months in 1608 to 1610, and a shell-hole in the cathedral gates recalls a failed siege by Wladyslaw IV in 1618. The young Peter I twice took refuge there. In 1744 Empress Elizabeth gave the cloister the dignity of a lavra, and the metropolitan of Moscow became its archimandrite.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917 the Soviet government closed the lavra in 1920, and its buildings were given to civic institutions or declared museums. In 1930 the monastery bells, including the Tsar-Bell of 65 tons, were destroyed. In 1945 Joseph Stalin's temporary tolerance of the church during World War II allowed the lavra to be returned to the Russian Orthodox Church, and divine service was renewed in the Assumption Cathedral on 16 April 1946.

It was the seat of the Moscow Patriarchate until 1983 and remains a prime centre of religious education, with more than 300 monks. It was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1993. Sergius of Radonezh and Boris Godunov are among those buried there.
tripartite-pact: Germany and Japan had technically been allies since the Anti-Comintern Pact of 1936, but the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of 1939 between Germany and the Soviet Union came as a surprise to Japan. In November 1939 the two signed an Agreement for Cultural Cooperation, which restored what has been called their reluctant alliance. The Tripartite Pact, also known as the Berlin Pact, was signed in Berlin by Joachim von Ribbentrop for Germany, Galeazzo Ciano for Italy and Saburō Kurusu for Japan, in the presence of Adolf Hitler.

Under Article 1 Japan recognised the leadership of Germany and Italy in establishing a new order in Europe, and under Article 2 they recognised Japan's leadership in a new order in Greater East Asia. Article 3 bound the three to assist one another with all political, economic and military means if one was attacked by a power not at present involved in the European War or the Japanese-Chinese conflict. Article 5 left unchanged each signatory's existing relations with the Soviet Union. The pact was to last ten years.

It was directed chiefly at the United States, but its practical effects were limited, since the Italo-German and Japanese theatres lay on opposite sides of the world and the partners' strategic interests differed. Its defensive clauses were never invoked. Joint technical commissions were agreed on 20 December 1940, yet the military commission in Berlin met only two or three times by 1943, and there were no trilateral naval talks.

Hungary joined on 20 November 1940, Romania on 23 November, Slovakia on 24 November and Bulgaria on 1 March 1941. Hungary had first sent notice of spiritual adherence, after Ribbentrop's speech seemed to invite new members, though Ciano opposed adding smaller states. Bulgaria signed after Germany needed to move troops through it. Yugoslavia signed on 25 March 1941, and the military coup in Belgrade two days later was followed by invasion by Germany, Italy and Hungary. The Independent State of Croatia, created from conquered Yugoslav territory, signed on 15 June 1941. Finland and Thailand declined to join, and German talks with the Soviet Union about joining went nowhere.

On 11 December 1941, the day Germany and Italy declared war on the United States, the three powers agreed not to make a separate peace with the United States or Britain. The historian Paul W. Schroeder describes the pact as virtually inoperative by December 1941. Its symbolic effect was larger: it persuaded the American public that Japan was acting in concert with Germany, and the charge that it coordinated aggression was part of the case at Nuremberg and at the Tokyo trials.
triple-alliance-1882: The man chiefly responsible for the alliance was Otto von Bismarck, the Chancellor of Germany. After unifying Germany in 1871 his main aim was to preserve the status quo in Europe, and he feared that France would find allies to help it regain Alsace-Lorraine. By promising aid to Austria-Hungary and Italy if they were attacked, he sought to make them somewhat dependent on Germany and unsympathetic to French adventures. Germany and Austria-Hungary had been closely allied since October 1879.

Italy had several motives. Its government was then controlled by conservatives who sympathised with the two monarchies, and Catholic Austria was a traditional protector of the Papacy, with which Italy had poor relations. Above all Italy sought allies against the French Third Republic. Italian anger at the French conquest of Tunisia in 1881, called the Slap of Tunis by the Italian press, pushed it towards the two monarchies, even though it had fought three wars against Austria-Hungary in the previous 34 years.

Each member promised mutual support in the event of an attack by another great power. Germany and Austria-Hungary were to assist Italy if France attacked it without provocation, and Italy would assist Germany in the same case. If Austria-Hungary and Russia went to war, Italy promised to remain neutral.

The treaty was renewed periodically. In February 1887 Italy gained a promise of German support for its colonial ambitions in North Africa, which proved empty. Bismarck pressed Austria-Hungary to accept consultation and mutual agreement with Italy on any territorial change in the Balkans or on the coasts and islands of the Adriatic and Aegean. In 1891 attempts to bring Britain into the alliance failed, though Russian diplomats widely believed they had succeeded. Romania, ruled by Carol I, also secretly pledged support on 18 October 1883.

The alliance was never comfortable. Italian opinion was unenthusiastic about an alignment with the former enemy of Italian unification, whose districts in the Trentino and Istria irredentists saw as occupied. Austria-Hungary's general staff kept plans for a war against Italy from at least 1903, and as late as 1911 its chief, Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf, urged a preemptive strike. Shortly after the alliance was renewed in June 1902, Italy secretly gave France a similar guarantee, and on 1 November 1902 the two agreed to stay neutral if the other was attacked. In 1909 Italy and Russia made the Racconigi Bargain.

When Austria-Hungary began a war in August 1914, Italy proclaimed neutrality, regarding Austria-Hungary as the aggressor, and it had not consulted Italy as the 1912 renewal required. After negotiating with both sides, Italy sided with the Triple Entente and declared war on Austria-Hungary. Romania likewise stayed neutral in 1914 and entered the war against the Central Powers on 27 August 1916.
triple-entente: After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871, Prussia forced France to cede Alsace-Lorraine to the new German Empire, and France built up its army to deter German aggression. Russia had been a member of the League of the Three Emperors of 1873 with Austria-Hungary and Germany, but rivalry in the Balkans prevented its renewal in 1887. Bismarck's secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapsed in 1890, and Russian leaders, alarmed at their isolation, joined the Franco-Russian Alliance in 1894. It was designed as a counter to the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.

Britain kept to its policy of splendid isolation through the 1890s. By the early 1900s it saw the German threat as having grown sharply, and when overtures to Berlin were not returned it turned to Paris and St. Petersburg. In 1904 Britain and France signed five agreements on spheres of influence in North Africa, mostly settling colonial disputes, which began the Entente cordiale.

The Tangier Crisis encouraged cooperation between Britain and France from their shared fear of German expansion. Russia had lost the Russo-Japanese War, which contributed to the Russian Revolution of 1905. In 1907 the Anglo-Russian Entente tried to settle disputes over Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet and to end the rivalry in Central Asia known as the Great Game, and it eased British fears about the Baghdad Railway. The Franco-Japanese Treaty of 1907 also formed part of the coalition. The Anglo-German naval race left an atmosphere of mutual hostility, and Lord Haldane's mission to Berlin in February 1912 failed.

The Entente was not an alliance of mutual defence, unlike the Triple Alliance and the Franco-Russian Alliance, so Britain was free in 1914 to make its own decisions. The Foreign Office official Eyre Crowe wrote that it was nothing more than a frame of mind. In 1914 all three powers entered the First World War as Allied Powers, and on 4 September 1914 they declared that they would not make a separate peace.

Historians continue to debate how far the alliance system caused the First World War. The alignment of Russia with France and Britain was controversial on both sides, since Russian conservatives distrusted the secular French and British and many French and British politicians disliked the tsarist regime. Mistrust lasted into the war, and British and French politicians expressed relief when Nicholas II abdicated in 1917. The British king withdrew an offer of asylum to the Romanovs, and France never raised the subject. The Triple Entente was the coalition that fought the First World War against the Central Powers.
tripoli-greece: Tripoli lies in the centre of the Peloponnese, at the western border of a large basin, a polje about 650 metres above sea level and roughly 30 kilometres long. It has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate with some continental features, and snow or sleet can fall between November and early April. The ground of the basin is karstic: water seeps into the underground through ponors rather than draining over the surface, so heavy winter rains can leave temporary lakes. Because the city is at the centre of the Peloponnese, it is a transport hub.

In the Middle Ages the place was known as Drobolitsa, perhaps from the Greek Hydropolitsa, Water City, or from the South Slavic for Plain of Oaks. It appears in a list of abandoned Byzantine sites of 1467. After the Ottoman conquest of the Morea the cultural and administrative centre of the Tegean plain moved from Mouchli to Drobolitsa, and after 1540 the settlement below the fortress, called Tarabluca, became the political centre.

In spring 1770, during the Greek uprising known as the Orlov Revolt, the revolutionary armies were halted outside Tripolitsa. Albanian mercenaries of the Ottomans killed 3,000 Greeks in a few hours on entering the city, and Osman bey, their leader, intervened to prevent its total destruction.

Before the Greek War of Independence, as Tripoliçe, it was an Ottoman administrative centre in the Peloponnese, the Morea Eyalet, often called the pashalik of Tripolitsa, with large Muslim and Jewish populations. Greek insurgents stormed it after a bloody siege in 1821 and exterminated the Muslim population. Ibrahim Pasha retook the city on 22 June 1825, after the Greeks had abandoned it. Before he evacuated the Peloponnese in early 1828 he destroyed the city and tore down its walls. The siege is the subject of the folk song Forty lads from Livadeia.

After the independent Greek state was established in 1830 the old Ottoman buildings, including the walls, were destroyed or demolished. Tripoli was renamed and rebuilt, and during the 19th and 20th centuries it became the administrative, economic, commercial and transport centre of the central and southern Peloponnese. It is the capital of the Peloponnese region and of the regional unit of Arcadia, and its municipality had 44,165 inhabitants in 2021. Tripoli is the flagship campus of the University of the Peloponnese, founded in 2000. Theodoros Kolokotronis, the pre-eminent general of the Greek War of Independence, is among its notable people.
tripura: Tripura is a landlocked state of about 10,491 square kilometres, bordered by Assam and Mizoram and by Bangladesh, and one of the Seven Sister States of North East India. Five ranges of hills, Baramura, Atharamura, Longtharai, Shakhan and the Jampui Hills, run from north to south with valleys between them, while Agartala stands on a plain in the west. The highest point is Betling Shib, at 939 metres. The climate is tropical savanna, with heavy monsoon rain from May to September, and more than half of the land is forest.

The Mahabharata, the Puranas and the Edicts of Ashoka are said to mention Tripura, and the Mahabharata names the region Kirat Desh, though it is unclear whether that land matched the modern state. The Twipra Kingdom ruled the area for centuries, but when its dynasty began is not documented. The Rajmala, a chronicle first written in the 15th century, lists 179 kings down to Krishna Kishore Manikya, who reigned from 1830 to 1850, but it is not a reliable source. The name is linked to the goddess Tripura Sundari, whose temple at Udaipur is one of the 51 Shakta pithas.

After 1947 Tippera district in the plains became part of East Pakistan, while Hill Tippera stayed under a regency council until 1949. On 9 September 1949 the Maharani Regent signed the Tripura Merger Agreement, making Tripura a Part C state of India. Partition cut it off: the road distance from Kolkata to Agartala grew from under 350 kilometres to 1,700. In 1947–51 an estimated 610,000 Bengali refugees entered, a number almost equal to the state's whole population, and about 1.038 million more came during the war of 1971.

Agartala is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Bengali, Kokborok and English. The 2011 census counted 3,671,032 people, and in 2001 Bengalis were almost 65 per cent of them, with 19 scheduled tribes, of which the Kokborok-speaking Tripuris are the largest. Most of the land belongs to the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council. The sculptures at Unakoti, Pilak and Devtamura show a fusion of organised and indigenous religious art.
trireme: The trireme developed from the penteconter, a single-banked warship with 25 oars on each side, and from the bireme, a two-banked warship of Phoenician origin. Biremes are common on vases and pottery fragments from the 8th century BCE, and the first references to three-banked ships come at the end of that century.

Modern scholars are divided on whether the trireme came from Greece or Phoenicia. Thucydides says the Corinthians introduced it to Greece in the late 8th century BCE, and Pliny and Diodorus took this to mean that it was invented at Corinth. Clement of Alexandria attributes it to the Sidonians. The first definite reference to triremes in battle is of about 525 BCE, when Polycrates of Samos contributed 40 to a Persian invasion of Egypt. By 490 BCE they were the backbone of the Persian fleet.

Excavated ship sheds at Zea in Piraeus, the main war harbour of Athens, were about 40 metres long and 6 metres wide, which with Vitruvius's allowance for each rower suggests a ship just under 37 metres long. Its draught was about 1 metre, and it could be beached easily. The ship had 170 oars, one man to each, two masts with square sails, and two steering oars at the stern.

The complement was about 200: the 170 rowers, a deck crew under the trierarch and a marine detachment. Crews were free men, not galley slaves. An Athenian crew in the Peloponnesian War typically had 80 citizens, 60 metics and 60 foreign hands. In Athens a wealthy trierarch paid to man and maintain the ship, which belonged to the city.

The trireme relied on speed and manoeuvre rather than boarding. Squadrons used the periplous, outflanking the enemy to strike the rear, and the diekplous, a charge to break the enemy line. In 483/2 BCE Themistocles persuaded the Athenian assembly to build 200 triremes with the income of the Laurion silver mines. The Persian fleet was defeated at Salamis, after a first clash at Artemisium.

In the Hellenistic period larger warships, the quinqueremes, replaced it as ramming grew less effective against armoured bows. Between 1985 and 1987 a trireme named Olympias was built at Piraeus on the advice of the historian J. S. Morrison and the naval architect John F. Coates. Crewed by 170 volunteers, it could turn through 180 degrees in one minute, and its trials suggest that ancient accounts of its performance were not exaggerated.
tristan-und-isolde: Richard Wagner called the work a music drama in three acts, to a German libretto of his own loosely based on Gottfried von Strassburg's 12th-century romance. He preferred the term Handlung, plot or action, to distinguish its continuous narrative flow, the endless melody, from conventional opera with its recitatives and showpiece arias, which he regarded with disdain. First conceived in 1854, it was inspired in part by the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer and by Wagner's relationship with his muse Mathilde Wesendonck.

Wagner had fled to Zurich after a warrant was issued for his arrest for taking part in the May Revolution of 1849, and there in 1852 he met the silk trader Otto Wesendonck, who supported him for several years. According to his autobiography, he decided to dramatise the legend after his friend Karl Ritter tried to do so.

In the first act Isolde, promised in marriage to King Marke, is carried by ship to Cornwall in the care of Marke's nephew Tristan, whom she scorns and blames. In the second, the lovers meet at night when Marke leaves on a hunt. They declare that only in the long night of death can they be eternally united. The knight Melot leads Marke to find them, and Marke is heartbroken that Tristan betrayed him.

In the third act Kurwenal has brought the wounded Tristan to his castle at Kareol in Brittany, where a shepherd's pipe announces whether a ship is in sight. Tristan curses the love potion and, when Isolde's ship is at last piped, tears the bandages from his wounds in his excitement. He dies with her name on his lips as she arrives at his side.

The music was composed between 1857 and 1859, but the opera proved difficult to stage. Proposals for Rio de Janeiro, Strasbourg, Paris and Karlsruhe came to nothing, and a Vienna production was abandoned in 1864 after over seventy rehearsals, which gave it a reputation as unperformable. It was premiered in Munich on 10 June 1865 under Hans von Bülow. The Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung called it an act of indecency.

The Tristan chord of its prelude marks a defining moment in the move away from traditional tonal harmony, and some scholars see in the opera the beginnings of atonality. It directly inspired Anton Bruckner, Gustav Mahler, Richard Strauss, Alban Berg, Arnold Schoenberg and Benjamin Britten, while Claude Debussy, Maurice Ravel and Igor Stravinsky formed their styles in contrast to it.
troad: The Troad, also called Troas, is a historical region in northwestern Anatolia. It corresponds with the Biga Peninsula in the Çanakkale Province of modern Turkey. It is bounded by the Dardanelles to the northwest and the Aegean Sea to the west, and separated from the rest of Anatolia by the massif that forms Mount Ida. It is drained by two main rivers, the Scamander (Karamenderes) and the Simoeis, which join in the area containing the ruins of Troy.

The Troad is first mentioned by that name in Hittite records as Taruiša. The identification was first put forward by Emil Forrer but was largely disputed by Hittite experts until 1983, when Houwink ten Cate showed that two fragments came from the same cuneiform tablet and that Taruiša and Wiluša (Troy) were correctly placed in northwestern Anatolia. Greek settlements flourished in the Archaic and Classical ages, as shown by the number of Greek poleis that coined money in their own names.

The region was part of the satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia of the Achaemenid Empire until its conquest by Alexander the Great. It then fell to the Seleucid Empire and passed to Rome's ally, the kingdom of Pergamon. The Attalid kings ceded Mysia, including the Troad, to the Roman Republic on the death of King Attalus III in 133 BCE. Under the Roman Empire it became part of the province of Asia and later of the smaller Mysian province Hellespontus, and it was important enough to have suffragan bishoprics. Under the later Byzantine Empire it belonged to the thema of the Aegean Islands, and after the Ottoman conquest it formed part of the sanjak of Biga.

In the New Testament the apostles Paul and Silas first visited Troas on their journey from Galatia to Macedonia. Paul also referred to Troas when he asked Timothy to bring the cloak he had left there. The change from "they" to "we" in Acts 16 and Acts 20 implies that Paul was joined by Luke when he went through Troas.
troia-apulia: According to legend, the ancient town of Aecae on this site was founded by the Greek hero Diomedes, who had destroyed Troy. Polybius and Livy mention Aecae during the operations of Hannibal and Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus in Apulia. Like many Apulian cities it joined the Carthaginians after the Battle of Cannae, but Fabius Maximus recovered it in 214 BCE after a regular siege. Pliny lists its people, the Aecani, among the inland towns of Apulia, and the Roman itineraries place it on the Appian Way between Aequum Tuticum and Herdonia, 29 to 31 kilometres from the latter.

That distance matches the position of modern Troia, and medieval chroniclers state that the present town was founded about the beginning of the 11th century on the ruins of Aecae. It was built as a fortified town by Basil Boioannes. Until it was overshadowed by Foggia it was an important strategic town in southern Italy, and was besieged several times, notably by the emperors Henry II and Frederick II. After Frederick's fall it sided with the Angevines and later, against them, with the Aragonese.

After the unification of southern Italy in 1861, Troia rebelled, and Savoy troops intervened with cannon. Cluverius mistook Aecae for Accadia, a village in the Daunian Mountains south of Bovino, but his error was corrected by Holstenius.

Troia stands on a hill of moderate height above the fertile plain of Apulia, 15 kilometres south of Lucera and 22 kilometres south-west of Foggia, and is a bishop's seat. Its main sights include the cathedral, an example of Apulian Romanesque architecture, and the Basilica of St. Basil from the 11th century. There are also the Baroque church of St. Francis, the Church of San Vincenzo from the 10th century, the Palazzo Principi d'Avalos and the Jesuits' Palace of the 16th century.

The Municipal Museum holds archaeological finds from the area and an art gallery. The Diocesan Museum, in an 18th-century Benedictine nunnery, and the New Museum of the Cathedral's Treasure house the medieval rolls of the Exultet.
trois-rivieres: Trois-Rivières lies on the north shore of the Saint Lawrence River at the mouth of the Saint-Maurice River, in the Mauricie region of Quebec. The name means three rivers and refers to the three channels into which the Saint-Maurice is divided at its mouth by two islands. François Gravé Du Pont, a geographer under Samuel de Champlain, first used the name in 1599, when sailing upriver he took the channels for three separate tributaries.

For thousands of years the area was frequented by Indigenous peoples. The Algonquin and Abenaki used it as a summer stopping place to fish, hunt and gather roots and nuts. Jacques Cartier described the site in 1535 and planted a cross on Saint-Quentin Island. In 1603 Samuel de Champlain recommended a permanent settlement, and the village was formed on 4 July 1634 under its first governor, Sieur de Laviolette. It played an important part in the fur trade with First Nations peoples and became the seat of a regional government in 1665. Ursuline nuns who arrived in 1697 founded its first school.

French rule ended in 1760, when the town was taken in the British conquest of Canada. On 8 June 1776 the Battle of Trois-Rivières was fought here during the American invasion of the province of Quebec. Its first foundry opened in 1738 and supplied iron, much of it shipped to France for the navy, for about 150 years. A fire in 1908 destroyed most of the city, including many buildings from the French colonial years; the Ursuline Monastery and the De Tonnancour Manor survived.

From the late 1920s to the early 1960s the city was known as the pulp and paper capital of the world. Industry declined later, and in the 1960s the city began to diversify its economy. The Old City was declared an historic sector in 1964 and the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières was founded in 1969.

Trois-Rivières is the economic and cultural hub of the Mauricie region, roughly halfway between Montreal and Quebec City, and French is the mother tongue of the great majority of its people. Its landmarks include the Forges du Saint-Maurice, a foundry dating from the 1730s, and the Notre-Dame-du-Cap Basilica. It has a major ice-free port on the Saint Lawrence.
trojan-war: In the Greek tradition the war arose from a quarrel among the goddesses Hera, Athena and Aphrodite, caused by Eris, the goddess of discord, who threw a golden apple inscribed to the fairest into the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. A shepherd, in fact the Trojan prince Paris, judged between them and chose Aphrodite, who caused Helen, the queen of Sparta, to fall in love with him.

When Helen left with Paris, her former husband Menelaus called on the kings and princes of Greece, who were bound by the oath of Helen's suitors to defend her marriage. Agamemnon sent emissaries to gather them. When the fleet reached Aulis the winds ceased, and in some versions Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to appease Artemis.

The Iliad covers four days and two nights in the tenth year of the siege. Agamemnon refused to return Chryseis, the daughter of Apollo's priest Chryses, and Apollo afflicted the Achaean army with plague. When Agamemnon was forced to give her up, he took Achilles's concubine Briseis. Enraged, Achilles withdrew from the fighting, and Zeus agreed to give the Trojans success in his absence.

Troy fell, according to the tradition, when the Achaeans entered the city and killed its sleeping population. Neoptolemus killed Priam at the altar of Zeus, and Menelaus took Helen back to the ships. Ajax the Lesser raped Cassandra on Athena's altar. The Trojan Horse does not appear in the Iliad; it became familiar through Virgil's account in the second book of the Aeneid.

The gods, angered by the sacrilege, decided that most of the Greeks would not return home. Agamemnon reached Argos safely and was killed there, in the oldest versions by Aegisthus. Ajax the Lesser drowned after a storm sent by Athena, and Nestor alone made a fast and safe return. Odysseus's ten-year journey home is told in the Odyssey, and Aeneas's flight to Italy in the Aeneid, whose hero carries the household gods that Romans claimed to preserve as guarantees of Rome's security.

Most classical Greeks thought the war historical, though Thucydides doubted that 1,186 ships were sent. Ancient authors gave dates for the fall of Troy between 1334 BCE and 1135 BCE. After excavations at Hisarlık, Troy VIIa, destroyed around 1180 BCE, has come to be regarded as the most likely Homeric Troy. Many scholars now accept a historical core in a Greek expedition against the city, but few think the Homeric poems faithfully represent it.
trondheim: Trondheim lies on the south shore of Trondheim Fjord, at the mouth of the river Nidelva, with an excellent and sheltered harbour. In the Middle Ages the river was deep enough for most boats, but in the mid-17th century an avalanche of mud and stones made it less navigable and partly ruined the harbour. Despite its northerly latitude it has a mild climate. Around the summer solstice the nights are light enough that no outdoor lighting is needed between 23 May and 19 July, while at the winter solstice the sun stands only slightly more than 3 degrees above the horizon at midday.

The settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post by the Viking king Olav Tryggvason, who named it Kaupangen, meaning market place. Shortly afterwards it came to be called Nidaros, the outlet of the river Nid. The district around it, Trondheim, meant the home of the Trønder people, and Trøndelag the law area of the Trønder. The city served as the king's seat and was the capital of Norway until 1217. From 1152 to 1537 it was the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros; it then became, and has remained, the seat of the Lutheran Diocese of Nidaros.

Nidaros Cathedral, begun in 1070, is the most important Gothic monument in Norway and was Northern Europe's most important Christian pilgrimage site in the Middle Ages, with routes leading to it from Oslo and from the Jämtland and Värmland regions of Sweden. Sverre Sigurdsson built the fortification Sverresborg in 1182 and 1183; it was burned in 1188 and had been restored by 1197. Kristiansten Fortress, built from 1681 to 1684, repelled invading Swedes in 1718 and was decommissioned in 1816. During the German occupation of Norway in the Second World War the city held a submarine base for the 13th U-boat Flotilla, and Vollan District Jail was used for prisoners of war and political prisoners.

Trondheim is a city and municipality in Trøndelag county, the third most populous municipality in Norway. It was incorporated as a city on 1 January 1838, and its present municipality was formed in 1964 by merger with four neighbouring municipalities, and enlarged again in 2020. The Norwegian University of Science and Technology and the research foundation SINTEF have their headquarters there, and the cathedral stands beside the Archbishop's Palace in the city centre.
troodos-mountains: The Troodos Mountains are the largest mountain range of Cyprus, lying roughly in the centre of the island and covering a third of its area, across most of its western side. The highest peak is Mount Olympus, also called Hionistra, at 1,952 metres. The range forms a significant rain shadow on the island. The name probably comes from one of two sources: the Greek words for three and road, referring to the three roads that lead to the mountain, or a phrase meaning the mountains of Adonis. The Cyprus cedar and many other plants and animals found nowhere else live there.

The mountains have been known since antiquity for their mines, which for centuries supplied copper to the entire Mediterranean. In the Byzantine period they became a centre of Byzantine art, as churches and monasteries were built in the mountains, away from the threatened coastline. The region is known for Byzantine churches and monasteries richly decorated with murals, of which the Kykkos monastery is the richest. Nine churches and one monastery in Troodos together form a World Heritage Site, first inscribed by UNESCO in 1985; they include Panagia tou Araka, Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis and Agios Ioannis Lampadistis at Kalopanagiotis.

Geologists value the range for an undisturbed ophiolite sequence, the Troodos Ophiolite. It rose slowly from the sea as the African and European plates collided, a process that eventually formed the island. Erosion exposed the former magma chamber beneath the mountains, revealing intact rocks and petrified pillow lava formed millions of years ago. Observations of the Troodos ophiolite by Ian Graham Gass and his colleagues were among the evidence that led to the theory of seafloor spreading.

The mountains hold resorts, villages in the valleys and on terraced hillsides, and many Byzantine monasteries and churches on the peaks. The climate is Mediterranean, with greater daily ranges in temperature than on the coast. Trees include the Turkish pine and golden oak, with Anatolian black pine higher up. The endangered Cyprus mouflon is the chief wild animal.
troy: The archaeological site of Troy consists of the hill of Hisarlık and the fields below it to the south. The hill is a tell, formed of strata holding the remains of more than three millennia of occupation. Nine main layers are identified, numbered with Roman numerals from Troy I, the earliest, to Troy IX, the latest, with sublayers marked by letters such as VIIa and VIIb. Relative dates come from comparing artefacts with those from other sites, and precise absolute dates are not always possible because radiocarbon dating has limited accuracy.

Troy I was founded around 3000 BCE beside a shallow lagoon and was notable for massive limestone fortifications. Troy II, built around 2550 BCE, was twice the size, with a lower town and a citadel divided into two precincts; its Megaron IIA is the biggest known building of its kind in the Aegean and Anatolian region. Troy VI–VII was a major Late Bronze Age city with a steep citadel and a sprawling lower town, in contact with Mycenaean Greece. Hittite records name a city of Wilusa, usually identified with it, though not all scholars regard the identification as firmly established. Sublayers VIh and VIIa show possible signs of violent destruction and are candidates for the setting of the later myths.

Troy VIII grew from about 700 BCE, when Greek immigrants began building, and lasted into the Roman era. Herodotus says that Xerxes sacrificed 1,000 cattle at the sanctuary of Athena Ilias on his march towards Greece. Ilion was destroyed in 85 BCE after an eleven-day siege by the Roman general Fimbria, then rebuilt after Sulla bestowed benefactions on it, and its new civic calendar took 85 BCE as its first year. Earthquakes around 500 CE devastated the city, and from the 4th century until the Byzantine era Ilion was the seat of a Christian bishop.

Interest in the site began with travellers who mistook Alexandria Troas for Troy. Charles Maclaren was the first to identify Hisarlık with confidence, in 1822, and Frank Calvert surveyed it in 1865. Heinrich Schliemann secured permission to excavate in 1868 and began his trench in April 1870; Wilhelm Dörpfeld, Carl Blegen and, from 1988 to 2005, Manfred Korfmann continued the work, the last revealing the lower city. Schliemann proposed Troy II as the city of legend, though later research showed it predates the Mycenaean era by several hundred years. The relationship between myth and reality remains unclear. The Turkish government created a Historical National Park at Troy in 1996, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.
troyes: Troyes lies on the Seine about 140 km south-east of Paris, within the Champagne wine region. Prehistoric evidence suggests that a settlement may have developed there as early as 600 BCE, and Celtic grave-mounds and artifacts have been found in and near the city. In the Roman era the town, called Augustobona Tricassium, stood at the meeting of many roads, above all the Via Agrippa, which led north to Reims and south to Langres and on to Milan.

Troyes was the civitas of the Tricasses, whom Augustus separated from the Senones. Little of the early Gallo-Roman city survives apart from scattered remains and traces of an aqueduct, and by the late Empire the settlement had shrunk. Its later name came from Tricassium or Tricassae. The people had become Christian by the fourth century and the city became the seat of a bishop.

The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, also called the Battle of Troyes, was fought nearby in 451, when Flavius Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I fought Attila. In 878 Louis the Stammerer received the crown of West Francia from Pope John VIII at Troyes. After Norman raids at the end of the ninth century the counts of Champagne chose it as their capital, and it remained the capital of the Province of Champagne until the Revolution.

In the Middle Ages it was an important international trading town, driven by the Champagne cloth fairs, and the troy weight for gold is named after it. Rashi, the commentator on the Bible and the Talmud, was born there in 1040 and founded an influential school. In 1417 John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, worked to have Troyes made the capital of France.

The Treaty of Troyes was signed there on 21 May 1420, betrothing Henry V of England to Catherine, daughter of Charles VI, and making Henry rather than the Dauphin the heir to the French crown. Joan of Arc and the Dauphin, later Charles VII, restored French control of the town in 1429.

Troyes is the capital of the department of Aube in the Grand Est region. Many half-timbered houses, mostly of the 16th century, survive in the old town, and it is designated a City of Art and History. Its Gothic churches include the cathedral of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul and the Basilica of Saint-Urbain, begun by Jacques Pantaléon, who became Pope Urban IV in 1261.
true-cross: The term True Cross refers to any relic claimed to be part of the original wooden cross on which Jesus of Nazareth was crucified. The Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodoxy, the Oriental Orthodox churches and some denominations of the Church of the East have all claimed relics of it as objects of veneration. There is no evidence that any particular relic is part of the original cross, and historians generally dispute their authenticity, as do Protestant and other Christian churches, which do not hold them in as high regard.

Some fourth-century historians and Christian legends say that Helena, the mother of the Roman emperor Constantine the Great, recovered the cross at the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem during her travels in the Holy Land in 326 to 328. The Life of Constantine by Eusebius of Caesarea, the earliest main source on the rediscovery of the tomb of Jesus, does not mention the cross.

About forty years after Cyril, a fully developed story existed. Gelasius of Caesarea recorded it in a lost Greek history before his death in 395, and Rufinus of Aquileia adapted it around 402. In it Helena tore down a temple of Aphrodite and found three crosses beneath the rubble. The cross of Jesus was identified, with the help of Bishop Macarius of Jerusalem, when it cured a mortally ill woman. A church was built on the spot and the relic divided, part staying in Jerusalem and part going to Constantine with the nails.

A silver reliquary at the Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre was shown periodically to the faithful. In the 380s the pilgrim Egeria described the veneration of the cross at Jerusalem in a long letter known as her Itinerary.

During the Byzantine-Sasanian war of 602 to 628 the Sasanian shah Khosrow II took the part held in Jerusalem as a trophy after capturing the city in 614. The Byzantine emperor Heraclius defeated Khosrow and regained it in 628, restoring it to Jerusalem on 21 March 630. Constantin Zuckerman has suggested that the Persians had actually lost the cross and that the wood Heraclius brought was a fake.

A Syriac tradition replaced Helena with a fictitious first-century empress named Protonike, and in 1260 Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend gave several accounts of the cross's origin in trees from Adam's grave. By the end of the Middle Ages so many churches claimed relics that John Calvin remarked that there was enough wood in them to fill a ship.
trujillo-peru: Trujillo lies on the Moche River, near its mouth at the Pacific Ocean, in the Moche Valley, on a coastal plain about 34 metres above sea level. It has a desert climate but is called the City of Everlasting Spring, because the Humboldt Current keeps temperatures moderate. The river has been used for irrigation since the time of the Moche and Chimú.

The area was long a centre of successive pre-European cultures. Huaca Prieta was occupied as early as 4700 BCE, and the Cupisnique, Moche and Chimú all developed here. Chan Chan, the largest adobe city of the ancient world, and the Temples of the Sun and Moon lie close to the modern city.

According to the historian Napoleón Cieza Burga, Diego de Almagro founded the first settlement in November 1534 as Trujillo of New Castile, after Francisco Pizarro's home city. It was placed among four Chimú settlements to create an alliance against the Incas. On 23 November 1537 King Charles I of Spain gave it the rank of city and a coat of arms, the first in Peru granted by the king. By 1544 it had around 300 homes and 1,000 inhabitants, with an economy based on sugar cane and wheat.

Led by the mayor and intendant José Bernardo de Tagle, the Intendancy of Trujillo declared independence from Spain on 29 December 1820. The Department of Trujillo, created in 1821, covered nearly half the country and was until 1825 the only stable area able to organise the new republic. In 1824 Simón Bolívar declared the city the provisional capital of Peru.

Trujillo is the capital of the La Libertad region and the third most populous city of Peru. Its historic centre, bounded by Avenida España where the city wall once stood, holds colonial and republican buildings and ten colonial churches. Chan Chan was designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1986. The city is known as the capital of the marinera, a traditional dance, and the poet César Vallejo lived there from 1910 to 1917. Irrigated lands produce sugarcane, rice and asparagus, and the shoe industry is a major employer.
truman-doctrine: At the conclusion of World War II, Turkey was pressured by the Soviet government to allow Soviet shipping free passage through the Turkish Straits, which connect the Black Sea with the Mediterranean. Turkey refused, and a show of naval force took place at the Straits. In Greece, the Dekemvriana clashes of December 1944 were followed by a period of persecution of leftists known as the White Terror, which contributed to the outbreak of the Greek Civil War in 1946, in which Communist Party of Greece guerrillas fought the government.

By late 1946 Britain informed the United States that its declining economy no longer allowed it to support the Greek government. In February 1946 the American diplomat George F. Kennan had sent his Long Telegram from Moscow, recommending a long-term strategy of containment. After Prime Minister Konstantinos Tsaldaris asked for help in Washington in December 1946, the State Department planned aid to both Greece and Turkey. Policy makers feared that if Greece were lost to communism, Turkey would not last long.

Truman needed the support of the Republicans, who controlled both houses of Congress. Senator Arthur Vandenberg backed him and advised him to appear before Congress and scare the hell out of the American people. Dean Acheson compared a communist state to a rotten apple that could infect a whole barrel. Secretary of State George C. Marshall, Kennan and others thought the draft of the address contained too much rhetoric, but Truman answered that the request would pass only if he played up the threat.

On 12 March 1947 Truman spoke to a joint session of Congress for eighteen minutes. He said that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures. He added that help should be primarily through economic and financial aid. Congress approved 400 million dollars in military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey by a large majority in May 1947.

The domestic reaction was broadly positive, though the columnist Walter Lippmann was sceptical of the open-ended pledge, and others pointed out that the Greek monarchy Truman proposed to defend was itself repressive. The doctrine was the first of a series of containment measures, followed by the Marshall Plan and the creation of NATO in 1949. The historian Eric Foner writes that it set a precedent for American assistance to anticommunist regimes throughout the world, however undemocratic.
tsar: Tsar, also spelled czar, is a Slavic title derived from the Latin caesar. It entered the Slavic languages through the Gothic kaisar and served as the equivalent of the Greek basileus, which referred to Byzantine emperors and the kings of the Bible. It was meant to denote an emperor in the medieval European sense, a ruler of the same rank as a Roman emperor who held it by the approval of another emperor or a supreme ecclesiastical official, but Western Europeans usually took it to mean king.

The first ruler to adopt the title was Simeon I of Bulgaria, after a makeshift imperial coronation performed by the Patriarch of Constantinople in 913. The Byzantine government recognised it in 924 and again in 927, after a decade of intensive warfare. Stefan Dušan of Serbia was crowned emperor at Skopje at Easter 1346, and his son Stefan Uroš V succeeded him in 1355. Bulgaria's Ferdinand I took the title again in 1908, and it lasted until the monarchy ended in 1946.

In Russia, church officials once called Yaroslav the Wise tsar, but other princes of Kievan Rus' did not style themselves so. Ivan III, who asserted independence from the khan in 1476, began using the title regularly in diplomacy with the West. Its growth was tied to Russian ambitions to be a third Rome after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, and Emperor Maximilian I recognised the Moscow monarch as an emperor in 1514. The first Russian ruler formally crowned tsar of all Russia was Ivan IV in 1547.

In 1721 Peter the Great formally adopted the title of Emperor, but tsar stayed in common use and was kept in the full title as the style of rule over states absorbed by the Russian monarchy, such as the Tatar khanates and the Georgian Orthodox kingdom. In the 18th century it was increasingly seen as inferior to emperor.

By 1815 it had come to be read in Russia as the equivalent of the Polish król, king, and the emperor took the title tsar of Poland. Among the indigenous peoples of Siberia and the Muslims of the Volga region, Central Asia and the Caucasus, Russian autocracy became identified with the White Tsar. In English, tsar has been used since 1866 as a metaphor for a person of high authority.
tsetse-fly: Tsetse flies are large biting flies that inhabit much of tropical Africa. They include all the species of the genus Glossina, which has its own family, Glossinidae, and they live by feeding on the blood of vertebrate animals. Adults are 0.5 to 1.5 centimetres long and fold their wings completely over the abdomen when at rest.

They have an unusual life cycle: a female develops one offspring at a time inside her uterus, feeding it with a milky secretion, and the larva leaves the uterus only in its third stage, when it crawls into the ground and forms a hard case. Glossina is almost entirely restricted to wooded grasslands and forested areas, and its species are divided into savannah, forest and riverine flies.

The tsetse is a biological vector of trypanosomes, single-celled parasites that cause trypanosomiasis. In humans this is sleeping sickness, caused by Trypanosoma brucei, which is invariably fatal if untreated. In cattle and horses it is called nagana, and it reduces the growth, milk yield and strength of farm animals and generally leads to their death. Some breeds of cattle are called trypanotolerant because they can survive and grow when infected.

In East Africa C. F. M. Swynnerton did much of the earliest research on tsetse ecology in the first half of the 20th century, and the species Glossina swynnertoni was named for him in 1922. Early control methods included slaughtering the wild animals the flies fed on: Príncipe was cleared of feral pigs in the 1930s, which ended the fly there.

Writers on environmental determinism have linked the tsetse to difficulties in early state formation where the fly is common. A 2012 study built a suitability index from population growth, climate and geospatial data and found that more suitable conditions for the fly were associated with weaker agriculture, urbanization and institutions.

Its authors concluded that the fly decimated livestock, forcing early states to rely on slave labour to clear land and preventing farmers from using animal fertiliser, which may have kept population density low. In the 19th century the rinderpest epidemic, introduced in 1887 in livestock brought by an Italian expeditionary force to Eritrea, together with the tsetse fly is said to have depopulated much of Africa. Land infested with tsetse is often farmed with hoes rather than draught animals.
tsu-mie: Tsu lies in the east-central Kii Peninsula, in central Mie Prefecture. It stretches across the width of the prefecture, from Ise Bay in the east to Nara Prefecture in the west, and it has an area of 711.11 square kilometres, making it the largest city in the prefecture by area. Parts of the city are within the Murō-Akame-Aoyama Quasi-National Park. It has a humid subtropical climate with hot summers and cool winters with little or no snowfall.

Tsu originally developed as a port town called Anotsu in the Nara and Heian periods. In 1498 the port was devastated by the earthquakes and tsunami of the Meiō era, including the 1498 Meiō Nankaidō earthquake, and its residents were forced to relocate.

The town was rebuilt as a castle town and a post station by the Tōdō clan, daimyō of Tsu Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate. During the Edo period it became a popular stopping point for travellers to Ise Grand Shrine, about 40 kilometres to the south-east. Tōjin Odori, a dance from the Wakebe-chō neighbourhood, began around 1636 as part of the festival of Tsu Hachiman Shrine and imitates the Joseon Tongsinsa, the Korean diplomatic missions to Edo-period Japan.

After the Meiji Restoration Tsu became the capital of Mie Prefecture. When the modern municipal system was established on 1 April 1889, Tsu was one of the original 31 cities proclaimed in Japan and the only one in Mie. It grew by annexing neighbouring villages between 1909 and 1943. The first bombs fell on 12 March 1945, and three heavy air raids in June and July destroyed about 73 per cent of the city centre by incendiary bombs. The worst raid, by about 70 B-29 bombers on 24 July 1945, killed an estimated 1,200 to 1,300 people.

On 1 January 2006 Tsu merged with the neighbouring city of Hisai and several towns and villages in the Age and Ichishi districts, forming the new city of Tsu, which became the largest in Mie by area. It is the administrative and educational centre of the prefecture. Mie University, the prefecture's only national university, is here. The ruins of Tsu Castle have been made into a downtown park, and Kitabatake Shrine and Yūki Shrine are notable local Shinto shrines.
tsuruoka: Tsuruoka lies on the coast of Yamagata Prefecture, bordering the Sea of Japan, and covers 1,311.53 square kilometres, which makes it the largest city in the Tōhoku region by area. Two main rivers run through it, the Akagawa and the Mogami. All three of the Three Mountains of Dewa lie at least partly within its limits: Mount Haguro, the smallest at 436 metres, Mount Gassan, the highest at 1,984 metres, and Mount Yudono at 1,500 metres. The winters bring heavy snowfall, and some neighbourhoods can expect up to 2 metres.

The area was part of ancient Dewa Province. In the Edo period it was the capital of the Shōnai Domain and a minor port for the kitamaebune coastal trade. After the start of the Meiji period it was organised as Tsuruoka Town in 1878. It became a city on 1 October 1924, the 100th city in Japan. It annexed the town of Kamo and nine neighbouring villages in 1955 and the town of Oyama in 1963. On 1 October 2005 the towns of Fujishima, Haguro, Kushibiki and Atsumi and the village of Asahi merged into it.

The Three Mountains are the core of the practice of Shugendō, often seen as a blend of Shinto and Buddhism. The Yamabushi, the men who practise it, believe in the Buddha but also that a god resides in all things in nature. The pilgrimage of the three mountains is understood to represent death and rebirth. Mount Haguro has a five-storied pagoda that is one of Japan's National Treasures, and a cedar more than 1,000 years old. The Yamabushi's vegan temple food is called shōjin ryōri.

In 2014 Tsuruoka was registered as a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy, in part because of more than 50 kinds of ancestral food crops that have remained intact for centuries. They include the minden eggplant and the Atsumi turnip. The city is also known for dadachamame soybeans and for its local rice. Thatch-roofed houses are among its symbols, and the Chidō Museum preserves one.
tsushima-island: Tsushima lies between the Tsushima Strait and the Korea Strait, roughly halfway between Kyushu and the Korean Peninsula. The Korea Strait splits at the archipelago into two channels, and the wider one, closer to the Japanese mainland, is the Tsushima Strait. The main island, once a single island, was divided in two in 1671 by the Ōfunakoshiseto canal and in three in 1900 by the Manzekiseto canal, forming North Tsushima and South Tsushima. The group also includes over 100 smaller islands.
It measures about seventy by fifteen kilometres. Forest covers about 90 per cent of the island, and there are few plains, so the islanders have lived mainly by fishing and trade.

In Japanese mythology Tsushima was one of the eight original islands created by the deities Izanagi and Izanami. Archaeological evidence suggests that settlers from the Japanese archipelago and the Korean Peninsula lived there from the Jōmon period to the Kofun period. The Chinese Records of the Three Kingdoms describes a country called Duì hǎi guó, commonly identified with Tsushima, as one of about 30 that made up the Yamatai union. Its families controlled Iki Island and traded with Yayoi Japan. A mountain castle on Jouyama, built in 667 by Emperor Tenji, housed border guards, and from the early sixth century Tsushima was an official province of Japan.

In the feudal period it was an important trading centre. Private trade between Goryeo, Tsushima, Iki and Kyūshū halted during the Mongol invasions of Japan between 1274 and 1281, and the Goryeosa records that in 1274 Korean troops of the Mongol army led by Kim Bang-gyeong killed a great number of people on the islands. Tsushima became one of the main bases of the Wokou, Japanese pirates, along with Iki and Matsuura. Korea at times placated the pirates with trade agreements and at times used force, and in 1389 General Pak Wi of Goryeo wiped out the Wokou on Tsushima.

In 1861 the Imperial Russian Navy tried to establish a base on the island, in what is known as the Tsushima incident. The plan had been made by Vice Admiral Ivan Likhachev, but the Russians withdrew under pressure from Vice Admiral John Hope, who commanded the British ships in Japanese waters on the orders of Sir Rutherford Alcock.

Tsushima is part of Nagasaki Prefecture, and Tsushima City, formed on 1 March 2004 from six towns, covers the whole island. Izuhara was the castle town of the Tsushima domain until the Edo period, and ancient stone walls still stand in its samurai street. The Ofunaeato ruins, docks created in 1663, served the Korean trade and the alternate attendance system. The sacred Mount Shiratake, 519 metres high, is a national natural monument for its primeval forest.
tuareg: The Tuareg are an Amazigh people who speak the Tuareg languages, known as Tamasheq in Mali, Tamahaq in Algeria and Libya, and Tamajeq in the Azawagh and Aïr regions of Niger. They are descended from indigenous Berber communities of North Africa. Some researchers tie the origin of the Tuareg to the fall of the Garamantes, who lived in the Fezzan from the 1st millennium BCE to the 5th century CE. The Lamtuna, a Sanhaja Berber tribe that formed the core of the Almoravid dynasty, were closely related to their ancestors.

In tradition the Tuareg moved south from the Tafilalt region into the Sahel under their founding queen Tin Hinan, believed to have lived between the 4th and 5th centuries. Her tomb at Abalessa in the Hoggar Mountains of southern Algeria bears traces of an inscription in Tifinagh, the Libyco-Berber script that the Tuareg still use.

The invasion of North Africa from the Middle East in the 7th century triggered migrations of Tuareg groups such as the Lemta and the Zarawa. Later, the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym Arab tribes moved into Tuareg regions in the 11th century and pushed the Tuareg south, into seven clans which oral tradition holds are descended from one mother. Tuareg people are credited with spreading Islam in North Africa and the adjacent Sahel.

At the turn of the 19th century, Tuareg territory was organised into confederations, each ruled by a supreme chief, the amenokal, with a council of elders from each tribe. They were sometimes called drum groups after the amenokal's symbol of authority. There were seven major confederations, including the Kel Ajjer, Kel Ahaggar, Kel Adagh, Kel Ayr and Kel Gres. When African states became independent in the 1960s, Tuareg territory was divided among Niger, Mali, Algeria, Libya and Burkina Faso. A Tuareg uprising in Mali in the 1960s was suppressed by the army.

Tuareg society has traditionally had clan membership, social status and caste hierarchies within each confederation. Its strata included nobles, clerics, craftsmen and unfree people, and slavery was widespread. The nobles carried arms, owned camels and collected tribute from their vassals. Culture is largely matrilineal, and men, not women, traditionally wear the veil, the indigo tagelmust, a combined turban and veil. The Tuareg are a pastoral people with an economy based on livestock, trade and agriculture. They have long organised caravans across the Sahara, such as the salt caravans from Agadez to Fachi and Bilma and from Timbuktu to Taoudenni. They are mostly Muslim, and their population is estimated at 1.2 to 3 million.
tubingen: Tübingen is a traditional university city in central Baden-Württemberg, 30 kilometres south of Stuttgart. It grew around the base of the fortress Schloss Hohentübingen and of the St. George's Collegiate Church, on both sides of the Neckar and Ammer rivers. The Neckar flows east through the city, just south of the medieval old town. To the north lies the Schönbuch, a densely wooded nature park, and the Swabian Alb rises to the south-east. The Schlossberg and the Österberg stand in the city centre, and large parts of the city are hilly.

The area was probably first settled in the 12th millennium BCE. The Romans left traces in 85 CE, when they built a limes frontier wall at the Neckar in confrontation with the Alamanni. Records of the castle of Hohentübingen go back to 1078, when Henry IV, King of Germany, besieged it. In the middle of the 12th century the Counts of Zollern were raised to Imperial Counts Palatine, with their seat at Tübingen. By 1231 it was a civitas, which meant the Crown recognised its civil liberties, a market and a court system.

In the later 13th century the town gained Augustinian and Franciscan monasteries and a Latin school, today's Uhland-Gymnasium. In 1342 the town and castle passed to the Counts of Württemberg. The clock tower of the Collegiate Church was begun in 1411. The Jewish community, centred on the Judengasse below the Rathaus, was expelled in 1477, the year the university was founded.

The university, Eberhard Karl University, is one of the oldest north of the Alps. In the 19th century it was associated with the German-patriotic student Burschenschaften, whose large fraternity houses remain a feature of the town. It was associated with the rise of National Socialism in the years between the world wars. Among those linked with the town are Philip Melanchthon, the astronomer Johannes Kepler, and Wilhelm Schickard, professor of Hebrew and astronomy and inventor of a mechanical calculator. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel and Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling studied there, and Friedrich Hölderlin studied, lived and died in the town, as did the theologian Ferdinand Christian Baur.

Tübingen survived the Second World War with its historic fabric almost wholly intact, and its old town, with crooked cobblestone lanes, half-timbered houses and the Rathaus on the central market, is one of the few Altstädte in Germany that is completely intact. Students make up almost a third of its 90,000 residents. After the 1960s the city expanded on the high ground to the north, and later into the Loretto and French Quarter on land that French military bases had left.
