It is the capital of a district and of an administrative region, and the university is its largest employer.
tudela: Tudela stands in the Ebro valley in Navarre, Spain, and is the second largest city of that chartered community. It is the capital of the agricultural region of Ribera Navarra. Excavations show that the area has been populated since the Lower Paleolithic, and the town has been inhabited continuously since Roman times. The Roman poet Martial recalls the town of Tutela in grateful verse in his Epigrams.

The town was taken by the Arabs during the Umayyad conquest of Hispania and was named Tatīlah. At the beginning of the 9th century its position on the Ebro made it strategically important, and it became the base of the Banu Qasi, a family of local magnates who had converted to Islam. They remained independent of the emirs and kept on-off alliances with the kings of Pamplona for the next century. As their power faded at the start of the 10th century, the town came under the influence of the Caliphate of Córdoba.

Muslims used Tudela as a bridgehead against the expanding Kingdom of Navarre. When Christians under Alfonso the Battler conquered it in 1119, Muslims, Mozarabs and Jews lived there. Relations afterwards appear to have been strained, and the Muslims were made to live in a suburb outside the walls. In 1157 the English scholar Robert of Ketton, the first translator of the Koran into Latin, became a canon of Tudela. The principal mosque was handed to the Catholic Church in 1121, and by the end of the 12th century work had begun on the cathedral.

Jews were banished in 1498, and Muslims and Moriscos were expelled in 1516 and 1610. Tudela was the last Navarrese stronghold of the Agramont party to surrender to Ferdinand II of Aragon's troops in the 1512 invasion. Marshal Lannes won the Battle of Tudela for Napoleon Bonaparte on 23 November 1808, and the railway station was built in 1861.

Tudela has about 35,000 inhabitants. The Cathedral of Our Lady of Solitude, built in the 12th and 13th centuries, includes Romanesque work such as the Door of the Last Judgement, with Gothic influence and Baroque additions. The Romanesque churches of Magdalene and San Nicolás also date from the 12th century, and examples of Mudéjar architecture remain.
tughlaq-dynasty: The Tughlaq dynasty was the third to rule the Delhi Sultanate. Tughlaq was the personal name of the founder, Ghazi Malik, rather than an ancestral designation, and historians use it for the whole dynasty as a convenience. His ancestry is debated, but he is usually considered to be of Turko-Mongol or Turkic origin. The Khalji dynasty had ruled before 1320. Its last ruler, Khusro Khan, lacked the support of the Muslim nobles, who invited Ghazi Malik, then governor in Punjab, to lead a coup. In 1320 he killed Khusro Khan and took the throne as Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq.

Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq built Tughlakabad, a city six kilometres east of Delhi with a fort considered more defensible against Mongol attacks. His son Jauna Khan captured Arangal in 1323 and annexed Kakatiya territory. According to many historians, including Ibn Battuta, Ghiyasuddin was killed by Jauna Khan in 1325, and Jauna Khan ruled as Muhammad bin Tughlaq for 26 years. His campaigns between 1330 and 1335 brought the sultanate to its territorial zenith, but they were expensive and the extended empire was hard to retain. Rebellions became routine, and the Deccan, Bengal, Sindh and Multan became independent.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised the land tax on non-Muslims tenfold in some districts of the Ganges and Yamuna region and twentyfold in others. Villages left their fields, and famines followed; Ibn Battuta, who arrived in 1334, noted a seven-year famine from 1335 near Delhi. The court historian Ziauddin Barani records bloodshed among Muslims as well. After a short rule by Mahmud Ibn Muhammad, his nephew Firuz Shah Tughlaq reigned for 37 years; Barani calls him the mildest sovereign since Islam came to Delhi. Civil wars broke out in 1384 and 1394.

In 1398 Timur defeated four armies of the Sultanate. Sultan Mahmud Khan fled, and Delhi was plundered for eight days and its population massacred. Khizr Khan, whom Timur is believed to have appointed viceroy at Delhi, entered the city on 6 June 1414 and founded the Sayyid dynasty.

The Tughlaqs managed their expanded empire by appointing family members and Muslim aristocrats as na'ib of iqta' provinces under contract. The na'ib deposited a fixed sum with the Sultan and kept a share of the taxes collected; excess collected from non-Muslims was split between na'ib and Sultan in a 20:80 ratio, which Firuz Shah changed to 80:20. Campaigns yielded loot and slaves, and the sultans patronised a slave market. The sultans, particularly Firuz Shah, also sponsored many construction projects and are credited with developing Indo-Islamic architecture.
tughril: Tughril was born most likely in the Central Asian steppes, where nomadic Oghuz Turks roamed in search of pasture. His name was the Old Turkic word for a bird of prey, possibly the crested goshawk. After the death of his father Mikail, he and his brother Chaghri were reportedly raised by their grandfather Seljuk, the eponymous founder of the dynasty, in Jand. The family seems to have converted to Islam, at least nominally, in this period. For decades the Seljuks served as mercenaries for warring factions in Transoxiana and Khwarazm in exchange for pasture for their herds.

They then asked Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni for leave to settle in Khorasan, where pastures were scarce for them in their old lands. Mahmud allowed it, and they crossed the Amu Darya and settled around Sarakhs, Farava and Bavard.

Under Mahmud's successor Masʽud I the Seljuks fought near Nasa in 1034, and Tughril took the city. In 1037 the Seljuk notables declared him sultan and a sermon was delivered in his name. His victory over the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 ended their rule in Greater Khorasan, and he made Nishapur his capital. He and Chaghri Beg, whose names were read together in the sermons and struck on coins, shared rule according to the Turkic custom of a khagan and a yabghu.

With the help of his half-brother Ibrahim Inal, Tughril conquered Jibal and Iraq-i Ajam between 1040 and 1054 and ended Buyid rule in those areas. He took Ray, later making Isfahan his capital, and brought Azerbaijan under his control. From 1048 Turcomans under Ibrahim began systematic campaigns into Byzantine lands. In 1055, at the invitation of the caliph al-Qa'im, he entered Baghdad and ended the Buyid dynasty by arresting its last ruler in Iraq, Malik al-Rahim. He later put down a revolt by Ibrahim Inal and defeated Arslan al-Basasiri, who had Fatimid backing.

Tughril died in Ramadan in 455 AH (1063), without an heir, near Ray, and was buried there in the Tughril Tower. He was known as devout, built many mosques and madrasas, followed the Hanafi school and, with his vizier Amid al-Mulk Kunduri, restricted other Islamic sects. Some sources describe him as a just ruler who avoided bloodshed, while others report oppressive conduct by him and his army.

His legacy was an administrative model that joined Turkic political tradition, regional customs and the religious legitimacy of the Abbasid caliphate. It made the sultanate a form of absolute rule that recognised the caliph's spiritual leadership but overshadowed his worldly power. Before the Seljuks Iran had been divided among warring local powers such as the Buyids, Kakuyids and Ghaznavids, and under Tughril peace and prosperity came to Iran and Mesopotamia.
tuileries-palace: The site lay just outside the walls of Paris, on land occupied by workshops that made tuiles, roof tiles. After the death of Henri II in 1559, his widow Catherine de' Medici planned a new residence close to the Louvre with space for a large garden. Between 1563 and 1568 she bought several plots, and construction began in 1564 with Philibert de l'Orme as chief architect. After he died in 1570 Jean Bullant took his place. The Day of the Barricades in 1588 halted the work.

Henri IV resumed construction in 1594 and built the Grande Galerie, which connected the Tuileries to the Louvre. Between 1659 and 1661, and again from 1664 to 1666, Louis Le Vau enlarged the palace for Louis XIV. The finished façade was 266 metres long.

The court occupied the palace from 1667 to 1672 and then moved to Versailles. Louis XV lived there from 1716 to 1722. On 1 December 1783 the first manned flight in a hydrogen balloon, by Jacques Charles and the Robert brothers, took off from its garden. On 6 October 1789 Louis XVI and his family were forced to leave Versailles for the Tuileries, and the National Constituent Assembly later met in its Salle du Manège. After the failed flight to Varennes in June 1791 the royal family was returned to Paris, and on 10 August 1792 a mob stormed the palace and massacred the Swiss Guards who defended it. The National Convention then met there during the Reign of Terror.

Napoleon Bonaparte moved in on 19 February 1799 and had Charles Percier and Pierre Fontaine redesign the interior. the House of Bourbon returned after his fall, Louis Philippe d'Orléans used the palace until 1848, and Napoleon III took up residence in 1852 and extensively redecorated it.

On 23 May 1871, during the suppression of the Paris Commune, twelve men under Jules Bergeret set the palace on fire with petroleum, tar and turpentine. The fire lasted 48 hours and gutted it, apart from the foundations and the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel. The walls stood for eleven years until the Third Republic had them demolished between February and 30 September 1883. Pieces of the stone were sold as souvenirs. The Tuileries Garden survives, as does the Axe historique running through the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe, which was once centred on the palace façade.
tukoji-rao-holkar-iii: Tukoji was born on 26 November 1890, the son of Shivajirao Holkar, Maharaja of Indore, and Maharani Sita Bai. His father abdicated on 31 January 1903, and as the new maharaja was only thirteen a council of regency governed until he came of age. He was educated at the Daly College in Indore and at Dehradun. On 6 November 1911 he was invested with ruling powers, and in the same year he attended the coronation of King George V in London.

As ruler he founded two orders, the Order of Merit of Holkar in February 1914 and the Order of Ahilyabai Holkar on 22 November 1920. In the New Year Honours of 1918 he was made a Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Star of India.

In January 1925 Mumtaz Begum, a courtesan and one of his mistresses, left his harem after what she described as repressive conditions and the death of her daughter, which she blamed on palace nurses. While performing in Bombay she met Abdul Bawla, a 25-year-old Memon businessman, who was threatened several times and told to send her back, and refused. On 12 January a group of assassins attacked the couple at Malabar Hill. Bawla was shot in the head and killed; Mumtaz Begum survived with a wound to the face after British officers who were nearby intervened.

She testified against nine accused, among them men of the maharaja's household. The court sentenced three men to death and three to life imprisonment. One of the latter, General Anandrao Gangram Phanse of the Indore army, escaped the death penalty after being represented by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The court did not formally hold Tukoji responsible, but under British pressure he abdicated on 26 February 1926 and left Indore.

After his abdication he lived mainly in France. He had married three times. His senior wife, Chandravati Gawade, whom he married on 16 March 1895 when both were small children, stayed in Indore and brought up their son, the new maharaja. His second wife, Indira Talcherkar, married in 1913, also remained there and became a patron of historical research bodies such as the Rajwade Historical Research Institute.

In 1928 he married Nancy Anne Miller, who before the wedding embraced Hinduism, was received into the Dhangar community and took the name Sharmista Devi Holkar; they had four daughters. The Bawla case inspired a film of 1925, Kulin Kanta, and two books. Tukoji died in Paris on 21 May 1978, leaving one son and six daughters.
tulln: Tulln lies in the centre of the Tulln Basin, which stretches to the Vienna Woods in the south, about 40 kilometres northwest of Vienna. Most of its built-up area is on the southern bank of the Danube. Because of its many parks and gardens the town is often called Blumenstadt, the City of Flowers. The municipality consists of several cadastral communities, among them Langenlebarn, Staasdorf and Mollersdorf, and the town proper has about twelve thousand inhabitants. It is the administrative seat of Tulln District.

The name Tulln is presumably of Celtic origin, and the place was settled before Roman times. It gained importance as the Roman fort of Comagena, also called Comagenis. In the last years of Roman rule Saint Severinus of Noricum is said to have visited the town and saved it from the barbarians. A Roman tower of the 4th century still stands. The town is first mentioned as Tullina in a deed of 859, when the area belonged to the Bavarian marcha orientalis.

Tulln became important as a residence of the House of Babenberg, who ruled as Austrian margraves from 976, and lost its significance after they moved their residence to Vienna. The first public clock tower is recorded here in 1372. On 6 September 1683 the Polish cavalry of King John III Sobieski joined Imperial forces and troops from Saxony, Bavaria and Baden at Tulln before the Battle of Vienna against the invading Ottoman army. In 1986 the town applied to become capital of Lower Austria, but Sankt Pölten was chosen.

Tulln has a large sugar-producing plant, and trade fairs, including camping equipment and boat shows, take place there. The Federal School of Aviation and several state institutions of Lower Austria, such as the fire brigade and the disaster relief service, have their seat in the town. According to the Nibelungenlied it was at Tulln that Attila the Hun saw Kriemhild and proposed to her, and a Nibelungen Fountain was dedicated to the episode in 2005. The painter Egon Schiele was born in Tulln, which has a museum dedicated to him. The Minoritenkloster, a convent, is among the sights.
tullus-hostilius: Tullus Hostilius came from a Roman family of Alban descent. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, its earliest known member, Hostus Hostilius, had migrated to Rome from Medullia and fell in the front ranks fighting beside Romulus against the Sabines. After the death of Numa Pompilius, the Senate appointed interreges, each serving for five days, and the Curiate Assembly elected Tullus king by acclamation. He still needed the auspices, the sanction of the gods, before entering office.

According to Dionysius, Tullus began by dividing the royal estates among landless Romans. He brought the Caelian Hill within the walls and lived there for a time. Livy records that after the conquest of Alba Longa he added ten squadrons of Albans to the cavalry, raising it from 300 to 600. Ancient sources credit him with the Curia Hostilia, the first senate house, and the Comitium, with the Fetial college, which conducted Rome's treaties and declarations of war, and with the Salii Collini, a second college of priests.

War with Alba Longa began with cattle raids across the border. Rather than fight a full battle, the Alban dictator Mettius Fufetius proposed that three brothers from each city fight for supremacy; Rome's champion, Publius Horatius, won. Later, in a war against Veii and Fidenae, Mettius held the Alban troops back on a hilltop and betrayed both sides. Tullus had him executed, destroyed Alba Longa, and brought its people to Rome as citizens. Leading Alban families, including the Julii, entered the Senate. Sources also record a Sabine war won at the Battle of the Malitiosa.

Livy says Tullus neglected the gods until omens and a pestilence came late in his reign. He fell ill, tried to perform rites from Numa's writings, and did the ceremony for Jupiter Elicius wrongly; lightning struck his house and burned it with his family. Dionysius gives another version, in which Ancus Marcius and his followers killed Tullus and his household on a stormy night.

Modern historians treat the early kings with scepticism, since Livy, Dionysius and Plutarch wrote at least five hundred years later. Most nonetheless accept that Tullus existed, because Tullus is a rare praenomen and the name Hostilius did not belong to a great Republican family. Some see his story as modelled on Romulus. Corneille's tragedy Horace (1640) and Jacques-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii (1784) draw on the legend of the duel.
tulsidas: Tulsidas was born Rambola Dubey, on the seventh day of the bright half of the month of Shraavana. The exact date and year of his birth are disputed among scholars and biographers. Tulsidas himself gives only a few facts about his life, and the early sources are the Bhaktamal of Nabhadas, a contemporary who calls him an incarnation of Valmiki.

Many believe he was a reincarnation of Valmiki. According to the Tulsi Prakash and some other works he married Ratnavali, and after she rebuked him for his attachment to her he left for Prayag and became a sadhu. Most stories about him are apocryphal and have been carried forward by word of mouth, since none was related by Tulsidas himself.

After renunciation he spent most of his time at Varanasi, Prayag, Ayodhya and Chitrakuta, and travelled to many other places. Tradition holds that he began composing poetry in Sanskrit in Varanasi, but that the verses he wrote by day were lost each night.

On the eighth night Shiva is believed to have ordered him in a dream to compose in the vernacular and to go to Ayodhya to write in Awadhi. He is generally believed to have died in 1623 at Assi Ghat in Varanasi, though the exact day and month are disputed.

Twelve works are widely considered to be his, six major and six minor, in Awadhi and Braj. The Ramcharitmanas, composed between 1574 and 1576, is his longest and earliest work, of around 12,800 lines in seven books, about one third the size of Valmiki's Ramayana. His other works include the Dohavali, the Vinaya Patrika, the Gitavali, and the Parvati Mangal and Janaki Mangal, on the marriages of Parvati and of Sita.

The Hanuman Chalisa is popularly attributed to him and bears his signature, though some authors doubt he wrote it. In his teaching Tulsidas holds that the Nirguna Brahman, without qualities, and the Saguna Brahman, with qualities, are one and the same, but he favours the Saguna aspect. Repeating the name of Rama is, in his view, the only means to reach God in the Kali age.

He sees no incompatibility between devotion to Rama and attachment to Shiva, and his writings aim to teach bhakti to Rama as the means of salvation, free and open to men of the lowest caste. The Tulsi Ghat in Varanasi is named after him, and the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple there is believed to stand where he saw Hanuman.
tumbuka-language: Tumbuka, or Chitumbuka, is a Bantu language of Central and Southern Africa spoken primarily in Malawi, Zambia, Tanzania and Zimbabwe. It is the native language of more than 13 peoples, among them the Senga, Tumbuka, Yombe, Phoka, Henga, Fungwe, Hewe, Northern Ngoni, Kamanga and Tonga, with 12 known dialects. The prefix chi- means "the language of". In 2024 there were approximately 7.1 million native speakers in Malawi, Zambia and Tanzania, and nearly 1,600,000 people spoke it as a second language in Malawi and Zambia.

As in other Bantu languages, nouns are grouped into noun classes by their singular and plural prefixes, and verbs, adjectives and pronouns agree with the noun through concords. Every verb has a subject prefix, as in ciŵinda ci-ka-koma nkhalamu, "the hunter killed a lion". A negative is made by adding yayi or cha(ra) at or near the end of the clause. Tone plays only a limited part: every word spoken in isolation has the same falling tone on the penultimate syllable.

All Tumbuka dialects have been affected to some extent by the Zulu language, chiNgoni, most of all in Mzimba District. The Ngoni originated from the Ndwandwe people, who were neighbours of the Zulu clan before they were conquered by the Zulu and assimilated into the Zulu identity. The language the Ndwandwe spoke was therefore nearly identical to Zulu. Most words of Zulu or Ndwandwe origin have Tumbuka counterparts that can be used interchangeably, and the Mzimba dialect has click consonants in words such as chitha, "urinate", which do not occur in other dialects.

In 1947 Chitumbuka was made an official language of Malawi for 21 years, along with Chewa and English. In 1968 Hastings Kamuzu Banda removed it under his one-nation, one-language policy, and it was taken out of the school curriculum, the national radio and the print media. With the advent of multi-party democracy in 1994, Chitumbuka programmes were started again on the radio.

Two systems of writing are in use. The traditional spelling writes banthu, "people", and chaka, "year", with b and ch; the new official spelling writes them ŵanthu and caka. There is also uncertainty over where to write r and where l, since [l] and [r] are allophones of the same phoneme.
tumkur: Tumkur is a city in the southern state of Karnataka, India, at an altitude of around 800 metres above sea level and about 70 kilometres northwest of the state capital, Bengaluru. The surrounding district has elevated terrain cut by river valleys, with hilly and forested areas such as the Devarayanadurga hill range, in the southern part of which the river Shimsha originates. Agriculture is supported by monsoon rainfall and favourable terrain, and major crops include coconut, areca nut, rice, ragi, groundnut and several oilseeds.

The origin of the name is uncertain. It is believed to have changed from Tumbe ooru, after the abundance of thumbe hoovu, a kind of flower, or from thamate ooru, after the folk percussion instrument thamate, which may have been used most here. Another account says that Gulur was the capital during the rule of the Cholas, and that because Tumkur stands high, guards on a hill beat a drum called the tumaki to sound alerts. The area is also called Kalpatharu Nadu, the land of coconut trees.

Tumkur was accorded the status of a city corporation on 28 August 2010. The central government approved the renaming of Tumkur and twelve other cities in October 2014, and it officially became Tumakuru on 1 November 2014.

At the 2011 census Tumkur had approximately 542,000 inhabitants, most of them Hindu, with Muslim and Christian minorities. Kannada, the official language of the state, is the language of the majority, and there are many Urdu speakers and small Telugu, Tamil and Hindi communities. The railway station lies in the centre of the city, on the Bangalore–Hubli main line. The Siddaganga Matha, a Lingayat monastery, provides free education and accommodation for more than 9,000 children; Shivakumara Swami was its president.
tunisia: Tunisia lies on the Mediterranean coast of north-west Africa, bordered by Algeria to the west and south-west and Libya to the south-east. It covers 163,610 square kilometres and has a coastline of about 1,300 kilometres. The Dorsal, the eastern extension of the Atlas Mountains, crosses the country north-eastward; north of it lies the Tell, a region of low hills and plains. The Sahel, a coastal plain on the east, is among the world's premier areas of olive cultivation, and much of the south is semi-arid and desert. Tunis, the capital, stands on a hill slope above the lake of Tunis.

Tunisia was inhabited by Berber tribes at the beginning of recorded history. Phoenicians began settling the coast from as early as the 12th century BCE, at Bizerte and Utica. Carthage, founded in the 9th century BCE, became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean after wars with the Greek city-states of Sicily. According to the Greek writer Timaeus of Tauromenium, Dido of Tyre founded it in 814 BCE, though this is regarded as legend. Its people worshipped Baal and Tanit. After the Second Punic War, in which Hannibal invaded Italy, Carthage was a client state of Rome until it was conquered in 146 BCE and made the province of Africa.

Arab Muslims conquered Tunisia in the 7th century CE, and the migration of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym tribes in the 11th and 12th centuries accelerated the process, and by about the 15th century the region was almost completely Arabised. The Ottoman Empire took control in 1546 and held it until the French conquest of 1881. Tunisia became independent as the Tunisian Republic in 1956.

The Tunisian Revolution of 2011 overthrew President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali after 24 years in power and set off the wider Arab Spring. A new constitution was adopted on 26 January 2014, and a constitutional referendum in 2022 made it a unitary presidential republic.

The population is 12.1 million, the vast majority Arab and Muslim. Arabic is the official language, and French serves as an administrative and educational language without official status. The European Union is the first trading partner: Tunisia signed an Association Agreement with it in July 1995, the first Mediterranean country to do so.
tunja: Tunja lies in the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian Andes, in the region known as the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, 130 kilometres northeast of Bogotá. The city centre stands at 2,820 metres above sea level, and the city ranges from about 2,700 to 2,900 metres, making it one of the higher cities of Colombia. It has a subtropical highland climate with little variation in temperature and a dry season from December to February. It is the capital of the department of Boyacá.

Before the Spanish conquest the settlement was called Hunza and was the seat of a Muisca ruler. According to Muisca tradition the prophet Goranchacha moved the capital of the northern Muisca from Ramiriquí to Hunza. Hunzahúa, who came from Ramiriquí, was elected supreme chief and took the title of hoa, great lord. Later the ruler Eucaneme avoided any aggression against the Europeans and sent them gifts, hoping to stop them while he hid his treasures.

Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada's expedition reached Hunza on 20 August 1537 and found Quemuenchatocha, the ruler, seated and dressed in gold; the conquerors took gold, emeralds and fabrics. He was succeeded by his nephew Aquiminzaque, whom the Spaniards accused of planning an insurrection. In 1540 Aquiminzaque was beheaded, which ended the dynasty of the zaques of Hunza. Captain Gonzalo Suárez Rendón founded the Spanish city on 6 August 1539 on the lands of Quemuenchatocha. The main square was laid out first, and in 1550 the outlines of the city were consolidated. The Franciscans arrived in 1550, the Dominicans a year later, the Augustinians in 1585 and the Jesuits in 1611.

Tunja is known for colonial religious architecture, and the Casa del Fundador Gonzalo Suárez Rendón is recognised as its oldest remnant. The city also holds the most surviving Muisca architecture, including the Hunzahúa Well, the Goranchacha Temple and the Cojines del Zaque. The Colegio de Boyacá, founded on 20 October 1822 by Vice President Francisco de Paula Santander, was the first public school in the territories of Venezuela, Ecuador, Panama and Colombia. Tunja has a large student population, and its main university, the Pedagogical and Technological University of Colombia, is a public one.
tunku-abdul-rahman: Tunku Abdul Rahman was born on 8 February 1903 in Alor Setar, Kedah, the seventh son and one of 45 children of Sultan Abdul Hamid Halim Shah. His mother, Cik Menyelara, the sixth consort of the Sultan, was of Thai descent. Kedah was afflicted by cholera and malaria, and several of his siblings died of illness. He studied in Malaya and graduated from St Catharine's College, Cambridge.

In January 1931 he joined the Kedah Civil Service as a cadet and became District Officer of Padang Terap, where he had the swamps drained to rid Kuala Nerang of malaria. He married Violet Coulson, which the regent Tunku Ibrahim had opposed, and a transfer to the isolated post at Langkawi followed. During the Japanese occupation, as District Officer in Kulim, he organised a vigilante corps to prevent looting. After a period of law study in England he qualified as an advocate and solicitor and became a deputy public prosecutor in 1949.

He won the leadership of UMNO in 1951, and in 1952 he formed the Alliance Party with the Malaysian Chinese Association and the Malaysian Indian Congress, holding that each community needed its own party. The Alliance won a landslide in the 1955 general election and he became chief minister. He offered amnesty to the communist revolutionaries of the Malayan Emergency and tried to end it at the Baling Talks, without success.

He led the Merdeka Mission to constitutional talks at Lancaster House in London in January 1956, and the Treaty of London secured independence. He proclaimed Malayan independence on 31 August 1957. As prime minister he was also foreign minister, and he led the Alliance to victories in 1959 and 1964. He oversaw the formation of Malaysia in 1963 with Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak.

Ethnic tensions grew, above all in the relationship with Singapore. After mutual provocations between UMNO and the People's Action Party under Lee Kuan Yew he resolved to expel Singapore, with separation taking effect on 9 August 1965. Violent unrest in the 13 May incident of 1969 followed the Alliance's reduced majority. He stepped down in 1970, succeeded by Abdul Razak Hussein.

In retirement he served as the first secretary-general of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. He had been president of the Asian Football Confederation from 1958 until 1977 and started the Merdeka Tournament in 1957. He died in Kuala Lumpur on 6 December 1990, aged 87, and was buried at the Langgar Royal Mausoleum in Alor Setar. He is recognised as the country's founding father, and places such as Putrajaya and several universities bear his name.
tuol-sleng: Tuol Sleng is in Phnom Penh. The site was a secondary school, Tuol Svay Prey High School, named after a royal ancestor of King Norodom Sihanouk. To hold the victims of purges important enough for the attention of the Khmer Rouge, its five buildings were converted into a prison and interrogation centre and renamed Security Prison 21 (S-21). The buildings were enclosed in electrified barbed wire, classrooms became tiny cells and torture chambers, and windows were covered with iron bars and barbed wire to prevent escapes and suicides. It was one of between 150 and 196 torture and execution centres established by the Khmer Rouge.

At any one time the prison held between 1,000 and 1,500 prisoners, who were repeatedly tortured and coerced into naming family members and associates, who were in turn arrested. In the early months most victims came from the previous Lon Nol regime, among them soldiers, officials, academics, doctors, teachers, students, factory workers, monks and engineers. Later purges brought thousands of party activists and their families, including senior figures such as Khoy Thoun, Vorn Vet and Hu Nim, officially arrested for espionage. Confessions ran to thousands of words and are believed to have been mostly false.

Most prisoners were held for two to three months. Killing prisoners outright was discouraged because the Khmer Rouge needed their confessions. Corpses were at first buried near the prison, but by the end of 1976 burial space had run out, and prisoners and family members were taken to the Boeung Choeung Ek extermination centre, fifteen kilometres from Phnom Penh. The prison had a staff of 1,720 under its chief, Khang Khek Ieu, known as Comrade Duch, a former mathematics teacher. Some staff themselves became prisoners.

In 1979 the prison was uncovered by the invading Vietnamese army, and Hồ Văn Tây, a Vietnamese combat photographer, was the first journalist to document it. The government of the People's Republic of Kampuchea reopened it as a historical museum memorialising the actions of the Khmer Rouge regime. The buildings are preserved, some rooms as they were when the Khmer Rouge were driven out, and several rooms are lined with photographs of prisoners. Paintings by Vann Nath, a former inmate spared because he could paint, show people being tortured.

On 26 July 2010 the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia convicted Kang Kek Iew of crimes against humanity; he died in 2020. In 2025 the site was designated a World Heritage Site as part of the Cambodian Memorial Sites.
tupac-amaru-ii: Túpac Amaru II was born José Gabriel Condorcanqui Noguera at Surimana, Tungasuca, in the province of Cusco, to Miguel Condorcanqui, kuraka of three towns in the Tinta district, and María Rosa Noguera. His parents died when he was twelve, and at sixteen he received a Jesuit education at the San Francisco de Borja school, founded for the sons of kurakas. He married Micaela Bastidas and succeeded his father as kuraka, inheriting 350 mules, so that he was both head of several Quechua communities and a regional muleteer.

He petitioned the authorities in Tinta, Cusco and Lima to relieve the tribute and the mining mita, the forced labour at Potosí, and met only refusal or indifference. He adopted the name Túpac Amaru II after his ancestor Túpac Amaru I, the last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State.

The rebellion began on 4 November 1780 with the capture and hanging of Antonio de Arriaga, corregidor of Tinta, accused of repeated abuses. Its immediate cause lay in the Bourbon reforms, which centralised administrative and economic control and laid heavier taxes and labour burdens on Native and Creole populations. It was not at first an independence movement but a protest against colonial abuses, often speaking in the king's name, though some of his followers, mainly poor peasants, artisans and women, hoped for a restored Inca order. On 16 November 1780 he decreed the abolition of slavery for Black people.

At Sangarará on 18 November 1780 his forces killed all 578 Spanish soldiers, but the rebels' killing without orders ended any hope of Creole support. His 40,000 to 60,000 followers were repelled from Cusco, where reinforcements had arrived from Lima. His wife Micaela Bastidas commanded a battalion and is often credited with sharper strategy than his. Betrayed by two of his own officers, he was captured.

On 18 May 1781 he was executed in the Plaza de Armas of Cusco, after being forced to watch the deaths of Micaela Bastidas, his eldest son Hipólito and others. The sentence called for his limbs to be pulled apart by horses; the attempt failed and the body was quartered by hand and beheaded. The authorities ordered his houses demolished, his relatives declared infamous and Inca dress and the identity of Inca outlawed.

The revolt continued under his cousin Diego Cristóbal Túpac Amaru and spread through Upper Peru. Although not an independence movement in the modern sense, the rebellion was the first large-scale revolt in the Spanish colonies, and Túpac Amaru II later became a symbol of social justice and resistance in Peru.
tupelo-mississippi: Tupelo lies in north-eastern Mississippi on Interstate 22 and U.S. Route 78, midway between Memphis, Tennessee, and Birmingham, Alabama. It covers about 51 square miles, and the 2020 census counted 37,923 people. The Tupelo area is also the headquarters of the Natchez Trace Parkway, which follows the route of an ancient trail used by indigenous peoples long before Europeans came and connects Natchez, Mississippi, to Nashville, Tennessee. Nearby are the Pharr Mounds, a complex of nearly 2,000-year-old burial earthworks of the Middle Woodland period.

The Chickasaw and Choctaw occupied the area before European settlement, and the French and British traded with them and sought alliances. On 26 May 1736 the Battle of Ackia was fought near the site of present-day Tupelo, where British and Chickasaw soldiers repelled a French and Choctaw attack on the Chickasaw village of Ackia. The French governor of Louisiana, Jean Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville, had sought to link Louisiana with Acadia and the other northern colonies of New France. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 authorised the relocation of the Southeast Native Americans to territory west of the Mississippi River, completed by the end of the 1830s.

The settlement was founded in 1860 on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and was first called Gum Pond, from the local tupelo trees known as blackgum. Union and Confederate forces fought in the area in 1864 in the Battle of Tupelo and the Battle of Old Town Creek. The town took the name Tupelo in honour of the battle and was incorporated on 20 July 1870.

By the early twentieth century it had cotton textile mills, which under segregation employed only white adults and children. On 7 February 1934 Tupelo became the first city to receive power from the Tennessee Valley Authority, and President Franklin Roosevelt visited this First TVA City in 1935.

On 5 and 6 April 1936 a tornado struck, levelling 48 city blocks and more than 200 homes and killing 216 people in the official count. It destroyed the Gum Pond neighbourhood. Because white newspapers did not report news about Black people until the 1940s and 1950s, historians estimate the real toll was higher. Elvis Presley, then a baby, survived it.

Tupelo is the seat of Lee County and the birthplace of Elvis Presley, and the Elvis Presley Birthplace is among its cultural institutions. The Tupelo National Battlefield and the Brices Cross Roads National Battlefield, about ten miles to the north, commemorate Civil War battles. A statue of the Chickasaw leader Piomingo stands in front of the city hall.
tura-river: The Tura is a left tributary of the Tobol in the basin of the Irtysh, flowing across the Tura Plain through the Sverdlovsk and Tyumen oblasts of Russia. It is 1,030 kilometres long, with a drainage basin of 80,400 square kilometres, and is navigable for 635 kilometres from its mouth. Near its source it is also called the Dolgaya. It begins at an elevation of 370 metres from the confluence of several streams southwest of the Khrebet-Uralsky railway station. The upper valley is narrow with steep slopes and a rocky bed, and in the lower reaches the flow is smooth. The main tributaries are the Salda, Tagil, Nitsa, Pyshma, Aktay and Is.

In 18th-century sources G. F. Müller explained the name from the Tatar word tura, meaning city, referring to the town of Chimgi-Tura on the river. Modern hypotheses link it to an Ural-Altaic root tur, meaning watercourse or body of water, which passed into several Ugric and Turkic languages. The Babinov Road, also known as the Sovereign's Road, was built along the river. Several cities lie on the Tura, from source to mouth Verkhnyaya Tura, Nizhnyaya Tura, Lesnoy, Verkhoturye, Turinsk and Tyumen.

The river freezes in November and thaws mainly in the first half of April, and ice jams sometimes accompany the break-up. Its flood lasts about two and a half months, and the winter low water lasts on average 140 to 160 days. The Tura is the primary source of water for the water supply of Tyumen. In the upper part of the basin lie deposits of copper, iron ores, gold and platinum, and the industries based on them are one of the main sources of pollution of the river. Three reservoirs, with a total area of 23 square kilometres, include the Verkhoturye Hydroelectric Station, and their construction changed the river's water regime.
turfan: Turpan, also written Turfan, is a prefecture-level city in the east of the Xinjiang autonomous region, about 150 kilometres south-east of Ürümqi, on the northern side of the Turpan Depression at about 30 metres above sea level. It has an extremely continental desert climate, with very hot summers, very cold winters and annual precipitation of only 15.7 millimetres. The ancient irrigation system and the summer heat allow the countryside to produce great quantities of high-quality fruit, and the region is China's largest raisin-producing area. The historical centre of the area has shifted, from Jiaohe to Qocho, also called Gaochang, and to Turpan itself.

The Jushi Kingdom ruled the area in the 1st millennium BCE until the Chinese Han dynasty conquered it in 107 BCE. Han and Xiongnu contended for it. After the fall of the Han in 220 the region was virtually independent. Tocharian-speaking people lived in Turpan and nearby city-states up to at least the 8th century, and many Han Chinese and Sogdians settled there. In 327 the Former Liang created the Gaochang Commandery here, and from 460 Gaochang was a vassal kingdom of the Rouran Khaganate under a Han Chinese king. Later kings of the Qu dynasty were vassals of the Göktürks.

The Tang dynasty conquered the region in 640 and renamed it Xi Prefecture. Sogdian and Chinese merchants traded extensively, and contracts found in the Astana Cemetery record sales of slaves. The Tibetans took Turfan in 792, and in 803 the Uyghurs seized it from them. After the Kirghiz destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in Mongolia in 840, many Uyghurs moved here. The Uyghurs set up the Idikut kingdom, also called the Kara-Khoja Kingdom, with its capital at Gaochang, which lasted from 856 to 1389. Its people were first Manichaean and later converted to Buddhism, funding the Bezeklik Caves. The kingdom became a vassal of the Kara-Khitans and then of the Mongol Empire.

German expeditions between 1902 and 1914 took paintings and other art to the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin, and many of the artefacts of Manichaean and Buddhist origin were later destroyed or looted during the Second World War. The Turfan fragments, over 40,000 manuscripts and fragments in 16 languages, are kept in the Berlin State Library. They hold Buddhist, Christian-Nestorian, Manichaean and secular texts, among them parts of the Gospel of Mani. Many texts survive because the Astana graveyard used discarded paper to make clothing for corpses. The conversion of the Buddhist population to Islam was completed in the second half of the 15th century.
turin: Turin lies in north-western Italy, mainly on the western bank of the River Po, surrounded on the west and north by the Alps and on the east by a high hill that continues the hills of Monferrato. Four major rivers pass through it: the Po and its tributaries the Dora Riparia, the Stura di Lanzo and the Sangone.

The Taurini, a Celto-Ligurian Alpine people, occupied the upper valley of the Po. In 218 BCE Hannibal, allied with their enemies the Insubres, took their chief town, Taurasia, after a three-day siege. In the 1st century BCE the Romans founded Augusta Taurinorum, a town of about 5,000 inhabitants within high walls; its Porta Palatina is still preserved. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town was held by the Heruli, Ostrogoths and Lombards, and passed to the Franks under Charlemagne in 773. The Counts of Savoy gained control after the marriage of Adelaide of Susa to Otto, son of Humbert Biancamano, and when the city was annexed to the Duchy of Savoy at the end of the 13th century it had 20,000 inhabitants.

Emmanuel Philibert, nicknamed Iron Head, made Turin the capital of the Duchy of Savoy in 1563. The French Empire annexed it with the rest of Piedmont in 1802, and in 1814 the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia was restored with Turin as its capital. That kingdom led the struggle for the unification of Italy, and Turin was the political and intellectual centre of the Risorgimento. It became the capital of the new Kingdom of Italy in 1861; the capital moved to Florence in 1865 and to Rome after the conquest of the Papal States in 1870.

Turin is the capital of Piedmont and is sometimes called the cradle of Italian liberty. Its architecture is predominantly Baroque, and part of the historical centre is inscribed in the World Heritage List as the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy. It is the base of Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo, and hosted the 2006 Winter Olympics.
turin-king-list: The Turin King List is a hieratic papyrus thought to date from the reign of Ramesses II, who ruled from 1279 to 1213 BCE. It is the most extensive list of kings compiled by the ancient Egyptians and the basis of most Egyptian chronology before his reign. The list is written on the back of a discarded tax register, which may mean the writer did not treat it as formally important; its main function is thought to have been as an administrative aid.

Its beginning and end are lost, with no introduction and nothing after the 19th Dynasty, so it may have been composed at any time from Ramesses II to as late as the 20th Dynasty. It is a sloppy copy of a more detailed original that rested on much older sources. Only the kings of the First and Second dynasties have both their length of reign and age at death.

The papyrus is divided into eleven columns. The first two hold the gods, spirits and mythical kings; the human kings follow, from the First Dynasty to the 17th, and perhaps once a twelfth column carried the 18th and 19th. It gives the length of each reign in years, with months and days for some, and sometimes groups rulers by family, roughly as Manetho's dynasties do. It includes ephemeral rulers and those of small territories who are unmentioned elsewhere.

It also lists the Hyksos kings of the 15th Dynasty, who ruled Lower Egypt and the Nile delta. They have no cartouches, and a sign marks them as foreigners, although foreign rulers are not usually listed in king lists. Kim Ryholt estimates that the list once held about 250 kings, with about 270 from Narmer or Menes to Ramesses II over some 1,800 years.

The circumstances of discovery are unknown. The Italian traveller Bernardino Drovetti bought the papyrus at Thebes around 1818. It was purchased at Livorno in 1820 and reached Turin in 1824, where the Egyptian Museum acquired it as Papyrus Number 1874. When its box was opened, it had crumbled into small fragments. Jean-François Champollion drew what he could read, and Gustav Seyffarth rebuilt it from the fibres of the papyrus alone, before hieratic could be read.

Giulio Farina published a new placement of fragments with a transcription, translation and commentary in 1938, and Ryholt published a new interpretation in 1997. Donald Redford has noted discrepancies between its names and monuments and other documents. About half the papyrus is still missing; it is now 1.7 m long and 0.41 m wide in over 160 fragments, and unpublished fragments were found in the museum's storage in 2009.
turkey: Turkey, officially the Republic of Türkiye, lies mainly in Anatolia, which makes up 97% of its surface, with a smaller part called East Thrace in Southeast Europe. Together they cover 783,562 square kilometres, and the Turkish straits and the Sea of Marmara run between them. The inland Anatolian Plateau grows more rugged towards the east, where Mount Ararat, the highest point at 5,137 metres, and Lake Van, the largest lake, are found. The Euphrates, the Tigris and the Aras rise in the east, and the country is divided into seven major regions.

The area has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic and holds some of the oldest Neolithic sites, among them Göbekli Tepe, close to 12,000 years old, and Çatalhöyük. Written records begin with clay tablets of about 2000 BCE from Kültepe, which belonged to an Assyrian trade colony. The Hittite kingdom, with its capital at Hattusa, lasted approximately between 1700 and 1200 BCE, and Phrygia was established around 750 BCE. Alexander the Great's conquests brought Hellenization, followed by Romanization under the Roman and Byzantine empires.

The Seljuk Turks began migrating into Anatolia in the 11th century. The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum ruled until the Mongol invasion of 1243, after which Turkish principalities emerged. From 1299 the Ottomans united them, and Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453. The Ottoman state entered World War I in 1914, and its government committed genocides against its Armenian, Greek and Assyrian subjects. After defeat came the Turkish War of Independence, the abolition of the sultanate and the Treaty of Lausanne. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first president, proclaimed the Republic on 29 October 1923.

Turkey has more than 86 million people. Most are ethnic Turks, and Kurds are the largest minority, with estimates ranging from 12 to 20% of the population because census figures have not recorded ethnicity since 1965. Ankara is the capital and Istanbul the largest city. The country is a presidential republic under the constitution approved by referendum in 1982, with a 600-member Parliament and 81 provinces.
turkish-war-of-independence: The Armistice of Mudros, signed on 30 October 1918, ended the First World War for the Ottoman Empire. The army was to demobilise, and Article VII gave the Allies the right to occupy the forts of the Straits and, in case of disorder, any territory threatened by insecurity. The Committee of Union and Progress dissolved itself, and its leaders Talât, Enver and Cemal fled, leaving a power vacuum. Sultan Mehmed VI sent Mustafa Kemal Pasha to restore order as inspector of the Ninth Army, but he became the leader of Turkish nationalist resistance.

Most historians date the war's start to the Greek landing at Smyrna on 15 May 1919, when hundreds of Turkish and about a hundred Greek soldiers and civilians were killed or wounded. Kemal landed at Samsun on 19 May and organised mass meetings. The Erzurum Congress drafted the National Pact, based on self-determination, and set up a Committee of Representation with Kemal as chairman.

On 16 March 1920 the Allies occupied Istanbul and arrested nationalist politicians, and the Grand National Assembly then convened in Ankara. Turkish forces defeated the French in the south, and in the east the army partitioned Armenia with the Bolsheviks, resulting in the Treaty of Kars in 1921. On the Western Front, the Greco-Turkish War, the regular army under İsmet Pasha fought the Greeks to a standstill at the First and Second Battles of İnönü. The Greeks won at Kütahya-Eskişehir and advanced on Ankara, but were checked at the Battle of Sakarya, and a Turkish counter-attack, the Great Offensive, expelled them.

The war ended with the recapture of İzmir, the Chanak crisis and an armistice at Mudanya. On 1 November 1922 the Assembly voted to abolish the sultanate, and Mehmed VI left on 17 November 1922, ending the monarchy of over 600 years.

The Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923 and more favourable to Turkey than Sèvres, was followed by the Allied evacuation of Istanbul. The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923, with Mustafa Kemal elected its first president, and he went on to introduce sweeping reforms. A population exchange between Greece and Turkey accompanied the end of the Ottoman era.

The war also reshaped Turkey's population. Historians note that the nationalists carried out massacres and deportations of Christian populations, continuing policies of the First World War: over a million Greeks were expelled, and the remaining Armenians of several districts were forced into French-mandate Syria. Greek and Armenian civilians were massacred in the fire of Smyrna. Muslims rose from 80% to 98% of the population. Some historians dispute the name war of independence, given the scale of civilian deaths among Christian minorities.
turkistan-city: Turkistan is the administrative centre of Turkistan Region in Kazakhstan, near the Syr Darya river, 160 kilometres north-west of Shymkent on the Trans-Aral Railway between Kyzylorda to the north and Tashkent to the south. Its name comes from the Turco-Persian phrase Hazrat-i-Turkistan, 'Saint of Turkistan', a reference to Ahmad Yasawi, a prominent 11th-century poet and Sufi who rests in the city. Earlier, and through much of the medieval and early modern era, it was called Iasy or Shavgar.

The city has an archaeological record reaching back to the 4th century. It emerged as a commercial centre after the decline of Otrar, an ancient city near the Syr Darya, and in honour of Ahmad Yasawi it became a hub of spiritual growth and Islamic education for the people of the Kazakh steppes. In the 1390s Timur built a domed mausoleum over Yasawi's resting place, one of the most notable architectural landmarks in Kazakhstan. The city also has a medieval bath-house and four mausoleums, one for Rabiya Sultan Begim, Timur's great-granddaughter, and three for Kazakh khans.

Before the Russian arrival in the 19th century Turkistan stood on the boundary between the Perso-Islamic oasis civilisation of Transoxiana to the south and the Kazakh steppes to the north. From the 16th to the 18th century it was the capital of the Kazakh Khanate and the political centre of the steppe. As Russia expanded and weakened the khanate, smaller southern states fell, and by 1864 the Russian general Veryovkin had captured Turkistan from the Kokand Khanate. It became part of the Syr-Darya Oblast in Russian Turkistan, briefly of the Turkistan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic after 1917–18, and in 1924 of the Kazakh ASSR.

The Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its image appeared on Kazakhstan's banknotes until 2006. According to local tradition, visiting Turkistan three times equals a single hajj to Mecca, and the city has been called the Second Mecca of the East; it draws thousands of pilgrims. In 2018 it became the administrative centre of the renamed Turkistan Region, and the 2019 census counted 165,000 inhabitants, Kazakhs and Uzbeks making up almost all of them.
turkmenbasy: Türkmenbaşy lies on the Türkmenbaşy Gulf of the Caspian Sea at an elevation of 27 metres, on the site where the dry bed of a former mouth of the Amu-Darya River once emptied into the sea. It has a cold desert climate with hot summers and somewhat chilly winters, and average annual precipitation of 125 millimetres. The city has been known by several names: Shagadam, Kyzyl-Su, meaning Red Water, Krasnovodsk, its Russian translation, and Türkmenbaşy.

In 1717 the Russian prince Alexander Bekovich-Cherkassky landed here and set up a secret fortified settlement. He intended to march an army up the dry riverbed and conquer the Khanate of Khiva. The expedition failed, and the Russians abandoned the settlement for over 150 years.

In 1869 the Russians came a second time, captured the settlement and named their fort Krasnovodsk. It served Imperial Russia as a base of operations against Khiva and Bukhara and against the semi-nomadic Turkmen tribes. The Trans-Caspian Railway had begun at Uzun-Ada on the Caspian, and its terminus was shifted north to the harbour at Krasnovodsk. The Russian station building dates from 1895, and the Church of St. Michael the Archangel was moved to the town from Uzun-Ada in the same year. The Armenian Apostolic church was built in 1903.

The town fell to the Red Army in February 1920. Krasnovodsk Oblast was formed on 21 November 1939 and was repeatedly abolished and restored until 1988. In 1942 a large part of the Polish Anders' Army, together with many civilians, was evacuated from the USSR through the port to Iran. On 8 October 1993 President Saparmurat Niyazov renamed the city Türkmenbaşy, meaning Head of all Turkmens, after his own self-proclaimed title.

Türkmenbaşy is a major port in Balkan Province in western Turkmenistan. Its seaport is Turkmenistan's main sea link to the west, with ferries across the Caspian to Baku, about 260 kilometres away, and it is the western terminus of the Trans-Caspian railway, which runs to Ashgabat. The country's largest oil refinery is here. Most of the population are Turkmens, who are Sunni Muslim, with Russian, Armenian and Azerbaijani minorities.
turku: Turku lies at the mouth of the Aura River in the south-western corner of Finland and covers both banks. The eastern bank, where Turku Cathedral stands, is the older and original centre; the western side, with Turku Castle, is the newer part. South-western Finland stayed below sea level for a long time after the Ice Age, and tectonic uplift turned the region from an outlying archipelago into a shoreline between about 3000 and 2000 BCE. In the Iron Age it was densely populated, and the word Finland once referred only to the area round Turku, which is why the province is called Finland Proper.

The Finnish name Turku is related to the word torg, meaning market. Pope Gregory IX mentioned the town of Aboa in his bull of 1229, and that year is now used as the founding year of the city. By the pope's permission of 23 January 1229 the episcopal seat was moved from Nousiainen to Koroinen, near the present centre. Because no reliable document records the founding, it has also been suggested that the city was founded in the 1280s or 1290s by the joint initiative of the king, the bishop and the Dominican Convent of Saint Olaf. Turku was the most important city in Finland under Swedish rule.

After the Finnish War, Sweden ceded Finland to Russia at the Treaty of Fredrikshamn in 1809, and the Russians entered Turku in October 1809 without resistance. Turku became the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland but lost the status in 1812, when Emperor Alexander I decided to move the capital to Helsinki. After the last great fire, in 1827, most government institutions were moved to Helsinki together with the Royal Academy of Turku, founded in 1640, which later became the University of Helsinki.

Turku is the oldest city in Finland and the regional capital of Southwest Finland, with about 210,000 inhabitants. It is officially bilingual in Finnish and Swedish. The Swedish-language Åbo Akademi was founded there in 1918 and the Finnish-language University of Turku two years later. Its port runs ferries to Stockholm and Mariehamn.
tutankhamun: Tutankhamun was born in the reign of Akhenaten, during the Amarna Period. His original name, Tutankhaten or Tutankhuaten, meant living image of Aten, reflecting the shift to Atenism that characterised Akhenaten's reign. When he became king he married Ankhesenpaaten, one of Akhenaten's daughters, who later changed her name to Ankhesenamun. They had two daughters who died at or soon after birth and were buried with him in his tomb.

Tutankhamun became pharaoh between 8 and 9 years of age, after the short reigns of Akhenaten's successors Smenkhkare and Neferneferuaten, and he took the throne name Nebkheperure. At the start of his reign the court was still at Amarna and the Aten was still acknowledged, but his court was trying to reconcile Atenism with the traditional religion. Activity at Amarna decreased during the first four years, and given the king's age the reversals of Akhenaten's policies must have been instigated by his advisors. His restorations of cults were recorded on the Restoration Stela.

He sought to restore diplomatic relations with other kingdoms, in particular with the Mitanni, and battles with Nubians and Asiatics were recorded in his mortuary temple at Thebes, both as Egyptian victories. He was one of the few pharaohs worshipped as a deity during their lifetime, as temples in Nubia and stelae at Karnak indicate. There are no surviving records of the circumstances of his death. Hawass and his team postulate that it resulted from a leg fracture, perhaps from a fall, combined with a severe malarial infection.

Tutankhamun's two known children were stillborn or died shortly after birth, and his death left no immediate heir. Ay, who performs the opening of the mouth ritual for him on the burial chamber wall, became pharaoh, and Horemheb, commander-in-chief of his armed forces, succeeded Ay. Horemheb completed the restoration of the traditional religion and had his own name inscribed on monuments that Tutankhamun had commissioned.

His tomb was unusually small for his status, and its entrance was lost under debris from later tombs and workers' houses. Howard Carter found it in 1922, with the patronage of George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon. It is the only royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings found in near-intact condition, with 5,398 items, among them a solid gold coffin, a face mask, thrones, bows and trumpets, and Carter took ten years to catalogue them. Rumours of a curse of the pharaohs followed the death of Carnarvon on 5 April 1923. In 1962 the Louvre held an exhibition of the treasures that drew 1.2 million visitors.
tutuila: Tutuila is part of the Samoan Islands and is the third largest island of that chain. It lies roughly 4,000 kilometres northeast of Brisbane and over 1,200 kilometres northeast of Fiji. It is a volcanic island of early Pliocene age, about 33 kilometres long and little more than 4.8 kilometres across at its widest point. The highest point is Matafao Peak at 653 metres.

Pago Pago Harbor, a large natural harbour, divides the island into two parts. The island has six terrestrial and three marine ecosystems, with lowland and montane rain forest. The National Park of American Samoa, established in 1988, protects part of the forest and coast, including two species of flying fox that Samoans regard as guardians of the forest and its people.

Polynesians first reached Samoa around 1000 BCE, and by 600 BCE they had a settlement on Tutuila at Tula. Around 1200 CE, in the reign of Momo, the tenth Tuʻi Tonga, the Tongans invaded and occupied Tutuila and other Samoan islands for nearly two centuries. Under the paramount chief Malietoa the Samoans rose against them, and Fau'au of Pago Pago led the local resistance that expelled the Tongans from Tutuila.

Jacob Roggeveen encountered the Samoan Islands in 1722, and Louis Antoine de Bougainville named them the Navigator Islands in 1768. Whalers and Protestant missionaries arrived in the early 19th century, and traders developed Apia on Upolu rather than Pago Pago as their station.

The US Navy saw Pago Pago as an ideal refuelling station for the new San Francisco-to-Sydney steamship service, and the United States Congress ratified a treaty for it in 1878. Great Britain and Germany also had interests, and in 1879 the three powers formed a tripartite government. Their dispute led in 1899 to a division of the islands: the eastern islands, including Tutuila, became American Samoa and the western ones came under European control. The US flag was raised on Tutuila on 17 April 1900.

Tutuila holds about 95 per cent of the population of American Samoa and some 68 per cent of its land. The capital, Pago Pago, stands on the harbour, and Pago Pago International Airport is on the island. American Samoa is an unincorporated and unorganized territory of the United States, and more than 90 per cent of its land is communally owned. Relics of the Second World War, including guns and bunkers around the harbour, survive on the island.
tuul-river: The Tuul River, also called the Tula River and in older sources the Tola, is a river in central and northern Mongolia. It is 882.8 kilometres long and drains an area of 49,840 square kilometres. It originates in the Khan Khentii Strictly Protected Area in the Khentii Mountains, in the Erdene sum of Töv aimag, and travels southwest until it reaches the territory of Ulaanbaatar. Its water runs through the southern part of the capital and continues westward in large loops.

On meeting the border of Bulgan aimag it turns north and runs along that border. After it enters Selenge aimag it discharges into the Orkhon River near the sum centre of Orkhontuul sum. The Orkhon flows into the Selenge River, which flows into Russia and Lake Baikal. The Tuul also flows along the Khustain Nuruu National Park.

The Tuul is sacred to the Mongols and is generally called the Hatan Tuul, meaning Queen Tuul. In Old Turkic sources it appears as Toɣla ögüz. The Secret History of the Mongols, of 1240, frequently mentions a Black Forest of the Tuul River, where the palace of Ong Khan was located.

The river is typically frozen over from the middle of November through the middle of April. Willow forests grow along its banks, and the river is home to endangered species of sturgeon. In 2014 almost 100 million cubic metres of water were withdrawn from it for domestic, livestock, cropland and industrial use, making it the most used river in Mongolia.
tuva: Tuva lies at the geographical centre of Asia in southern Siberia, and its capital, Kyzyl, stands near the geographic centre of the continent. The republic is a mountain basin about 600 metres above sea level, encircled by the Sayan and Tannu-Ola ranges, and mountains and hills cover over 80 per cent of its territory. Its highest point is Mongun-Tayga, at 3,970 metres. There are over 8,000 rivers, including the upper course of the Yenisei. It borders Mongolia to the south.

The territory was controlled by a succession of powers, among them the Xiongnu, the Rouran Khaganate, the Tang dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Yuan dynasty. From 1758 to 1911 Tuva was part of China's Qing dynasty, administered through Outer Mongolia. During the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 a separatist movement formed among the Tuvans, and on 17 April 1914 Tuva became a Russian protectorate as Uryankhay Krai. In 1918 and 1919 it was occupied by the White Russian troops of Alexander Kolchak, later by China, until the Bolsheviks expelled the Chinese in 1921.

On 14 August 1921 the Bolsheviks established the Tuvan People's Republic, popularly called Tannu-Tuva, formally independent between the World Wars. Its capital was renamed Kyzyl, meaning red, in 1926. A coup of 1929, carried out by five young Tuvans trained in Moscow, replaced Chairman Donduk Kuular, and Buddhist and Mongol influences were then curtailed. The Soviet Union annexed Tuva in 1944, with the approval of its Little Khural but without a referendum. Tuva signed the treaty creating the Russian Federation on 31 March 1992.

The Republic of Tyva is a republic of the Russian Federation, with 336,651 inhabitants at the 2021 census, more than a third of them in Kyzyl. Tuvans make up most of the population and speak the Tuvan language, a Turkic language. Tuvan and Russian are both official. Tuvan throat singing, in which the singer produces a fundamental tone and an overtone together, is a defining tradition. Tibetan Buddhism, first met in the 13th and 14th centuries, coexists with shamanism, which is preserved as part of traditional culture.
twelver-shiism: The term Twelver rests on the belief that twelve male descendants of the family of Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib to Muhammad al-Mahdi, are Imams with religious and political authority. The division of Islam into Shia and Sunni traces back to the crisis over the succession to Muhammad. According to Tabatabai the word Shia first referred to the partisans of Ali at the time of Muhammad himself. Ali moved the capital of Islam to Kufa and fought Mu'awiyah, who refused him allegiance. The death of Husayn played an important part in the spread of Shi'ism in Iraq, Yemen and Persia.

Twelvers believe that the Twelve Imams are divinely appointed spiritual and political successors to Muhammad, with special knowledge and authority to guide the Muslim community. They hold that Muhammad and the Imams must be free from error and sin, a doctrine called Ismah. Twelvers differ from the Isma'ili and Nizari branches in the number of Imams and the line of succession, and in rejecting the abrogation of Sharia laws. Their theology rests on the Quran and on hadiths from Muhammad and the Imams, especially Jafar al-Sadiq, and has been shaped by events such as the Battle of Karbala and the occultation of the twelfth Imam.

Many Twelvers add Ali is the viceregent of God to the Shahada. Their jurisprudence is called Ja'fari. The Usuli school accepts ijtihad, or rational effort, while the Akhbari school relies on the hadith of the Prophet and the Imams alone.

In the 10th century Baghdad was the centre of Mu'tazila theologians, whose ideas affected Shia thinkers. Abu Sahl al-Nawbakhti fused Mu'tazili theology with Imami thought, while Ibn Babawayh of Qom answered them from the hadiths. Al-Shaykh al-Mufid, Sharif al-Murtaza and Shaykh al-Tusi were the leading figures of the Baghdad school, and al-Muhaqqiq al-Hilli of the school of Hillah brought ijtihad into jurisprudence.

In 1501 Isma'il I took power in Iran, founded the Safavid dynasty and declared Twelverism the official religion of his empire, although most of the larger cities were Sunni. Shia scholars were brought in to set up seminaries, and religious authorities were appointed for all major cities. Twelver Shi'ism is the largest branch of Shia Islam, and Iran is the only country where it is the state religion.
twentieth-dynasty-of-egypt: The Twentieth Dynasty was the third and last dynasty of the Egyptian New Kingdom. With the Nineteenth Dynasty it forms the Ramesside period, so called because so many rulers bore the name Ramesses. After the death of Queen Twosret, last pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty, Egypt entered a period of civil war, as the Elephantine stela of Setnakhte attests. Her fate is uncertain: she may have died peacefully or been overthrown by Setnakhte, who was probably middle-aged. The cause of the war is unknown because historical records are lost.

Setnakhte ended the conflict and founded the dynasty. He stabilised Egypt and may have driven off an attempted invasion by the Sea Peoples. He ruled for about three or four years before his son Ramesses III succeeded him.

Ramesses III defeated a Libyan invasion in his fifth year and, in his eighth, a confederacy of Sea Peoples, including the Denyen, Tjekker, Peleset, Shardana and Weshesh, in the Battle of Djahy and the Battle of the Delta. In his twenty-ninth year the workmen of Set Maat, now Deir el-Medina, held the first labour strike recorded in history when their rations could not be supplied. A harem conspiracy in which Queen Tiye sought to put her son Pentawer on the throne ended in the king's death, and his heir Ramesses IV had about thirty conspirators put to death.

Later reigns were weaker. Ramesses V ruled no more than four years, and workmen at Set Maat had to stop work at times for fear of raiders, presumed Libyan. Under Ramesses IX, tomb robbery trials found many tombs broken into. Three sons of Ramesses III assumed power as Ramesses IV, VI and VIII, and droughts, low Nile floods, famine and corruption limited the capacity of any king.

A consistent theme was the loss of pharaonic power to the High Priests of Amun. The Wilbour Papyrus, thought to date from Ramesses V, shows that most land in Egypt was controlled by the Temple of Amun, which had complete control of finances. Under Ramesses XI, the last king, the High Priests of Amun at Thebes became the de facto rulers of Upper Egypt, while Smendes controlled Lower Egypt even before the king's death.

A period of chaos followed his death, ended by Smendes, who founded the Twenty-First Dynasty at Tanis. The dynasty is generally considered to mark the beginning of the decline of ancient Egypt, coinciding with the Bronze Age Collapse and the onset of the Third Intermediate Period. Although it defended Egypt against the Sea Peoples, its trade routes were damaged as most trading partners had been destroyed.
twenty-fifth-dynasty-of-egypt: The Twenty-fifth Dynasty, also called the Nubian Dynasty and the Napatans after their capital Napata, was the last dynasty of the Third Intermediate Period. It originated in the Kingdom of Kush, in present-day northern Sudan, and most of its kings saw Napata as their spiritual homeland. The dynasty was highly Egyptianized, using the Egyptian language and writing and showing an unusual devotion to Egypt's religious, artistic and literary traditions. Scholars have criticised the term Black Pharaohs, because it suggests that other dynasties did not share southern origins.

Piye, spelled Piankhi in older works, invaded Egypt from Napata and recorded his victory on the Stele of Victory, which names him Pharaoh of all Egypt. Tradition holds that Shabaka brought the Nile Valley under Kushite rule, but recent archaeological evidence shows that he ruled after Shebitku, not before. Shabaka restored monuments and temples and moved the capital to Memphis.

Taharqa's reign was prosperous, with a large Nile flood and abundant crops. He gave gold to the temple of Amun at Kawa, built or restored works at Jebel Barkal, Kawa, Qasr Ibrim and Karnak, and raised the largest pyramid in the Nubian region at Nuri. The imperial ambitions of Assyria made war inevitable. Esarhaddon invaded Egypt in 674 BCE and was defeated, according to Babylonian records, but in 671 BCE he conquered northern Egypt and captured Memphis. Ashurbanipal later advanced as far south as Thebes, and Taharqa retreated to Nubia, where he died in 664 BCE.

His successor Tantamani sailed north from Napata to Thebes, where he was ritually installed as king, and reconquered Egypt as far north as Memphis. Psamtik I returned with Ashurbanipal, Tantamani fled to Nubia, and the Assyrians sacked Thebes in 663 BCE. Psamtik I became the first ruler of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty and in 656 BCE sent a large fleet south to Thebes, peacefully taking control of Upper Egypt.

The dynasty ruled Egypt for less than a century, but it holds an important place in Egyptian history for its restoration of traditional Egyptian values, culture, art and architecture. It revived the building of pyramids for dead rulers, at El-Kurru and Nuri, about 1,000 years after Egyptian burial methods had changed. Its successors continued their kingdom in Nubia at Napata and then at Meroë. Psamtik II destroyed the monuments of the Kushite kings in Egypt, erasing their names, and sent an army to Nubia in 592 BCE. Even so, the memory of Shabaka survived, and Egyptians named a street after him in Late Period Memphis.
tycho-brahe: Tycho was born Tyge Ottesen Brahe on 14 December 1546 at his family's seat at Knutstorp in Scania, then Danish, the oldest of twelve siblings. He was heir to several of Denmark's most influential noble families, and both his grandfathers and all his great-grandfathers had served on the king's Privy Council. In 1566 he went to study at the University of Rostock. On 29 December of that year he lost part of his nose in a sword duel with his third cousin Manderup Parsberg, after a drunken quarrel over who was the better mathematician, and he wore a prosthetic nose for the rest of his life. His family had expected him to enter politics or law but supported his choice of the sciences.

Tycho devoted himself to more accurate instruments, enlarging the sextant and the quadrant, and mounted them underground on the bedrock once he realised that wind and the movement of buildings affected them. King Frederick II granted him an estate on Hven and money to build Uraniborg, the first large observatory in Christian Europe. In De nova stella of 1573 he refuted the Aristotelian belief in an unchanging celestial realm, and he showed that comets were not atmospheric phenomena. He could not reconcile Copernican heliocentrism with Aristotelian physics, so he devised a system in which the Sun and Moon orbit the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun.

After Frederick's death in 1588 Tycho's influence at court declined, and in 1597 he was forced by the new king to leave Denmark. He was invited to Prague, where he became imperial astronomer and built an observatory at Benátky nad Jizerou.

Tycho fell ill after a banquet in Prague and died eleven days later, on 24 October 1601, aged 54. Before dying he urged Johannes Kepler to finish the Rudolphine Tables using Tycho's own planetary system. Kepler used Tycho's records of the motion of Mars to deduce his laws of planetary motion. Tycho's planetary model was soon discredited, but his observations were an essential contribution to the Scientific Revolution. Danish scholarship often depicted him as a mediocre scholar and a traitor to the nation, but from the second half of the 20th century scholars reassessed his significance.
typewriter: The typewriter was invented in small steps by many people working independently or in competition over several decades, as the automobile, the telephone and the telegraph were. Historians have estimated that some form of it was invented 52 times. The Hansen Writing Ball, invented by Rasmus Malling-Hansen of Denmark in 1865, went into commercial production in 1870 and was the first typewriter sold. It printed only capital letters and was still reported in use in European offices in 1909.

Each key of a typewriter causes one character to be printed on paper by striking an inked ribbon against the page with a type element. The first commercially successful machine was patented in 1868 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, by Christopher Latham Sholes, Frank Haven Hall, Carlos Glidden and Samuel W. Soule. The clockmaker and machinist Matthias Schwalbach made the working prototype.

Sholes and James Densmore bought out the others and agreed with E. Remington and Sons, then known for sewing machines, to sell it as the Sholes and Glidden Type-Writer, which gave the machine its name. By about 1910 the manual typewriter had a fairly standard design of typebars striking a ribbon against a cylindrical platen.

Manufacturers at first found it hard to sell. Buyers compared a Remington costing 125 dollars with a pen costing a penny, and some recipients of typed letters felt insulted. Makers trained customers and referred typists to employers, and business colleges began to teach typing. Remington assumed the machine would be used for taking dictation and operated by a woman, and women filled many clerical posts during the First World War. Mark Twain bought a Remington in autumn 1874 and was using it for correspondence by December. The typewriter was also an early accessibility tool for blind people, and Sir Francis Campbell began adapting one with Braille output in 1875.

The Sholes and Glidden machines established the QWERTY layout, which remains the standard for English-language keyboards, and variants such as the French AZERTY and German QWERTZ arose for other languages. Typewriters were a fixture of offices until the 1980s, when personal computers began to replace them, and IBM sold its typewriter division in 1991. Habits such as typing two hyphens for a dash, and terms such as backspace, carriage return and cc for carbon copy, descend from the machine.
typhus: Typhus is a group of infectious diseases that includes epidemic typhus, scrub typhus and murine typhus. Common symptoms are fever, headache and a rash, typically beginning one to two weeks after exposure. Epidemic typhus is caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii and spread by body lice, scrub typhus by Orientia tsutsugamushi and spread by chiggers, and murine typhus by Rickettsia typhi and spread by fleas.

Epidemic typhus, the most severe form, generally occurs in outbreaks where poor sanitation and crowding are present. Without treatment, death may occur in 10 to 60 percent of cases. The antibiotic doxycycline is the treatment. The name comes from the Greek tûphos, meaning hazy or smoky, a word for delusion, and typhus is a different disease from typhoid fever.

Typhus has been described since at least 1528. The first reliable description appears in 1489, during the siege of Baza in the War of Granada, when the Spanish lost 3,000 men to enemy action and a further 17,000 to typhus. Gaol fever, common in English prisons where inmates were crowded into dark, filthy rooms, is believed to have been typhus.
