In 1750 it killed the Lord Mayor of London and many court officials at the Old Bailey, next to Newgate Prison.

Epidemics occurred routinely across Europe from the 16th to the 19th centuries. Typhus may have killed more than 10 percent of the German population in the Thirty Years' War. In Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812, more French soldiers died of typhus and dysentery than were killed by the Russians.

An epidemic in Ireland between 1816 and 1819 killed an estimated 100,000 people, and typhus with typhoid fever is said to be responsible for 400,000 deaths in the Great Irish Famine of 1846 to 1849. In the First World War typhus ravaged the armies of the Eastern Front, with over 150,000 deaths in Serbia alone. In 1922 the epidemic in Soviet territory peaked at some 20 to 30 million cases in Russia, and during the civil war it killed 2–3 million people.

Rudolf Weigl developed the first typhus vaccine in the interwar period; it did not prevent the disease but reduced mortality. In the Second World War typhus killed prisoners in camps and ghettos, among them Anne Frank and her sister Margot at Bergen-Belsen. Epidemic typhus is now rare.
tyrol: Tyrol is a historical region in the Alps of northern Italy and western Austria, with an area of 26,673 square kilometres. It consists of the Austrian State of Tyrol and, in Italy, the Province of South Tyrol and the Province of Trento, along with a few municipalities of Veneto and Lombardy. Its largest cities are Innsbruck, Trento and Bolzano. The main chain of the Alps runs across it, along the border between North and South Tyrol, and the Brenner Pass, at 1,370 metres, is the lowest pass across that chain. The Ortler, at 3,905 metres, is the highest mountain. German and Italian are the main languages, with Ladin, Cimbrian and Mócheno as minority languages.

The earliest evidence of settlement is from the Tischofer Cave, about 28,000 years ago. In 15 BCE Roman forces under Drusus and Tiberius conquered Tyrol and organised the provinces of Raetia and Noricum. In the Middle Ages most of the region fell to the Duchy of Bavaria, created about 555, while the south, including Bolzano, remained with the Lombards. Christianity spread through the bishoprics of Brixen and Trento. The County of Tyrol took shape in the 12th century, and Innsbruck became a centre of European politics and culture when Emperor Maximilian I took up residence there.

From the mid-16th century Tyrol was ruled by younger sons of the Habsburg emperors until all Habsburg lands came under Emperor Leopold I in 1665. From the time of Maria Theresa it was governed from Vienna in major matters, and in 1803 the lands of the bishoprics of Trent and Brixen were secularised and added to the county. The Tyrolean Rifles, a militia authorised by Maximilian I in 1511, became known in 1809, when peasants rose against the French-Bavarian occupation under Andreas Hofer in four battles at Bergisel. In 1919 the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye divided Tyrol into the Austrian state and the Italian region of Trentino-Alto Adige.

Tyrol has long been a transit route between northern and southern Europe, and the Brenner Railway, opened in 1867, runs from Innsbruck to Verona. Tourism is the most important economic sector, helped by railways in the 19th century and the Brenner motorway in the 1960s, and agriculture and forestry shape the landscape; apples and wine are grown in the south. The Tyrol-South Tyrol-Trentino Euroregion, a cross-border body, has had its own legal entity since 2011. The arms of Tyrol show a red eagle on a silver field.
tyrrhenian-sea: The Tyrrhenian Sea lies off the western coast of Italy. The islands of Corsica and Sardinia bound it on the west, the Italian Peninsula, in the regions of Tuscany, Lazio, Campania, Basilicata and Calabria, on the north and east, and Sicily on the south. Its maximum depth is 3,785 metres. The International Hydrographic Organization defines its limits by lines across the Strait of Messina, from Sicily to Sardinia, across the Strait of Bonifacio and along the north from Cape Corse in Corsica to the Italian coast. The sea contains smaller islands such as Capri, Elba, Ischia and Ustica, and the eight Aeolian Islands lie in its southern part, north of Sicily.

It lies near the meeting of the African and Eurasian plates, and mountain chains and active volcanoes such as Mount Marsili are found in its depths. It is a back-arc basin that formed during the Neogene as the Calabrian slab rolled back towards the south-east. Episodes of fast and slow retreat formed first the Vavilov basin and then the Marsili basin, which are separated by an undersea ridge, the Issel Bridge. The same process gave rise to submarine volcanoes and to the active volcano Mount Stromboli.

The name derives from the Greek name for the Etruscans. Hesiod, in the 8th century BCE, first mentions them, describing them as living in central Italy alongside the Latins. The Etruscans lived along the coast of modern Tuscany, Latium and Campania, and they called the water the Sea of the Etruscans. In Greek mythology the cliffs above the sea were believed to house the four winds kept by Aeolus: the Mistral from the Rhône valley, the Libeccio from the southwest, and the Sirocco and Ostro from the south.

The main Italian ports on the sea are Naples, Palermo, Civitavecchia, Salerno, Trapani and Gioia Tauro, and Bastia lies on Corsica. The maritime facilities called the port of Rome are at Civitavecchia, about 68 kilometres north-west of the city, since Rome itself has no port. Its islands include Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, the Tuscan Archipelago, the Pontine Islands, Procida and the Aeolian Islands.
tyrtaeus: Almost everything known about Tyrtaeus comes from two entries of the Suda, a Byzantine encyclopedia compiled in the 10th century CE, and from accounts that were mostly deduced from his poetry or invented. Ancient writers disagreed about his origin. Pausanias told of a lame and stupid Athenian schoolteacher whom the Athenians sent to Sparta in response to an oracle. Modern scholars generally think the story was an Athenian invention, and conclude that he was a native of Laconia, because in one fragment he counts himself among the Heraclidae whom Zeus gave to Sparta and addresses Spartan warriors with authority.

His poems arose from two crises. One was civil unrest that threatened the authority of kings and elders; Aristotle recalls that some Spartans, hard pressed by war, demanded a redistribution of land. The other was the Second Messenian War, which followed the Spartan conquest of Messenia in the 8th century BCE.

Tyrtaeus was chiefly an elegiac poet, and his works were thought to fill five books. About 250 lines or parts of lines survive, through quotations and papyri. The Suda names a Constitution, generally treated as another title for the Eunomia, which stressed the role of divine providence in the state and the cooperation of kings, elders and people. It also names Precepts in elegiac couplets and war songs, and later writers add marching songs in anapaests, whose authenticity is doubtful.

The three longest fragments are complete or nearly complete poems on the ideal warrior and the glory or disgrace that follows his choices. One describes hoplites fighting foot against foot, shield against shield and breast against breast. His language is largely Homeric even though his audience spoke Doric, and a line on dying fighting for the fatherland echoes Hector's speech in the Iliad. He holds that patriotic military valour is the highest form of arete, which can be reached only among comrades, and he names no individual warriors.

In the 4th century BCE, when his poetry was an established classic, Spartan armies on campaign were made to listen to it. Plato quotes his elegy on arete in the Laws. Some modern scholars believe he helped turn Sparta from its arts toward military austerity, though others see no real evidence for this.

During the Renaissance he came to be seen as the prototype of the artist who uses his talent to urge his countrymen to fight for freedom, partly through a story in Plutarch's Life of Cleomenes, in which King Leonidas praises him. A bronze statue of a hoplite raised in the central square of Sparta in 2006 carries one of his poems in modern Greek.
